                               PREFACE



This book has grown out of eight years of close collaboration among its
authors. From the very beginning we decided that its content should
come out as the result of a truly common effort. That is, we did not
"distribute" parts of the text planned to each one of us. On the contrary,
we made a point that each single paragraph be the product of a
common reflection. Genuine team-work is not as usual in philosophy as
it is in other academic disciplines. We think, however, that this is more
due to the idiosyncrasy of philosophers than to the nature of their
subject.
    Close collaboration with positive results is as rewarding as anything
can be, but it may also prove to be quite difficult to implement. In our
case, part of the difficulties came from purely geographic separation.
This caused unsuspected delays in coordinating the work. But more
than this, as time passed, the accumulation of particular results and
ideas outran our ability to fit them into an organic unity. Different
styles of exposition, different ways of formalization, different levels of
complexity were simultaneously present in a voluminous manuscript
that had become completely unmanageable. In particular, a portion of
the text had been conceived in the language of category theory and
employed ideas of a rather abstract nature, while another part was
expounded in the more conventional set-theoretic style, stressing intui-
tivity and concreteness. Consequently, at a certain point we decided to
split up the material into two texts - one of a more elementary and
concrete character (which eventually resulted in the present book), and
another one of a more abstract general nature, which we hope to be
able to conclude in the future. Even the present text, however, has
different levels of complexity. In particular, the degree of formal
sophistication in the first chapter is considerably higher than in the rest.
Ws: felt the technicalities of the first chapter were necessary in order
to make sure that we were building our program on formally solid
foundations - thereby responding to some criticisms of our previous
writings. Nevertheless, those readers interested in the implementation
of the program rather than in its foundations may skip the first chapter
without substantial loss of understanding for the rest.
                                    xi
xu                               PREFACE

     In spite of the splitting of the material into two books, one of which
 is left for the future, we by no means consider the present book as a
 really finished piece of work on its own level. It is much more the
 presentation of a program than anything else. In it we sketch, frequently
 with very broad brush strokes, how our view of scientific theories might
 be extended to characterize the totality of scientific knowledge -
 perhaps even the totality of empirical knowledge - both from a
 synchronic and a diachronic perspective. By sketching this rather
 ambitious program we do not necessarily intend to suggest that carrying
 it out would be worth the resources required to do so. However, we do
believe that it is conceptually interesting, and perhaps even techno-
logically and didactically useful to represent substantial fragments of
knowledge in the way we describe here. We also find certain interesting
philosophical questions illuminated by considering various ways the
total program might be carried to completion. Our discussion of these
issues will presuppose some knowledge of naive set theory and some
knowledge of specific empirical theories. We have tried to maximize the
audience that can appreciate at least some of the examples by choosing
them from diverse areas of empirical science as well as by including
some of a rather trivial character that presuppose little knowledge.
    In choosing our examples as well as in choosing the other material to
be discussed, we have drawn on a considerable body of published
material pertaining to what has come to be called the "structuralist
view" of scientific theories, as well as on critical studies of this view and
other works that in some way or other show a similarity of purpose and
approach. Qf course, not only philosophical or meta-scientific literature
but also some scientific texts relevant to the specific examples dealt
with have been used. However, it is not our aim here to provide
an overview of this literature - much less a critical, integrative and
evaluative overview. We have mentioned those authors and writings
that have been influential on our reflections and results at the end of
each corresponding chapter. This means that the bibliography we
present is explicitly a topical one, even at the cost of some redundancy.
We have, by no means, addressed all the interesting philosophical
issues in this literature, nor have we replied to all our critics. We have
chosen to address only those issues and criticisms that appear germane
to our present purposes. In this same vein, we have not attempted to
trace the development of our own thinking on the matters we discuss
here. The reader familiar with our earlier work will find some reformu-
                                PREFACE                                 XIll


lations and revisions of previously published material without explana-
tion of why we prefer the present formulation. In many cases, the
reformulation is warranted only by the desire for uniformity, economy
or elegance of notation. In other cases, substantial errors were cor-
rected. Our aim with this book has been to make the discussion here
"self-contained". Among other things, it should serve as an introduction
to this way of looking at empirical knowledge.
    Besides the authors quoted in the text, we would like to mention
explicitly all those friends, colleagues, and students which, in the course
of many discussions all these years through, have shared with us their
insights and criticisms. Some of them even had the patience to read

a more or less definite shape and kindly made their comments about

able to mention all those persons that responded with such a stimulat-
ing interest towards our work. But some of them we may mention at

                              OVERVIEW



                          0.0 INTRODUCTION

This book is about the structure of knowledge. By 'knowledge' we mean
'reasoned, true belief'. This entails that knowledge consists of things like
propositions or statements. By 'structure' we mean simply the way in
which the truth values, or probability values, of statements are inter-
dependent. Our account of the structure of knoweldge, however,
requires something more than statements and logical relations among
them. Indeed, we may appear to give so much attention to these other
elements that the propositional nature of knowledge is ignored. We find
these other elements essential to exhibiting the complexity of the
structural features we find in common examples of knowledge. Our
attention to these features and the somewhat elaborate technical appa-
ratus we employ to describe them should not, however, obscure our
essentially conservative and conventional views about the nature of
knowledge.
   For us, empirical science is the paradigm example of knowledge.
Paradigm examples of empirical science are the contents of textbooks
and professional journals associated with various subdisciplines of
physics, chemistry, biology, geology, psychology, linguistics, sociology,
anthropology, economics and some other disciplines commonly prac-
ticed in academic settings. We shall confine our account of the structure
of knowledge to the kind of knowledge exemplified here - empirical
knowledge - without venturing a definition of 'empirical knowledge'.
Were we pressed for a definition, we would begin from a sociological
perspective. Empirical knowledge is the product of a certain kind of
social activity. To define 'empirical knowledge' is to distinguish the
kinds of social activities that produce it from other kinds of social
activity. Traditionally, ways of characterizing empirical knowledge have
appealed in some way to the concept of "perceptual knowledge". Ours
would not obviously do this. What would apparently replace appeal to
perceptual knowledge in our account would be a description of certain
characteristic ways in which sub-groups of an empirical scientific
                                    xv
xvi                           OVERVIEW

community transmit scientific information. Whether this could be done
in an ultimately satisfactory manner without appeal to the concept of
perceptual knowledge remains, for us, an open question. That we would
take this tack in defining empirical knowledge is, in part, a consequence
of our account of the structure of empirical knowledge. Just how this is
so will become clearer as our story unfolds. Our discussion in Ch. VIII
bears most directly on this issue.
    In restricting our attention to empirical knowledge of the kinds
exemplified in the literature of professionalized empirical science, we
clearly intend to rule mathematical knowledge out of consideration.
This may appear surprising to some since the account we offer of the
structure of empirical science gives such great prominence to the
mathematical aspect of empirical theories. However, it should be clear
that, on our account, empirical science is an activity quite distinct and
quite different from "pure" mathematics. All of the empirical science we
will explicitly reconstruct in this book makes use of mathematics in
essential ways. Our methodology for representing scientific knowledge
also makes heavy use of mathematical tools. But these facts do not
entail that we view empirical science as identical, or even structurally
similar, to mathematical science. On the other hand, it is not obvious
that mathematical knowledge does not exemplify some of the structural
features we find in empirical knowledge. We doubt that it exhibits all of
them, but we are not prepared to defend this conjecture. To do so
would require a deeper understanding of mathematical knowledge than
we now have.
    It is considerably less clear that restricting our domain in this way
rules out "common sense" empirical knowledge - for example, our
pre-scientific or naive knowledge about the behavior of middle-sized
physical objects like chairs, books and animals. While we find some
mathematical tools essential to our methodology, these same tools
might as easily be used to represent empirical knowledge that does not,
itself, make essential use of recognizable pieces of mathematical
science. Indeed, our discussion of the global structure of empirical
science in Ch. VIII suggests that a fully adequate account of our
paradigm kind of empirical knowledge, with our methodological tools,
would ultimately require using these same tools to describe naive
knowledge. We have not undertaken to do this, though some related
work is available [6, 71. Whether it can be done and how doing it would
illuminate the nature of more "scientific" empirical knowledge is an
interesting question that remains open at this point.
                               OVERVIEW                                xvii

    Somewhat more explicitly, our investigation intends to provide a way
 of describing various "parts" of empirical science as well as the way
 they are embedded in a highly complex structure or "architectonic". We
 share with Kant the view expressed on the front piece that it is in the
 properties of this structure or architectonic that one should look to find
 the "essential" features of empirical knowledge - to discover the
 essential ways in which empirical knowledge differs from "mere" true
 belief and from other forms of knowledge. We offer no general
 epistemological theory here - we do not try to define 'empirical
 knowledge'. Our present aim is more modest. We want to provide a
 description of those structural features of empirical knowledge which,
we think, could serve to distinguish it in an interesting way from other
 things. We want to do this for some paradigm examples of empirical
 knowledge. From these examples, and surely others as well, an adequate
account of empirical knowledge may ultimately emerge. This view
commits us to a certain kind of "holism". We believe that those features
of empirical science that fully distinguish it from non-scientific enter-
prises can only be seen clearly by viewing sufficiently "large" fragments
of scientific knowledge. That is, they are only apparent when one has a
sufficiently "global" perspective. However, our holism is restrained.
Even from a "local" perspective certain essential features, or necessary
conditions, for empirical science may be apparent. An adequate charac-
terization of empirical science may ultimately turn out to have a
structure similar to modern expositions of differential geometry in
which global structure is determined by conditions on local structure
together with conditions on "intersections" of local structures. We are
not now in a position to provide such an account. At this point, it is
more metaphor than theory. However, it is this metaphor which has
guided our work.
    The somewhat grandiose aims just mentioned, should not obscure
the essentially representational nature of our enterprise. First, we
develop certain formal, methodological tools and then we use the tools
to represent the structure of some specific examples of empirical
science and their development over time. In terms now current among
workers in artificial intelligence, we develop a "representation scheme"
for scientific knowledge. We then test the adequacy of that scheme by
applying it to "reconstruct" certain fragments of empirical science. The
primary criterion by which we judge the adequacy of our reconstruc-
tions is this. The reconstruction of each particular piece of science
should "generate" in a systematic, standardized, and natural way the
xviii                          OVERVIEW

essential properties of that piece and the central claims associated to it
by the average users of that piece (the "experts"). At this level, we
clearly do not seek to "evaluate" the content of empirical science. There
are however secondary criteria for evaluating our representation
scheme to be applied lexically with respect to the first, primary cri-
terion. They include "consistency", "elegance" and "economy", as well
as "perspective". Consistency, is clearly a normative concept in this
context. There is occasionally a tension between this criterion and the
first. However, when its application is mitigated by sufficient charity
toward empirical scientists supplemented by technical ingenuity its
force is considerably diminished. Elegance and economy are technical
virtues about which we have little new to say. "Perspective" is more
interesting. In a restricted sense 'perspective' means "historical perspec-
tive". Our representations of scientific knowledge should be "histori-
cally neutral" in the sense that knowledge in every historical time
period should be treated in the same way. That is, there should be no
explicit or implicit "bias" in our representation scheme that would,
for example, reconstrue and reevaluate the science of one historical
period in terms of the science of another. For example, an account of
the history of mechanics that attempted to reformulate all earlier
mechanical theories in the conceptual framework of quantum mechanics
would lack historical perspective. It is at this point, that our enterprise
apparently diverges from some other attempts to reconstruct physical
theories. In the broader sense, 'perspective' should apply across fields
and disciplines in science as well as across the history of a single
discipline. For example, an attempt to reconstruct thermodynamic
theory with a representation scheme that required embedding the
fundamental entities of the theory in a spacio-temporal manifold would,
in our view, lack perspective. Most simply, "perspective" requires that
the representation scheme be "neutral" with respect to all the theories
to which it is applied.
    There are at least two ways in which our methodology may appear to
lack perspective of the kind we have just described. First, it might
appear that some parts of empirical science, not to say empirical
knowledge in general, could be "distorted" by forcing them into the
mathematical formalism we employ. "Field sciences" such as historical
geology and botany have been suggested to us as examples' of this
possibility. Such sciences appear to contain a significant component
of taxonomy and knowledge about how to use this taxonomy for
                               OVERVIEW                                 xix

 classification of specific individuals. It is apparently this latter sort
 of knowledge that some feel would be distorted by austere formal
representation. In reply to this, we only note that knowledge of this
kind is also associated with physical theories - paradigm examples of
successful application of our methods. Recognizing which force laws
might be expected to apply to a specific mechanical system "found in
nature" is, so it appears to us, the same kind of problem as identifying
the geologic period to which a specific formation belongs or identifying
the botanic category to which a specific plant belongs. In our methodo-
logical framework, all these situations would be described as allocating
intended applications to theory-elements in a specialization net (see Ch.
IV). Admittedly, we do not have a completely adequate account of how
this is done - for any kind of theory. But we see no reason to expect
that the partial account we now have, as well as improvements on it,
will not be generally applicable. Indeed, the apparatus of mathematical
taxonomy (cf. e.g. [8)) may, we conjecture, have interesting applications
outside the typical taxonomic sciences in explicating the notion of
"intended application".
    Second, there might be generally accepted examples of empirical
science - at least at some stages of their development - that simply
will not yield the kind of formal structure we demand. The "formative
period" of thermodynamics discussed in Sec. V4) may be such an
example. The most plausible suggestion here appears to be that these
periods are characterized by a multiplicity of "small theories" - theory-
elements in our terminology - with relatively short lifetimes. These
"mini-theories" are not linked with each other and very weakly linked
with the rest of empirical science. The "web of theory" here is thinly
woven and easily tom. This, we suggest, is what makes these periods in
the development of scientific knowledge look less like science and more
like other social activities - e.g. normative political theory. The concept
of empirical science may· ultimately be best explicated as an ordering
relation - activities or areas of discourse may be regarded as "more
scientific" than others. We do not know whether this view would suffice
for all examples of "pre-scientific" activity. But, were it adequate, then
no essentially new methodology would be required. Further investiga-
tion appears to be required to decide the issue. We note here that a
"thin" structure of links may well characterize things like the formative
period of thermodynamics and contemporary sociological theory and
yet not characterize our naive theories about physical objects and
xx                             OVERVIEW

 people. Naive common sense may tum to be "pre-scientific" in quite
 a different way than the formative periods of professional scientific
 practice.
    Our architectonic for science may be summarily described in the
 following way. At any given time, empirical science consists of a large,
 but finite number of elementary units or "building blocks" which we call
 'theory-elements'. A theory-element is the smallest unit of empirical
 science that has all the features required to say something interesting
 about the world. Very roughly, theory-elements consist of a "vocabu-
 lary" or "conceptual structure" and some empirical law formulated with
this vocabulary together with a specification of the things to which this
law is intended to apply. Theory-elements correspond to one common
conception of a scientific theory exemplified by "Newton's theory of
gravitation". Theory-elements are the key feature in a local picture of
empirical science. However, they, never, in fact, appear in isolation and
there is at least some reason to believe that they could not be intel-
ligibly used if they did (see Sec. VIII. 5). They appear in clusters linked
together by what we call 'intertheoretical links'. Intertheoretical links
serve to transmit "information" between theory-elements. Among other
things, empirical interpretation of at least some of the vocabulary in a
given theory-element is provided by its links to other theory-elements.
Intertheoretical links tie together theory-elements with the same vocab-
ulary and different laws into "specialization nets" which correspond to
another common conception of a scientific theory exemplified by
"classical particle mechanics". Intertheoreticallinks also serve to repre-
sent much. discussed relations among theories such as reduction and
equivalence. These links may be formulated precisely, but in many
interesting cases they will be approximate. Global empirical science
then is represented as a "net" or "complex" of theory-elements tied
together with intertheoretical links of various kinds. Each theory-
element makes a statement about the things to which it is intended to
apply. What this statement is, depends both on the theory-element, its
immediate environment in the complex and perhaps on its more remote
environment. This statement may be formulated exactly but, in general,
it will be approximate. Empirical science may change over time in three
fundamentally different ways. First, the things to which the laws in
individual theory-elements are expected to apply or known to apply
may grow or diminish. Second, theory-elements may appear and dis-
appear from the complex. Finally, intertheoreticallinks between theory-
                               OVERVIEW                                  xxi

elements may appear and disappear from the complex. Some features
of global structure considered in Ch. VIII suggest that the first mode of
change may be explicable in terms of the last two. That such a construct
serves to depict many interesting features of empirical science is the
thesis of this book.
   Our strategy in defending this thesis is to begin with a local picture
of empirical science focusing on theory-elements. We shall move in-
crementally to provide accounts of increasingly larger fragments of
empirical science. To the extent that we are able, these accounts will
be illustrated by examples of reconstructions of specific cases. This
strategy was chosen primarily for reasons of pedagogic efficacy. Regret-
tably, it entails that our first accounts of local fragments of science will
be only approximately correct from the perspective of a more global
account. The alternative of beginning with the global account and
moving from it to a description of the local account could have avoided
this problem. But, this tack appeared to us to require too much sacrifice
of intuitive understanding and motivation. In the next few pages we will
describe our present strategy in somewhat more detail.

              0.1 STRUCTURE SPECIES AND MODELS

The fundamental intuition underlying our approach is that the smallest
significant or interesting parts of empirical science - things like
empirical laws - are best characterized, not as linguistic entities, but as
model-theoretic entities - classes of set-theoretic structures. In Ch. I
we say what we have to say about the intuitive justification for this
approach. We try to give some intuitive content to the idea of a model
of a theory that is independent of the specific apparatus used to
describe models. Our hope here is to convince the reader that our
model-theoretic approach has at least as much prima facie intuitive
plausibility as its competitors.
   We then move on to introduce the specific technical apparatus we
shall use to talk about models for theories. To this end we employ a
slight variant of the Bourbaki concept of "structure species" [3]. Our
primary motivation here is to provide some foundational basis for the
familiar means of characterizing model classes by means of defining
set-theoretic predicates. This may be regarded as a partial response to
criticism [19, 17, 21] of earlier, naive uses of set-theoretic axiomatiza-
tion by some of us [22]. This material is somewhat technical and may be
xxii                           OVERVIEW

avoided, at some cost, by those ready to accept the use of naive set-
theoretic axiomatization. Apart from the discussion in Ch. I, essential
use of the concept of structure species is made only in Sec. V1.7, to
discuss the linguistic aspects of the reduction link.
    In choosing to conceive model classes as structure species we have
ignored one feature of them that is significant in at least some empirical
theories. Structural relations among models of the same class such as
isomorphism play a key role in theories such as particle mechanics.
They are needed to characterize "invariance prin,ciples" which might
plausibly be argued to be essential features of these theories. Technical
means to append these features to classes of models conceived as
structure species are at hand. We need only take the structure species
to be the object class of a category and the structural relations among
its members as the morphism set of the category. It appears that the
material in this book could be expounded from a category-theoretic
foundation of this sort. The gain in this would be that a more adequate
ontological account of mechanical theories might be provided and
certain obvious inelegancies in the discussion of these theories could
surely be avoided. That the same could be said for all the theories we
consider is less obvious. While it appears that model classes associated
with all theories we consider can be endowed with a plausible morph-
ism concept, in most cases they do not appear to have the key role they
have in mechanical theories. In most cases they amount to no more
than things like "scale transformations" for metric concepts. Certainly,
laws in these theories are invariant under scale transformations. But this
fact does not appear as significant to these theories as invariance under
kinematic transformations does for mechanical theories. Some have
suggested that category theory provides an elegant and "deep" under-
standing of some of our fundamental concepts such as "intertheoretical
link" (see e.g. [11 D. We find this idea stimulating, but its philosophical
implications remain to be assessed. The cost of adopting a category-
theoretic formulation is the introduction of considerable technical
complexity - especially in the concept of intertheoretical link - and
the consequent diminution of the accessibility of the material. Here
again, we have opted for technical simplicity and accessibility, leaving
the possibly more adequate, but surely more formidable approach for
another occasion.
   In considering model classes associated with a theory it is expendient
and, indeed essential, for later discussions of specialization links (Ch.
                              OVERVIEW                               XXlll


IV) to distinguish between the "vocabulary" associated with a theory
and the laws formulated in this vocabulary. Here ''vocabulary'' is under-
stood intuitively to include what some have called "analytical truths"
about the concepts in question. One dividend of the structure species
concept is that it allows us to move some way in making this distinction
precise. This is discussed in Sec. 1.2. Making this distinction allows us
to distinguish two model classes associated with the basic units of
empirical science - those consisting of all structures that contain the
requisite vocabulary and satisfy the "analytical truths" which we call
"potential models" and those which in addition satisfy substantive
empirical laws which we call models. These ideas are illustrated in Ch. I
by extensive measurement theory, Jeffrey decision theory, classical and
relativistic collision mechanics and classical particle mechanics.

                       0.2 THEORY-ELEMENTS

Theory-elements, the simplest significant part of empirical science,
consist of a purely formal, mathematical part which we call a 'theory-
core' and a class of intended applications. The potential models and
models belong to the theory-core. They can be characterized in a
purely formal way. In contrast, the intended applications can not be
captured by purely formal characterization - at least not from a local
perspective. In Sec. ILl, we say what can be said about intended
applications at the local level and return to the question again in Sec.
11.6, with the additional apparatus of intertheoreticallinks at hand. Here
we effectively see only a single theory-element and its immediate
neighbors. Intended applications still elude formal characterization and
the account of intended applications remains incomplete. We finally
consider this question from a fully global perspective in Sec. VII1.S.
Here we conclude that it may be, at least in principle, possible to
characterize intended applications formally. But pragmatic difficulties in
doing this are formidable.
   Besides potential models and models, the formal theory-core con-
sists of constraints, which characterize connections or relations among
different applications or models of the same theory. The presence of
constraints in the formal core is a consequence of our view that most
empirical theories have multiple intended applications which are usually
required to be interrelated in some specific ways. The constraints serve
to make the required interrelation explicit in our representation of the
XXIV                           OVERVIEW

 theory. The formal core also contains some intertheoreticallinks which
 characterize the theory-element's "essential" connections to other the-
ories - represented by other theory-elements. Finally, the formal
 theory-core contains a class of partial potential models - fragments
 of the potential models that can be understood or interpreted in-
 dependently of the theory-element in question. The intended applica-
 tions are seen to have the formal structure of partial potential models.
 Partial potential models are first characterized with a purely local,
 theory-relative theoretical/non-theoretical distinction among compo-
 nents of potential models (Sec. 11.3) and once again with the help of our
 concept of intertheoretical links (Secs. 11.5 and 11.6). We return to this
 question from a fully global perspective in Sec. VIII.2.
    Theory-elements have an empirical claim associated with them. It is
 a proposition or statement - what the theory-element claims about the
 world. We formulate the empirical claim with the help of the notion of
 the content of a theory-element (Sec. 11.7). The content of a theory-
 element is the class of arrays of partial potential models that are
"compatible" with the laws, constraints and intertheoretical links asso-
ciated with the theory-element. The empirical claim is simply that the
set of intended applications is a member of the content.
    In Ch. III we note that some theory-elements are "basic" with respect
to a "specialization relation" to be considered in detail in Ch. IV. We
then proceed to exhibit the basic theory-elements for classical collision
mechanics, relativistic collision mechanics, classical particle mechanics,
Daltonian stoichiometry, simple equilibrium thermodynamics, Lagran-
gian mechanics and pure exchange economics. All these examples have
been treated in the literature from our methodological perspective in
various places cited in Ch. III. The specific manner of treatment has
differed ranging from the rather crude early efforts with classical
particle mechanics and Lagrangian mechanics in [221 to [21. At the risk
of repetition, it appeared to us useful to collect these examples together,
correct known mistakes in them and present them in a unified manner.
In subsequent chapters these examples will be emended to provide
further illustrations of our methodology. We feel that the totality of
these illustrative examples presented in a unified form provides the
strongest argument we can muster for the efficacy of our methodo-
logical tools and their philosophical consequences.
                              OVERVIEW                                xxv

                          0.3 THEORY-NETS

In Ch. IV we take up again the main thread of our exposition moving
now one step away from a local view of empirical science. Here we
consider sets of theory-elements all having the same conceptual appa-
ratus - the same potential models and partial potential models - but
possibly differing in their laws, constraints and intertheoretical links.
Such sets of theory-elements ordered in specific ways by a specializa-
tion relation - a kind of intertheoretical link - correspond to one
common conception of an empirical theory. The concept of empirical
claim may be extended from theory-elements to theory-nets in several
ways (Sec. IV.3). These ideas are illustrated by classical collision
mechanics and in more interesting ways by classical particle mechanics
and simple equilibrium thermodynamics.


        0.4 THE DIACHRONIC STRUCTURE OF THEORIES

 Up to this point in our exposition we will have presented the apparatus
 required to describe the structure of empirical science at a single
specific time in its historical development. The most complex construc-
tion required for this purpose is a theory-net. Theory-nets correspond
to one common intuitive idea of "an empirical theory". However, there
is a, perhaps still more common, conception of an empirical theory in
which it is an entity with a history of development over time. For
example, classical particle mechanics began with Newton and his con-
temporaries and developed over time as an identifiable "cultural entity"
up to, at least, the late 18th century. In Ch. V we extend our formal
apparatus to provide a means of describing one important way in which
empirical theories develop over time. This type of development cor-
responds roughly to what Kuhn [9] has called 'normal science'. To this
end we define the concept of "theory-evolution". The concept of a
theory-evolution rests on the conncept of a theory-net. A theory-
evolution is a temporally ordered sequence of theory-nets subject to
some rather strong additional conditions. Intuitively, a theory-evolution
is a changing theory-net - rather like a "living" net, growing and
shrinking over time.
   Our account of theory-elements and theory-nets will not be purely
formal. At certain crucial points we shall be forced to appeal to
irreducibly "pragmatic" concepts describing the relation between em-
xxvi                          OVERVIEW

pirical scientists and the theories they use. When we come to speak of
theory-evolutions, pragmatic aspects of the matter become even more
significant and must be supplemented with socio-historical concepts as
well. We find that we require five basic pragmatic and socio-historical
concepts - historical periods, historical precedence, scientists, scien-
tific communities and scientific generations - to elucidate the concept
of a theory-evolution. These concepts are discussed and characterized
as precisely as we can in Sec. V.l. Using these concepts, theory-
evolutions are defined formally in Sec. V.2. At this point, several types
of theory-evolutions are distinguished. Among these is "paradigm-
guided evolution" which corresponds more closely to Kuhn's normal
science than does the more general concept of a theory-evolution.
Using this concept, it becomes possible to provide rather precise
empirical tests of the claim that specific empirical sciences developed
over time in the manner of Kuhnian normal science. We consider in
some detail the theory-evolutions associated with classical particle
mechanics (Sec. V.3) and simple equilibrium thermodynamics (Sec.
VA). In the latter case, our account departs somewhat from the usual
account of the matter. For this reason, we defend it with some attention
to examination of primary historical sources.

               0.5 INTER THEORETICAL RELATIONS

In Ch. II we introduce the idea that certain links to other theories are
essential to the nature of theory-elements. In Ch. VI we begin to
reconsider a theory-element's possible connections with other theory-
elements from a somewhat broader point of view. We begin by broaden-
ing the concept of "intertheoreticallink" to include connections between
potential models as a whole - without necessarily referring to their
specific components (Sec. VI. I ). We call these 'global intertheoretical
relations'. Ultimately in Ch. VIII, we arrive at a picture of large
fragments of empirical science - even the whole of empirical science -
in which global intertheoretical links play an essential role as the
"mortar" that holds the theory-element "building blocks" together. The
discussion in Ch. VI sets the stage for this more synoptic and systematic
discussion by considering several familiar intertheoretical relations
regarded as global intertheoretical relations.
   As examples of global intertheoretical relations, we reconsider first
the relations of specialization and theoretization already introduced
                               OVERVIEW                               xxvii

in connection with the discussion of theory-nets and non-theoretical
concepts (Sec. VI.2). Next we consider the reduction relation (Sec. VI.3)
- first for the rather simple example of the reduction of classical
collision mechanics to classical particle mechanics and then for the
more complicated example of the reduction of classical rigid body
mechanics to classical particle mechanics. Generalizing from features of
these examples, we define a general concept of reduction (Sec. VI.4).
Next, we focus on the relation of "empirical equivalence" - roughly,
equivalence of content at the non-theoretical level - and consider the
example of the equivalence of Lagrangian particle mechanics and
classical particle mechanics (Sec. VI.5). We then move on to consider a
stronger concept of equivalence which requires some connections
between the theoretical concepts in the theory-elements, illustrating
these with the equivalence relation between metric and relational
formulations of Euclidean geometry (here viewed as an empirical
theory) (Sec. VI.6).
   Finally, we tum to consider some issues about reduction involving
explicit reference to language. We do this to bring our views on the
growth of scientific knowledge into the same area as those authors who
prefer a "linguistic" formulation of the issues. First, we consider whether
our concept of reduction justifies speaking of one theory's being
"derived" from another. Then we consider whether reduction entails
"translation". And finally, we consider the issue of "incommensurable
theories". This material draws on our discussion of structure species in
Sec. I.2 and is somewhat technical in nature.

                        0.6 APPROXIMATION

Having laid out the basic ideas required for our account of the archi-
tectonic of science, we then tum our attention to elaborating these ideas
in the direction of accounting for the inexactness or approximate nature
of most real empirical knowledge. Though usually ignored by philoso-
phers of science, the approximate nature of scientific knowledge is one
of the most salient features of the professional literature in which this
knowledge is reported as well as in discussion of technological applica-
tions of this knowledge. Any adequate representation of scientific
knowledge must, we believe, offer a suitable means of depicting the
approximate character of this knowledge.
   We distinguish four types of approximation in empirical science (Ch.
xxviii                         OVERVIEW

VII). Roughly these have to do with "idealizations" made to construct
models, approximations made to subsume already idealized intended
applications into the content of a theory-element, approximations made
in substitution of one (usually "simpler") empirical law for another, and
finally, approximate relations between entire theory-elements like, for
example, the "approximate" reduction of classical particle mechanics to
relativistic particle mechanics. With the exception of the first type,
idealization, we succeed in extending our formal apparatus to provide
a formal account of each type of approximation. The formal basis for
this treatment is the topological concept of a "uniformity" derived from
Bourbaki. This concept, however, requires considerable emendation to
make it formally suitable for the context of empirical science. To this
end we define an "empirical uniformity" (Sec. VII.2). Still more refine-
ment is required to narrow down on the kinds of approximations that
are actually used in empirical science. We attempt to provide necessary
conditions for approximations used in formulating empirical claims
(type two approximation). Later on, we use these ideas to provide an
approximate version of the empirical claim of a theory-element and
also extend these ideas to theory-nets and theory-evolutions thus
dealing with the third type of approximation. Intertheoretical approxi-
mation is considered in Sec. VII.3.
   Our treatment of approximation should not be taken as a substitute
for a treatment of probabilistic reasoning in empirical science. We view
probabilistic reasoning in empirical science, as elsewhere in human
affairs, to be a means of dealing with "uncertainty". We believe ''uncer-
tainty" and "inexactness" are distinct concepts. Here we have dealt with
inexactness. We do not address the role of uncertainty in empirical
science in this book. Our view is that uncertainty in empirical science
requires no· special treatment. There is (or should be) a uniform account
of probabilistic reasoning that applies to "ordinary affairs" and empirical
science as well. We are aware that this claim is controversial. To argue
seriously for it would require detailed consideration of such theories as
statistical mechanics and quantum mechanics where probability plays an
essential role. We do not treat these examples here simply because we
are not prepared to do so at this time.

            0.7 THE GLOBAL STRUCTURE OF SCIENCE

In our final chapter (Ch. VIII) we consider the possibility of employing
                               OVERVIEW                                xxix

 the methods developed in the preceding chapters to increasingly larger
 fragments of empirical science. Here we have in mind, first, fragments
larger than single theory-nets or theory-evolutions - for example,
 classical mechanics as a whole including statics, rigid body mechanics,
hydrodynamics, various formulations of particle mechanics as well as
 the underlying kinematical theories. Still larger fragments - for example,
 classical physics including kinematics, classical electrodynamics and
 classical statistical mechanics - are intended as well. In a somewhat
 speculative way we consider still larger fragments like "natural science"
 and even "all of empirical science". Our motivation here is not to urge
that an army of philosophers be deployed to the task of representing
all of empirical science in our architectonic scheme. Rather, it is to
characterize as precisely as we can what must be "left over" - left out of
the formal representation - whenever we reconstruct some fragment
torn from the fabric of empirical science. It is only by understanding
how the whole fabric is woven that we can understand how the "loose
ends" of the fragments we have in hand can "in principle" be rewoven
into the whole.
    In Sec. VIII.1 we generalize the concept of intertheoretical link
introduced in Chs. II and VI and introduce the concept of a theory-
 holon - a collection of theory-elements connected by intertheoretical
links. Links here are so conceived that each ordered pair of theory-
elements is connected by, at most, one non-trivial link - the intersec-
tion of all the links connecting individual components in the elements.
This formulation implicitly assigns a "direction" to the links in a theory-
holon so that the complex has the structure of a directed graph satisfy-
ing some additional conditions. Intuitively, the direction of the link may
be understood to indicate something like "presupposition" and/or
"temporal precedence". We do not elaborate on the intuitive interpreta-
tion. In Sec. VIII.2 we define the concept of an entailment link and use
it to provide a precise definition of 'theoreticity' of a component of a
theory-element in a theory-holon. This discussion makes precise the
ideas sketched more intuitively in Secs. 11.5 and 11.6. The basic intuitive
idea is that other theory-elements connected to a given theory-element
T by entailment links provide T -independent means of measuring some
of the components appearing in T. Thus the concept of T-theoreticity
can be defined in a purely formal way provided one has at hand a
formal reconstruction of the "immediate neighborhood" of T in a
theory-holon.
xxx                            OVERVIEW

   We examine some of the graph-theoretic properties of theory-holons
in Sec. VIlI.3 including "paths" between theory-elements and in Sec.
VIIl.4 we apply these properties to consider the way in which the
non-theoretical structures and intended applications of a single theory-
element in a holon are determined by the global properties of the holon.
Roughly, the idea is that models for the theory-elements in a holon that
"interpret" theory-element T and that are consistently linked to models
of other theory-elements in the holon partially determine the intended
applications of T via their links to T in a purely formal way. More
intuitively, T's intended applications are partially determined by the
theory-elements that interpret it and their links to the rest of the theory-
holon. As the theory-holon in which T is embedded is enlarged to
include increasingly larger parts of empirical science, this partial formal
determination narrows down to include fewer and fewer things that are
not "genuine" intended applications of T. One may conjecture that, as
the theory-holon approaches the whole of empirical science - or
perhaps the whole of empirical knowledge - only the genuine intended
applications will remain. Of course, for any reconstruction of a local
fragment of empirical science, the genuine intended applications will be
included in the formal definition of the kind we suggest, but so will
many other things. The point is, so we conjecture, that we can always
rule out more of these "pseudo-intended applications" by enlarging the
reconstructed complex to include more of empirical science. Every
fragment tom from the fabric has loose ends, but the larger the fragment
the less significant they become relative to the fragment.
   In Sec. VIIl.S we consider some alternative possibilities for the global
structure of a theory-holon. We contrast two views about this structure
which we call 'foundationalism' and 'coherentism'. Foundationalism is
the view that the theory-holon representing the global structure of
science may not contain closed paths. The consequence of this view -
that there are some "bed-rock" theory-elements upon which the rest of
empirical science rests - is considered in some detail. This examination
reveals some apparently serious problems for foundationalism. We then
examine a strong form of coherentism that maintains there are no
loop-free paths and consequently no bed-rock theory-elements. Though
we do not defend this view, we do suggest some ways in which it
appears more tenable than foundationalism.

 Throughout the book we have attempted to use the standard notation
 of set theory and, more generally, of the mathematical sciences. We
 have tried to avoid notation specific of symbolic logic; only in a few

                  MODELS AND STRUCTURES



                          1.0 INTRODUCTION

In this chapter we introduce the idea of model-theoretic representation
of scientific theories or scientific knowledge. To begin, we will use the
term 'scientific theory' in a rather loose, intuitive sense. In the course of
our discussion in the remainder of this work, this term will become
more precisely defined - partly in terms of the concepts introduced in
this chapter.
   We shall begin with an intuitive discussion of the idea of a "model"
for an empirical theory (Sec. 11). We note that the concept of a model
for a theory can be broadened in a natural way to permit us to speak of
"potential models" for a theory. The distinction between models and
potential models closely parallels the well-known distinction between
lawlike and non-lawlike sentences. We introduce the concept of a
"structure species" to provide a general framework for talking about
classes of models for theories and to elucidate the distinction between
the models and potential models of empirical theories (Sec. 1.2). Con-
ceiving classes of models as structure species may be viewed simply as
an elaboration of the familiar idea ofaxiomatizing a theory by defining
a "set-theoretic predicate" (Sec. 1.3). We discuss some of the well-
known limitations of this approach to specifically empirical theories. In
particular, we consider the implicit commitment to multiple models of
empirical theories entailed by this approach and the inherent difficulty
in specifying just the "empirically interesting" models or potential
models with this approach (Sec. 1.4).
   Throughout this chapter, we shall use the theory of extensive mea-
surement as an illustrative example. We shall conclude the chapter with
brief· treatments of several more examples (Sec. 1.5-7) - Jeffrey
decision theory, classical and relativistic collision mechanics, and clas-
sical particle mechanics - which will be considered in more detail and
greater sophistication in later chapters.



                                     1
2                            CHAPTER ONE

               I.1 MODELS AND POTENTIAL MODELS

Whenever a scientific theory has attained a certain degree of maturity
 and conceptual determinacy, we can set about identifying its models
 - those things the theory deals with. The basic units of our analysis
 of scientific theories will be models - not statements, as in other
 approaches to the foundations of science. Theories which have not
 attained the level of determinacy where its models can be identified, fall
 out of the scope of the present work. This should not be understood as
 an evaluative judgement. There might be subjects of inquiry where, for
 whatever intrinsic or extrinsic reasons, no theories with actually identifi-
able models can be devised. Of course, one could then raise the
 question whether it still makes sense to try to construct "theories" in
 such cases. This is not a question to which we shall give any answer in
the present context.
    We understand the term "model" here in the sense of modern logic
and model theory. In ordinary language and in informal contexts within
empirical science, the term "model" is used in an ambiguous way. If we
consider the term "model" with respect to the relationship between a
"picture" of something and the thing "depicted", it appears that "model"
is sometimes used in the sense of picture and sometimes in the sense of
the thing depicted. The two meanings are logically converse, so that one
can be defined through the other by just transforming the phrase "x is a
model of y" into "y is a model of x". Empirical scientists tend to use
"model" in the sense of "picture", as when they say that a certain set of
equations "is a model" of some subatomic phenomena or certain real-
life market situations. Logicians and mathematicians consistently use
"model" in the sense of the thing depicted by a picture (= by a theory).
Since this second use of "model" is well-established and clearly defined
in the formal sciences, it is the one we are going to adopt here.
Therefore, instead of saying that certain equations are a model of
subatomic or economic phenomena, we propose to say that the sub-
atomic or economic phenomena are models of the theory represented
by those equations.
    This use of "model" in the sense of "the thing depicted" is by no
means restricted to logic and mathematics. It also appears in ordinary
language, e.g. when one says that a woman is the model of a painting.
Here, the model is the person depicted and the painting is the picture of
it. The logician'S and our use of "model" is consistent with this artistic
usage.
                      MODELS AND STRUCTURES                                3

    Models are, therefore, those "things" depicted by a theory. A theory
 normally has many different models. By being all models of the same
 theory, they have something in common. Roughly speaking, what they
 have in common is that they all share the same structure. But this is still
 too general a characterization. By "sharing the same structure" we mean
essentially two different things at the same time: That they can be all
 subsumed under the same "conceptual framework" and that they all
 satisfy the same "laws". It is important to make this distinction for our
 analysis of scientific theories. Things that can all be subsumed under
 the same conceptual framework of a given theory are sometimes called
"possible realizations", "possible models" or "potential models" of this
theory. We shall adopt the latter term here. The class of all potential
models of a theory T will be denoted by Mp(T). Potential models which
not only belong to the same conceptual framework but, in addition,
satisfy the laws of the same theory T, will be the (actual) models of T.
Their class is denoted by M(T).
    In order to clarify the distinction between potential and actual
models, let us first illustrate it by way of the example of a rather simple,
but widely applicable theory: the theory of extensive structures. This
theory tells us under what conditions the objects of a given domain D
can be measured by means of an additive numerical function. (Well-
known examples of additive functions are length, volume, and mass.)
In the domain D there must be given a relation of "precedence"
(symbolized by ";$") and an operation of "concatenation" (symbolized
by "0") having such properties that we can always find a function on the
real numbers f which satisfies the following two conditions with respect
to precedence and concatenation:
  (1)      For all a, bED:      a ;$ b ifff(a) ~ f(b)
  (2)      For all a, bED:      f(a 0 b) = f(a) + f(b).
When the axioms of the theory of extensive structures (to abbreviate as
"EXT") are all satisfied, it can be proved that there is always a real
function f satisfying (1) and (2), and moreover that this function is
unique up to the following scale transformation: If there is another J'
also satisfying (1) and (2), then there is a positive real number r such
that, for all a E D,
           f(a) = r· J'(a).
The properties that are necessary and sufficient in order to obtain this
result for the domain D together with precedence and concatenation
4                            CHAPTER ONE

are the following. Precedence must be a transitive and connected
relation on D; concatenation must be a dyadic function on D (i.e.
an "operation" on D); further, precedence and concatenation must be
related to each other in a number of different ways: Concatenation
must be associative, commutative and monotonous with respect to
precedence, and finally the so-called "Archimedean" property must be
satisfied. Let us express all these properties a bit more precisely. To do
this, let us first introduce some convenient abbreviations.
           a -< b means: a ~ b and not b ~ a
           a - b means:    a ~ band b ~ a.
           na is the concatenation of object a with itself n successive
           times: na = a 0 . . . 0 a, n times. Concatenation is supposed
           not to be idempotent, i.e. a 0 a '" a.
The desired properties are systematized in the following definition of
the predicate "is an extensive structure".
M(EXT): x is an extensive structure iff there exist D, ~,o such that
    (1) x=(D, :$,0)
    (2) D is a non-empty set
    (3) ~ is a binary relation onD
    (4) for all a, b, c E D: (if a .~ band b :$ c then a ~ c) and
        (a ~ b or b :$ a)
    (5) o:D X D .... D
    (6) for all a, b, c E D: a 0 (b 0 c) - (a 0 b) 0 c
    (7) for all a, bED: a 0 b - boa
    (8) for all a, b, c E D: a :$ b iff a 0 c :$ b 0 c
    (9) for all a, b, c, d E D there is n E N such that a -< b
        implies na 0 c ~ nb 0 d
This stipulation uses three basic notions: D, ~ and o. Conditions
(2)-(5) specify the "type" or structure of each one of these notions
taken, so to speak, "in isolation". The remaining conditions state some
relationships between them: that 0 is associative and commutative with
respect to :$ «6) and (7)), and that 0 is monotonous with respect to
 ~ (8). (9) expresses the so-called Archimedean property in a general
version. Intuitively speaking, this last axiom entails that any given objet
of D, however "large" it may be, can be "surpassed" by al)Y other object
by concatenating the last with itself a suitable number of times.
   It is methodologically interesting to distinguish two groups of condi-
                     MODELS AND STRUCTURES                               5

 tions or axioms within this list: axioms (1)-(5) and axioms (6)-(9).
 The first group tells what kind of notions constitute the theory: a "base"
 set D, of which nothing is said but that it is non-empty, a transitive and
 connected relation and a dyadic function O. In set-theoretic terms, :::;
 and 0 can be considered as sets as well, namely as "derivative" sets
 constructed out of D: ;$ is a subset of D X D whereas 0 is a subset of
 D X D X D. The second group of axioms (5)-(8) states what we could
 call some law-like connections between ;$ and o. We could express
 this distinction in a somewhat more general way: The first group of
 axioms tells what structure each of the fundamental notions must have
 so that a triple of the form (D, ;$, 0) might be considered as a possible
 candidate for an extensive structure. The second group states the
 "substantial" connections that have to be satisfied for this possible
 candidate to be really an extensive structure.
    Now, the distinction between potential and actual models of the
 theory of extensive structures as systematized in M(EXT) is settled
 through the distinction made between both groups of axioms. We can
say that conditions (1)-(5) determine the "conceptual framework" to
which all potential models of EXT must belong, whereas conditions
(6)-(9) express the "law-like connections" which the models of this
theory have to satisfy. In other words, (1)-(5) determine MP(EXT)
while the addition of (6)-(9) to Mp determines M(EXT).
    By means of this example we have only illustrated and made plausi-
ble the distinction between potential and actual models, but we have
not yet drawn this distinction in a systematic way, i.e. we have not yet
defined general notions of actual and potential models. Although in all
examples of theories we shall analyze and also in the general considera-
tions connected with them the distinction between potential and actual
models turns out to be very helpful and natural, the question of how to
draw this distinction in general is more difficult than it appears at first
glance. The difficulty in principle arises from the well-known difficulty
with the concept of lawlikeness which has been discussed in classical
philosophy of science for decades. Roughly, the distinction between
actual and potential models is parallel to the distinction between law-
like and non-lawlike axiomatic statements. It is well-known that tradi-
tional philosophy of science did not succeed, despite years of hard
work, in arriving at a systematic explication of this latter distinction.
Our approach appears to afford some insight into this distinction which
has eluded the more traditional linguistically oriented approaches.
6                            CHAPTER ONE

   To see this, let us consider how the common structure of all exten-
sive structures has been determined in M(EXT) above. According to
this definition, extensive structures are "things" constituted by exactly
one base set D (which is not further specified), two sets $ and 0
constructed out of D in a standard set-theoretic way (we shall say that
 $ and 0 are "typified" in terms of D), and a list (call it {Ad) of
sentences expressing the basic features of the constructed sets as well as
of their inter-relationships. This is the structure common to all models
of EXT. If we would like to consider not the structure of all models of
EXT but only the structure of all potential models of EXT, we would
say that this is constituted by just D, $, 0, and a sublist {Aj} of
sentences Ai - namely, the list obtained by dropping axioms (6)-(9).
In the first case, we say that D, $, 0, and {Ai} constitute the structure
species of the models of EXT, in the second case, we say that D, $,0,
and {Aj} constitute the structure species of the potential models of
EXT.

                1.2 TYPES AND STRUCTURE SPECIES

The way of viewing theoretical structures illustrated above can be
generalized to any theory. Accordingly the structure species of any
theory would be constituted by
    (a) a natural number (expressing the number of base sets);
    (b) a finite number of typifications (expressing procedures for con-
        structing new sets, relations or functions out of the base sets);
        and
    (c) set-theoretic sentences (formulas) expressing the conditions that
        have to be satisfied by the basic notions of the theory or relating
        some of them with each other (expressing "laws").
To be more precise, we first need the auxiliary notion of a typification.
Intuitively, a typification is a statement expressing that some given set R
has a definite set-theoretic type over other, given, sets D 1, ••• , D k •
Such an indication of the set-theoretic type is necessary for the rela-
tions or functions occurring in a theory, for otherwise one could not
know what kinds of arguments the function takes or the relation applies
to.
    Consider, first, the example of EXT. We have two relations occurring
in the potential models of EXT: "$" and "0". The typification of $
                      MODELS AND STRUCTURES                                 7

 states that :$ is a binary relation on the (single) base set D, and the
 typification of 0 expresses that 0 is a ternary relation on D. Now for
 arbitrary D, a binary relation on D is just an element of Po( D X D)
 and a ternary relation on D is an element of Po(D X D X D). The
 sentences ":$ E Po(D X D)" and "0 E Po(D X D X D)" are such that
 "D", ":$" and "0" can be replaced by other symbols, say, "D"', ":$'"
 and "0"', in a way which will preserve the typification. The sen-
 tences resulting from these replacements, ":$' E Po(D' X D')" and
 "0' E Po(D' X D' X D')" still are typifications, now of ":$ ", and "0'"
 over D'. From these observations it can be seen that the essential
 feature of a typification is given by the structure of the respective
 formula to the right of "E", and that the special symbol for a base set
 occurring in that formula ("D" or "D'" above) does not matter. What
 matters are the "forms" Po(' X .) and Po(' X • X .) where the dots
 indicate argument places to be filled by symbols for sets. These forms
 can be regarded as rules for the construction of more complicated sets,
out of given sets. If we "apply" Po(' X .) to the set D we obtain the
more complicated set Po( D X D).
    In general, we may want to start with more than a single base set,
say, with D 1, ••• , D k • Then in the above "forms" we have to replace the
dots by indices i E {I, ... , k} indicating which one of D 1, ... , Dk has
to go into the argument place held by the index. So Po(3 X 2) would
indicate that D3 has to go to the place held by "3" and D2 to the place
held by "2". That is, Po(3 X 2) "applied to" sets D 1, ... , Dk (k ~ 3)
yields PO(D3 X D 2).
    In general we only have to say what an "admissible form" is. Such
forms we shall call k-types, k indicating the number of (base) sets to
which the form is to be applied. The general definition of k-types is by
induction; more complicated k-types are constructed step by step from
simpler ones. Each k-type a can be imagined as a rule for constructing
a distinguished set of "type" a from k given arbitrary sets D 1, ••• , D k •
For any k-type a we write a(D 1, ... , Dk) in order to denote the result
of "applying" a to given sets D 1, ••• , D k • The simplest k-type a
is given by a number i ~ k: a == i. The result of applying i to sets
D 1, ... , Dk is defined to be just Di • Next, if some k-type a has already
been constructed then we stipulate that Po( a), too, be a k-type. If
a == i according to the first step, then a 1 = Po( a) is a k-type, and its
application a1(D 1, ... , Dk) to sets D 1, ... , Dk is defined to be given by
the application of i (== a) to D 1, ... , Dk and by subsequent application
8                              CHAPTER ONE

of the power-set operation to the resulting set, i.e. al(D I, ... , D k ) =
Po(a(Dt> ... , D k » = Po(Dj ). Another inductive step allows to proceed
from two "given" (i.e. already constructed) k-types at> a z to the new
k-type (al X a z). If, for instance, a l == j (i ~ k) and a 2 == Po(i) (with
i ~ k) then a 3 == (i X Po(i» is a k-type. The application of a 3 to sets
D I, ... , D k , a 3(D I , ••• , D k ), is defined as follows: apply a l and a z to
D I, ... , Dk and then take the cartesian product of the two sets so
obtained. In the example, al(D I , . . . , D k ) = Dj , az(D I , . . . , D k ) =

In order to characterize the set-theoretic formulas Aj which express the
laws of theory T we could proceed in a purely syntactic way talking
about formulas, free variables and typifications. Instead, we prefer to
talk about (set-theoretic) structures and about formulas applying to
such structures. To this end we start from DI-l. By specifying the
number k of base sets, the number n of relations, functions or pre-
dicates, and correspondingly n k-types aI' ... , an for the latter the
conceptual frame of a theory is fixed. We integrate these items into
what we call a type in DI-2 below. A type comprises complete informa-
                       MODELS AND STRUCTURES                                 9

tion about the syntactic properties of a theory's vocabulary. It tells how
many sorts of things (objects) the theory is talking about (the number of
base sets), it tells how many basic predicates are used (the number n of
typifications), and it tells how many arguments of which types each
predicate has (the k-type a i for the i-th predicate). Each type deter-
mines a class of set-theoretic structures of that type (DI-2-b).

 A structure of type "t consists of a collection of base sets D 1, ••• , D k ,
 Ab ... , Am· and a collection of predicates Rb ... , Rn such that the
 latter are typified over the former. If "t is a given type then "t determines

 denote by "Str("t)". Conversely, if we have a given class of set-theoretic
structures such that any two such structures have the same numbers of
base sets and relations, and such that the relations are typified in the
 same way in any two structures, then this class uniquely determines
 some type "t, namely that type "t for which all structures of the class are
 structures of type "t. In formal logic, our types are the types of many-
sorted, higher-order finite languages.
    In defining the concept of a type we have introduced a distinction
among the base sets by distinguishing two numbers k and m. Cor-
respondingly, the structures of such a type contain two kinds of base
sets: D 1, ••• , Dk and A 1, ••• , Am. This distinction we introduce for
convenience. Our intention is to be able to separate purely mathe-
matical sets (like the set N of natural numbers, or the set ~ of real
numbers) from other base sets which are empirically interpreted (lik~
the set D in the example of EXT above). Such a distinction occurs in
many empirical theories and it would be tedious to include a full
development of all the mathematics included in stating the theory.
10                            CHAPTER ONE

In such cases it is convenient to treat mathematical base sets as
"antecedently available" and interpreted, and to state only the proper
empirical part of the theory in an explicit way. By means of the above
distinction this can be done without complication. If necessary, base
sets of the first kind (DI' ... , Db which obtain an empirical inter-
pretation) are called principal base sets whereas those of the second
kind (AI' ... , Am' which have a purely mathematical interpretation)
are called auxiliary base sets.
    Now we can introduce the third part of a structure species men-
tioned earlier, namely the list of sentences or axioms. This can be
done most easily if we use the phrase "a formula applying to a struc-
ture". By this phrase the following is meant. Consider a structure
x = (DI' ... , D k , AI' ... , Am' R I, ... , Rn) of some type T. All the
items occurring in this tuple are sets, and the symbols printed here on
the paper ("Dt, ... , "R n") are symbols for sets. Now with symbols for
sets and with the usual symbols from set theory and logic we can build
formulas. Let A denote such a formula. We write A(u) in order to
denote that the symbol "u" (which is to denote a set) occurs in A, and
similarly A(u l , ... , un) if the symbols "u l", ... , "un" occur in A. We
write A[u l , ... , unl in order to denote that at most "u l", ... , "un" occur
in A as symbols denoting sets (except bound variables). Then we can say
that a formula A applies to structure (D I' . . . , Rn) iff at most the symbols
"D I ", ••• , "Rn" occur in A as symbols for sets (besides bound variables),
i.e. iff A has the form A[DI' ... , Rnl. This means, in other words, that A
is a formula built up from (some of, or all) the symbols "D I ", ••• , "Rn"
by means of the usual set-theoretic definitions, that is, with "E", "=",
quantifiers, brackets and bound variables as further stuff.
    All the formulas Ai of a structure species are required to apply to
some structure of the type T which is given in the first two parts making
up a structure species. We thus have the following definition.

   The general concept of a structure species goes back to Bourbaki's
foundational work in mathematics (see [3]). However, note that our
definition of a structure species is weaker than Bourbaki's in that we do
not require the formulas Ai to be "invariant under canonical trans-
formations". Roughly, some formula Ai applying to structures of type T
12                            CHAPTER ONE

 is invariant under canonical transformations if its truth-value does not
 change by substituting some structure x by another one x' which is a
 "bijective image" of x. That is, if x and x' can be obtained from each
 other by means of bijective mappings between the principal base sets
 and by corresponding changes of the relations Rj (while the auxiliary
 base sets are kept fixed) then: A;(x) is true iff A;(x') is true. Requir-
 ing this kind of invariance has interesting formal consequences: con-
 servation properties may then be proved. Formally, invariance under
 canonical transformations amounts to an analogue of the well-known
 isomorphy theorem in first-order logic. So, this kind of invariance
 requires that all the "objects" occurring in the principal base sets are
 really unspecified objects which may be replaced by others without
 affecting the truth of statements of the form "A;(x)". All properties of
 those objects have to be made explicit by means of the relations Rj • In
 the present set-theoretic frame this kind of invariance cannot be
proved, for set-theoretic formulas in general do not preserve their
truth-value under bijective mappings (consider "x ~ y" as an example).
In spite of the formal attraction exerted by this invariance condition we
 choose not to impose it in general for this would represent a strong
formal restriction of the way in which theories have to be represented.
In some real-life examples of empirical theories, requiring such an
invariance condition would force us into a very complicated representa-
tion of the theory.
    In general, DI-3 is still a bit restrictive in the following sense. In the
course of introducing a class of potential or actual models we do not
want to state explicitly the numbers of base sets and the k-types. Of
course, these have to be determined somehow. As in the example of
EXT we prefer to specify these items in the same way as the laws,
i.e. by means of set-theoretic sentences. Usually, the number of base
sets can simply be read off from the tuples occurring in the head of a
definition. It is clear that instead of stating a k-type we just can write
down the corresponding typification. Instead of introducing the I-type
Po(1 XI) for ";$" in EXT we simply have stated one more "axiom",
namely that ;$ is a binary relation on D (M(EXT)-2». We shall
generally adopt this way of introducing structure species. Of course,
DI-3 could be restated in a way capturing precisely this way of writing
down concrete definitions of a structure species. Roughly, a structure
species then would be given by a fixed number of typifications where all
typifications operate on the same number of base sets, together with a
list of "proper" axioms A;. It is routine and tedious to go into the
syntactic details of such a definition.
                     MODELS AND STRUCTURES                             13

    The most convenient way to proceed is this. We keep the general
 form of DI-3. In applications of DI-3 we do not make explicit the
 type 7:. Instead, we use some of the formulas Ai in order to express
 typifications. Note that DI-3 does not rule out some of the Ai being
 typifications.
    The formulas Ai can be called the theory's "constitutive statements".
 They could also be called "axioms" or "laws". However, the term "law"
 is normally used in a more restricted and pragmatic sense. We come
 back to the concept of a law below.
    Notice the following point in our example. All formulas of M(EXT)
 which are typifications belong to the formulas determining the structure
 species of the potential models of EXT. On the other hand, the theory's
"substantive claims" (6)-(9) all belong to the structure species of the
 actual models. Thus, one could be tempted to express the general
distinction between potential and actual models in the following way.
 One might say that the class of potential models of a given theory is
determined by structure species whose constitutive formulas Aj all
express typifications and nothing but typifications. On the other hand,
the class of actual models would be determined by structure species
determined not only by typifications but also by "real laws" like (6)-(9)
inM(EXT).
    However, this dichotomy between typifications and laws would be
too hasty, as the example of EXT itself shows. For, among the formulas
determining the potential models of EXT we have decided to take also
(4) and (5). Now, (4) is not a typification at all but a description of
some set-theoretic properties of ;$. And (5) only in part includes the
typification 0 E Po(X X X X X) (implicitly); it entails moreover the
statement that 0 is univocal to the right (and therefore is a function).
This, again, cannot be considered a typification. One could question
whether or not such formulas could be labelled "laws". But so much
is clear: They are certainly not lawlike connections of different con-
structed relations, which is the sense of "law" we are propounding here.
In the case of more complex theories this difference is still more
striking. For example, in physical theories using metric parameters,
besides typifications and "real laws" the structure species will be deter-
mined by statements of the sort "term t is a twice differentiable
function". Clearly, such a statement is not a typification in the sense of
DI-l. But it would also be awkward to say that it is a physical law. It is
rather a mathematical characterization of some formal properties the
term must have so that we get the structure we want. It is typical of
such mathematical characterizations that they are formulas in which,
14                             CHAPTER ONE

besides the base sets, there occurs only the term we are characterizing.
In other words these formulas do not express connections between the
different notions of the theory that are not base sets. Connections are
stated only in the law(s) of the theory. Let us call formulas whose role is
to restrict the form of isolated (non-base) terms characterizations for
short. In the framework of a structure species ~ characterizations can
be defined sharply.
DI-4:        If ~ = (k, m, ai' ... , an, AI' ... , As> is a structure species
             and i ::;;; s then Ai is a characterization iff Ai contains
             besides set-theoretic symbols and symbols for base sets, only
             symbols for precisely one relation.
For example, each of the requirements (2)-(5) of M(EXT) contains
a characterization. Each characterization determines exactly one rela-
tional (i.e. non-base) notion in terms of the base sets and auxiliary base
sets.
   Now we can state a criterion for distinguishing the potential from the
actual models of any theory: All the formulas Ai of the structure
species determining a potential model will be either typifications or
characterizations. The structure species determining an actual model
will contain, in addition, formulas which are neither typifications nor
characterizations.

        1.3 SET-THEORETIC PREDICATES AND LAWLIKENESS

Let us settle these ideas a bit more precisely. To do this, let us notice
first that the potential models have to be introduced as set-theoretic
structures (in the sense of DI-2) whereas structure species are not
structures but rather an heterogenous assortment of numbers, k-types
and formulas. So the first thing to do is to introduce the notion of a
structure of a structure species.
