As already pointed out, models will be certain kinds of potential models,
whose corresponding structure species contains not only typifications
and characterizations, but other kinds of formulas as well. These
additional formulas might normally be called "laws", some of them even
"fundamental laws". The notion of a law (or of a lawlike statement)
is essential to circumscribe the subclass of models within a class of
potential models. The problem, however, is that in spite of much
discussion on lawlikeness within traditional philosophy of science, we
still lack an adequate set of precise necessary and sufficient conditions
as a criterion for a statement to be considered a "law". It is likely that
no such set of conditions can ever be found that would appear satis-
factory to everybody since the notion of a law is a strongly historical,
discipline-dependent kind of notion.
    Nevertheless, some weak necessary conditions (like universal quanti-
fication or non-tautologous character) can be stated on which every-
body agrees. We shall not engage in a discussion of what minimal list of
necessary conditions for lawlikeness should be adopted.
    However, in the case of developed empirical theories we would like
to propose a further necessary condition for fundamental lawlikeness,
16                           CHAPTER ONE

which does not appear to have been considered in the literature. If the
theory in question has more than just one basic relation a formula will
be considered a law within this theory only if it states a non-trivial con-
nection between different non-base terms. Therefore, in such theories
characterizations are excluded from the range of laws. Of course, there
are "degenerate" cases of very simple theories where only one non-base
term appears and therefore the fundamental law of the theory cannot
but be a characterization of this term also. For such simple theories, the
laws coincide with some characterizations and therefore the class of
potential models coincides with the class of actual models. But this
situation is not typical for empirical science. (It is rather typical for
theories from elementary mathematics). Developed empirical theories
contain many non-base terms and their fundamental laws express
connections between them.
   The previous discussion has led us to a somewhat clearer explication
of the concepts of characterization and law in general - an explication
which is at least sharper than what has come out from the proposals of
the traditional approach - which seems to be adequate for mature
empirical sciences. This explication also allows for a more precise
distinction between the class of potential models and the class of actual
models.

    In standard approaches to the philosophy of science the language of
a theory plays a central role - due to the received view according to
which philosophical analysis is nothing but analysis. of language. For
some authors, a theory is just a set of sentences of a certain language.
We do not want to deny that language is an important part of every
theory. But we believe - and this is an essential tenet of our approach
- that in the study of the structure and development of empirical
science language has not a big role to play. This belief is mirrored in
our concept(s) of an empirical theory which will not contain a language
as an explicit part. It would, of course, be a serious misunderstanding to
say that therefore we have dispensed with language altogether. The
formal concept of a language known from logic comprises two features,
namely a collection of basic (non-logical) symbols - the non-logical
vocabulary -, like individual constants, predicate constants, function
constants of given, fixed "types" (arity), and some rules of how these
non-logical symbols may be combined (together with logical ones) in
order to form sentences (formulas, terms etc.). Obviously, a species ~
of structures completely describes the non-logical vocabulary of a
corresponding theory. Each relation R; occurring in the structures of ~
is typified by some k-type a; so that we know how many arguments of
which kinds R; can take. Thus each k-type a; corresponds to a specifi-
cation of some non-logical symbol of a language, and the collection of
all k-types corresponds to specifying the non-logical vocabulary of the
language. Also, the number of different sorts of variables is specified in
a type 'T by means of the number k + m of base sets. What is left open
in our account is the way in which sentences are formed out of basic
symbols, variables, and other logical symbols. But such formation rules
do not play any role in empirical science, and that is why there is no
18                          CHAPTER ONE

need to specify them. (Reference to "quantum logic", by the way, is not
to the point here.) We may safely say that - for our purposes - a type
 i completely describes the language corresponding to the species of
structures ~.
   These remarks point to a natural way of dealing with "terms" in our
 approach. A term t is a symbol in some language. By interpreting the
language we arrive at "structures for" the language and in such a
structure, term t denotes some particular entity. If t, for instance, is a
function-symbol with n argument places then the denotation of t in
some structure for the language will be a function mapping n-tuples of
"objects" on other "objects". In this model-theoretic picture about the
relation of language and "reality" (as represented by a model of set
theory) a term is just a symbol in the language denoting all entities of
appropriate type which occur in all possible structures for the language.
According to what was said in the last paragraph the two components
of this picture - language and structures for the language - are also
present in a species of structures ~. The language of ~ is given by
{aI' ... , an} and the structures for this language are just the structures
of species ~. As long as the particular token which denotes a symbol of
the language is not relevant we may take the symbols "a;" themselves as
(tokens of) the symbols of the language. Then we can say that symbol
"a;" in a structure x of species ~ denotes the entity Rj (i.e. the i-th
relation occurring in x).
   This way of dealing with language in terms of species of structures
without treating language as an explicit component will prove to be very
convenient. We therefore introduce some terminology concerning the
"terms" of a language which is given by ~. Since we concentrate on
potential models in the following (species of structures being only an
auxiliary device for their definition), it is convenient to relativize our
use of "term" to a given class of potential models from the outset.

           ai is called a term of Mp or the i-th-term of Mp. Sometimes

                     MODELS AND STRUCTURES                             19

Among the laws determining the models of a theory, normally there
 will be at least one which is distinguished from the rest by being of a
 more general and schematic character. It might be called the "funda-
mental law(s)" of the given theory. We have no general criterion for
 deciding, in any case, whether or not a given law should be considered
 as fundamental. The distinction between "normal" and ''fundamental''
laws is rather intuitive. Nevertheless, in many concrete examples of
 theories we are able to tell which of the conditions defining the models
is to be regarded as fundamental. For example, we shall see that in
 classical particle mechanics, there is no doubt that Newton's Second
Law is fundamental; in thermodynamics we shall encounter the so-
called fundamental equation of state; in collision mechanics, the fund a-
mental law is clearly the law of conservation of momentum; in Lagrange
mechanics this role is played by Lagrange's equations, and so on.
Though we have no formal criterion at hand, it seems that an unmis-
takable characteristic of fundamental laws is that they connect all, or
almost all, ofthe theory's terms in just one 'big' formula.
    Let's add here a remark concerning the distinction between potential
and actual models which is of purely technical nature. In the recon-
structions of some of the empirical theories that will be presented in the
following we shall always make a distinction between Mp and M and
we shall write down and give names to the corresponding set-theoretic
predicates. But in the case of Mp we shall not always sharply distinguish
typifications from characterizations. Often we shall express a typifica-
tion and a characterization which both concern one and the same
concept by one single comprehensive formula. This will be done only
for stylistic reasons. Also we shall omit those typifications and charac-
terizations which refer to purely mathematical entities (like Nand IR).
We shall assume that such so-called auxiliary sets already are typified
and characterized in the appropriate axiomatizations of the correspond-
ing mathematical theories.
    In the remainder of this chapter we shall reconstruct the potential
and actual models of a number of more or less complex theories
belonging to empirical science along the lines just expounded. We shall
define the corresponding so-called set-theoretic predicates determining
the class of potential and the class of actual models of each theory. A
set-theoretic predicate for the potential models of a theory is defined
by the following sorts of conditions: (a) statements about the set-
theoretic properties of the base sets; (b) typifications of the basic
20                          CHAPTER ONE

relations and (c) characterizations of the basic relations. We have
already said what kinds of statements typifications and characteriza-
tions are. For completeness let us say a word here about the descrip-
tions of the base sets. They will not always be of the simple kind we
have encountered in the example of EXT of just requiring that the base
set be non-empty. Sometimes, more substantial requirements involving
notions of some developed areas of pure mathematics will be put on a
base set; for example, that it should be a Boolean algebra or a set
isomorphic to an interval of real numbers. We shall admit any kind of
strong requirements in the description of the base sets as long as these
requirements only involve notions taken from mathematical theories.
   For the set-theoretic predicates corresponding to the actual models,
we have to add a fourth sort of conditions: (d) laws. Conditions (d)
have to be always carefully distinguished from conditions of the kind
(b) and (c). On the other hand, though in a totally neat reconstruction
we should also distinguish conditions (b) from (c) explicitly, for reasons
of economy of exposition we shall usually write down typifications and
characterizations of each relation in just one condition. The reader will
have no trouble in sorting them out in each case. By doing this, he will
also be able to find out the structure species of each set-theoretic
predicate. Finally, we shall not explicitly write down the conditions for
the auxiliary base sets (like integers and real numbers), since their
properties will be assumed to be already known from mathematics.

                I.4 PLAUSIBLE INTERPRETATIONS

Before we turn over to the task of reconstructing the potential and
actual models of some concrete theories, it is convenient to discuss the
general problem of interpretation of the models of any empirical theory
in formal terms. According to the way we have introduced these
notions here, any "normal" theory will have a great number of models
- not just one. To be more precise, in normal theories it can be proved
that neither the class of potential models nor the class of actual models
determined by a given structure species will be singletons. Actually, in
"mathematized" theories those classes will be infinite. More intuitively,
this means that any theory can be interpreted in many different ways,
which are all equally legitimate from the formal point .of view. In
particular, the interpretations can be "purely mathematical" (e.g. numer-
ical) or they can be empirical. For example, in· the case of EXT
                      MODELS AND STRUCTURES                               21

 we could include a purely numerical model which is rather obvious:
 Interpret D as the set of real numbers, :$ as just the numerical
 equal-or-Iess relation, and 0 as numerical addition. Then, the structure
 (IR, :$, 0) obviously satisfies the set-theoretic predicate "is an extensive
 structure". But, of course, the most interesting models of EXT are those
 that include a domain of empirical objects. A typical example is this.
 Take D as a class of (potentially infinite) sets of rods, so that each
 element of D is a set of rods all having exactly the same length. Then
 interpret the relation :$ between two sets of rods a and b as establish-
 ing that any rod in a is not longer than any rod in b; and interpret Oas
 the (physical) operation applied to two sets a and b which consists in
juxtaposing one rod of a to one rod of b. Under certain idealizing
 assumptions (like the possibility of building ever longer rods), the
 structure of the so interpreted terms D, :$ and 0 happens to be an
 actual model of EXT. Many more examples of a similar kind both in
pure mathematics and in empirical science could be added.
    This multiplicity of models for any given systematized theory to a
great extent is due to the fact that in the course of introducing the
 structures of a ~-species nothing specific is said about the base sets.
For example, in the case of EXT nothing is said about the content of
the only base set D. It can be any set of objects of any kind.
    There is, in principle, nothing wrong with this multiplicity of possible
interpretations of the base sets. This multiplicity is not only good for
pure mathematics. In fact, we claim that multiplicity of models is also
the normal situation in empirical science - a situation which explains
the fruitfulness of developing mathematically expressed theories for
empirical phenomena. It is clear that EXT is an interesting empirical
theory in spite of its elementary character precisely because of the great
variety of interesting models it has. This is also the case in most
theories developed in pure mathematics (which have models not only
inside mathematics but also - at least idealized ones - in the "outside
world").
    Nevertheless, when we come to theories developed in empirical
science for exclusively empirical purposes, one might argue on intuitive
grounds that we should put some restrictions on this extreme variety
of potential and actual models. For example, one might want to exclude
purely numerical models from theories like mechanics, or thermo-
dynamics, or perhaps even from EXT. One might want to say that all
the models of such theories, whatever their diversity, have to contain
22                           CHAPTER ONE

 base sets which are sets of physical objects, to say the least. This should
 not only be required of actual, but also of potential models. The reason
 would be this. The intention behind the use of potential models in
 empirical theories is that they describe some physical (empirical)
 systems or ranges of phenomena which are "reasonable" candidates for
the theory's application. It might turn out that these candidates do not
 satisfy the theory'S lawlike statements after all; but this does not
imply that they were unreasonable from the start. For example, it was
 reasonable to try to apply Newtonian mechanics to optical phenomena
and chemical reactions because these things were physical phenomena
after all - though, in the long run, they proved to be recalcitrant to a
fruitful treatment within this theory. They were plausible potential
models of Newtonian mechanics. On the other hand, it is clearly not
plausible to try to apply Newtonian mechanics to numbers. It is also
very doubtful whether it would be plausible to try to apply Newtonian
mechanics to such phenomena as love and hatred among people. Of
course, the boundaries between "plausible" and "implausible" candi-
dates are rather fuzzy. But that much should be clear: Structures whose
base sets do not contain any empirical objects should be excluded
from the range of "plausible candidates", i.e. of potential models of an
empirical theory. If we were interested in establishing a criterion for
drawing a sharp boundary between pure mathematics and empirical
science we would use this idea: The first discipline would consist of
theories not putting any (semantic) constraint on the content of the base
sets of their models; empirical science consists of theories which do
put such constraints - which differentiate between "plausible" and
"implausible" potential models on some pre-theoretic grounds.
    These considerations about the semantics of empirical theories can-
not be explicated in formal terms. Some (weak) necessary conditions
for "empirical plausibility" can be formalized within the construction of
particular theories; but others can only be left to something like the
"physicist's intuitions" or some other pragmatic decision procedures.
We shall come back to this point in the next chapter when we come to
the discussion of the notion of the intended applications of a given
theory. For the time being, we will be content with noting that these
semantic constraints on the multiplicity of really applicable models will
not be reflected in our formal concepts of potential and actual. models
of a given theory; these definitions will not include any hint at the
empirical interpretation of the base sets. The latter is left for another
                      MODELS AND STRUCTURES                               23

 step in the reconstruction of empirical theories. We want clearly to dif-
ferentiate the "purely structural" or "purely formal" aspects of a theory
from its more "semantic" or "pragmatic" features.
    Before ending our general discussion of potential and actual models
we can give a first rough and provisional description of what it means
to apply a theory to a certain range of phenomena. We will try to
explain this in terms of potential and actual models. The issue is related
to the distinction between conceptualizing a certain range of phe-
nomena and making an empirical assertion about them. When con-
fronted with some given "data" or "phenomena" we might want to use a
theory T to ''understand'' them, to "explain" them, to "predict" them, -
in short,we might want to apply T to those data. To do this, the first
thing we try is to conceptualize the domain I of data in terms of T, i.e.
to use the concepts appearing in potential models of T to refer to I. We
create a potential model of T for I. This is the more "conceptual" aspect
of the application of a theory. The next step is to make an assertion
about I in terms of T - an assertion with empirically testable con-
sequences. We then assert that I satisfies the fundamental laws of T,
which, of course, only makes sense if I has already been conceptualized
in terms of T. In other words, we make the empirical assertion that the
potential model considered is also an actual model of T. This empirical
assertion can be either true or false. If it turns out to be true, we can say
that we have applied T to I successfully.

                  1.5 EXAMPLE: DECISION THEORY

To illustrate the main points of the general discussion so far as well as
the problems encountered when trying to identify the potential and
actual models of a given theory we have chosen two examples of
empirical theories of different disciplines: decision theory and collision
mechanics. Though they are somewhat more complex in structure than
EXT, they are still simple enough to make the reconstruction proce-
dures easy to grasp. The full reconstruction of collision mechanics will
be left for Ch. III. For the time being, our main purpose in reconstruct-
ing these theories is one of illustration.
   Our exposition of each theory will proceed in two steps: We first
determine its potential models and subsequently its actual models. The
method used to determine both kinds of structures is the semi-formal
axiomatic method known as "definition of a set-theoretic predicate",
24                           CHAPTER ONE

 which we have already illustrated in the case of EXT: A set-theoretic
 predicate is defined through the conditions (axioms) that have to be
 satisfied by the basic notions of the theory in question. This predicate
is, so to speak, the "family name" of all structures we call potential,
 respectively actual, models of the given theory. The predicate defined
 by the conditions determining the actual models will be called the
''fundamental predicate" of the theory in question.
    In each of the following cases, the predicate naming the potential
 models of the theory will be the same as the fundamental predicate with
 the word "potential" placed before; afterwards, we go on to determine
 the actual models by defining the fundamental predicate (whose con-
ditions include the fundamentallaw(s)).
    We start by reconstructing the potential and actual models of a
theory slightly more complicated than EXT: decision theory in the
version propounded by Jeffrey, referred to by "DEC". This theory
clearly belongs to the behavioral sciences. It only makes sense to try to
apply it to human beings or, at most, to developed organisms and
machines.
    Jeffrey's decision theory deals with the way people (ideally) make
decisions in situations where they have a ranking of preferences among
different alternatives, whose outcomes are only incompletely known in
advance. The basic intuitive idea is that in such situations people ideally
tend to render their preferences in some way compatible with the
expected utilities of their decisions as well as with the probability that
the different possible alternatives actually take place or not. To put it
briefly, the task of decision theory is to tell how people's utilities and
personal probability judgements hang together.
    In our systematic exposition of decision theory the basic individuals
will not be persons or organisms but rather propositions. They are all
we need in this context. These propositions are supposed to describe
the different alternatives a person is factually confronted with (or,
rather, he/she believes he/she is confronted with) as well as the dif-
ferent ways this person can react to them, i.e. the decisions he/she
takes. These propositons should obey the rules of classical logic; that
is, the set of propositions admitted in a decision-theoretic structure
together with the logical operations of conjunction A, disjunction V,
and negation -=-, must constitute a so-called Boolean algebra (cf. [8], p.
246). In particular, this implies that among all propositions we shall
have two selected ones: the tautologous or "universal" proposition
                     MODELS AND STRUCTURES                               25

denoted by i and the contradictory proposition denoted by 0, with
their well-known properties.
   Besides the base set of Boolean propositions we need an auxiliary
base set: the set of real numbers, fR. The other basic notions of DEC
(obtained from the base sets by typifications) will be two dyadic
relations called, respectively, utility U, and probability P. U will just be
characterized as a real-valued function. The characterization of P will
be richer. We shall require that P together with the Boolean algebra of
the base set be a probability space.

     (1) x = (B,IR, U,p)

               1.6 EXAMPLE: COLLISION MECHANICS

We now tum over to theories of physical sciences. Our first example is
one of the simplest "real-life" theories to be found in physics: collision
mechanics. Historically, it was also one of the first physical theories to
be treated in a quasi-axiomatic, mathematical way. Its basic concepts
and laws were already developed within the Cartesian program for the
physical sciences in the middle of the 17th century, before the advent
of Newtonian mechanics. Frequently, if collision mechanics is treated
in standard expositions at all, this is done within the framework of
Newtonian mechanics, so to say, as a "sub-theory" of the latter. This
might have some practical justification. But for conceptual as well as
historical reasons we think it is more adequate to reconstruct collision
mechanics as a theory by itself before Newtonian mechanics.
    We shall reconstruct two versions of collision mechanics: classical
and relativistic collision mechanics. The second is slightly more com-
plex than the first and its main interest lies in its applicability to some
processes in elementary particle (high-energy) physics, whereas the
classical version is applicable to macroscopic collisions only.
    In the classical version, collisions are described by giving the veloc-
ities of each particle before and after the collision. Nothing is said
about the phenomenon of collision itself. This is treated as a sort of
"black box", whose "inputs" are the velocities of all particles before
collision and its "outputs" are their velocities afterwards. The actual
paths of the particles are irrelevant to this theory.
    Therefore, all basic notions we need to describe classical collisions
are a finite, non-empty set of colliding particles p, a set of two time
instants T = {fl' f 2 }, where fl denotes a moment "before" and f2
denotes a moment "after" the collision, and a velocity function v
assigning a three-component vector (one component for each direction
in space) to each particle at each time. Further, in order to formulate
the theory's fundamental law we have to introduce a real-valued func-
tion called the mass m of each particle, which is a constant factor over
time. We shall come to speak on the differences of semantic and
functional status between velocity and mass in the next chapter. For the
time being we treat velocity and mass on the same footing. The only
difference between velocity and mass we can notice now is summarized
                        MODELS AND STRUCTURES                          27

in their respective formal characterizations: While velocity is a time-
dependent vectorial function whose range are triples of real numbers
(classical) mass is a time-independent scalar function whose range are
the positive real numbers.
   From what has just been said, we can already figure out what the
base sets of the models will be. We need three base sets: the set P of
particles, the set of instants T and the auxiliary base set IR of real
numbers.
   Further, there will be two basic relations, velocity and mass, typified
as a relation over particles, time and real numbers and as a relation
over particles and real numbers, respectively. All this is systematized in
the set-theoretic definition of the potential models as follows.
MP(CCM): x is a potential classical collision mechanics (x E Mp(CCM)
         iff there exist P, T, v, and m such that
     (1) x=(P, T,IR,v,m)
     (2) P is a finite, non-empty set

     (4) v:PX T-.1R3

so-called "law of conservation of momentum" which says that the total
sum of the products of mass and velocity of each particle must remain
the same before and after the collision.

In order to reconstruct relativistic collision mechanics we make two
modifications to the previous framework. First, to account for "rela-
tivistic effects" on moving bodies mass must be taken not as a constant
function of each particle, but as a velocity-dependent, and therefore
ultimately time-dependent function. That is, the typification of mass will
change. Secondly we shall introduce a new basic notion into the theory,
viz. an "existence function" which tells whether or not a given particle
exists at time ti • This would not make sense in classical physics, where
28                               CHAPTER ONE

particles are supposed to exist before as well as after the collision, but it
makes sense when we come to the application of collision mechanics to
elementary particle physics, where some particles appear or disappear
in the course of a collision. There is nothing specifically relativistic
about this existence function; in principle, it could also be introduced
into the framework of CCM. But since its introduction was prompted
by the experimental results in high-energy physics, where the only
workable framework is that of relativity, it seems natural to include the
existence function only in the relativistic version of collision mechanics.

        1.7 EXAMPLE: CLASSICAL PARTICLE MECHANICS

 Having reconstructed the basic structures of DEC and collision
 mechanics we want to proceed to a more important and more complex
 theory which also serves as a paradigm for many discussions in the.
 philosophy of science: classical particle mechanics (CPM). It is pro-
 fitable to reconstruct CPM immediately after collision mechanics
 because CPM can be regarded logically as well as historically as a
generalization and an enrichment of collision mechanics. The enrich-
 ment mainly consists in adding the concept of force to the concepts of
 collision mechanics. This allows to treat a great number of dynamic
 systems which collision mechanics was not able to. treat because its
 range of applications was much narrower from the beginning.
     The fully reconstructed structure of CPM is not only richer but also
much more complicated than that of collision mechanics. There are
several aspects relevant for philosophy of science which do not play an
important role in DEC and collision mechanics but which are essential
for the identification of CPM. We shall come back to this. Here we
only want to introduce Mp and M (as in the other examples).
     CPM deals with all possible motions of particles which are con-
sidered as mass-points in space and it is assumed that these motions are
caused by forces. The concept of force is not explained any further but
introduced as an undefined basic concept. In any case force must be a
vector-valued function.
    Just as collision mechanics historically is connected with the name
of Descartes so CPM is associated with the name of Newton -
therefore it sometimes is called "Newtonian mechanics". But this name
is a bit misleading because modern formulations differ from the original
Newtonian formulation in some essential respects. They basically are
generalizations of the original formulation. But more important is
the fact that CPM is not the only mechanical theory attributable to
Newton. Among others, he also developed hydrodynamics and the
mechanics of rigid bodies. So, the expression "Newtonian mechanics" is
ambiguous.
    In the following definition, sp denotes the function obtained from s
by keeping argument p of s fixed, i.e. sp(t) = s(p, t) for all t E T.
c1 denotes the inverse function of c l ; its existence is guaranteed because
of the requirement that c 1 be bijective.
Mp(CPM): x is a potential classical particle mechanics (x E Mp(CPM))
         iff there exist P, T, S, s, m, f, cl , C2 such that

 of time and S the set of points of space. Instead of considering just a
 discrete set of instants, as in CCM, we now take something like a
 continuous time interval T during which the particles are considered.
 c1 and Cz are coordinatizations of time and space respectively and
 separately (which is an essential feature of classical theories). c1 maps
 points of time into the real numbers, while Cz maps points of space into
 real 3-vectors. c1 and Cz are bijective and therefore induce the struc-
 tures of IR and 1R3 on T and S. In this way, time and space are supplied
 with their usual, classical structures. s is the position function which
 assigns to each particle p and point of time t a point of space, namely
 that point of space at which particle p is situated at time t (p's position
 at t). So "s(p, t) = a" means "particle p at time t is in position a".
Usual formulations of mechanics introduce a position function which is
 differentiable (at least twice) with respect to time. Since T and Shave
no proper intrinsic structure, differentiability of s cannot be formulated
without using the coordinatizations Cl and Cz. We cannot require that s
itself is differentiable - this makes no sense - but we can require that
 C z 0 sp 0 c1 be differentiable. If we look at the following diagram we
see that this function goes from IR to 1R3 and therefore is a suitable
candidate to be differentiable. sp might be called the position function
of particle p or p's path. m, as in CCM, is the mass function.
     We do not want to identify space and time with IR to 1R3 which we
conceive of as purely mathematical entities. Points of space and time
are not mathematical entities, they are physical entities. In order to
take account of this fact we have to introduce the base sets T and S.
This is in accordance with the genuine "Newtonian spirit" in classical
mechanics, which views space and time as real ("absolute") physical
entities. Accordingly, the position function s (other than, say, the
velocity function in CCM, for which no such spatial identification is
needed) has to be viewed as assigning physically real "places" to
particles at given times. Also, a rather rich structure of space and time

force values with no definite total sum. We do not require - and here
we differ from other treatments - that the total sum always be con-
vergent. We do not need to require this because in actual models this
logically follows from Newton's second law.
