                      THEORY-ELEMENTS



                         Il.O INTRODUCTION

In this chapter we discuss the simplest kind of set-theoretic structure
that may be identified with, or serve as a logical reconstruction of an
empirical theory. We call these structures 'theory-elements'. Theory-
elements consist of two parts - a purely formal, mathematical structure
K which we call a 'theory-core' and a class of 'intended applications'.
Roughly, the formal core K is used to "say something" about the
intended applications I. This distinction is introduced in Sec. 11.1 and
the remainder of the chapter is devoted to discussing different com-
ponents of the theory-core (Secs. 11.2-11.4), the intended applications
(Sec. 11.6) and the form of the claim made with the core about th~
intended applications (Secs. II.S and II.7). Theory-elements are elemen-
tary empirical theories in two senses. First, they are the smallest set-
theoretical entities that may have empirical claims associated with them.
Second, more complex, non-elementary, "molecular" empirical theories
are all built from theory-elements that are linked in specific ways
(Ch. IV). Paradigm examples of theory-elements in our sense are
"fragments" of theories associated with specific laws - for example,
the theory of elastic forces, the classical theory of gravitational forces
and the theory of van der Waals' gases. Theories in the "larger" sense
such as classical particle mechanics will be construed as linked collec-
tions of "elementary" theory-elements.
   In Ch. I potential models and models were introduced to describe
respectively what we might call the conceptual framework of a theory-
element and the empirical laws formulated within this framework.
These are regarded as a part of the theory's formal core. In addition,
the theory-core contains "constraints" which describe "connections" or
"relations" among different applications of the same theory (Sec. 11.2)
and intertheoretical links which describe essential connections between
applications of the theory in question and other, different ,theories
represented by different theory-elements (Sec. 11.3.2). Finally, the core
contains a class of "partial potential models" - fragments of the
                                   36
                          THEORY-ELEMENTS                                 37

potential models that can be understood or interpreted independently
of the theory in question. Partial potential models are first characterized
in terms of a theory-relative theoretical/non-theoretical distinction
among the components in the potential models. This distinction is first
introduced in a rather intuitive manner (Sec. 11.3.1). The connection of
this distinction to the traditional theoretical/non-theoretical dichotomy
is discussed at this point. We return to treat this distinction again,
with the help of our concept of intertheoretical links, in two somewhat
different ways in Sec. 11.3.3 and Sec. 11.3.4. In the course of doing this, a
set-theoretic characterization of "measurement method" or "determina-
tion" is developed and illustrated with examples (Sec. 11.3.3).
   Our explication of the empirical claim associated with a theory-
element begins with a characterization of the "content" of the element
(Sec. 11.5). Roughly, the content of a theory-element is the class of
arrays or sets of partial potential models that are "compatible" with the
laws, constraints and intertheoretical links associated with the theory-
element. The claim is simply that the intended applications are a
member of the content. We continue our discussion of the limits on
formal description of the intended applications in Sec. 11.6.

            ILl CORES AND INTENDED APPLICATIONS

Standard analyses of empirical theories presuppose that all we need in
order to identify the essential components of a theory is the distinction
between (actual) models and potential models. However, if we look
more carefully at the way real empirical theories are built up, we see
that more components have to be distinguished in order to identify a
theory'S complex structure accurately.
   First, we find out that empirical theories, in contrast to theories of
pure mathematics, cannot be reduced to components describable in
purely formal terms (as is the case for M and Mp). In addition, they
have associated with them some informal descriptions of the particular
"chunks" of reality which they are intended to apply to. It is our view
that such descriptions are not somehow "external" to the theory (as
many philosophers of science have assumed) but rather belong to the
theory-concept itself. In addition to the theory's "formalism" we need a
set of informal descriptions of its domain of applications. This second
component usually can be found in textbooks only implicitly - in-
dicated perhaps by the sort of empirical problems that can be solved by
38                          CHAPTER TWO

 means of the formalism. We consider this component to be a part of the
 identity of a theory because without it we would have no way to know
 what the theory is about, we would not even know whether we are
 dealing with an empirical theory at all. Take the case of an advanced
 scientific theory, where quite a few abstract terms expressed in mathe-
 matical language appear, and let us ask whether by just considering the
 theory'S formalism we would be able to tell which part of the world the
 theory describes, or for what purposes the theory is useful. The general
 answer to this question is that we cannot tell. For, even by assuming
 that the formalism is adequate for describing some part of the world,
we shall be able in general to go over to quite different phenomena
 described by the same formal means. This is indicated by a well-known
 theorem of logic, namely, that structures isomorphic to models of a
theory are again models of that same theory.
    Thus, in order to know what a theory is about we have to include
an informal description of its intended applications, as a part of the
identity of the theory in question. Such a component cannot be iden-
tified in a purely formal way, since this would immediately entail the
difficulty explained above. Let us call this component "the domain of
 intended applications", and let us denote it by I (to remind us of its
 intentional nature).
    Though I cannot be identified in completely formal terms, the
conditions describing it may have different degrees of precision. As we
shall see later on, some of them can be stated formally by using the
structural descriptions of the models of the theory. Some other con-
ditions, though being stated in informal, everyday language, can have a
rather precise meaning. The latter are necessary (but not sufficient)
conditions about the way the base sets of the theory have to be
interpreted. Let us call these descriptions "general conditions for the
intended interpretations of the base sets" - abbreviated as "basic
intended interpretations". The meaning of the terms appearing in them
is more or less well-determined by a general semantics of the scientists'
"everyday" language, involving very general (and weak) rules of inter-
pretation for such terms as "particle", "state", "commodity", "person",
etc. No such general semantics is available so far, so we leave this issue
here as an open project; but the minimal requirements we put on the
base sets when dealing with some concrete examples in Chapter III will
point to the place where this project should impinge on the structural
reconstruction of theories.
                          THEORY-ELEMENTS                                 39

   The explicit introduction of formalizable structural descriptions and
of basic intended interpretations does not exhaust all the means at our
disposal to draw the boundaries of the domain of intended applications.
There are two further means strongly pragmatic in character. First,
there is the so-called "paradigmatic method", which roughly consists in
starting with some concrete "core examples" of application of the
theory and trying to enlarge the set of these applications step-by-step
through intuitive considerations of analogy. The second way is the so-
called "method of autodetermination", by which the theory's formalism
itself is left with the "responsibility" of deciding, in many cases, what its
applications are to be. The combination of the paradigmatic method
with the method of autodetermination gives rise to a step-by-step
determination of the theory's empirical domain in the course of its
historical evolution. (This is what has been called "normal science").
More about this will be said later in this chapter and in Chapter V.
   Summarizing what has been said so far, we can distinguish two major
components of a theory's identity: a structurally formalizable one, and
another "more empirical" part, which can only partially be charac-
terized in a precise way. The second part we have just called "the
domain of intended applications", I; let us call the first part "the
(formal) core", K. Accordingly, we could define a theory as an ordered
pair consisting of a core K and a domain of applications I. However, for
reasons which will clearly be appreciated in Ch. IV, we shall call such a
structure not a "theory", but a "theory-element". Theory-elements are,
so to speak, the simplest cases of theories.
DII-l:     T is a theory-element iff there exist K and I such that
              T= (K, I)
           where
             (1) K is a theory-core
             (2) I is a domain of intended applications of K
For all that has been said up to this point, one could think that the core
of a theory-element reduces to the sets Mp and M. However, this can
be an accurate description of· a theory's core only in very simple and
"degenerate" cases. Normally, three further components are needed in
order to make up a theory's formal identity.
   First, as we have already argued, M will normally not be a singleton,
nor will I be. On the contrary, the normal case is that we find a large
40                           CHAPTER TWO

variety of models (and correspondingly of applications) for a given
theory. With the possible (and doubtful) exception of general relativity
theory, no actually existing theory can claim to have the whole universe
as its only model; real theories apply only to different parts of it. Their
applications are not "cosmological", but "local". Now, all these different
models and applications do not appear in isolation, but rather "tied up"
through some formally describable interconnections. These we call
"constraints". They also belong to K.
    A second addition we have to make is the distinction between
theoretical and non-theoretical terms within the conceptual frame Mp.
This distinction has a long and controversial history in the philosophy
of science, but we will treat it here in a quite different spirit, without
claiming that our treatment solves all the epistemological and onto-
logical problems which have usually been associated with the distinc-
tion. The sort of distinction we find useful for reconstructing empirical
theories is roughly this. There are concepts in Mp which appear to be
specific of the conceptual framework of the theory T in question, in
the sense that their meaning depends on T. These concepts we call
T-theoretical. Some other concepts in M p ' on the contrary, have a
meaning independent of T, e.g. they can be determined by other -
underlying - theories. These concepts we call T -non-theoretical.
    Finally, we have to take account of the fact that, normally, empirical
theories do not appear in isolation. They appear in connection with
other theories, and some of these "intertheoretical" connections are not
just "accidental" but essentially belong to the identity of the theory
itself. That is, the theory cannot be used or applied, or even re-
constructed, by disregarding its intertheoretical connections to other
theories. These we call a theory's "(intertheoretical) links". They also
belong to a theory's core. Now, we go on to deal with all these
components in detail.

                          11.2 CONSTRAINTS

Usually a theory is applied to concrete, bounded phenomena. A certain
class of phenomena - a system - is taken into consideration, other
phenomena not relevant for the system - and usually separated from it
in space and time - are neglected. This is so for most theories in
physics. Even in physics there are very few cases of theories which may
really be supposed to deal with the whole of our universe as "one big"
                          THEORY-ELEMENTS                               41

application. The only example of this sort we can think of is the alleged
case of general relativity theory. But even such an exceptionable case
would not put any restriction to the scope of our approach. Since one
big universal application can be regarded as a special case of "local"
applications, we shall concentrate on the latter case. By "local" we mean
"bounded to a part of the universe".
   But if theory T has local applications there is an immediate difficulty
connected with these. Local applications may overlap in space and
time, they may influence each other (even if they are separated in space
and time), certain properties of T's objects may remain the same if the
objects are transferred from one application to another one. Any
connection of this sort will be captured by what we call constraints.
Constraints express physical or real connections between different
applications but they also can express mere conceptual connections.
How can we treat these interconnections? Let us consider some
examples.

112.1 Extensivity of Energy in Equilibrium Thermodynamics
Simple equilibrium thermodynamics (SETH) will be formally treated in
Chapter III. Here, we shall discuss only informally one of SETH's
various constraints which is equally important and illuminating: the
extensivity of energy.
   Without going into details of the description of thermodynamical
systems let us assume that each thermodynamical system (for example,
a given amount of gas within a container that is being heated up) can
acquire various states and in each state has a specific energy. The
energy is expressed by a real number U(z) where z is a state
of the thermodynamical system x. Suppose that by describing thermo-
dynamical systems we obtain structures which form the set Mp(SETH)
of potential models of thermodynamics. Each description contains at
least the components just mentioned: state and energy. The concept of
a "thermodynamic system" cannot occur in potential models as a basic
concept, for any potential model as a whole corresponds to a thermo-
dynamical system.
   Now one central feature of thermodynamics is that usually it is
applied to rather small systems like a gas in a box or a liquid in ~
suitable bottle, and the question of interest is how such systems interact,
if they are brought into contact with each other. As such "concatena-
42                          CHAPTER TWO

tions" of thermodynamical systems are systematically treated in SETH
we have to consider a concatenation operation 0 among thermo-
dynamical systems (potential models). Since this concatenation cannot
be defined in terms of other basic concepts it has to be treated as a
basic notion on its own.
   As an example consider two boxes filled with gas (see Figure II-I).
Each box represents a thermodynamical system. But we also can
concatenate both boxes in the following way. We put them together and
take off the two walls on which they are made to touch (see Figure II-I,
b and c).


                   (a)




                   (b)




                   (c)



                                                  x o x'




                                  Fig. II-I.

The result of this operation again is a thermodynamical system denoted
by x 0 x'.
   Generally speaking, we have two systems x and x' which are in
states z and z', respectively. x has an energy function U assigning to
each state z of x its value of energy U(z), and x' has energy function U'
with values U'(z'). If we concatenate x and x' we obtain a new.system
x". We write x" = x 0 x' in order to indicate that x" has been obtained
by concatenation of x and x'. If X is in state z and x' in state z' then x"
                         THEORY-ELEMENTS                                43

also will be in some specific state z" which we find convenient to
denote by z 0 z' in order to indicate that it arose by concatenation. If
the concatenated system x 0 x' is to be a full blown thermodynamical
system it must of course have its own energy function U" associating to
each of its states z" an energy value U"(z").
   Now we can ask whether there is a systematic connection between
U" and the energy functions U and U' of the original systems. In
fact, questions of this type are not only reasonable: they are crucial
for SETH and quite a lot of SETH's laws consist of answers to
such questions. In the case of energy the answer is this. The energy
U"(z 0 z') of the compound system x" which arises from concatenation
of x and x' and which is in state z 0 z' due to the fact that x is in state
z and x' in z', is just the sum of the original systems' energies in their
respective states, i.e.
           U"(z 0 z') = U(z) + U'(z').
This requirement should be satisfied by any two thermodynamical
systems which are concatenated. That is, it has the general form of the
scheme:
   (A)     if x, x' E Mp and x is in state z and x' is in state z' and
           x 0 x' is in state z 0 z', then
               U"(z 0 z') = U(z) + U(z')
This is the requirement of the extensivity of energy, that is, the require-
ment that energy be additive with respect to concatenation.
    What is the precise form of this requirement within our model-
theoretic set-up? Obviously, there is some quantification over potential
models going on here, but we cannot quantify over all potential
models, since we may always construct sets of potential models that
don't fulfill the extensivity of energy. Rather, the general requirement
implicit in scheme (A) is that we shall only admit collections of poten-
tial models in our theory that agree with the extensivity condition. That
is, the quantification is restricted to some subset X of Mp(SETH):
  (Ax)     For any three potential models x, x', x" in X: if x" = x 0 x'
           and x, x', x" are in states z, z', z 0 z', respectively, then
           U"(z 0 z') = U(z) + U'(z')
Subsets X of Mp(SETH) having the property (Ax) represent "admis-
sible" combinations of potential models. They are admissible in satisfy-
44                           CHAPTER TWO

ing the requirements of extensivity. That is why we may call such a
condition on sets of potential models a "constraint".
    Formally, we can lump together all admissible combinations thereby
obtaining a set which derivatively may also be called a "constraint" and
denoted by C. The elements of C are characterized by some sentence
(like (Ax) above) containing quantification over potential models, and
therefore they will be sets of potential models.


11.2.2 Equality Constraint in Classical Mechanics

In classical particle mechanics (CPM -         compare Ch. I), we find an
 example of so-called "equality constraints"; the equality constraint for
mass. Consider a system (a potential model of CPM) containing the
earth, the moon and a rocket which is going to be sent from the earth to
the moon. In order to bring down the rocket softly on the surface of the
moon it is necessary to know the rocket's mass. With a given mass mr
of the rocket, if we were to calculate and programme velocities and
accelerations induced by the machinery during the landing manoeuvre,
the landing would be successful only if mr has the correct value. If mr is
too big the rocket will crash on the moon, if mr is too small the rocket
will drive back into space. (This is the situation of a well-known
computer game.)
    How is mr discovered? First, the mass of the empty rocket as well
as the mass of fuel are determined on the earth. This can be done
by means of well-known methods depending on certain empirical
generalities and well grounded physical properties of the materials like
homogeneity and density. Then the length of the journey and the
amount of fuel needed during this time is calculated. This number is
subtracted from the original mass and thus the desired value mr at the
time before the landing is obtained.
    What matters here is that the mass of the empty rocket on the earth
is the same as the mass of the empty rocket on the moon. This fact is so
evident that usually it will not be stated explicitly. But it could be well
imagined that the masses of bodies change, depending on their posi-
tions in space or on their positions relative to other bodies or on their
velocities (as in relativity theory). This not being the case is an essential
assumption of CPM. If, in the example above, the mass of the empty
rocket were to change during its travelling we would have to use a law
                         THEORY-ELEMENTS                               45

describing this change in quantitative terms in order to land it on the
moon softly.
   The straightforward formulation of this assumption about mass is to
say that a particle's mass depends on that particle, and on nothing else.
However, this statement makes sense only "inside" one single model of
CPM. If CPM were to deal only with one big model (application), viz.
the universe, then the above formulation would do. But CPM is .not
such a universal theory - even if physicists engaged in philosophical
reflections sometimes claim so. Actually, CPM always is applied to
systems bounded in space and time - subsystems of the universe. CPM
has many different "local" applications which, of course, may overlap.
In the above example two different applications are involved. The first
application is that in which the rocket's mass on the earth is deter-
mined. The second application contains the earth, the moon and the
rocket during the voyage. The rocket which appears in both applica-
tions has the same mass in both applications. This is an instance of the
equality constraint for mass in CPM.
   In general this constraint may be stated as follows. Whenever we
have two mechanical systems (potential models of CPM) and a particle
occurring in both systems, the particle's mass must be the same in both
systems. In other words, we get the scheme:
   (B)     if x, x' E Mp and m is the mass function of x and m' the
           mass function of x', then: for all particles p, if P occurs in
           x and x', then m(p) = m'(p).
As before, the precise formulation of this constraint says that, for· any
suitable subset X ~ M p ' we must require that:
   (Bx)    For all potential models x, x' of X with corresponding mass
           functions m, m' and for all particles p: if p occurs in x and
           in x' then m(p) = m'(p)
Again, sets of potential models for which (Bx) is true may be called
"admissible" combinations of potential models, "admissible" in the
sense that they are admitted with respect to the requirement of mass
not depending on "external" factors. By collecting all such admissible
combinations we obtain a class C which will be called the equality con-
straint for mass in CPM. In general, equality constraints work like this.
Some function - representing a property of the objects of the theory -
is considered. The equality constraint for that function then requires
46                           CHAPTER TWO

that objects occurring in different applications (potential models) yield
the same function value (have the same property expressed by this
function) in these applications.
   Of course, not all empirical properties of systems will satisfy this
requirement: as an obvious counterexample think of the taste of one
and the same economic agent (his utility) - a property that may vary as
the agent changes the country, that is, as he changes from one deci-
sional context (a potential model of DEC) to another one.

11.2.3 The General Notion of a Constraint

Some general features can be extracted from the above examples. We
said that constraints single out certain admissible combinations of
potential models. The requirements discussed in the examples «Ax)
and (Bx) above) are properties of sets of potential models and usually
there are many sets of potential models possessing these properties. So
the constraint C will consist of all these sets, i.e. C ~ Po(M p). We may
assume C to be not empty. C being empty would mean that there is no
combination of potential models that is allowed by the theory. In view
of the fact that singletons are limit cases of combinations this would
mean that even single potential models are not allowed by the theory.
Such a theory would be useless. Third, the empty set is not contained in
C. This is just because it would not make sense to allow for a "com-
bination of zero potential models".
   Two further properties of constraints cannot be directly read off
from the examples. They will become plausible only if we look at how
constraints function in the formal core of a theory, and how they "work
together" with the other components of a core. Therefore, at the
moment we simply state these properties and leave their justification for
a later stage. The first property is that for each potential model x of the
theory the singleton {x}, i.e. the admissible combination consisting of
x only, is an element of the constraint C. That is, every singleton
constitutes an admissible combination. The second property we call
transitivity: if an admissible combination X is in C, and if Y is any
subset ("sub-combination") of X then Y is admissible, too. That is, the
process of narrowing down a given combination is transitive.
   Although transitivity will hold in most examples, there are 'cases of
constraints not being transitive. Intuitively, these constraints require a
certain number of potential models (e.g. three) to exist (see for example
                            THEOR Y - ELEMENTS                          47

C4(SETH) in Chapter III). We shall therefore introduce two kinds of
constraints: "simple" constraints which need not be transitive and
"transitive constraints". It has to be stressed that most constraints are
transitive.
   By summarizing all requirements just discussed we obtain a general
characterization of constraints.

DII-2:       If Mp is a class of potential models, then
         (a) C is a constraint for Mp iff
                (1) C ~ Po(Mp)
                (2) C ~ 0 and 0 ~ C
                (3) for all x E Mp: \ x} E C
         (b) C is a transitive constraint iff
                (1) C is a constraint for Mp
                (2) for all X, Y: if X E C and Y ~ X then Y E C


11.3 THEORETICITY, PARTIAL POTENTIAL MODELS, AND LINKS

11.3.1 An Intuitive Idea of Theoretical Concepts

The question of theoreticity is a semantical issue, it is a question
connected with the determination of the meaning of scientific terms.
Basically, the question is how to determine a given concept. In order to
determine some concept we have to tell where, to what, and under
which conditions, it applies. We have to say which kinds of things or
entities can be subsumed under it (are instances of it). We have to
determine the class of those instances. In order to determine, for
instance; the concept "hermaphrodite" a general method has to be
specified according to which one can decide whether a given object is
an hermaphrodite or not.
    If the concept is definable in a scientific context then the problem of
its determination is transferred to those further concepts in terms of
which the first one is defined. "Hermaphrodite", for instance, is defined
as "living being which is male and female simultaneously". According to
this definition in order to determine whether some given object is a
hermaphrodite we have to know under what conditions an object is a
living being, and when it is male or female. But it is clear that nominal
definitions, even if iterated, at some point will not lead any further. We
48                           CHAPTER TWO

then have to stop with definitions and to use specific empirical methods
which eventually could settle the issue of conceptual determination.
    The question of how metrical concepts are determined is of special
interest to us because metrical concepts are of major importance in
science. A metrical concept in some concrete situation is represented
by a numerical function, that is, a function taking real numbers as
values (like the mass function in CPM). To determine such a function
amounts to giving general criteria according to which we can find out
the real number, the function-value, which by the function is ascribed to
a given object (argument). In the case of mass we have to specify how
to find out for a given p, the number m(p), representing particle p's
mass. In general, for concepts which are not explicitly defined such
determinations are performed by means of methods of measurement,
whether direct experimental or indirect methods involving calculations.
   This has to be kept in mind when the problems of theoreticity are
discussed. The distinction between concepts specific for a given theory
T, and concepts not specific for T has played an important role in the
development of philosophy of science in the last forty years. The
distinction is closely connected with the question of how we can
provide an "empirical basis" for a theory, i.e. a frame of concepts by
means of which the theory can be controlled, or by means of which we
can find out when the theory functions correctly, and when not. The
"empirical basis" of a given theory T should include those concepts
which, in a sense still to be made precise, are not specific for T. T's
other concepts will belong to T's theoretical "superstructure".
   Traditional philosophy of science attempted to draw a universal
distinction between "theoretical" and "observational" terms in a way
relative to our total system of knowledge. There were attempts to
establish this dichotomy by means of general semantical criteria (with
special weight put on the theory of perception) which are independent
of the existence of concrete scientific theories.
   According to our view such a universal account is inadequate for the
task of reconstructing single theories and their empirical bases. First, all
criteria of observability proposed up to now are vulnerable to serious
objections. Second, these criteria would not contribute to our task
because in all advanced theories there will be no observational con-
cepts at all - at least if we take "observational" in the more philo-
sophical sense of not involving any theory. Third, it can be shown that
none of the concepts of an advanced theory can be defined in terms of
observational concepts.
                          THEORY-ELEMENTS                                 49

    The really fruitful task is to distinguish between concepts which can
be determined and therefore controlled independently of a given theory
 and those for which this is not so. A bit more precisely, given a theory
T we want to distinguish between those of T's concepts the determina-
 tion of which in principle does not presuppose the laws of T (i.e. T's
 actual models) and those for which the application always will depend
on the existence of some actual model. Concepts of the first kind we
 call T-non-theoretical, and those of the second kind T-theoretical. Note
that the distinction therefore is always relativized to T.
    In order to grasp the relevance of this distinction for our programme
of reconstruction let us consider the example of CPM. The basic
concepts are P, T, S, c j , c z, s, m, f and the question is: for which of
these concepts is CPM needed as far as meaning is concerned?
    Let us begin with P. One could start by advancing a general a priori
argument purporting to show that the concept of a particle is not
theoretical in mechanics: P is the common ontological basis for all of
CPM's concepts - i.e. in our language: P is a base set of the theory.
The meaning of the ontological base of the theory should be - so one
could argue - semantically independent from the theory itself for
otherwise we would not know from the beginning what the theory
speaks about, we would not know whether the theory makes sense at
all. This argument in principle can be applied to all empirical theories:
it would be a characteristic of all empirical theories (in contrast, e.g., to
mathematical or metaphysical theories) that their base sets can be
semantically determined independently of the theory in question. This
is the only guarantee for the theory having empirically testable content.
There must be at least several applications of the theory in which the
base sets are determined either pre-theoretically in ordinary language
or by means of underlying theories. Only under this assumption the
theory's empirical application seems to be possible.
    This argument is certainly plausible and, we think, it leads to con-
sequences which in principle are correct. But our strategy is to be very
careful with general a priori arguments in the philosophy of science.
Therefore we want to examine the argument and its consequences
thoroughly for the example of P as a base set of CPM.
    An opponent could object that the concept of a particle is not
independent of CPM; after all "CPM" means classical particle mechanics.
which indicates that the concept is specific of CPM. This sounds rather
dogmatic or like playing with the word "particle". But our opponent
could try to further back his claim: "You cannot determine whether
50                          CHAPTER TWO

something is a particle system unless you apply CPM to it." This
statement is ambiguous. If it means that the concept of a particle can
only be used in a physically meaningful way in the conceptual frame of
CPM or of some theory presupposing CPM, then we agree. But this
does not mean to presuppose the validity of the laws of CPM, i.e. the
existence of actual models. Just this was one of our reasons to draw a
distinction between the conceptual frame and proper laws (i.e. between
Mp and M). The question is whether any application of the concept of a
particle to an arbitrary object is dependent in principle on the fact that
Newton's laws hold in the domain considered. This certainly is not the
case. It might well happen that we arrive at a good determination of the
concept in the frame of Mp even though not a single proper law is valid
in the domain considered. We therefore assume that the base set Pis
not theoretical with respect to CPM, i.e. it is CPM-non-theoretical.
   In order to discuss the question of theoreticity for the rest of CPM's
basic concepts, it is convenient first to pinpoint the criterion of the-
oreticity in a way usable for the case where measurement is involved,
since the determination and, therefore, the understanding of the mean-
ing of the rest of CPM's concepts is intimately connected to the
problem of how real numbers are assigned in a non-arbitrary way to
physical entities. (This is what "measurement" amounts to.) When the
determination of a concept involves some kind of measurement (as is
the case for T, S, c1, c2 , s, m, and f), we shall assume that the question
of its theoreticity can be reduced to the question of whether all
methods of measurement being available for that concept presuppose
the laws of the theory under consideration or not. This idea is ex-
pressed in the following informal criterion of theoreticity, which is just
a specification of the general semantical criterion introduced at the
beginning:
  A concept whose determination involves some kind of measurement
  will be called theoretical with respect to theory T if all methods of
  measurement involved in its determination have to be conceived as
  models of T or as presupposing some models of T.
We do not wish at this point to advance some general arguments
purporting to show that this way of understanding the question of
theoreticity for the metrical case is intuitively adequate. We hope that
this will be seen, first, by comparing the criterion just stated with the
general intuitive idea expressed at the beginning of this section and,
                          THEORY-ELEMENTS                                51

secondly, by looking at the way this criterion functions when con-
fronted with concrete examples. Let us only add a general remark
which may give this criterion at least some prima facie plausibility. In
accordance with current philosophical semantics we may assume that
the meaning of a concept is highly dependent on (though not neces-
sarily identical with) its concrete use; in the case of a metrical concept,
it is clear that its use may be described correctly only if one knows how
to measure it. Methods of measurement therefore constitute at least an
essential component of the meaning of metrical concepts. Let us now
come back to the basic concepts of CPM.
    What about T? As before the decision would be easy if we just say:
all base sets are non-theoretical. But in spite of the a priori plausibility
of such a statement we do not want to accept it without examination. T
is not an arbitrary set but has to be chosen such that it represents a
specific period of time. In order to understand T we therefore must
understand what a period of time is. And the question is whether we
need CPM for that. Now, a period of time in the sense we need this
notion for CPM may be explicated as a sequence of events showing
some kind of qualitatively apprehensible repetition, the whole sequence
being mapped into a sequence of real numbers. The time we need for
CPM is a metrical time. This means that the question of determination
of time in CPM goes hand in hand with the question of determining the
coordinatization C j • Actually, for the present purposes both concepts
are inseparable. Our question is, then, whether we may determine the
pair <T, c j > without presupposing CPM. Now, the determination of
<T, c j > is the business of chronometry, i.e. the theory of some stan-
dardized procedures to fix T and c j known as "clocks". The question
of the CPM-theoreticity of T and its accompanying c j , then, comes
down as the question whether we need CPM in order to determine
what a clock is. The answer is that in some cases in fact we need CPM,
namely in those cases in which <T, c j > is determined by means of
mechanical clocks. But this is not so in all cases. Chronometry is more
than the theory of mechanical clocks; some of its applications are
non-mechanical clocks - as is easily seen from the history of time
measurement. Astronomical, hydrological, physiological, biological, and
other kinds of "clocks" have been either found or devised since antiq-
uity which do not presuppose the laws of mechanics. We conclude that
T and its companion C j are CPM-non-theoretical.
   The case of S and its coordinatization c2 is somewhat more involved.
52                           CHAPTER TWO

 The reason is that their determination, at least in part, involves the
 position function s (which we shall discuss immediately) and, through
 it, indirectly T and C 1 . However, essentially the same kind of argument
 as for T and c 1 may be applied to the "complex" (S, cz, s) and we shall
 reach the same conclusion. To see this, notice first that the space we
 need for CPM is a structure of point-like "places" to which we may
 assign real vectors in a conventional though not arbitrary way. We need
 to fix one privileged place as the "origin" (to which Cz assigns (0, 0, 0»)
 and at least a few other places that are in some definite spatial relation-
 ships to the origin. (Usually, Cz is taken to assign to these other places
 the values (1, 0, 0), (0, 1,0), and (0,0, 1).) Clearly, this determination
 of places and their accompanying cz-values may proceed in a way that
has nothing to do with the laws of mechanics. Only rather elementary
 optico-physiological procedures are necessarily involved. Also, at this
stage s is not involved either. It is for determining the rest of S and Cz
that we usually need the interplay with the methods of measuring
position in general. Thus, at least for a part of Sand cz, it is clear that
they may be determined without assuming CPM. Strictly speaking, this
should suffice to make S and Cz CPM-non-theoretical. On the other
hand, adding s into the picture (which we need for the major portion of
S and cz) only reinforces this conclusion.
     Indeed, if we ask for the status of s in CPM with respect to
theoreticity then according to our criterion the answer is rather clear:
we can measure (i.e. determine) position or distance without somehow
presupposing the laws of CPM. The use of position, distance; and the
concepts of velocity and acceleration derived from the former plus time
is not specific of mechanics. All these concepts can be determined
in preceding theories, e.g. in physical geometry, in optics and in
kinematics. In these theories, corresponding methods of measurement
can be described which do not presuppose any models of CPM. There-
fore, also s is CPM-non-theoretical and with it, to the extent that the
determination of S and Cz depends on s, it is also made sure that all
spatial (and kinematic) notions of CPM are CPM-non-theoretical.
     As far as the concept of force is concerned, considerations of
methods of determination lead also to a clear-cut result - although in
the opposite direction. Generally speaking, the specific meaning of the
physical (non-anthropomorphic) concept of force is determined by
Newtonian mechanics. If there is at all a concept specific for CPM then
it is force. More concretely, this is implied by the fact that without
                          THEORY-ELEMENTS                                53

 admitting some mechanical laws, no forces at all can be determined
 (measured or calculated). Every experimental device to measure force
 presupposes, by its very construction, the validity not only of Newton's
 fundamental law but also of some more special mechanical law as well
 (e.g. the law of gravitation or some law of elasticity). More about the
 measurement of force will be said in a later section of this chapter on
 methods of determination.
    The concept of mass is a bit more problematic. On the one hand it
 is an historical fact that the unique determination of the concept of
 inertial mass and its clear distinction from the concept of weight was
 made possible only by Newtonian mechanics. Before that theory, mass
 and weight were always confused. On the other hand, in spite of this
 historical fact, one can object that a concept of mass can be introduced
 by certain conventions without presupposing CPM. Usually one thinks
 of an independent theory about the structure of matter, for instance an
 atomistic theory. The mass of a body would be given just by the
number of its atoms. Newton himself already tried to use such a theory
when he characterized mass as "quantitas materiae". There are no
formal objections against this procedure, but it is difficult to see how
 such a convention could be applied empirically. We cannot count the
atoms of a macroscopic body. A further difficulty is that, according
to Daltonian chemistry, atoms of different substances have different
masses. One certainly can imagine that other, more refined conventions
of the kind of "quantitas materiae" finally would lead to a correct
definition of mass which also would be practically applicable. But up to
now we do not know of such proposals. Of course, there also are
kinematical definitions of mass (e.g. by Mach) according to which mass
simply is a factor of proportionality for the acceleration or velocity of
interacting bodies. Or there are dynamical definitions which define
mass as the quotient of total force by acceleration. But such "defini-
tions" presuppose CPM in principle. The kinematical definition uses
the principle of actio-reactio, the dynamical definition uses the concept
of force itself and the basic law of CPM.
    To decide the issue let us try a more pragmatic analysis of methods
of measurement for mass. There are many such methods. The case in
which knowledge of force and applicability of Newton's laws is presup-
posed and mass is calculated by the quotient of force by acceleration
can be neglected. For it is clear that in these cases it is presupposed that
the system under consideration is a model of CPM. All kinematical
54                          CHAPTER TWO

 determinations of mass by means of the interactions of two particles in
 which mass is determined as a factor of proportionality either of the
 respective accelerations or the velocities of the colliding particles
 presuppose the actio-reactio principle (and moreover, implicitly, the
 basic law of CPM). Often masses are measured by means of coil
 springs where a change of position is "observed". But in this proce-
 dure, among others, Hooke's law (or some similar law of elasticity)
 which is a special law of CPM is used. Therefore it is presupposed that
 the system is a special model of CPM. Finally we have the classical
method to measure mass by means of an equal arms balance. One
 could say that equal arms balances are not systems of CPM and that
 therefore we have found a CPM-independent method for determina-
tion of mass. But here we have to examine the conceptual connections
very carefully. It is true that an equal arms balance is not a model of
 CPM in a straightforward sense. For a formal description of an equal
arms balance would make explicit that we use the concepts of a rigid
body and of angular momentum which do not occur in CPM. An equal
arms balance is a model of rigid body mechanics. On the other hand we
can show (in Ch. VI) that rigid body mechanics can be reduced to
CPM in a strict and precise sense. But if one theory T can be reduced
to another theory T' this means that T semantically presupposes T'
- even though the relation of presupposition may not be seen im-
mediately. If this semantical interpretation of reduction is accepted and
if we assume that the presupposition relation is transitive then we can
conclude in the present case that the use of an equal arms balance
for the determination of mass presupposes CPM - via rigid body
mechanics and reduction.
    If we assume that the set of methods of measurement for mass
discussed up to now is representative of all possibilities of determining
mass, then we have shown that all these methods presuppose the
applicability of CPM to the system under consideration - and there-
fore that mass is CPM-theoretical. It is certainly no a priori truth that
all methods of measurement for mass which occur in the literature in
principle can be reduced to the cases just discussed. Rather this is a
hypothesis in the philosophy of science which seems to be well
grounded' for the time being.
   Therefore with respect to the basic concepts of CPM we come to
the following result: there is a semantical and pragmatical distinction
between two groups of concepts of CPM. On the one hand there are
                         THEORY - ELEMENTS                              55

 P, T, S and s. On the other hand there are m and f. The distinction,
 expressed comprehensively, is that the first concepts are not specific for
 CPM, viz. they can be determined or measured in at least some cases
 of application without presupposing that we have models of CPM.
 Concepts of the second group are specific for CPM: the use of these
concepts always presupposes CPM. Concepts of the first kind we call
 CPM-non-theoretical, those of the second CPM-theoretical.
   The discussion of this example has shown that the theoreticallnon-
theoretical distinction makes sense for developed theories and that we
come to rather plausible results in a specific example. At least this
occurs if we concentrate on theories which can be identified rather
precisely and if we pose the question of theoreticity relative to such a
given theory.
   From the fact that theoreticity of a concept can be meaningfully
decided on only relatively to a given theory we see that the property of
being theoretical or non-theoretical is not an "intrinsic" property of a
concept but can change from one theory to the next. A concept which
is non-theoretical with respect to one theory can be theoretical with
respect to a preceding theory. We have already mentioned the fact that
the position function occurs as a basic concept in kinematics which
precedes mechanics, and it is very likely that there it is theoretical. On
the other hand the CPM-theoretical concepts can occur, of course, as
non-theoretical in other theories. Mass and force are non-theoretical in
thermodynamics and stoichiometry.
   From this discussion we can distil a general conjecture and a semi-
formal criterion concerning the question of theoreticity.
   Criterion of theoreticity:
  A concept t is called theoretical relative to theory T (or just T-
  theoretic'al) iff every determination of (a relation belonging to) t in
  any application of T presupposes the existence of at least one actual
  model ofT.
Conjecture:
  In every mature empirical theory T a meaningful distinction can be
  drawn between concepts which, according to the above criterion, are
  T -theoretical, and concepts which are not (i.e. which are T -non-
  theoretical).
It may be remarked that we speak about "determination" of a concept
56                           CHAPTER TWO

 and not only about its "measurement". "Measurement" would apply
only to metrical functions but not to qualitative concepts. And even in
the case of metrical functions we cannot always say that the determina-
 tion of their values is a measurement in the strict sense (i.e. that it
implies use of devices, experimental observations and empirical control
of other parameters). In many cases determination amounts to calcula-
tion only. Determination includes measurement but not vice versa.
    We also have to note that we have left unexplicated the term "to
presuppose" which occurs in our formulation of the criterion and which
is frequently used in our discussion. We could make it more precise
(and we shall do it below) within our set-theoretical apparatus and so
arrive at more precision. But for the moment we do not want to do so.
We want to give a formulation which also applies to theories which
resist to a formal reconstruction in set-theoretical terms. We just appeal
to the intuition of the presupposition relation and we only want to
remark that the kernel of this intuition coincides with the concept of
semantic consequence.
    Before we turn to more precise treatments of theoreticity we have to
introduce some more conceptual apparatus in order to express the
distinction between theoretical and non-theoretical terms. That is, we
have to add another component to those making up a theory-element.
    The distinction between theoretical and non-theoretical terms can be
drawn at the "purely conceptual" level of potential models. We have to
split up each potential model in such a way that we can find out which
part of it corresponds to its theoretical part and which one corresponds
to its non-theoretical part. It is most convenient to draw a distinction
between structures consisting of (all and only) the non-theoretical
concepts on the one hand and structures consisting of all of the theory's
concepts on the other hand, i.e. its non-theoretical and its theoretical
ones. The latter structures are of course just the potential models
themselves, the former are of a new kind, and we call them partial
potential models. They are so to speak truncated potential models
(whence the label "partial") - truncated in so far as the theoretical
functions and relations are cut off. (According to the above hypothesis
that the base sets will never be theoretical the truncation will affect only
the functions and relations.)
    We shall consequently denote the potential models of a theory in the
following way:

relations t l , ••• , tq • Note that this ordering in which all non-theoretical
relations precede the theoretical ones presupposes that we know which
terms are theoretical even when we start introducing the potential
models. However, it is clear that this ordering is completely arbitrary
and has been chosen merely for matters of convenience. With some
further notational conventions we could easily free ourselves from a
particular order of the terms' occurrences in the potential models. The
class of all partial potential models then can be defined relatively to
given classes Mp(T) and M(T) as follows.

necessary.
    It is clear that to each potential model (D I , ••• , tq ) there corre-

many "extensions" obtained by adding suitable relations t l , ... , tq.

11.3.2 Intertheoretical Links Determining Non- Theoretical Terms

In the above considerations of theoreticity we came to characterize
T-non-theoretical terms as those which can be determined by means of
other theories which do not presuppose T. This characterization is
58                          CHAPTER TWO

rather weak. Often it will be the case that a much stronger condition is
satisfied, namely that T -non-theoretical terms can only be determined
by means of other theories which do not presuppose T. The bearing of
this on the interpretation of a theory is straightforward. If the stronger
version of non-theoreticity is satisfied then T's partial potential models
can get their interpretation and their meaning only through other
theories "preceding" T. Even if non-theoretical terms can be deter-
mined by means of T in some cases' (i.e. even if the weaker version
of non-theoreticity is satisfied) there will be other cases of determina-
tions for these terms in which theories different fro)1l T are used and
presupposed.
   This necessitates some transfer of information from theories dif-
ferent from T to theory T. The information consists of data which
are obtained in the course of some determination of a term which is
non-theoretical in T. Clearly such transfer contributes to the interpreta-
tion of Mpp(T). It is part of the determination of the meaning of the
terms occurring in T's partial potential models, and therefore it is an
essential component of T itself.
   We will take this into account and introduce what we call inter-
theoretical links which represent the transfer of data from theories T' to
theory T. Later on we shall see that the representation of this connec-
tion is only one of the aspects which intertheoretical links allow us to
capture. But for the moment let us concentrate on this connection.
   A typical example of intertheoretical links of the kind under discus-
sion is given by theories containing "purely non-theoretical" axioms, i.e.
axioms containing no T-theoretical terms at all. Such axioms actually
belong to or are derivable from theories T' preceding T and need not
appear expressly in the reconstruction of T. They are presupposed in T,
and for this reason they are used implicitly in the application of T.
   For example, in the case of CPM we do not explicitly state the
kinematical axioms which determine position and .the chronological
conditions for the measurement of time. But since the partial potential
models of CPM are constituted by time and position, we can say that
such kinematical and chronological conditions, though (apparently)
alien to CPM, also constitute this theory by determining its "external"
boundaries of applicability. The only reason for not stating them
explicitly when reconstructing CPM is because we assume that' they are
already stated in some other, presupposed theories.
   However, in a completely adequate formulation of the theory in
                         THEORY-ELEMENTS                               59

question they should appear as a sort of "hybrid" conditions belonging
to two (or more) theories simultaneously. Later on, we shall encounter
cases of links that are still more conspicuous in determining the theory's
identity and therefore may not be disregarded at all, not even in
simplified formulations. That is, we shall find cases of links of a theory
T to other "surrounding" theories whose role consists not only in
determining T's non-theoretical structures but also in narrowing down
the choice of admissible theoretical terms of T by tying them somehow
to the theoretical terms of other theories. These further kind of "the-
oretical" links are, in a sense, even more specific of a given theory than
the ones we have just dealt with and therefore also belong to a com-
plete reconstruction of a theory. However, it is not convenient to deal
with them in detail at this point, so we just note their existence and ask
the reader for patience.
    Intertheoreticallinks have so far been neglected in the logical recon-
structions of theories because, in most cases, they do not explicitly
appear in the standard axiomatizations of those 'theories. Because of
their intertheoretical character it is difficult to identify them when
reconstructing a single theory. But once the existence and importance
of intertheoretical links is admitted, the question necessarily arises:
What kind of general framework should we use in order to reconstruct
them? Or, to put it in slightly different terms: At what point in our
reconstruction of scientific theories should they appear?
    A first possible answer to this question is this. We could add the
conditions expressing the links to the axioms determining the actual
models of the theory, since their role in restricting the range of poten-
tial models actually used is similar to that of "normal" fundamental
laws. Formally, there would be nothing wrong in doing this. However,
this way of understanding the links would obscure their intertheoretical
character. Also, there would be some redundancy, for they would
appear in the actual models of both linked theories T and T'. There-
fore, it seems more adequate to separate clearly the axioms determining
the actual models of T from those intertheoretical restrictions linking
some functions of T with some functions of T'.
   Another possible way of dealing with links would be to separate
them completely from the concept of a (single) theory and to consider
them as purely external to the theories they link. That is, links would
not be essential to the identity of a theory, but rather a sort of
accidental feature of the way theories relate to each other. Since a
60                          CHAPTER TWO

 substantial portion of this book will be devoted to intertheoretical
relations like reduction, equivalence, and approximation, taken as
 relations external to theories, the natural move would seem to be to
 deal with links in that context. Nevertheless, though this treatment of
links is plausible for some very elementary theories like EXT, which we
 can clearly identify without taking into consideration its links to other
theories, it does not seem plausible in other cases. A close analysis of
 existing expositions of most theories makes us aware of the "symbiotic"
mode of existence of these theories with respect to others. Furthermore,
 as later examples will show, there are theories that cannot be clearly
identified, and therefore applied to, without some knowledge of the
form of their intertheoretical links. Even their historical origin shows
their dependence upon other theories. Thus, in such cases, interthe-
oretical links appear to belong to the "essence" or identity of the
theories in question. Again, there would be nothing formally wrong in
reconstructing links in all cases as purely external relations among
theories. And, in some cases, this might be the most appropriate thing
to do. But we claim that this is not always going to be the most natural
way of reconstructing specific examples of theories. Therefore, we pro-
pose to introduce a general notion into the whole structure of each
single theory which allows to deal with "essential" intertheoretical links
whenever they are required - in quite the same way as we introduced
the general notion of a constraint for expressing relations among
models. Admittedly, this new notion gives rise to the introduction of
further complexity in the explicit structure of any given theory, but we
think that this complexity mirrors the actual complexity of science: For
one thing, scientific theories cannot be fully reconstructed as isolated
units, they have to be reconstructed as linked elements of "global
science".
    In order to formalize the general notion of an intertheoretic link we
have to take into account the fact that intertheoretical links restrict the
potential models of two theories T, T' simultaneously. Therefore they
could simply be defined as relations on Mp(T) X Mp(T'). This is the
concept of an abstract link we shall introduce below (DII-4a), which is
useful for general considerations: When it is not necessary to know
precisely which terms are really involved in a particular link, we may
regard the link just as linking full potential models. On the other hand,
in other contexts (especially when reconstructing specific examples of
linked theories) it is more convenient to refer to the corresponding
                           THEORY-ELEMENTS                                   61

functions or relations in the two theories that are so linked. For this
purpose, we introduce the notion of a (concrete) link. To take into
account the functions linked with each other we shall not denote these
functions directly but rather the places they occupy in the tuples
constituting the potential models. It is expedient to introduce the
following notation.
   For any given natural numbers iI, ... , in let .1f(T, iI, ... , in)
   denote the class of all tuples (R;,1 ... , R;)   n

II.3.3 An Informal Criterion of Theoreticity
Our account of theoreticity can be made more precise if we try to
analyze measurement or methods of determination in terms of the
structures already introduced. We shall describe here only one of
several possibilities, and we shall restrict ourselves to rather simple
situations which nevertheless will be realized in nearly all examples of
this book. Up to the end of this section we shall consider a class Mp
of potential models and a class of models M ~ Mp subject to the
following assumptions:
     (1)   Any x E Mp has exactly m + 1 basic relations, denoted by
           rl,···,rm,t
   (2)     all the r l , . . • , r m , t occurring in potential models are
           functions taking real numbers as function values.
Assumption (1) means that we restrict ourselves to the investigation of
exactly one theoretical term t. The general case of several theoretical
terms can be treated similarly, we only would need a more complicated
notation. Since in this context the auxiliary bases AI' ... , Al will play
no explicit role we shall omit them in the notation, thus writing


for the potential models of Mp. Moreover, we use (as before) the
phrase "f is T-theoretical". Since we do not yet know how a theory
T precisely looks like, this phrase is not yet very clear. In fact, the
following considerations are relativized to given classes Mp and M,
rather than to a given theory T. The phrase "t is T-theoretical" should
be regarded as an elliptical version of "t is theoretical with respect to
Mp and M, and T has Mp and M as sets of potential models and
models respectively".
   The first intuition we have of a T-theoretical function t is that all
determinations of t "essentially depend" on the use of T. The main step
in order to make this precise is to explicate the notion of a "method of
determination" .
   Paradigm cases of methods of determination are methods of mea-
                            THEORY-ELEMENTS                                   63

surement used in the laboratory. Three features seem to be common to
every experimental set-up which is claimed to yield measurements.
There are certain functions r l , . . . , rm which can be forced to take
given numbers as their values. There is another function t whose values
are read off (i.e. measured) from the experiment. Third, the values to
be read off must be uniquely and systematically determined in terms of
the chosen values of r l , . . . , rm. The crucial observation is that, usually,
the functions r l , . . . , r m , t involved in an experiment together with
suitable domains D I , ... , Dk will form a potential model (Dj, ... , D k ,
r l , . . . , r m , t) of some theory. The concrete situation in which values of
t are determined (or measured) - i.e. in most cases the situation of a
concrete experiment - can be thought of as a potential model of some
corresponding theory. We therefore can identify concrete situations of
measurement (of determination) with certain potential models. These
potential models must satisfy two conditions.
   (1)      In these potential models the values of t must depend on
            r l , . . . , rm in a systematic way;
   (2)      the values of t must be uniquely determined.
Condition (1) means that the determination of some value of t (the
measurement) does not work for just one set of chosen values r l (a l ),
... , rm(am). It means that the determination works for many different
sets of values rl(a{), ... , rm(a~), j = 1, 2, .... Moreover, the deter-
mination must work not only if in one experimental set-up the values of
r l , . . . , rm are varied but also if other instruments of measurement of
the same type are used, i.e. it must work also in a different but similar
experimental set-up. One should speak of a "method" of determination
only if thi~ method works in a whole class of situations. All the
situations (or potential models) are similar in that they allow for the
determination of t through r l , . . . , rm by the same method.
      So we have a class Mm of potential models. All members of Mm have
in common the property of representing the performance of some
measurement according to a certain method of determination. This
property may be expressed by a sentence A which applies to potential
models of T (in the technical sense introduced in Ch. I). We shall
write A(x) and A(DI' ... , D k, r l , . . . , rm , t) where x = (DI' ... , Db
r l , . . . , r m , t) is a potential model. Sentence A expresses that there is a
systematic connection between (the values of) t and (the values of)
r l , . . . , rm which intuitively can be stated as follows. Whenever D I, ... ,
D k , r l , . . . , rm , t satisfy A then t can be determined by r l , . . . , rm
64                              CHAPTER TWO

 according to a specific method of determination. In many cases A will
be a "real law". But in other cases the label "law" would be too much
for such a sentence; it might have a rather modest scope. We shall use
the term theoretical systematization to cover "real laws" as well as
equations of systematic import.
   Condition (2) above is necessary, for if in an experiment represented
by (D I , ••• , Db rI , ••• , rm, t) for given values of rI , ••• , rm we would
obtain quite different values for t in repeated performances, we would
not say that we have measured or determined t. By using a theoretical
systematization A (representing a method of determination) uniqueness
of t can be expressed easily. t is uniquely determined by rI , ••• , rm and
A if for given Db ... , Db rI , ••• , rm: A(DI , ••• , rm, t) holds at most
for one t, i.e. for all t, t': if A(DI , .•• , rm, t) and A(D I , ••• , rm, t') then
t = t'. By combining these two aspects of theoretical systematization
and of uniqueness we obtain formal definitions of "method of deter-
mination" and of" t-determining model".
DII-5:       Let Mp be a class of potential models.
         (a) Mm is a method of determination for t in Mp iff there exists a
             sentence A such that
                (1) A applies to elements of Mp
                (2) Mm={(D(, ... ,t) E M/A(D(, ... ,t)}
                (3) for all D(, ... , Db r(, .. , , rm and all t, t': if
                    A(D(, ... , rm , t) and A(D(, ... , rm , t') then t = t'
         (b) x is a t-determining model iff there exists a method of
             determination Mm for t in Mp such that x E Mm
Often, methods of determination will not determine t uniquely but only
up to certain given transformations of scale. For instance, the method
of determining the mass of some particle p by letting it collide along
a straight line with some other particle p' and by calculating their
mass-ratio by means of their velocities before and after the collision
does not uniquely determine the mass function involved. By means of
this method only mass-ratios are determined. It is then said that mass is
determined up to a positive factor or up to the transformation of scale
consisting in a multiplication with a positive factor. For by choosing one
particle and by letting its mass-value be a E ~, a > 0, all of the mass
function is uniquely determined. Other kinds of measurement yield
different versions of uniqueness. In measuring temperature by means of
a thermometer the temperature is determined only up to two real
                           THEORY-ELEMENTS                                 65

 numbers (representing the "zero-point" and the ''unit''). It is not difficult
 to modify DI/-5 such that these indeterminacies "up to transformations
 of scale" are taken into account. The only thing we have to do is to
 replace the equality ( = (' in DI/-5-a3 by some weaker expression of
 equivalence: ( - t'. The precise definition of the equivalence relation -
will vary from case to case according to the type of invariance
prevailing, but in all cases we have a proper equivalence relation. If
 DII-5-a is relativized to such a given equivalence relation we arrive at a
criterion which also can be applied to more realistic methods of
determination including invariances of scale.
    With these notions let us try to formulate our criterion of T-
theoreticity. The intuition we have of aT-theoretical term t is that
all the methods of determination of (relations belonging to) term t
"essentially depend" in some sense on the use of theory T. But what
does it mean to "depend essentially" on a theory? An obvious move is
to say that this just means "presupposes theory T". Term t then would
be T-theoretical if every determination for ( presupposes T. Now in
some philosophical contexts "to presuppose" means "logically implies".
So ( would be T -theoretical if every determination for ( would logically
imply T. If we switch from "determination" to a corresponding (-
determining model this means: any (-determining model implies T.
Here "implies T" can only mean "satisfies the axioms of T". Since a
t-determining model satisfying the axioms of T is just a model of T, we
arrive at the following formulation. Term ( is T-theoretical if every
t-determining model is a model of T. Or, in other words, if the set of all
t-determining models is included in M(T), or if any method of deter-
mination for t is contained in M(T).
    The intuitive idea of theoreticity thus is the following. Term t being
T -theoretical means that ( can be determined only if T's fundamental
laws are presupposed. In other words: The determination of ( only
works in situations in which T's fundamental laws are satisfied.
    If we take the criterion in this formulation we run into difficulties.
Intuitively, these difficulties arise from our having characterized methods
of determination in a purely formal way. Essentially, a method of deter-
mination involves only formal uniqueness. But it seems to be clear
that we always can produce sentences by which term t is uniquely
determined, even though such sentences may have nothing to do with
theory T - except using T's concepts. Formula A in DII-5 can be
chosen in a completely arbitrary way possibly "circumventing" the
66                          CHAPTER TWO

fundamental law. For interesting theories T the class of all possible t-
determining models will always contain artificially contrived structures.
These may appear for various reasons. T's mathematical apparatus may
be so strong that we can explicitly define "bizarre" but unique terms.
Fictitious T*'s may be invented to derive connections formulated in the
vocabulary of T. Even "reasonable" candidates for methods of deter-
mination may turn out to be unaccepted by practising scientists simply
because in T's history they have "not yet" been used.
   Consider, for example, the following sentence A:

           for all pEP, t E T and all i E N: (i = 1 and f(p, t, i) =
           9,81)or(i> 1andf(p,t,i)=O)

which is stated in the vocabulary of CPM. Sentence A uniquely deter-
mines the force function f in terms of CPM. Note that the determina-
tion of f is totally independent of the other relations of CPM (those
different from!). Clearly, A yields a method of determination.

           Mm = {y/A(y) 1
satisfying DII-5. But A does not imply Newton's second law. So
according to the above formulation of the criterion A would prove that
f is non-theoretical with respect to CPM, for there is a method of
determination (given by A) which is not a subset of M(CPM). Intui-
tively, A is contrived in that it makes no use of concepts different from
f f is "defined" by A in a purely mathematical way.
   There is a way out of this difficulty, a way, however, in which logical
rigour cannot be conserved and pragmatics is involved. This way con-
sists of referring to the existing expositions of theory T in the charac-
terization of methods of determination and t-determining models.
Roughly, we require the sentence A in a method of determination to
consist of (reformulations of) statements actually occurring in existing
expositions of the theory. By existing expositions here we mean books,
papers, articles, manuscripts or taped lectures.
   There are two reasons why this restriction of methods of determina-
tion to existing expositions should work. First, artificially constructed
examples of methods of determination which do not imply the theory
are ruled out. They just do not occur in existing expositions. ,Second,
and more importantly, our reference to existing expositions is in the
spirit of theoreticity. Only those methods of determination are relevant
for theoreticity that "come from" the theory.
                          THEORY-ELEMENTS                               67

   A problem still arises from the fact that we want to speak of existing
expositions of theory T while at the moment we are trying to explain
what a theory is, not yet having a clear picture of an empirical theory at
hand. But we have already described potential models and models for a
theory, and these two components usually are sufficient to distinguish a
"theory" as described in textbooks from other different theories. If we
know how the potential models and models look like we can speak of
the theory those potential models and models belong to. Thus by
starting with classes Mp and M of potential models and models we can
speak of the theory having M and Mp as components, and of existing
expositions of that theory. By restricting methods of determination or
t-determining models to those occurring in existing expositions of the
theory having M and Mp as components we obtain adequate methods
of determination and t-determining models (see DII-6a below).
   It may be mentioned that the term "existing exposition" is not as
vague as it seems to be at first glance. The existing expositions of a
theory at time to can be defined as all written or printed material to be
found on our planet at time to which uses the basic concepts of that
theory. Clearly, this "definition" does not exclude contrived counter-
examples. One might point to some crazy "private scientist" hiding in
his drawer an extraordinary world-formula written in terms of some
known theory. Or one might point out some futuristic novel in which
future physicists are described using formulas quite different from those
used by physicists today. Such examples, we think, can be excluded by
referring to real groups of scientists (where "real" indicates a group
containing more than one member). The only difficulty with existing
expositions then consists in surveying all of them. Such a survey cannot
be achieved in practice today. But it can be thought of in principle
without difficulties, and it should be possible in the near future with the
help of data banks.
   By referring to existing expositions we now can state our informal
criterion of theoreticity.

DII-6:       Let Mp be a class of potential models and M ~ Mp a set of
             models within Mp.
         (a) x is an adequate t-determining model in Mp iff x is a
             t-determining model in Mp and the sentence A of DII-5
             is a version of formulas or statements occurring in exist-
             ing expositions of the theory having M and Mp as com-
             ponents.
68                           CHAPTER TWO

       (b) (Criterion of Theoreticity)
           t is T-theoretical iff T is a theory with classes MP(T) and
           M(T) of potential models and models, respectively, and for
           all x: if x is an adequate t-determining model in Mp then
           x E M(T)
The criterion can be formulated still differently if we use the notion of a
potential model x being T -dependent. Let us say that potential model x
is T-dependent iff x is a model of T. Then the criterion reads as
follows: t is T -theoretical iff every adequate t-determining model is a
T -dependent model. This formulation brings out more clearly that T
plays an essential role in determining t.
   In order to better understand the concept of a method of deter-
mination and of at-determining model let us consider two examples.

11.3.3.1 Spring balance determination of weight in CPM. Our first

example fruitfully we have to reconstruct its conditions in more detail.

Condition (3) expresses that the two particles move on a straight line.
