below.

113.4 A Formal Criterion of Theoreticity
Let us now turn to the second criterion of theoreticity which can be
expressed in purely formal terms. The basic intuition here is about
non-theoreticity. A term t is non-theoretical in theory T if there is no
T -admissible method of determination for this term, that is, there is no
means of determining its extension by means of T or using T. In order
to fix the meaning of such a term it is therefore necessary to use other
theories different from T, and we already introduced the concept of
intertheoretical links by means of which such terms get their meaning.
Conversely, a term is T -theoretical if there is some T -admissible
method of determination for t. That is,in some cases, namely in those
corresponding to theoretical concepts, it will become possible to deter-
mine a term's extension by using the basic axioms of T and therefore by
presupposing T. The crucial point in the new definition is to explicat~
what we mean by saying that a method of determination is "T-
admissible". The first thing to note is that the notion of T -admissibility
74                          CHAPTER TWO

we have in mind here has to be distinguished from the concept of
T -dependence as introduced in the previous section. Roughly speaking,
T -admissibility presupposes T -d~pendence but not conversely; it is a
stronger notion. Our present explication of T -admissibility is based on
an idea of U. Gahde and makes essential use of a general notion of T's
invariances. The intuitive idea is that aT-dependent method of deter-
mination for term t will moreover be T -admissible if it has a general
kind of invariance wrt t; and then we shall say that t is T -theoretical if
there is at least one such method of determination for t which is
T -admissible in this sense.
   Up to the end of this section let again Mp and M be classes of
potential models and models respectively and such that the elements of
Mp have the form
             x = (D I , . .. , D k; AI,' .. , AI; rl , • .. , rm , t).
Now, let us denote by 'x[t']' the result of substituting t' for t in x
(where t' is always assumed to be of the same type as t). Consider a
method of determination Mm for t in the sense of DII-5a above. We
shall say that Mm is T -admissible if, in addition to being T -dependent
(Le. in addition to the condition Mm ~ M), it satisfies the condition that
it is invariant wrt any change of t when such a change still is compatible
with T's fundamental laws. That is, Mm has to be invariant under
transformations of the form x ..... x[!'] for which x[t'] still is a model.
More precisely, in order for Mm to be T-admissible, the following
condition must be satisfied:
  (3)      Mm ~ M and, if x E Mm and x[t'] E M, then x[!'] E Mm
Intuitively, such a general invariance implies that, if a given model x is
used to determine t uniquely, then the structure which comes out of x
by substituting !' for t can also be used to determine t' uniquely
without violating T's fundamental laws. We can now state our formal
criterion of theoreticity.
DII-9:     (Formal Criterion of Theoreticity)
           Term t is formally T-theoretical iff T is a theory with classes
           Mp(T) and M(T) of potential models and models respec-
           tively, and there is aT-admissible method of determination
           for t (i.e. there is aT-dependent method of determination
           Mm for t, such that: for all x and all t': if x E Mm and
           x[t'] EM then x[!'] E Mm).
                         THEORY-ELEMENTS                                75

Accordingly, t is formally T-non-theoretical if there is no method of
determination for t which is T-admissible in the sense of (3) above. In
other words: t is formally T -non-theoretical if, for all subclasses of M
satisfying the invariance condition (3) with respect to t, we find out that
none of them may be regarded as a method of determination of t; more
concretely, this means that, if t is a metrical term, none of them will
determine the values of t uniquely.
   Clearly, this formal criterion can be applied to all of T's terms,
including the non-functional ones. And if in DII-5a the equality t = t'
is replaced by some weaker "scale equivalence", we arrive at a more
general version of the formal criterion as introduced in DII-9, which
covers all cases of measurements in which invariances are involved.
   As brief examples for the application of this criterion consider CPM
and CCM. In CPM the formal criterion of theoreticity guarantees that s
is formally T-non-theoretical. For it can be proved that any subclass
M* ~ M satisfying the invariance condition (3) is invariant under
Galilei-transformations (see Balzer [2]), which means that no such M*
may determine the values of s uniquely; therefore, no such M* is a
method of determination for s; conversely, no method of determination
for s can be T-admissible, which is what the formal criterion for T-non-
theoreticity requires. On the other hand, m, for instance, is formally
CPM-theoretical because there is at least one method of determination
of masses which is both T -dependent and satisfies (3). This is Mach's
method for determining masses uniquely (up to a proportional scale
transformation) out of acceleration rates in systems of pairs of interact-
ing particles. It can easily be checked that this method satisfies the
conditions required: It is CPM-dependent (it implicitly presupposes the
validity of Newton's Second Law), it is invariant in the sense of (3), and
it determines masses uniquely up to a scale transformation. Consider
now the case of velocity v in CCM. This function is formally CCM-
non-theoretical: Take any model x E M(CCM), that is, any system of
collision satisfying momentum conservation. By keeping the same
masses (i.e. the same particles) colliding you can provide those particles
with different initial velocities and will therefore get different final
velocities without thereby violating the law of momentum conservation;
that is, out of a model x you may construct practically any model xlv']
with an arbitrarily chosen velocity function v'. Therefore, no such class
of models of CCM may be used as a method for determining velocities
uniquely. On the other hand, m is formally CCM-theoretical. The
76                          CHAPTER TWO

method of determining mass by collision (Hermes' method) given by
 DII-8 is easily seen to be CCM-admissible.
   This last example also illustrates a possible source of conflict if the
purport of our two criteria of theoreticity is not well understood. For,
the result obtained by the formal criterion of theoreticity, namely that
mass is T -theoretical both in CPM and in CCM, seems to run counter
the intuitive idea that a term can be theoretical in one theory only, viz.
in the theory which it belongs to as a specific term. In fact, according
to our previous (pragmatic) criterion of T-theoreticity, mass is only
 CPM-theoretical but not CCM-theoretical since there are methods of
mass measurement in CPM that are not equivalent to methods of mass
measurement provided by CCM. For example, measuring mass by first
measuring weight by means of a dynamometer (i.e. by presupposing
some Newtonian law of elasticity) and by dividing thereafter the result
obtained by the terrestrial acceleration constant (i.e. by presupposing
some special form of CPM's fundamental law) is a way to measure
mass that presupposes the laws of CPM but not those of CCM. There-
fore, the two proposed criteria of theoreticity seem to contradict each
other. However, the conflict is only apparent, since the two criteria are
not intended to be generally equivalent. The pragmatic criterion of
theoreticity looks at the question of a term's theoreticity from a global
point of view within the whole of science (or at least within a discipline)
and it settles the question by taking into account, among other things,
intertheoretical relations. On the other hand, the perspective from
which the formal criterion of theoreticity is applied is a local one within
science: it considers just one theory, disregarding any possible inter-
theoretical relations. Frequently, the global and the local point of view
for theoreticity will coincide, but this needs not always be the case, as
our example shows.
   Since the original intuitions behind both criteria and the conse-
quences drawn from them seem to be plausible enough, one may
wonder what the source of such a divergent result may be and whether
we should not abandon one criterion in favor of the other - or both
altogether. The answer is that both criteria play an important role in
detecting significant features of the semantic structure of a theory. The
division between T-theoretical and T-non-theoretical terms founded in
the formal criterion points to the internal structure of T when we make
abstraction of the rest of the scientific context, whereas this same
                          THEORY -ELEMENTS                               77

 context is what comes into play when we apply the pragmatic criterion.
 And the important thing to notice about this context is that it may
 be historically changing, thereby possibly modifying the property of'
 theoreticity. From the "local" point of view, theoreticity is an ahistorical
 property of the terms of a theory, which only depends on the way a
 theory appears to be constructed. On the other hand, from the "global"
point of view theoreticity is a property that may change as new theories
and new relations among them emerge. Again, the case of CCM may
illustrate this point. It is not too far-fetched to view our formulation
of CCM as a logical reconstruction of a theory that existed indepen-
dently for some time in the seventeenth century, before the advent of
Newtonian mechanics: CCM belonged to the core of what has been
called "Cartesian mechanics" (most explicitly developed by Huygens).
We can safely assume that, for the period of its independent existence,
CCM was a theory with one theoretical term, viz. mass. (Huygens had
already conceived mass in our modern sense.) The formal criterion
of theoreticity does justice to this historical fact by establishing the
theoreticity of mass in CCM when we disregard all other theories. That
is, the result obtained by the formal criterion is a trace of a historical
situation. As CPM appeared and became well-established the situation
changed in the global context: CCM became subsumed under CPM (as
we shall see later on) and CCM's mass became thereby non-theoretical
because CPM got the priority for methods of mass measurement: mass
measurements in CCM were only accepted in case they were reflected
in CPM. But CCM conserved its own structure, and this means that
mass appears as T-theoretical within that structure.
    These considerations also shed some light on the relation between
our different accounts of theoreticity. It has become clear now that the
informal account is more restrictive in admitting terms as T -theoretical.
For there, the concept of determination is used in a very informal
and pragmatic sense covering all kinds of methods of determination
including those available in other theories different from T. And the
more methods of determination are admitted, the smaller t's chance
of being T -theoretical. In the precise formulation of our criteria of
theoreticity we have restricted our considerations to methods of deter-
mination which can be represented in the conceptual frame of T. These
formulations are therefore more restricted in their application. Their
application will yield correct results only in cases where other methods
78                           CHAPTER TWO

of determination which cannot be expressed in T's vocabulary, can be
neglected. In the case of CCM, methods of measuring mass by using
force laws cannot be represented by potential models of CCM.
   Our precise criteria of theoreticity therefore both have to be re-
garded as "special cases" of the general picture expressed in the first,
intuitive account. They can be applied only to special examples in
which all relevant methods of determination can be represented in the
theory under consideration. Of course, the precise criteria can be
extended to cover those more complicated cases, too, but this can be
done only at a later stage by referring to whole arrays of theories
(introduced as 'theory-holons' in c;hapter VIII) rather than to single
theory-elements.


                  11.4 THEORY-CORES EXPANDED

Up to this point we have dealt with the general features of all the
components which make up what can be called the formal structure of
a theory. This formal structure we call "a theory-core". The notions
involved in the characterization of a given theory-core K(T) are: the
potential models, the actual models, the constraints, the partial potential
models, and the intertheoretic links. Since ill a given theory there
normally will not appear just one constraint or just one intertheoretical
link, but a few of them, it is convenient to have a "global" notation for
the totality of constraints as well as of links.
DII-IO:    If CI(T), ... , CiT) are all the constraints for Mp(T)
           relevant for T then GC(T):= n {C I(T), ... , Cn(T) }
GC(T), the global constraint belonging to Mp(T) is just the intersection
of all constraints for Mp(T). Each member of GC(T) is a set of potential
models satisfying all the constraints taken together. Note that we may
not introduce the set of all possible constraints in the sense of DII-2
because this totality is much too large in order to be useful.
   As for the definition of the global intertheoreticallink we can follow
a similar strategy.
DII-ll:   (a) If LI(T), ... , Ln(T) are all the intertheoretical links
              between MP(T) and other classes Mp(Tj), i = 1, ... , n,
              relevant for T then for i ~ n we define
              lj(T) = {x E Mp(T)/3a3x'3a'(x, a, x', a') E Lj)}
                        THEORY-ELEMENTS                               79



The members of GL(T) are potential models of T which satisfy all the
theory's links with other theories. We call GL(T) "the global link
belonging to Mp(T)".
   Now we are in a position to define a theory-core formally as an
entity constituted by five different components: a class Mp (the class of
potential models), a class M of (actual) models, a class Mpp of partial
potential models relative to Mp and M, a global constraint GC, and a
global intertheoretical link GL. The "basic material" are the potential
models of Mp out of which the other components are "constructed" via
the relevant distinctions. We obtain the following formal definition:

DII-12:   K(T) is a theory-core iff there exist Mp(T), Mpp (T) , M(T),
          GC(T), GL(T) such that:
      (1) K(T) = (Mp(T), M(T), Mpp(T), GC(T), GL(T».
      (2) Mp(T) is a class of potential models
      (3) M(T) is a class of models within Mp(T)
      (4) Mpp(T) is the class of partial potential models given by
          Mp(T) and M(T)
      (5) GC(T) is the global constraint belonging to Mp(T)
      (6) GL(T) is the global link belonging to Mp(T)

                   11.6 INTENDED APPLICATIONS

 At the beginning of this chapter we introduced a set I of intended
 applications which is determined independently of the formal apparatus
 of the theory. In our meta-theoretical account, intended applications
 represent the phenomena a theory deals with. But our point of view is
 not that of a philosopher who is puzzled by questions like how it is
 possible to obtain knowledge about "the phenomena". Our attitude
 is much more descriptive, and if we look at what is "given" for an
 empirical theory we take the point of view of that very theory - in
 contrast to the "absolute" point of view of the philosopher. What is
 given for a theory depends on which other theories are available, a
fact which is only too roughly expressed by the term "background
 knowledge". More specifically, what is "given" for a theory are the
 "facts" established in other theories. Our concept of intertheoretical
links was introduced to provide among other things a precise means for
 expressing this relation. What is found to be an "admissible" relation Ri
in a model of one theory, may be used as "given" in the search for
models of another theory; and in case of success one will have two
models linked with each other in our technical sense.
    By collecting and lumping together everything that may be obtained
from "surrounding" theories by means of all relevant links we obtain
the partial potential models of a theory, as already described. Thus,
partial potential models in a natural way represent what is given for a
particular theory T in terms of its surrounding theories. It is most
economical and most natural to assume that the intended applications
of T have the structure of partial potential models. We assume this in
the following, that is, we assume that I(T) ~ Mpp(T). This assumption is
not only reasonable on the basis of general considerations, it also is
backed by studying how scientists talk and how they argue in the
context of an "application" of a theory.
    In the light of the previous discussion Mpp might be called the set
of all possible applications of a theory. But among these there always
will be undesired applications which have really nothing to do with
the theory in question. Consider for instance a partial potential model
(P, T, IR, v) of CCM. Such a structure will count as an intended
application of CCM only if P, T, and v represent particles, time-
instants, and a velocity function, respectively. But nobody can be
prevented from constructing a structure (P, T, IR, v) as fullows. As P
                         THEORY-ELEMENTS                               87

 take the set of inhabitants of a village, as T the set consisting of two
species of 'commodities', say "cow" and "pig" and v(p, t) E ~3, finally,
is found out by counting the number of cows or pigs (depending on
which species t denotes) owned by person p. This number written
down three times yields a vector v(p, t) E ~3. Thus we have a well
interpreted structure (P, T, ~, v> E Mpp(CCM). But this structure, of
course, has nothing to do with classical collision mechanics (rather it is
part of an economic structure, compare PEE in Ch. III).
    This example dramatically shows what has been argued abstractly
before, namely that intended applications of a theory cannot be charac-
terized by purely formal means. We can say something precise, namely
that an intended application is a partial potential model, but we cannot
be precise about every feature of intended applications.
    In most physical texts the term "application" is used as an abstract
term. Typical "applications" are e.g. the harmonic oscillator, the pen-
dulum, the Stern-Gerlach experiment, etc. Here the word "application"
obviously denotes the class of all concrete systems which have the
"right" characteristics for the respective label. The pendulum consists of
all concrete systems or situations in which there is a particle suspended
with some thread near the surface of the earth in such a way that the
particle can swing back and forth. Of course, this description is not
ultimately precise. We shall always find situations in which there might
arise doubts about whether the object in front of us is a pendulum or
not ~ for instance, if the thread is made of rubber and the particle
besides swinging back and forth also oscillates towards the earth and
back. Physicists tend to say that "what is an application depends on the
concrete situation under consideration". Although there is some truth in
this phrase we cannot leave it at that. To accept it without qualification
would leave room for the view that all applications of a theory are
chosen with the help of that very theory, a view which neglects the role
of experience. In the examples just mentioned we have some ideas
about how intended applications have to look like. Roughly, a "good"
pendulum must be similar to those concrete pendulae which we have
already seen at work. Quite a number of necessary conditions come to
our mind if we think how a pendulum has to look like. On the other
hand, it seems plausible that, provided a list of necessary conditions is
given, we always can think of new situations in which there is doubt
about the sufficiency of these conditions.
   So we have two features of the abstract concept of an application.
88                            CHAPTER TWO

First, we can state that there is a similarity relation connecting "con-
crete applications". On the one hand there is a similarity between
certain concrete applications of the same type, e.g. the similarity
between different pendulae. On the other hand there is a similarity
among all concrete applications belonging to one theory, e.g. applica-
tions of mechanics being similar in containing particles. Second, this
similarity relation cannot be described very precisely. There is only
a kind of family resemblance among the different applications. This
vagueness applies to both kinds of similarity: similarity among applica-
tions of the same type and similarity "across" different types.
   Though similarities of the first kind are important enough we shall
not take them into account at the present stage. To do this would
require treating I as a subset of Po(Mpp) rather than as a subset of M pp ,
and our apparatus would be complicated by this a great deal. We prefer
to stick to requiring that I ~ Mpp and we leave an explicit treatment of
classes of similar systems as forming one "application" as a special
problem of describing certain special forms of empirical claims (see
below), namely claims taking these similarities into account. We sum-
marize these considerations in the following "definition", which contains
the only necessary conditions about I that can be formalized at this
point.

DII-16:   I is a set of intended applications for K only if
      (1) K = (M p, M, M pp ' GC, GL) is a theory-core
      (2) I ~ Mpp

Members of I will be called "intended applications".
    The question of how I can be determined cannot be answered, as we
have seen, in a purely formal way by giving a set of "axioms". But even
if we think of some more liberal methods which still lead to a sharp
demarcation of I - as for instance an exhaustive list - we run into
difficulties.
    The method of determination of I which can be extracted from
historical developments of actual theories proceeds in two steps. In a
first step some few explicit examples - "paradigms" - are mentioned
which can be treated with the help of the theory. In most cases it is the
founder(s) of the theory who give(s) these examples. Formally this
amounts to giving a finite list of partial potential models Xl' ..• , x n • If
by 10 we denote the set of all applications occurring in this list then all
members of 10 are intended applications. These are the "paradigm"
                         THEORY - ELEMENTS                             89

cases about which there are no doubts. In a second step I then is said to
contain all those systems which are sufficiently similar to systems
belonging to 10 . It is open how "similarity" here can be made more
precise, and it is clear that it can be made precise only up to a certain
degree.
   This "paradigmatic method" of determination of I clearly leaves
room for changes during the development of a theory. New, additional
paradigms may be introduced and commonly accepted standards of
similarity may be overthrown or newly established.
   On the other hand some features of I are likely to remain identical
through a theory's whole development. Among these there are at least
the following two. Concrete intended applications can always be de-
scribed or conceptualized as partial potential models and the base sets
will always have the same basic intended interpretations.


11.7 IDEALIZED THEORY-ELEMENTS AND EMPIRICAL CLAIMS

We now have described and discussed in detail all the components
necessary to make up a theory-element. Theory-elements are the
smallest units of conceptual apparatus which can be used to formulate
idealized empirical claims. We use the attribute "idealized" in order to
indicate that such theory-elements still are not realistic in a sense,
namely insofar as they do not express and take into account the fact
that practically all empirical theories contain features of approximation.
In fact, the empirical claim associated with a theory-element (see the
next section) will always be only approximatively true, that is, the claim
will have to be blurred in order to be true. We postpone a discussion of
features of approximation to Ch. VII. In the meantime, up to Ch. VII,
we will be sloppy about the distinction between idealized theory-
elements and ("realistic", "approximative") theory-elements, and just
speak of "theory-elements" instead of "idealized theory-elements".
Mature theories usually are built out of several such idealized theory-
elements (compare Ch. N). This is why here we speak of theory-
elements. By summarizing the previous definitions we obtain:
DII-17:   T is an idealized theory-element iff there exist M pp , M p, M,
          GC, GL and I such that
      (1) K = (M p, M, M pp ' GC, GL) is a theory-core
      (2) T=(K,I)
      (3) I ~ Mpp
90                           CHAPTER TWO

For future reference we introduce the notions of content, theoretical
content and isolated content of a given theory-element T. These are
defined just as the concepts introduced earlier with reference to a given
theory-core K which we now take to be the core of T. That is, for a
given theory-element T = (K, I) we set

           Cn(T) = Cn(K),         the content of T
           Cnth(T) = Cnth(K),     the theoretical content of T
           cn(T) = cnCK),         the isolated content of T.

It goes without saying that in the examples the symbol "T" will be
replaced by the respective· symbol we choose to denote the theory in
question. Thus, in the context of, e.g., CCM we shall write Cn(CCM),
Cnth(CCM) etc. Similarly, we shall use the restriction functions r(K),
r(K) and f(K) with "K" replaced by "T", thereby obtaining expressions
like reT) or r(CPM).
    A theory-element T = (K, I) may be regarded as an instrument for
formulating empirical claims. We do not think that this statement forces
on us any particular epistemological position like instrumentalism, or
anti-realism with respect to theoretical terms, as has sometimes been
claimed by critics of our program (cf. e.g. [8] and [30]). Our main
intention here is to give an account of how to construe empirical claims
which we find in scientific practice, and this account does not seem to
fit squarely into such labels as "instrumentalism", "anti-realism" or their
opposites for that matter.
    To formulate precisely the empirical claim associated with a given
theory-element T = (K, I), a first attempt may be this: All intended
applications can be supplemented by theoretical terms such that the
resulting structures are models. However, empirical claims of this form
for most examples turn out to be trivial. That is, they can be proved to
be logically true. The proof usually consists in showing that an arbitrary
partial potential model can be augmented to a model by suitable
theoretical terms.
    What we need in addition, and what in most cases renders empirical
claims non-trivial, are the constraints and links. They express cross-
connections among potential models and among theories, and they
allow only for combinations of potential models subject to certain
restrictions. By requiring the augmentations of intended applications
not only to be models but also to form a set satisfying the constraints
and links, the latter can be used to sharpen the claim.
                          THEORY -ELEMENTS                               91

   Formally, the claim can be best understood if we try to think of a
core K as an instrument for selection as already discussed above.
Suppose we are given sets Mp and Mpp. Since Mpp is a set of all
possible applications of some theory we can interpret Po(Mpp) as the
set of all combinations of applications for such a theory. Each element
of Po(Mpp) is a set of possible applications and therefore a candidate
for the set I of intended applications.No~onsider those elements of
Po(Mpp) which can be augmented to a set of models which in addition
satisfies the constraints and links. Usually, not all elements of Po(Mpp)
will have this property. So we can say that M, GC and GL are used as
means of selection for picking out certain elements from Po(Mpp) or for
picking out a subset of Po(M pp ).
   What is picked out has already been described precisely: namely
Cn(K). Clearly, CoCK) depends on how GC, M and GL look like. If we
change M, GC or GL, then CoCK) will change, too. The elements of
Cn(K) may be described as combinations of partial potential models
which can be "subsumed" under the theory, or which can be "treated by
means of" T, or to which T can "be applied successfully".
   The empirical claim of theory-element T = (K, I) consists in the
statement that I, the set of intended applications, belongs to the content
of K. For the same reasons mentioned in the previous section we also
add the attribute "idealized" here. The empirical claim formulated in
DII-18 is a formally precise and sharp one, it is just true or not,
provided that I is regarded as given. However, realistic claims of
theories which are down to earth and not completely elementary will
always contain features of approximation; they claim that I is in Co (K)
"up to some degree of approximation". We shall deal with these fea-
tures in Ch. VII, and again just talk of "empirical claims" instead of
"idealized empirical claims" up to Chapter VII.
DII-18:    If T = (K, I) is a theory-element then the idealized empirical
           claim of T is that I E Cn(K)
Since I is described independently of K we cannot know whether
I E Cn(K) is true unless we have sufficient information about I. There
are, however, two cases in which we need no information about I at all.
These are the cases of T being inconsistent or trivial. T is inconsistent if
Cn(K) = 0. In this case no I can produce a true empirical claim. So,
regardless of how I looks like, we know the true-value of the empirical
claim in advance: it is false. T is trivial if Cn(K) = Po(Mpp), that is, if
every possible combination of partial potential models belongs to the
92                          CHAPTER TWO

content of K. In this case, too, we know the truth-value of the empirical
claim without regard of I. For, however 1 may look like, it is a subset of
Mpp and therefore it is contained in CoCK). In this case we say that T
(or K) has no empirical content.

DII-19:    If T = (K, I) is an idealized theory-element then T has no
           empirical content iff CoCK) = Po(Mpp)

   It is a somewhat oversimplified picture to imagine that 1 is described
in a way that is completely independent of K. Although there is
historical evidence for paradigmatic examples and even for certain
similarities, a quite usual feature of 1 is that of autodetermination.
The principle of autodetermination says that, after a theory has been
established, the theory itself is used as a means to determine its set of
intended applications. More precisely: the core K may be used in order
to determine whether some partial potential models belong to 1 or not.
This happens in three steps. First, one checks whether a given partial
potential model x can be augmented to a model. Second, it may be
checked whether x belongs to a combination X - given, for instance,
by a strong similarity - such that X can be augmented to satisfy the
constraints. Third, x's membership to 1 has to be decided depending on
whether x satisfies certain links or not.
   Often, discussions of the diachronic development of empirical science
suggest that, at each instance of its development, a scientific theory is
confronted with "anomalies", that is, with intended applications which
resist incorporation into a fully true empirical claim. This suggests that
we may introduce the notion of a theory being only "partially true in its
set of intended applications" and the notion of a "partial empirical
claim" of the theory. If the theory is represented by a theory-element a
partial empirical claim may be defined easily.

DIl-20:    If T = (K, I) is an idealized theory-element, and 0 ~ 10 ~ 1
           then the partial (idealized) empirical claim of T wrt. 10 is
           that 10 E CoCK)

We may use this restricted version of empirical claims for narrowing
down the class of all "possible" theory-elements in meta-scientific
investigations to a more adequate class of those theory-elements which
have at least some true partial empirical claim associated with them.

             SOME BASIC THEORY-ELEMENTS



                        1II.O INTRODUCTION

In this chapter we reconstruct some full-grown examples of well-
known empirical theories. They are: classical and relativistic collision
mechanics, classical particle mechanics, Daltonian stoichiometry, simple
equilibrium thermodynamics, Lagrangian mechanics and pure exchange
economics. In each single case, we systematically reconstruct all the
components of the (basic) theory-element along the lines exposed in the
two preceding chapters. The reason why we speak of basic theory-
elements here is this. The particular theory-elements reconstructed in
this chapter will prove to be "basic" in the sense that they are the base
on which some other "derived" theory-elements rest. The meaning of
this will become clearer in the next chapter, where we introduce the
notion of a theory-element being a specialization of some other theory-
element. Roughly speaking, a theory-element is basic when it "prevails"
over a number of different theory-elements as its specializations but
when it is not a specialization of another theory-element itself. This
immediately leads us to notice the ambiguity of the term "theory":
Sometimes it means a single (possibly basic) theory-element; sometimes
it means a whole net of inter-related theory-elements with a basic
theory-element prevailing over them. In this chapter we are only
interested in the basic theory-elements of the theories mentioned above.
   Thus, the reconstruction of the above-mentioned empirical theories
in this chapter will be incomplete in the sense that only their most
fundamental parts will be the object of our formal analysis. For some of
them, the more special laws they contain will be dealt with in the next
chapter. In another sense, the reconstruction of the theories in this
chapter will also be incomplete: We shall not state many theorems that
are derivable from the basic axioms of each theory and which usually
appear in standard expositions of the theory in question. The reason, of
course, is that we are not engaged in a scientific exposition of these
theories but in a meta scientific analysis of them, so that the many more
or less empirically useful theorems that may be derived from an
                                   95
96                         CHAPTER THREE

axiomatic presentation of a theory are of no concern to us. However, in
some cases we have broken this rule, and we have explicitly stated and
derived some (object-scientific) theorems which might enlighten the
logical structure of the theory or which, though not usually proved in
standard textbooks, have some intrinsic interest. We have applied this
strategy especially to the cases of stoichiometry, thermodynamics, and
exchange economics. In other cases, the theorems are rather of a
metatheoretical nature (e.g. in the case of mechanics).
    According to the distinctions introduced in the preceding chapters,
the following components have to be identified in order to get a
complete reconstruction of a particular theory-element: the class of
potential models, the class of actual models, the class of partial poten-
tial models, the constraints, the inter-theoretical links, and the intended
applications. For reasons of expository perspicuity we shall change the
ordering a bit: After defining the potential models, and before the
actual models, the partial potential models, the constraints and the
inter-theoretical links are identified, we say a word about the intended
applications. As already pointed out, the intended applications cannot
be characterized in a purely formal way; therefore, no definition of a
set-theoretic predicate for the intended applications should be expected.
The identification of the intended applications depends on strongly
pragmatic and diachronic considerations, some of which will be dis-
cussed with detail later on in this book. Here, we restrict ourselves to a
minimal semantic determination of the (non-auxiliary) base sets in form
of some very general necessary conditions for their empirical interpre-
tation. These conditions (which do not belong to the formal structure,
i.e. to the core K of a theory-element) will be subsumed under the label
"basic intended interpretation". For any given x E M(T), they express
some (weak) necessary conditions for asserting that r(x) E I(T).
    The potential and actual models of CCM and RCM, have already
been identified in Ch. 1. However, for more systematicity let us repeat
those definitions here.

of determination. If we restrict our consideration to methods of deter-

clearly, m will turn out to be CCM-theoretical. For all other methods
of determination known to us which do not presuppose conservation of
momentum essentially involve concepts of theories different from CCM
and thus cannot be represented as potential models of CCM. Deter-

using an equal-arms balance. In this case there also are included further

for the discussion of theoreticity of mass in CCM.

111.1.3 Constraints for CCM
For CCM we can formulate two constraints: an equality constraint C 1
for mass, and a constraint C z expressing the extensivity of mass. The
equality constraint requires that the mass of a particle p does not
change when p occurs in different applications (described by different
potential models). That is, the "outer" conditions around p do not affect
p's mass. This certainly is part of the idea that mass is an intrinsic
property of particles. Extensivity of mass intuitively means that under
concatenation of particles the masses of the particles are added. That is,
if two particles are put together or are concatenated then the mass of
the new, compound particle is just the sum of both single particles'
masses. This constraint can be formulated only if we introduce as a new
basic concept that of concatenation. Concatenation is represented by a
function 0 which to any two particles occurring in arbitrary potential
models of CCM assigns the result of putting together both particles. We
can imagine concatenation in a way such that both particles are fixed on
                  SOME BASIC THEORY-ELEMENTS                           99

each other. But the function 0 will be defined for any two particles, and
so it also covers abstract cases where the two particles are isolated from
each other in reality, and are put together merely conceptually.

The question of theoreticity here can be settled even more easily as in

CCM. The velocity function v as well as the existence function e are

volves very sophisticated methods in the case of RCM it does not
presuppose conservation of momentum. The determination of e may be
performed by means of photographic plates: the spots on the plate
indicate the existence of particles. Determination of m, on the other
hand, always presupposes conservation of momentum. It is tempting to
point out possibilities analogous to those existing for the determination
of m in CCM: methods of determination by means of special force laws
plus the basic laws of mechanics (now in relativistic form), or by means
of other devices (like the equal-arms balance in case of CCM). But such
possibilities up to now have to be regarded as mere speculation. There
exists hardly any textbook treating relativistic mechancis in a general
way analogous to Newtonian mechanics; usually only the special cases
attached to electrodynamics are treated. Those methods of determina-
tion of m which would be analogous to the non-CCM-dependent ones
do not work for elementary particles, and devices analogous to equal-
arms balances do not exist in this domain. It is only by means of the
basic law of RCM that physicists determine (or calculate, as they say)
the masses of elementary particles. We conclude that m is RCM-
theoretical. The investigation of whether our formal criterion of the-
oreticity yields the same result has not been performed yet.

III.3. 1. 1 The logical status of force in CPM. There has been a long
dispute - which still is not settled - among physicists and philos-

helpful to add some remarks on this issue. First, and most important,
both alternative views - that f is definable and that it is not - are not
104                         CHAPTER THREE

really inconsistent with each other, because they presuppose different
formulations of CPM. Defenders of f's definability (see e.g. [26, 34,

the second law in the form

as a definition of f in terms of m and s (via C 1, C2 and r). That is, the
resultant force acting on each particle is explicitly defined. Clearly this
approach is formally different from ours. We start with component
forces h: P X T ~ ~3 as basic notions which cannot be defined by
Newton's second law. For this law is meant to hold for resultant forces.
If we would use it to define component forces by infinitely many
axioms

we would run into trouble with systems where more than one com-
ponent force is present (as considered in the example of Ch. I). For
unless in such a system all the component forces are equal - which
usually is not the case - we obtain a contradiction:
   m(p)D2r(p, a) = f(p, cI ( a), i) oF f(p, cI ( a), j) = m(p)D 2r(p, a)
   for i oF j
Thus by starting with component forces it is unacceptable to use the
second law as a definition of component forces. The only way, there-
fore, of formulating this law is the one used above. But then one could
prove fs undefinability by Padoa's principle:

So the alternatives are: (1) to define resultant forces by means of
Newton's second law or (2) to start with component forces, to formu-
late the second law for the resultant forces defined in terms of the
component forces, and to accept component forces as undefinable.
   Alternative (1) has the advantage of yielding a straightforward
approach to the measurement of force. Force - i.e. resultant force

- is measured by measuring mD2 r. But even adherents of this alterna-
tive admit the existence of component forces. They admit that under
favorable circumstances the resultant forces should be viewed as split
up into component forces. It just turns out to be useful to decompose
the different forces acting on each particle according to their origin. But
as soon as this decomposition is accepted, approach (1) faces the same
kind of non-definability of the component forces as we do from the
beginning. For the decomposition of a given "resultant" force into
component forces is - logically speaking - completely arbitrary as
long as there are no further axioms introduced. Thus, from a purely
pragmatic point of view nothing seems to be gained by sticking to the
first approach. Of course, one might be willing to offer other, meta-
physical, arguments in favor of alternative (1) but these are of no
concern to us here.

111.3.3 Constraints for CPM

In CPM there are three natural constraints: equality constraints for
mass and force, and extensivity of mass. The equality constraint C j for
mass is the same as in CCM and was already discussed intuitively in
Ch. II. It requires any particle's mass to be independent from the system
in which the particle occurs. The constraint C2 for extensivity of mass
also is the same as in CCM. It requires that relative to some given
concatenation operation (which is represented by a new basic notion)
mass behaves as additive under concatenation. The equality constraint
C3 for force is new. It requires that the i-th component force acting on
particle p at time t is the same, irrespective of the system p belongs to.
106                        CHAPTER THREE

This formulation assumes that, in fact, some particle p may occur in
two different systems at the same time. Intuitively, this may happen if
the systems overlap both in space and time. For instance, the system
consisting of earth and moon in such' a way overlaps with the whole
solar system. C 3 in this case would require the gravitational force acting
on the moon in the smaller system to be the same as the gravitational
force acting on the moon in the whole system. Although this is not so if
we look at things quite accurately, physical calculations work with such
or similar assumptions. Roughly, C 3 requires that by neglecting the
influence of other systems on the system under consideration, the
forces of the latter do not become "too false".

theories open and make the idealizing assumption that there are no

10 • The same could be said of "the projectile" and "the harmonic

                I1I.4 DALTONIAN STOICHIOMETRY

I1I.4.1 The Potential Models of DSTOI
Daltonian Stoichiometry (DSTOI) is a theory about "weight relations"
in chemical reactions. It "explains" certain observed regularities in the
weights of chemical substances consumed and produced in chemical
reactions. The basic idea of "pure" DSTOI as introduced by Dalton
sometime before 1807 is the "atomic theory of matter". Chemical
substances are viewed as generally consisting of specific kinds of
complex "atoms" ("molecules" in modern terminology). Complex atoms
are constructed from elementary atoms. Chemical reactions are viewed
as "rearrangements" of the elementary atoms in the chemical substances
participating in the reaction. In its pure form, DSTOI makes no use of
the laws of Gay-Lussac, Dulong and Petit, or Avogadro that are some-
times associated with it in modern expositions of stoichiometry. (For a
detailed discussion of the historical development of stoichiometry in the
first half of the 19th century see Glymour, [171, pp. 226-43.)
    As conceived by this theory, a "chemical reaction" consists of a finite
set C of "chemical substances" - e.g. water, lime, marsh gas, gold etc.
- and two assignments of weight to each substance indicating the
amount of each substance consumed and produced by the reaction.
Often, substances that are consumed in a reaction will not be produced
                  SOME BASIC THEORY-ELEMENTS                           109

 in the same reaction. In this case, we may say that the weights assigned
 to the substances present before the reaction are those that "combine
without residue" to produce those weights assigned to the substances
that appear after the reaction. Generally, we (though Dalton did not)
may think of the same substance being both produced and consumed in
a reaction. In this case, we must think of the weight assigned to it before
the reaction as completely disappearing and the weight assigned to it
after the reaction appearing as the result of the reaction. If we arbi-
trarily let "tl" denote "before the reaction" and "t2" denote "after the
reaction", and denote by "C" the set of (names of) substances involved
then we can think of a chemical reaction as having the formal structure
of a quadruple <C, T, IR, w) where C is a non-empty, finite set; T =
{tl' t2l, and w: C X T -+ IRt. "w(s, t) = a" means that a (grams
or whatever) of substance s were present at "time" t. In particular,
"w(s, t 1) = a" means that a grams of s were present before the
reaction and "w(s, t 2 ) = 0" means that all of s was "used up" in the
reaction. The members of C in applications of DSTOI are to be
thought of as "pure" chemical compounds that can be assigned a single
chemical formula. Such substances are sometimes called "daltonides"
to distinguish them from other substances - "bertholides" - whose
chemical formula is different depending upon such things as the manner
of preparation. In simply describing a chemical reaction, however, we
do not assume chemical substances have been assigned a chemical
formula. Thus, simply as members of C, they may be referred to only
by their common pre-theoretical names - e.g. by "common salt" and
not by "NaCl". Strictly speaking, the values of the w-function are to be
interpreted as "masses", though the chemical literature commonly refers
to them as "combining weights". Thus, in applications of DSTOI the
values of the w-function may be thought to have been determined using
an analytical balance or some other instrument for determining the
masses of macroscopic bodies. Note that the same set of substances
may appear in reactions with different combining weight functions.
Different combining weight functions correspond to different "sizes" or
"scales" of the reaction as well as to simply measuring the combining
weights in different units.
    Essentially, DSTOI is a theory that tells us something about what
kinds of chemical reactions actually occur in nature. To do this it makes
use of several additional concepts. First, it assigns chemical formulas
to substances which tell how "molecules" of the substance are made
110                          CHAPTER THREE

 up of "atoms". Formally speaking, this is the way Dalton's "atomic
 hypothesis" enters into his stoichiometric theory. Though Dalton prob-
 ably thought of atoms as "very small particles", this conception of the
 atoms plays no real role in pure DSTOI. The chemical formula for the
 substance "water" is H 2 0 - meaning that a molecule of water consists
 of two hydrogen atoms, symbolized by H, and one atom of oxygen,
 symbolized by O. For the moment, let "F" denote the set of all
 "chemical formulas". Then DSTOI contains a "formula function" f -
 an assignment of a unique member of F to every member of C. That is,
f is an injective function from C into F: f: C ..... F. That f is required to
 be a function means that the theory is committed to dealing only with
 "daltonides".
    Second, DSTOI assigns "coefficients" of a "chemical equation" to
 the reaction, e.g. 2(H2) + 1(02) ..... 2(H20). The reaction equation coef-
ficients in this equation are the integers 2, 1 and 2. Note that the
numeral "1" before "0 2 " is usually omitted in writing the formula,
nevertheless the coefficient of oxygen is the integer 1. The coefficients
in a chemical reaction indicate the "proportions" in which the sub-
stances must be present if they are to react "without residue". Formally,
the coefficients are just integers assigned to the substances before and
after the reaction. So DSTOI uses a function k from eXT into the
non-negative integers N: k: eXT ..... N.
    Finally, "molecular weights" are assigned to chemical formulas.
These molecular weights are interpreted as the relative masses of atoms
and molecules of different substances - relative to the mass of one
atom of hydrogen which serves as the unit. Formally, "molecular
weight" is a function Jl from the set of chemical formulas F into the
positive real numbers, i.e., fi: F ..... ~+. Thus any full theoretical descrip-
tion of a reaction in terms of DSTOI yields a structure <c, T, N, ~, w,
F, f, k, fl). The real numbers ~ provide the range for the w- and
fl-functions. We may think of members of the set F of chemical
formulas as simply strings of symbols formed from some finite set of n
"elementary formulas" E (n) - the formulas that will ultimately be
assigned to "elementary" chemical substances and usually will consist of
just one or two letters which abbreviate the name of the elements. At
present the value of n is slightly more than 100. Typical members of
E(n) are: 0, Li, Fe. Typical, non-elementary members of F are: H 2 S04 ,
NaCI, CO 2 , We take formulas literally to be strings of symbols in the
Latin alphabet plus Arabic numerals, and usually we shall simply let the
                  SOME BASIC THEORY-ELEMENTS                          111

 symbol or string of symbols serve as a name for itself. Consider how
 the formula H 2 S0 4 is constructed from the elementary formulas H, S
 and O. We might think of it as being constructed with a "concatenation"
 operation * in the following way: H*H*S*O*O*O*O. Thinking of it in
 this way the subscript "2" that decorates H in the formula just indicates
 that H has been concatenated with itself two times, and similarly with
the subscript "4" of O. We don't really need the subscripts, they just
 save writing. Even if we choose to use a "shorthand" notation for
 repeated concatenations of the same elementary symbol, we don't have
to use the subscripts. We might just as well write H2*S*04, or
 2H*S*40.
    Concatenation * has to have certain formal properties. The first thing
to note is that it's a binary operation. We can think of H 2 0 being
constructed in two iterations of this operation: (H*H)*O. It seems
apparent that the order of concatenation is irrelevant. That is, we could
just as well think of H 2 0 being constructed as H*(H*O). This is to say
we take it that (H*H)*O = H*(H*O) and, in general, that the con-
catenation operation * is associative. It is somewhat less obvious
whether * is commutative. Are the formulas H 2 0, OH 2 , HOH to be
regarded in DSTOI as the same chemical formula? Clearly, convention
dictates that "water" is assigned the formula H 2 0 and not OH 2 or
HOH. But, could we in DSTOI assign, say HOH, to something other
than "water"? For example, might we not find it convenient to dis-
tinguish two forms of "water" - one assigned H 2 0 and the other
assigned HOH? Indeed we might. But it is difficult to see how we might
distinguish these forms of water solely on the basis of "combining
weight relations" - the data of DSTOI. Thus, it seems that as long as
we confine our use of chemical formulas to DSTOI, the concatenation
relation is commutative. That is, for example: Na*CI = CI*Na.
    These considerations suggest that we take the set of chemical for-
mulas F to be a part of a structure IF = (F, *, E(n», where E(n) is a
finite set of n elementary formulas, * is an associative and commutative
binary "concatenation" operation such that every member of F is
constructed from members of E(n) by iterations of the *-operation. It is
formally convenient to have the "null formula" - the formula that
consists of no symbols - to facilitate expressing formulas in terms of
their elementary formulas. If we call the null formula "A", then our
structure of chemical formulas is IF = (F, *, A, E(n». On this account
of the matter, the structure of chemical formulas IF is an n-dimensional
112                         CHAPTER THREE

We choose not to mention 'Yj as a primitive because the axioms

    There are a few further remarks worth making about this way of
viewing chemical formulas. First, it should be evident that the actual
members of E(n) are not important. That E(n) consists of the Roman
letters "H", "He", "Li", "Be", ... is a convention. We express the fact
that it is a convention in TIII-6 below. Second, any way of numbering
the members of E(n) is also conventional in DSTOI, though not
in some other theories that also employ the concept of a chemical
element. The number of members in E (n) is not conventional, though
the limits that DSTOI alone can put on its value are not narrow. It is
clear that we have not captured all the standard notation for chemical
formulas. The common practice of writing certain "radicals" or of
writing the "water of hydration" elude our characterization. Assuming
that these conventions can be made precise, there are no real problems
representing them formally. One might have to add some additional
concatenation operations that would be iterated in a specific order. It
should be noted that the concept of ''valence'' does not appear in our
account of chemical formulas. This is simply because it is clearly not a
part of the conceptual apparatus of DSTOI. It is however worth noting
how one would add it. The concept of valence is essentially a means of
putting limitations on what counts as an acceptable chemical formula.
That is, it picks out a subset of the set F we have characterized here. It
does this with the help of some additional conceptual apparatus -
roughly, "valence numbers" assigned to members of E(n).
    Two chemical reactions represented by structures x and x' may be
"identified" when the structures x and x' are isomorphic in a sense to
be precisely defined below. This accounts for the usual way of talking
about reactions as "types of reactions". Any such type is just a class of
isomorphic reactions in our sense. In addition to "identity" there also is
some interest in weaker forms of "similarity". Similarity of two reactions
x, x' may be expressed by the existence of some mapping cp between
corresponding sets of objects of x and x' which preserves the "structure
114                         CHAPTER THREE

III.4.2 The Models of DSTOI
There are three non-trivial laws that must be satisfied in the actual
models for DSTOI. The first tells us how the molecular chemical
formulas are determined by the molecular weights of "atomic" chemical
formulas. It tells us, for example, that Jl(H20) = 2Jl(H) + Jl(O). The
second tells us that chemical equations must be "balanced" - that is,
the sum of the atoms of each element appearing in the equation must
be· the same before and after the reaction. If, for instance, the reaction
is described by 1P2 0 S + 1H2 0 --+ 2HP0 3 then the sum of O-atoms
before the reaction is (5 X 1) + (1 X 1) = 6. The requirement of these
sums being balanced leads to simple equations for the coefficients.
For example, the coefficients in k(hydrogen)H2 + k(oxygen)02 --+
                    SOME BASIC THEORY-ELEMENTS                                             115

k(water)H 20 must be chosen so that 2 X k(hydrogen) = 2 X k(water)
and 2 X k(oxygen) = 1 X k(water). Finally, the ratios of combining
weights of substances in the reaction are equal to the ratios of the
products of their reaction equation coefficients and molecular weights.
For example,

             w(oxygen)                    k(oxygen) X ,u(02)    1 X ,u(02)
In addition to these laws there is the "obvious requirement" that
coefficients have the value 0 iff the combining weight is O.

DSTOI. This is simply because we didn't require that the coefficients
be "reduced to lowest terms".


III.4.3 The Partial Potential Models of DSTOI
Whatis it that DSTOI claims about the world, or what kind of claims
can we make by means of DSTOl's models? A rough answer is this.
We collect data from real chemical reactions, and we claim that these
data "yield" models of DSTOI. Intuitively, we may imagine a model
of DSTOI as being "broken up" into "atomic fragments" of the form
w(s, t) = a, f(s) = r, k(s, t) = n, fl(r) = m which can be regarded as
118                        CHAPTER THREE

 set-theoretic propositions. We observe some real reaction and we try
 to read off or to determine otherwise all those atomic propositions
 necessary for a full description of the reaction as a potential model. The
 claim then is that the potential model obtained, in fact, is a model of
 DSTOI, that is, the functions (j), J, k, fl "put together" piecemeal from
 all the "observed" data satisfy the laws stated in M(DSTOI).
     On this account there is a difficulty with the functions J, k and fl.
How can we determine the values of these functions from a given
 chemical reaction? Obviously, reactions do not carry with them the
formulas of the substances involved, and it is less drastically obvious
but equally true that this also holds for the k-coefficients and the
molecular weights. Intuitively, it is clear that J, k and fl are theoretical
terms in DSTOI. They cannot be "directly observed" but are intro-
duced in order to organize the observed data. Observed data are data
about different substances involved in a reaction, and about their
combining weights. That is, the observed data can form a structure
<C, T, N, IR, (j)), at best.
     But then the above account of the empirical claim of DSTOI needs
modification, for structures of the form <C, T, N, IR, (j)) cannot be
claimed to be models of DSTOI - they simply have the wrong type.
According to our general view the empirical claim of DSTOI has the
following form: it is claimed that for all structures <C, T, N, IR, (j))
which are obtained from real chemical reactions there exist functions
J, k and fl which, together with C, T and (j), form a model of DSTOI.
In other words, each real, "non-theoretical" structure <C, T, N, IR, (j))
can be extended to a full theoretical model <C, T, N, IR, IF, (j), J, k, fl)
by suitable "theoretical functions" J, k and fl. Here, we regard the
components N, IR and IF as purely mathematical items. IF provides the
range for the [-function in the same way IR provides the range for the
(j), k and fl-functions. If there is any distinction to be made here, it is
just that IR is unique, while IF is unique at best up to isomorphisms.
    These intuitive considerations can be made somewhat more precise
by means of our informal criterion of theoreticity. Applying this
criterion, we see at once that (j) is DSTOI-non-theoretical. There are
systems for the determination of masses which are not models of
DSTOI, for instance systems in which analytical balances are used. In
contrast, J, k and fl are DSTOI-theoretical. This becomes clear if we
think about how to determine specific formulas, reaction equation
coefficients and molecular weights. Roughly, we get all three in the
                 SOME BASIC THEORY-ELEMENTS                          119

same way. We assume that a chemical reaction is a model for DSTOI
and then try to figure out what formulas, reaction coefficients and
molecular weights are needed to make it a model. This is not quite
the whole story, and more will be said below. It might seem intuitively
natural also to regard IF or at least the elementary formulas E(n) as
DSTOI-theoretical. We capture a part of this intuition by noting that
the formula assignment function f is theoretical. F is theoretical in the
sense that it appears only in the theoretical structures of DSTOI
because it is needed to provide the range for f The non-theoretical
structures of DSTOI we call combining weight structures.
Mpp(DSTOI):     x is a combining weight structure for DSTOI (x         E
                Mpp(DSTOI)) iff there exist C, T and w such that
            (1) x = <C, T, N,~, w);
            (2) MP(DSTOI)-(2)-(4) are satisfied
Mpp(DSTOI) contains all possible non-theoretical descriptions of
chemical reactions. Among these there are the descriptions of real
reactions that have taken place or are intended to be carried out. Those
real reactions which practitioners of DSTOI are interested in we collect
in the set I(DSTOI) of intended applications of DSTOI.
   The empirical claim of DSTOI stated above, namely that all in-
tended applications can be extended to models, now can be precisely
formulated:
           I(DSTOI) <;; f(DSTOI)(M(DSTOI))
Intuitively, the claim is that every combining weight structure in
I(DSTOI) can be "filled out" with a formula structure IF, a formula
assignment function f, reaction coefficients k and molecular weights #
in a way that satisfies the laws of DSTOI. This claim is not trivial.
According to TIII-5, in systems satisfying two further plausible con-
ditions the claim is not true unless the reaction "conserves mass" in the
sense that the sum of the combining weights before and after the
reaction are equal.
   Note that the truth of the claim offered here requires only that there
be some IF, f, k and # that satisfy the laws. There might be several.
Moreover, the same substance could be assigned different formulas
and different molecular weights in different reactions. That these pos-
sibilities are not ruled out suggests that something is missing from this
formulation of the empirical claim of DSTOI.

III.4.4 Constraints for DSTOI

What is missing are the constraints which practitioners of DSTOI use
to draw and to exploit in order to get a more and more detailed picture
of the whole range of substances, elements and their possible reactions.
The most obvious constraint consists of assigning the same formula to a
substance, irrespective of the particular reaction in which the substance
is involved. Another obvious constraint is given by the assignment of
the same atomic weight (as a special case of molecular weight) to any
element, irrespective of the particular reaction.
   Two potential models satisfy the constraint for formula assignment
(C, (DSTOI) below) if any substance occurring in both structures gets
the same formula by the f-functions in both structures. Similarly, two
potential models satisfy the constraint for atomic weights (C 2 (DSTOI)
below) if any element occurring in both structures gets assigned the
same atomic weight by the ,u-functions in both potential models. The
constraints we need are as follows.
C,(DSTOI): for all X: X E C,(DSTOI) iff 0 "# X ~ MP(DSTOI)
           and for all x, x' EX: IFx = IFx'

            s E Cx n Cy thenfx(s) = fis)

    Some remarks concerning these constraints are in order here. Note,
first, that X and X' may be in C,(DSTOI) even though the ''uniform''
formula structure IF appearing in all members of X is different from the
IF' appearing in all members of X. On the other hand, for X E
C3 (DSTOI) it is required that every member of the common set of
elements E(n) be assigned to a chemical substance appearing in some
Cx of some member x of X; that is, the set E(n) has to be minimal in
                   SOME BASIC THEORY-ELEMENTS                        121

the sens~ of not containing redundant elements which would not occur
in any formula for any substance. C3 (DSTOI), therefore, may be called
the 'minimal elements constraint'.

111.4.5 Links for DSTOI

There are at least two important links DSTOI has to other theories
reconstructed in this book and which for this very· reason deserve
explicit mention at this point. One is a link with thermodynamics
and the other a link with rigid body mechanics. In the next section
(Sec. 111.5) we shall reconstruct simple equilibrium thermodynamics
(abbreviated as 'SETH') and we shall thereby see that the identification
of the latter theory would not be complete without the formulation of a
link from DSTOI to SETH which is essential to the latter theory. This
is the link that "imports" mole numbers from DSTOI into SETH. In
fact, DSTOI appears as a theory "underlying" SETH in the sense that it
provides SETH with one of its SETH-non-theoretical concepts. How-
ever, this link should not be considered as an essential constituent of
DSTOI's identity, since it clearly plays no unavoidable role in the use
of DSTOI. Therefore, the DSTOI-SETH-link we shall reconstruct in
the next section is not a part of DSTOI itself (according to our general
identity criteria).
   On the other hand, there certainly is at least one link we should
consider as an essential constituent of DSTOI in a complete recon-
struction of this theory: the link which provides DSTOI with the values
of the w-function. Typically, these values are determined by means of
an analytical balance, which means that to determine w we usually need
to assume some model of a mechanical theory: rigid body mechanics
(RBM). (If the analytical balance used to determine weights did not
satisfy the laws of RBM, we would not say that it determines any "real"
weights at all.) This means that for DSTOI we essentially need a link L j
between M(RBM) and Mp(DSTOI). For reasons of perspicuity, RBM
is a theory to be reconstructed much later in this book (see Ch. VI).
Nevertheless, anticipating the results of our analysis in Ch. VI, let us
point out that any model x E M(RBM) has the form:
           x = (B, T, S, N, lR, c j , c2 , U, cp, R, M, e, F, p).
Of all the constituents of x, for the present purposes we need to take
only B, T and M into account. B is a singleton {b} where b is "the
122                       CHAPTER THREE

body" considered. T is a time interval. M E IR+ is the mass of b and
has to agree with the momentum of inertia e through a complicated
relationship - but we may forget about this for the moment. (Through
M among other things, RBM is, in tutn, linked to CPM and its mass
function m, but this is again a complication we need not take into
account here.) Now, the RBM-DSTOI-link roughly says that for each
potential model of DSTOI the weight of its substances must coincide
with the value of M for some model of RBM. More formally, the link is
this (according to the notation introduced in Sec. 11-3-2).

           L l (DSTOI) ~ M(RBM) X
               n(RBM, 1,2,11) X Mp(DSTOI) X n(DSTOI, 1,2,6)

determined by the following condition:

           For all x E M(RBM) and x' E Mp(DSTOI):
           (x, (Bx, Tx, Mx), x', (Cx" Tx" wx'» E L l (DSTOI) iff there
           are s E Cx ' and t E Tx n Tx ' such that
       (a) s = U Bx
       (b) wAs, t) = Mx

Notice that this link is a many-many relation because, on the one hand
for a given potential model of DSTOI containing different "substances"
SI, . . . , sn' n different models of RBM have to be used to weigh them.
On the other hand, since M is a RBM-theoretical concept (see Sec.
VI-4), intuitively speaking to the same substance conceived as the body
b, different "empirically equivalent" M-values may be assigned. These
facts imply that a single model of DSTOI may be linked to several
models of RBM and vice versa. This is not at variance with our general
concept of a link since we have not required in general that links be
functions but just relations. (This case, by the way, shows that it would
be inadequate to conceive links as functions.)
   Assuming that L l (DSTOI) is the only essential link of DSTOI to
some other theory, we may introduce the global link as follows.
           GL(DSTOI) := Al (DSTOI), where Al corresponds to L l .


III.4.6 The Theory-Element of DSTOI and Its Claim
With the preceding discussion we have completed the explication of the
                  SOME BASIC THEORY-ELEMENTS                           123

several components of the theory-element of DSTOI so that we can
define
           K(DSTOI) := (Mp(DSTOI), M(DSTOI), Mpp(DSTOI),
             GC(DSTOI), GL(DSTOI»)
and
           T(DSTOI) := (K(DSTOI), I(DSTOI»)
We now can formulate the empirical claim of DSTOI in a more
satisfactory way. Intuitively, the claim is that the intended applications
- non-theoretical descriptions of real, "intended" reactions determined,
among other things, through the link LI - can be extended to a set of
models which are linked to each other by GC(DSTOI).
    More concretely, the claim is that the members of I(DSTOI) can be
filled out with a single formula structure IF, an array of formula func-
tions f, reaction equation coefficient functions k and molecular weight
functions Ji. In each individual reaction, IF together with these functions
must satisfy the laws of DSTOI. Moreover, each of the elements in
IF must be assigned a chemical substance in at least one member of
I(DSTOI); the array of i-functions must assign the same formula to the
same chemical substance in all the reactions in I(DSTOI) in which the
substance participates; the array of Ji-functions must assign the same
formula the same molecular weight in all members of I(DSTOI). Of
course, the reaction coefficient functions k may assign the same sub-
stance different coefficients in different reactions.
    It is worthwhile to elaborate a bit about the intuitive significance
of the empirical claim of DSTOI. First, consider the effect of the
minimal elements constraint C 3 (DSTOI). Suppose It = {YI' ... , Yn} ~
I(DSTOI) describes the chemical reactions known to us at time t and
the empirical claim for It is true. Now suppose we discover some
additional chemical reactions {Yn + I' . . . , Ym} ~ I(DSTOI) and add
them to the original "successful" intended applications to obtain an
empirical claim for It+1 = {YI"'" Yn' Yn+I,"·' Ym}· Suppose further
that there is no way to make this further claim true using 1Ft - the
formula structure used to make the claim for It true. But we can add
another elementary formula to E (n)t and obtain 1Ft + 1 which can be
used to make the claim true for It + I' Intuitively, we have discovered
then a new "chemical element". Now the minimal element constraint
will not let us use 1Ft + 1 to fill out It because the "new element" is
124                        CHAPTER THREE

superfluous for It. But, clearly, 1Ft still works for It and it will satisfy
the minimal element constraint. This shows that the theoretical con-
tent of DSTOI is "non-theoretically transitive" in the following sense.
Whenever Xl E Cnth(DSTOI) and X 2 is a subclass of Xl then also
X 2 E Cnth(DSTOI). This property allows for a cumulative develop-
ment of DSTOI in the direction of expanding the range of intended
applications: the inclusion of new intended applications will not force
us to exclude intended applications from I(DSTOI) in order to keep
the empirical claim true.
    Supposing the claim of DSTOI is true for I, it is natural to ask
whether the theoretical components needed to fill out I to a class of
models for DSTOI are determined up to the maximal amount of
uniqueness established by TIII-6. There are really two questions here.
What does an I have to be like in order to determine the theoretical
components in all its members up to the maximal degree of unique-
ness? Is the actual range of intended applications I(DSTOI) like this?
The answer to the second question, in the case that I is the range of
intended applications actually associated with this theory, is clearer
than the answer to the first. The main problem with "pure" DSTOI
was that it did not provide unique determinations of formulas and
molecular weights in very many actual reactions that were included in
its range of applications. Indeed, a good part of the history of chemistry
in the early 19th century can be understood as trying to figure out what
to add to "pure" DSTOI to keep the claim of the theory true and
determine formulas and molecular weights uniquely. It turned out
ultimately that Avogadro's law filled the bill (see Glymour, [17], pp.
226 ff.). Although no longer of genuine scientific interest, it is of
some philosophical interest to know the answer to the first question.
The philosophically interesting question here is whether DSTOI is
inherently incapable of affording maximally unique determinations of
formulas and molecular weights or whether it is just due to the "per-
versity of nature" that the chemical reactions actually available don't
overlap in ways that will afford maximally unique determinations.
    Now that we have the claim of the full theory at hand we can state
two further theorems. The first of these corresponds to the "law of
simple multiple proportions" first proposed by Dalton about 1803. It is
usually stated in the following way: "When two elements combine to
form more than one compound, the weights of one element which

         IlLS SIMPLE EQUILIBRIUM THERMODYNAMICS

III.5.1 The POlential Models of SETH
Thermodynamics is not one single theory but a whole array of theories
- in quite the same way as the label "mechanics" does not denote one
single theory. but the whole array of mechanical theories. The simplest
full-blown thermodynamical theory is what we call "simple equilibrium
thermodynamics" - the theory reconstructed in this section. As much
as classical particle mechanics can be viewed as a sort of "paradigmatic"
theory for the whole of mechanics, simple equilibrium thermodynamics
(in the following abbreviated as "SETH") plays the role of a paradigm
for equilibrium thermodynamics.
   Before the advent of so-called "irreversible thermodynamics", thermo-
dynamics characteristically dealt with states of systems in equilibrium.
128                        CHAPTER THREE

This is why some authors have proposed to call this discipline "thermo-
statics" instead of "thermodynamics". However, this terminological
proposal is not completely convincing, since dynamical considerations
also play some role in at least certain parts of the discipline, for
example in Gibbs' principle, as we shall see when we come to formalize
it.
    The potential models of SETH contain a set Z of states, a set I of
indices for chemical substances, a set ze of "phases of equilibrium", and
functions V, N, U, S, assigning to each state a real number denoting,
respectively, the volume, the mole number, the energy and the entropy
of the system in that state. N, in addition, depends on indices for the
different chemical substances of which the system consists. Intuitively, a
potential model can be imagined as a description of a thermodynamical
system running through a sequence of states.
    Not all kinds of systems are admitted within the scope of SETH.
This theory is intended to apply only to so-called "simple systems".
They are described roughly as systems that are macroscopically homo-
genous, isotropic, uncharged, and chemically inert, that are sufficiently
large so that surface effects can be neglected, and that are not acted on
by electric, magnetic or gravitational fields (compare Callen, [91, Ch. 1).

Mp(SETH): (a) x is a potential simple equilibrium thermodynamics
              (x E Mp(SETH)) with respect to cp iff there exist Z, I,
              ze, V, N, U, S such that
                  (1) x = (Z, N, IR, I, ze, V, N, U, S)
                  (2) Z is a non-empty set
                  (3) cp: Z -> IR is bijective
                  (4) I ~ N is finite (we write I = (i l , . .. , iJ where
                          i l < iz < ... < in)
                  (5) ze ~ Po(Z) is finite and not empty
