              (x E Mp(SETH)) iff there is some cp such that x E
              Mp(SETH) wrt cp
                  SOME BASIC THEORY-ELEMENTS                             129

Basic intended interpretation: Z is the set of successive states taken by
a given physical system undergoing a process.
    Z is just a set of states. But it is sometimes identified with the system
itself: This could be misleading since the notion of a system is used
in an ambiguous way in the literature on the foundations of thermo-
dynamics. Sometimes, by "system" a spatio-temporally localized material
entity is meant. This is not the present sense. Our "systems" have to be
interpreted as abstract processes: continuous sequences of states (and
states are abstract, non-localized entities).
   The fact that the elements of the base set of our reconstruction of
thermodynamics are interpreted as abstract, non-localized entities and
that, consequently, space and time do not appear as basic concepts of
this theory, may appear as an inadequate feature of our reconstruction.
Following a Kantian line of reasoning, one may claim that space and
time should appear as basic concepts of any scientific theory, or at
least, of any theory of physical science. It might be argued that without
a spatio-temporal framework we cannot understand nature. However,
we do not see any clearly compelling reasons for this claim. Whatever
the metaphysical or epistemological motivations for it might be, we
have not found any formally sound argument for introducing space
and time in the reconstruction of this particular example of thermo-
dynamics. When we look at existing expositions of this theory, we find
that thermodynamics makes no essential use of space and time. It
would be ad hoc to introduce these notions in the axiomatization of the
theory. To be sure, when the practical consequences of the application
of thermodynamics are considered, we find spatio-temporally localized
systems. Similarly, we see that space and time are involved when we
consider the connections of thermodynamics to some mechanical the-
ories. Nevertheless, admitting these facts does not affect our view of the
theory's identity. Space and time are not needed to display thermo-
dynamics' formal structure nor to provide a general interpretation of its
basic concepts. The Kantian prejudice in favour of space and time as
synthetic a priori categories applicable to the totality of science has
some plausibility when we only consider mechanical theories (as Kant
himself did). But we know now that mechanical theories are not the
only possible kind of theory in physics, much less in the whole of
science. There is no reason to force all theories into a spatio-temporal
conceptual framework.
   The set of states Z needs some minimal structure which already puts
some restriction on its possible empirical interpretation. This structure
130                         CHAPTER THREE

is imposed by the bijective function cp, and it is needed in order to
apply the usual notions from analysis. Thus we say that S, for instance,
is smooth which means that i'p 0 S: IR1 ..... IR1 is smooth. We shall write DS
etc. as a shorthand notation for D( i'p 0 S). Also the notions of (relative)
maxima and minima, and of neighbourhood are to be understood in
terms of cpo That S has a relative maximum at Zo means that i'p 0 S has a
relative maximum at cp(zo). The reader will have no difficulties in filling
in these notions very precisely, if he wants to do so.
    ze is intended to be the set of all sequences of states within Z which
are in (total) equilibrium (with respect to SETH). That is, the whole
process represented by Z may alternatively undergo, in a finite number
of times, phases of equilibrium and of non-equilibrium. At least one
phase of equilibrium is required. The theory's laws, as we shall see, are
formulated for equilibrium states only. With the exception of the rather
new branch of "irreversible thermodynamics", all classical thermo-
dynamic theories "deal with" equilibrium states only, that is, their laws
are stated just for equilibrium states. This fact has led some authors
to maintain that the only systems possibly considered in "ordinary"
thermodynamics are just sets of equilibrium states (quasi-static pro-
cesses). If this had to be taken literally, then a consequent logical
reconstruction of SETH should take the term "state" as synonymous to
"equilibrium state". Curiously enough, even authors who seem to follow
this point of view in their introductory remarks (as Callen, [9]), when
the time has come for the concrete application of the general principles
of the theory, more or less implicitly assume the existence of non-
equilibrium states. They make assertions like: "if the system were not in
equilibrium, this would trigger a process such that ...". The concept of
a non-equilibrium state is certainly not meaningless, even if one is
applying equilibrium thermodynamics. Non-equilibrium states are
unavoidable, especially for an adequate interpretation and application
of Gibbs' extremum principle, and for the determination of the entropy
of composite systems. The restriction of the formalism to quasi-static
processes would make the theory unmanageable.
   Each phase of equilibrium of the system is supposed to be a sub-
process of the total process Z. That is, no "isolated points" among the
equilibrium states are admitted. This is entailed by the requirement that
for each e E ze cp( e) be an open interval. This condition is necessary
for guaranteeing the applicability of differentiation techniques to equi-
librium states. Physically, it does not mean any serious restriction of the
                   SOME BASIC THEORY-ELEMENTS                               131

 theory's scope. We are only interested in equilibrium situations which,
 so to speak, "endure for a while".
    The set of all equilibrium states is given by U    ze.  Since we are going
to use this set rather frequently, it is convenient to given it a special
name. Let us call it E.
    The primitive functions of SETH are volume V, mole numbers N,
energy U, and entropy S. All other metrical parameters appearing in
standard expositions of simple thermodynamics, like (absolute) tem-
perature, chemical potentials, enthalpy, free energy etc. can be defined
in terms of the preceding set of functions and their derivatives.
    Usually, instead of a single dyadic mole numbers function N, an
indeterminate set of different mole numbers functions N I , ••• , N n
(one for each chemical substance in the system) is introduced. How-
ever, it is more expedient to "summarize" the whole array of n
functions N I , ••• , N n in just one function N which is not only defined
on states but also on a finite set I of natural numbers. Each natural
number of this set is to be regarded as an index denoting a particular
substance in quite the same way as in CPM the index "i" in f(p, t, i)
denotes a particular force acting on p.
    In the following two concepts of mono tonicity are needed. The first
one corresponds to the standard notion of a function being mono-
tonically dependent on the values taken by its argument(s). The second
one corresponds to monotonicity in a derivative sense: we shall say that
a function f is monotonic wrt g if f does not decrease iff g does not
decrease either, which of course implies that f increases or keeps
constant iff g increases or keeps constant. This second, not so usual
sense of mono tonicity is particularly interesting for thermodynamics.
Let us state all this more formally.
    Assuming a fixed base for ~m, for any m, we shall say that a function

   Let f and g be two real-valued differentiable functions defined over
the same domain D. We say that f is monotonic wrt g iff, for all
xED, Df(x) ~ 0 iff Dg(x) ~ O. Clearly, this sort of monotonicity is
an equivalence relation between functions.

Condition (5) in (a) expresses the fundamental law of SETH. It for-
malizes the fundamental correlation between entropy and the rest of
thermodynamic parameters: In each equilibrium state the entropy is
determined through an unspecified functional F by energy, volume,
and mole numbers. In many textbooks, this functional correlation is
written in form of the equation "S = S( U, V, NJ', which is meant to
express, of course, that the values taken by the entropy (in equilibrium
states) depend on the values taken by. energy, volume, and mole
numbers. In our formulation, this dependence is represented by the
functional F. We call this function - the arguments of which are not
states, but tuples of real numbers - an "entropy determination". We
could say that the entropy is determined by the values of energy, etc.
"in the F way". The particular form of F can be different for different
kinds of systems (we shall see examples in the next chapter). Partic-
ular forms of F are specified through special laws of the theory.
M(SETH)-5 as stated in the core of SETH, does not specify anything.
It is a "general frame law". In a way analogous to Newton's second
law in CPM, this thermodynamic frame law is not "falsifiable". For
a given simple system, we try to apply the theory with a specific F; if
we do not get the desired results, we do not say the theory is falsified:
We just try another form of entropy determination (compare TIlI-IO)
below).
   By putting the entropy in a functional dependence of the other
primitives of SETH through F we say that we have chosen the
"entropy representation" of thermodynamics. But the requirements of
                   SOME BASIC THEORY-ELEMENTS                            133

fS being smooth and strictly increasing allow us to take any other of the
primitive functions and put it in an appropriate functional correlation
with entropy and the rest - for equilibrium states. In particular, we
could put the energy in a functional dependence of the rest. This would
be the "energy representation" of thermodynamics.

of hydrodynamics and equilibrium thermodynamics. This, of course, is
a metatheoretical hypothesis about the way this link is always used in
expositions of thermodynamics. Secondly, the link in question is a link

primarily we state the link between P on the one side and V and fV on

SETH, U depends on iV, it follows that in those states U also depends
on P. This further dependence is what is usually meant in textbooks
when a relationship between pressure and the differential of energy is
stated. This statement we obtain here as a corollary of the link.

111.5.3 The Partial Potential Models of SETH
Let us consider now the question of SETH-theoreticity, i.e. the distinc-
tion between SETH-theoretical and SETH-non-theoretical concepts.
Volume is a concept clearly belonging to physical geometry. There are
methods of determination of V (stereometric methods) which obviously
do not imply the fundamental equation of SETH. Hence, V is SETH-
non-theoretical. I and N are concepts of chemistry. In order to deter-
mine chemical substances and mole numbers chemists do not always
use thermodynamical methods. This indicates that I and N, too, are
SETH-non-theoretical.
   On the other hand, it also seems quite clear that entropy is not a
concept that would have any sense in an "SETH-ignorant" world.
Historically, the entropy concept was born with thermodynamics
proper; it is a SETH-specific concept, if there is anyone to be con-
sidered so. The decision appears to be more difficult to take in the case
of energy. Historically, the notion of (inner) energy grew up from a
combination of the concepts of "work" and "heat". For simple systems,
work is clearly a mechanical concept while heat is not mechanical.
Thermodynamics was primarily developed to account for the phe-
nomenon of "heat". Shall we then say that energy is partially theoretical
and partially non-theoretical with respect to thermodynamics? This
138                       CHAPTER THREE

would make no sense in the present formulation, because we have
introduced energy as one primitive concept; and so do most modern
quasi-axiomatic expositions of thermodynamics. Work and heat may be
introduced, if necessary, as defined concepts at a later stage.
   There have been attempts to expound methods for an "operational"
determination of energy in laboratory terms. But it is easy to see from
the descriptions used in these attempts that the pretended "direct
measurability" of energy depends on assumptions which only make
sense within thermodynamics. For example, one may try to show that,
in some cases, energy can be determined by measuring mechanical
work alone, that is, through an SETH-independent concept. In the case
of simple equilibrium thermodynamics, mechanical work is measured
by the product of pressure and change of volume. By means of the link
between energy and pressure formulated in the previous section, energy
could be determined through this kind of work. But this mechanical
determination of energy depends on a number of assumptions whose
exact formulation would be impossible without SETH's conceptual
apparatus. One has to assume, first, that some simple systems can be
enclosed by perfectly adiabatic walls; secondly, that they satisfy an
equation of the form
  (1)      DU(z) = T(z)' DS(z) - P(z)· DV(z),
i.e. that no change in the amount of the chemical substances present is
occurring; thirdly, that if the process which takes place within the
adiabatic walls is performed quasi-statically, the change of entropy will
be zero. From (1) and DS(z) = 0 one may determine the change of U
by measuring the compression work P(z)· D V(z). But this all means
that we have assumed laws and concepts of SETH being applicable to
the system. In particular, (1) is nothing but a special form of the
fundamental law of SETH (M(SETH-S) as given by TIIl-13). In this
case, our criterion of theoreticity can be applied in a quite plausible
way and we may draw the general conclusion that every determination
of energy values of a thermodynamic system relies on the SETH-
specific assumption that equation (1) is valid, and that concepts like
"adiabatic" and "quasi-static" may be applied. This makes the conclu-
sion plausible that energy is to be regarded as an SETH-theoretical
concept.
    Finally, we have to put the question of SETH-theoreticity with
respect to the concept of equilibrium, which is not a metrical function
                  SOME BASIC THEORY-ELEMENTS                           139

but a monadic predicate. That is, we have to ask whether the applica-
tion of the predicate "is in equilibrium" to a given state z of a potential
model implies that we are presupposing a model of SETH. Perhaps one
would think that it is very easy to decide whether a system is in
equilibrium or not without knowing anything about SETH: The ques-
tion could be settled by purely "observational" means: The system is in
equilibrium if and only if it is quiescent. But this would be a very naive
point of view. As a rule, one cannot be sure that the system is in
equilibrium without applying the theory itself. Here we have an
example of a concept which is not a function, the determination of
which, however, presupposes the application of the theory. We may
conclude that ze is SETH-theoretical. Thus, SETH's partial potential
models can be described as follows.

           x = (Z, N, IR, I, ze, V, N, U, S), x E Mp(SETH) wrt cp

The empirical claim formulated with M(SETH) alone is trivial.

   So we need links and constraints in order to obtain a non-trivial
empirical claim. In fact, some of the most interesting "laws" of SETH in
the present frame have to be expressed as constraints. We shall con-
sider quite a number of them.


III.5.4 Constraints for SETH
Most constraints of thermodynamics have to be formulated by using a
concatenation operation "0", whose properties and role are similar to
the concatenation operation already introduced in mechanics to express
additivity of mass. But concatenation appears to be more significant in
thermodynamics than in mechanics.
   Let us first explain the structure and role of thermodynamic con-
140                                       CHAPTER THREE

catenation in physically intuitive terms. Suppose the system described
by a model x consists of a gas enclosed in a box. Only one wall of the
box is not totally unpermeable. Suppose the same is true for another x'.
Let us concentrate on the energy functions U and U'. If the system in
state z E Z has energy U(z), we can imagine some later state Zl in
which the energy U(ZI) is less than before: U(ZI) ~ U(z). Intuitively,
this might happen because some of the molecules have left the box by
passing through the distinguished wall. A similar situation is possible
for x'. So far, there is no connection between x and x'. Whatever the
energy U(z) in x in state z may be, this does not give us information
about the energy U'(z') in x' in state z'. Moreover, we cannot know
whether and how the decrease of energy in x depends on the change in
x'.
    But let us now concatenate both systems in such a way that the
distinguished walls come to lie exactly on each other as shown in Figure
III-l. (Part of the considerations issuing from this example already were
put up in Ch. II when we introduced the notion of constraints for the
first time; but now we can be more precise in our discussion and make
use of the conceptual frame of SETH at hand.)

   Intuitively, this combined system is closed. Its total energy is just the
sum of both parts' energy. How can we describe this more precisely?
   First, we introduce a concatenation operation for states of different
models. Out of two states z and z' of models x and x' the concatena-
tion operation (which we denote by "0") forms a new state z 0 z'.
Intuitively, this is the state of the system resulting from the combination
of the two original systems. It is most natural to imagine the com-
bination of two systems as a putting together of both systems in such a
way that some kind of interaction is possible (as depicted in Figure
                   SOME BASIC THEORY-ELEMENTS                           141

III-1). Any two states of the original systems then uniquely determine a
corresponding state of the total system.
   Having understood this intuitive idea it must at once be stressed that
it only covers a very special case. Concatenation of two systems need
not necessarily be performed in space. The general, abstract situation is
this. We have two systems x and x' which may interact or not. Now,
conceptually, we build the concatenation of both systems' states. This
can be done even if x and x' do not interact and do not change. That is,
we formally establish a binary function 0 on the sets of states Z and Z'
of x and x', i.e. from Z X Z' into a new set of states Z". The difficulty
here is to determine the new set of states Z" independently of Z and
Z'. It appears that the elements of Z" only come into being as con-
catenations of states in Z and Z'. On the other hand, they cannot be
defined explicitly in terms of Z and Z', since we have no means to
describe exactly how the states of Z and Z' have to be combined. We
must assume that the concatenation of states forms a set of states
belonging to some reasonable potential model of SETH. That is, we
must assume that for any two systems x and x' in Mp(SETH) there
exists an x" in Mp(SETH) with a set of states Z" such that the con-
catenation of two states of x and x' always is a member of Z". Again, as
in the case of mechanics, 0 cannot be defined explicitly. We assume
that an operation 0 can be established on the union of all the states of
potential models such that to any two states it assigns their concatena-
tion. Formally, there exists an operation 0 such that
           0: I; X I; ..... 1;, where
            I; := U {Zxlx E Mp(SETH) l
Intuitively, I; contains all states occurring in any of the potential models
of SETH. Thus 0 is added to the basic concepts of SETH.
   Now, we can ask, referring back to our example: If two systems are
combined by 0, what is the effect on the energy functions U, U', and
 U"? As we argued in the discussion of the example of Figure III-1, we
expect the energy U" of the combined system to be just the sum of the
energies of the original systems. That is, for any two states Z E Z
and z' E Z' we expect U"(z 0 z') to equal U(z) + U'(z'). Indeed, this
additivity requirement is generally accepted in SETH. Note that all the
considerations about concatenation were necessary only in order to
state the additivity of energy (as well as the other constraints to follow)
in precise terms.
142                        CHAPTER THREE

    Clearly, this requirement on the energy function works "across"
 different applications. For it requires that for any two applications there
 exists a third application consisting roughly of the concatenation of
 both original applications which is connected with the latter in a
 specific way. This requirement is of crucial importance for SETH. For
 if we could not concatenate different thermodynamical systems in
 different ways the whole theory would degenerate into a very poor
 fragment of nearly no practical interest. Constraints are central in
 thermodynamics.

compound system will attain an i -equilibrium corresponding to gi iff
the total entropy attains a maximum. Similarly for the energy: if the
total entropy is kept constant, then the system attains an i-equilibrium
iff the energy has a minimum.

III.S.S Links for SETH
In previous sections we already introduced and discussed the role of
a link between thermodynamics and hydrodynamics, viz. L1 (SETH)
linking the differential quotient of energy with respect to volume to
pressure.
   Another link that would certainly belong to a complete presentation
of SETH would be one relating volume as it appears in SETH to some
underlying theory of physical geometry or of the fundamental measure-
ment of length. However, since it is not clear to us which of these
underlying theories should best be chosen nor exactly how the link
looks like, we leave its concrete formulation as an open question and
introduce the link only as an undefined L 2 (SETH).
   On the other hand, a further link we are in a position to state
explicitly and which also is quite essential for the application of thermo-
dynamics is the one relating the mole numbers appearing in models of
SETH to the molcular weights of DSTOI. Informally, the mole number
of a substance present in a given system may be determined as the ratio
of the total weight of that substance to its characteristic molecular
weight (sometimes also called "molar mass" - cf. Callen, [91, p. 8).
Since we already have reconstructed Daltonian stoichiometry, which is
the theory determining molecular weights, there is, in principle, no
problem in stating this link within our frame. It should only be remem-
bered that, though the weight function w directly applies to a given
substance, the molecular weight does not directly apply to substances
but rather to formulas corresponding to these substances; this is why

                  111.6 LAGRANGIAN MECHANICS

III.6.1 The Potential and Actual Models of LAG
We consider Lagrangian mechanics as a distinct theory not to be
identified with classical mechanics. Its basic concepts and fundamental
law are different from those of CPM. However, Lagrangian mechanics
has a sort of symbiotic relationship to Newtonian mechanics. Actually,
Lagrangian mechanics (denoted by "LAG") is sometimes expounded in
textbooks with an explicit statement of its relationship to CPM. This
means that the intertheoretical links will play a very important role in
the reconstruction of LAG. We shall deal with those links here in detail.
   The reason for treating LAG after SETH - and not in immediate
150                        CHAPTER THREE

connection with CPM - is that LAG is an abstract theory in the same
way SETH is, and that after having seen a "non-mechanical" abstract
theory it is easier to see the difference between "concrete" CPM and
"abstract" LAG. Instead of "particles" and "positions" LAG is about
"degrees of freedom" and "generalized coordinates". The latter are
abstract entities which in some cases can be regarded as Cartesian
coordinates but must not be regarded so in general. The leading idea
behind LAG is to provide a "scalar" (i.e. non-vectorial), "equivalent"
description of mechanics. The key to this description is energy. The
theory is built upon kinetic energy which, for a single particle, is
defined by 1!2m(Dr)2. Along with its non-vectorical formulation come
the generalized coordinates. By the transition from Cartesian to gener-
alized coordinates the assignment of three dimensions to each particle
in the description of the system is abandoned. If we collect the different
position functions rp from CPM into a single, vector-valued function
 r*: IR ~ IR3n, defined by r*(t) = (r(PI' t), ... , r(Pn' t) (where P =
{PI' ... , Pn}), then r* yields a complete kinematical description of the
system with particles P. Range(r*) = IR3n is called the phase-space. For
many n-particle systems, however, the image r*(IR) in the phase-space
has less than 3 n dimensions. This is a typical case where generalized
coordinates are introduced. Instead of describing the systems by r*
one introduces as many generalized coordinates as are necessary. Their
number, h, is at least equal to the dimension of r*(IR) and is called
the number of degrees of freedom of the system. A system with h
degrees of freedom needs h independent generalized coordinates for
its description.
    We could use the connection to Cartesian descriptions in order to
explicitly define the minimal number of degrees of freedom by means
of r*(IR). But it seems too restrictive to consider only systems which are
described by independent coordinates. Therefore we treat this number
as a basic concept. The other concepts of LAG are time, generalized
coordinates ij - which generalize the concept of position function
- kinetic energy K and generalized forces Q.

III.6.2 The Partial Potential Models of LAG
As concerns theoreticity it is not difficult to see that h, T, c and ij are
LAG-non-theoretical. LAG, among other things, deals with n-particle
systems where h = 3n and T, ij are time and Cartesian position
function, respectively. And, among these systems, certainly there are
systems for which h, T, c and ij are determined - as in CPM - in a
theory-independent way. The determination of K - even in such non-
abstract systems in which h, T and ij are interpreted in a "Cartesian"
way - presupposes a determination of mechanical mass and therefore
presupposes CPM, or "equivalently", LAG. In case of abstract systems
we have no idea at all how to determine K without the theory. The
same is true for Q. SO the partial potential models look like this.

III.6.3 Constraints and Links for LAG
It is difficult to see how in this abstract formulation constraints could be
introduced. Typically, equality constraints are "fixed on" particles. But
particles are replaced here by degrees of freedom, so equality con-
                    SOME BASIC THEORY-ELEMENTS                        153

straints loose their meaning. We have no identity criteria for degrees of
freedom and we cannot say whether a degree of freedom is the same in
two different systems. Another possibility is to "fix" an equality con-
straint on the generalized coordinates. If two systems have the same
generalized coordinates then their theoretical functions, K and Q
should be the same. But this does not express something like an inner
property of some entity, rather it amounts to the triviality of excluding
different theoretical terms from the treatment of one and the same
system. (Note that our meta-theoretical notion of constraints has
nothing at all to do with what is usually called "constraint" in LAG.)
   Intuitively, constraints for LAG make sense only if we interpret LAG
through Cartesian coordinates, or, in other words, if we link LAG to
CPM. In fact this link is essential for LAG. Without it the abstract
theory would be hard to understand and hard to use. LAG's link with
CPM is defined as follows.

The link essentially contains a function X which maps points of the
154                       CHAPTER THREE

generalized phase-space: <q(l, t), ... , q( h, t) into values of the
Cartesian position function of the system. We have to imagine x and y
as potential models describing the "same" physical system in the two
different frames. Under this assumption it must be possible to "trans-
late" the description in terms of generalized coordinates into a descrip-
tion with a position function. This translation is provided by X. X takes
as "input" information about all generalized coordinates at a certain
point of time t, and some distinct particle p. As "output" X yields the
position of p at time t. Since this connection is required for all p
and t, it yields the Cartesian position function in terms of generalized
coordinates. The connection between particles and degrees of freedom,
i.e. between P and h, is not made explicit by X. It is, of course,
contained in X implicitly. Condition (2.2) is a condition of "well-
behavedness" of X. Intuitively it requires that X be smooth but since
this makes no sense for a function like X we have to use coordinatiza-
tions. Conditions (3) and (4) of the link require the usual appropriate
identities between kinetic energy and mass times velocity squared on
the one hand, and work in the Lagrangian and the Newtonian repre-
sentations on the other.
    By means of this link every potential model of LAG is connected
with a potential model of CPM. And via this connection every potential
model of LAG can be regarded as a different, "equivalent" description
of some potential classical particle mechanics. On the other hand, the
link permits a treatment of Lagrangian systems without explicit re-
ference to mechanical particle systems, that is, a "pure" mathematical
treatment which neglects the connection between generalized coordi-
nates and Cartesian position functions.

111.6.4 The Theory-Element of LAG

As intended applications of LAG one could imagine, first, the usual
mechanical systems, and second, abstract systems. But it is not clear
how abstract systems are tied to real systems by means of the para-
digmatic method discussed in Ch. II. Even if we admit that the para-
digm applications all are ordinary mechanical systems we do not know
by what standards of similarity we can come to abstract systems. We
must conclude that among LAG's intended applications there, do not
occur systems in which hand q describe abstract entities. Rather, the
intended applications all seem to tJe mechanical systems which could be
described as potential models of CPM as well.
                 SOME BASIC THEORY-ELEMENTS                            155

   But still there seems to be a difference between I(LAG) and I(CPM).
For I(CPM) seems not to contain systems in which "physical con-
straints" (which are not to be confused with our constraints) are
present. Physical constraints are requirements on the generalized
coordinates (or the position functions) in one single model. They
express, for instance, that some of the particles of the system are rigidly
connected with each other. One of the main domains of application of
LAG are just systems in which these physical constraints are essential.
LAG allows to treat them much more elegantly than CPM does. So
among the intended applications of LAG we should expect to find
description of systems with physical constraints, for instance coupled
pendulae (pendulae connected by rigid rods).

     T(LAG) := (K(LAG), I(LAG) where
     K(LAG) = (Mp(LAG), M(LAG), Mpp(LAG), GC(LAG), L(LAG)
     where GC(LAG) is determined by "translating" GC(CPM) into
     LAG by means of L(LAG), and I(LAG) ~ Mpp(LAG) is such that
     the elements of I(LAG) are as those in I(CPM), presumably
     submitted to physical constraints.


                111.7 PURE EXCHANGE ECONOMICS


III. 7.1 The Potential and Actual Models of PEE
Pure exchange economics is a very basic part of microeconomics as
presented in textbooks. The object of exchange economics is indicated
in its name. It deals with exchange processes. Exchange lies at the heart
of every economic system if we understand by economic system a
system in which people interact for the sake of their own provision.
   For the purpose of illustrating a logical reconstruction of an eco-
nomic theory we may concentrate on the simplest form of exchange.
More sophisticated and realistic versions may be treated as specializa-
tions or extensions, once the basic structures are understood clearly.
The simplest case is that of mere exchange without production and
without money. It is difficult to imagine that such systems can still be
found in our present-day world. But even if more realistic specializa-
tions of the simple original systems did not exist, there would still be
some point for the philosopher of science to reconstruct this crude
theory because it actually appears in expositions of micro-economics.
156                        CHAPTER THREE

   Our reconstruction will deal only with what is called pure exchange.
This theory assumes different quantities of different commodities to be
given. How these commodities are produced and how they come to be
distributed initially among the different individuals is ignored in the
present context. It is simply assumed that an initial distribution of the
commodities among the individuals is given. What the theory describes,
then, is how people try to increase their utilities by exchanging these
commodities. Although no concept of time is involved it is helpful to
imagine the situation as evolving in three steps. Initially, a distribution
of commodities qO is given. In a second step, exchanges are performed
until nobody wants or can exchange any more. The latter may occur if
some person has come to a point where he needs all his commodities
for his own provision. In the final stage, after exchanges have been
performed, we have a new distribution of commodities. The theory tells
us that this process is governed by certain rules. If the individuals act
according to these rules, then the new distribution will satisfy certain
requirements which can be stated in the form of axioms. This is the
essential "trick": Instead of stating axioms about actions one uses
axioms describing distributions which are the results of such actions.
This allows us to formulate the axioms in economic terms. If the theory
directly referred to actions, one would need basic concepts describing
certain human activities. Such concepts, besides being hard to deal with,
are not typically economical. Although· by reading textbooks in eco-
nomics one might get the impression that the authors are formulating
theories about the economic behavior of individuals (i.e. about human
actions), a deeper analysis shows that they only use a realistic language
as a way of talking. In fact, they are referring to prices, quantities of
commodities and utilities - and not to the underlying human actions.
   Let us come to the formalization of the structures of the theory of
pure exchange economics (abbreviated as PEE). A potential model of
PEE is aq entity consisting of a set J of individuals, a set G of kinds
of commodities, a function ij, giving the total quantities of each kind
of commodity, an initial distribution qO, a price function p, a utility
function U and a set of final distributions E.

Mp(PEE): x is a potential pure exchange economy (x E Mp(PEE)) iff
         there exist J, G, ij, qO, U, p, E such that
     (1) x = (1, G, IR, ij, qO, U, p, E)
     (2) J is a finite, non-empty set

       (3) G = {il,' .. , im } ~ N where i l < i2 < ... < im

    For reasons of convenience we use natural numbers in order to refer

111.7.2 The Partial Potential Models of PEE
As far as the question of theoreticity is concerned it is clear that
quantities of commodities can be measured in a PEE-independent way.
So qO and ij are PEE-non-theoretical. The utility function U is PEE-
non-theoretical, too. In order to determine utilities one can resort to
preferences. Preferences may be determined without using or pre-
supposing exchange theory, and by knowing enough about a person's
preference relation one may be able to infer this person's utility func-
tion. Technically speaking such an inference is expressed by relating
utility functions U to "underlying" preference relations :5 in the follow-
ingway:
  (1)       foralla,b:a:5 biffU(a) ~ U(b)
The most natural way of depicting this situation is by means of a link
which "imports" data about preferences from some theory of pre-
ferences by transforming these data into data about utility-values in
PEE. In the light of our informal criterion of theoreticity the con-
siderations above suggest that utility is PEE-non-theoretical because
there is a means of determining U which does not presuppose PEE.
Also, our formal criterion af theoreticity in the present case yields a
160                        CHAPTER THREE

clear-cut result, namely that U is formally PEE-non-theoretical. Intui-
tively, this is due to the fact that PEE's axioms do not permit any
formal determination of U in terms of the other concepts of PEE.
   The remaining relations, namely price, p, and the final distributions,
E, are PEE-theoretical. In case of the price function the argument is
this. In the models of PEE the prices are to satisfy rather strong
conditions. At those prices, final distributions have to exist. That is,
prices have to be such that people can maximize their utilities with
respect to these prices, or, more precisely, with respect to the budget
restriction in which the prices play an essential role. If final distribu-
tions were what economists call equilibrium distributions then we might
say that the prices occurring in models of PEE have to be equilibrium
prices. Actually, the concept of equilibrium as used by economists
besides maximization of utilities comprises another condition, namely
that all markets be cleared:
           for all g E G and q E E:    I      q(i, g) =    I      qO(i, g).
                                      i E J               i E J


But even if this additional requirement need not be satisfied in models
of PEE - so that prices need not be equilibrium prices proper - our
reference to the concept of equilibrium should have cleared the situa-
tion. Roughly, though not quite correctly, the price function in PEE
expresses equilibrium prices. Now consider any method for the actual
determination of prices which refers to prices "read off" from the
economic system and which is thus independent of PEE. Such a
method cannot guarantee that the prices actually determined will be
equilibrium prices. So one would not say that by means of such a
method one really had determined prices. The only way to guarantee
that the "external" determination of prices yields "correct" results, i.e.
the prices of PEE, "equilibrium prices", is to assume that PEE is valid
during the determination. That is, in any "correct" determination of p,
PEE has to be presupposed. In the light of our criterion of theoreticity
this means that the price function is PEE-theoretical. And the argument
remains valid if "equilibrium price" is replaced by "price as determined
in models of PEE" because the latter concept is an essential part of the
former.
   In addition to these intuitive considerations it could be proven that
according to our formal criterion of theoreticity prices are formally
PEE-theoretical, too. We therefore conclude that p is PEE-theoretical.
                  SOME BASIC THEORY-ELEMENTS                          161

   Finally, with respect to E the situation is this. In order to determine
E it is necessary and sufficient to have a method for determining
whether a given distribution q belongs to E or not. But this can be
done only by checking whether the conditions for E stated in the
definition of the models of PEE are satisfied. If q is to be in E the
conditions have to obtain. Since these conditions are just the axioms of
PEE we have stated, then q can be in E only if the system under
consideration is a model of PEE, which means that according to our
criterion of theoreticity E is PEE-theoretical. We note that this is the
case with respect to the formal criterion of theoreticity, too.

IIL7.3 The Theory-Element oj PEE
We do not introduce constraints or links in the present reconstruction
of PEE. On the one hand, there appear to be no interesting constraints
on the PEE-theoretical notions. The values of the theoretical prices are
fully dependent on each particular market considered; and the same
goes for the equilibrium of the final distributions. Perhaps we could
advance the hypothesis that the inexistence of non-trivial constraints is
a common feature of primitive economic theories like the present one.
This, among other things, might explain the poor predictive capacities
of such theories.
   As for links, in a completely neat reconstruction of PEE we should
at least explicitly introduce the above-mentioned link PEE must have to
some underlying theory of preferences in order to determine its utilities.
However, since the nature of such underlying theory is not all clear, we
leave the specific form of this link as an open question here.
   The set I(PEE) of intended applications is hard to describe. We can-
not point out a single concrete situation which is commonly accepted
by economists as a standard example of PEE. There are no paradigms.
But we must not conclude that therefore PEE is not an empirical
theory at all. Unlike the applications of physical theories, the concrete
situations to be treated by PEE - e.g. some specific village at some
specific time - are difficult to record. First, they are very complex,
162                       CHAPTER THREE

second, one cannot reproduce situations that are similar even in a weak
sense of "similarity". A moment's reflection on what is involved in the
description of a partial potential model of PEE should convince us that
real situations have existed (or still do exist) which can be described as
partial potential models of PEE. For all we need are sets of individuals,
kinds of commodities, and an initial distribution.
    It may be noted that a survey of the literature in theoretical econom-
ics suggests that theoretical economists are not interested in empirical
applications of their abstract concepts. Some authors conclude that
economics is a "pure" science in contrast to "empirical" ones like
physics. However, a similar picture is obtained from reviewing the
literature of some theoretical branch of a natural science. In physics
textbooks or journals on theoretical physics we rarely 'find references to
some concrete real system or application; in spite of this fact it is
maintained that theoretical physics is empirical. To our mind, the
deeper ground for the widespread mistrust of the empirical character
of theoretical economics lies in the fact that the interplay between
theoretical and experimental ("applied") branches in the natural
sciences functions in a well standardized way, whereas in economics
this interplay (with econometrics at the "applied" side) is not yet
developed to the same extent as in the natural sciences.

                          THEORY-NETS



                         IV.O INTRODUCTION

The term "scientific theory" is ambiguous; or better: polisemic. It can
mean a number of identifiable different things. Sometimes just a law
(i.e., in our terminology, a condition determining a model) is meant.
Sometimes, the use of the term "theory" corresponds to the "theory-
elements" we have defined in Chapter II and exemplified in Chapter III.
In many cases the intuition behind the usage of the term "theory" is
still more embracing. "Theory" can mean something like a whole array
of inter-connected theory-elements, all of which have "the same struc-
ture". The present chapter is devoted to the reconstruction of such
"bigger" entities, which we shall call "theory-nets". They correspond to
what is probably the most wide-spread intuition about what a theory is
like. Still, sometimes an even more embracing notion of "theory" can be
met. A "theory" then is something which develops in time preserving a
sort of genidentical identity (like a person or a community). In this case
we shall speak of a "theory-evolution". Such entities can also be defined
within our present metatheoretical framework, as will be seen in the
next chapter. There might still be other meanings of the term "theory"
but we need not embark on a philological investigation for our present
purposes.
    We discuss the fundamental relation of "specialization" that holds
between individual theory-elements in the same "theory" in Sec. IV.l.
We illustrate it with two simple examples from classical collision
mechanics (CCM). "Theory-nets" composed of theory-elements related
by specialization are discussed in Sec. IV.2 and again illustrated by
classical collision mechanics. Various alternative ways of extending the
concept of "empirical claim" from theory-elements to theory-nets are
considered in Sec. IV.3. In Secs. IV.4 and IV.S these ideas are illu-
strated by more interesting examples of classical particle mechanics
(CPM) and simple equilibrium thermodynamics (SETH).



                                  167
168                        CHAPTER FOUR

                       IV.l SPECIALIZATIONS

When we reconstruct the conceptual structures of the standard exposi-
 tions of a "theory", very often we do not encounter just one theory-
 element in our sense. Normally, we find many. And they often appear
interrelated by a sort of hierarchical ordering.
    It would be inadequate to say that the theory expounded is just one
of these theory-elements, the rest being only a sort of inessential
"appendix". For example, it would be intuitively inadequate to say that
"the theory of classical particle mechanics" reduces to the theory-
element we have reconstructed in the preceding chapter as CPM.
Besides the primitive concepts (particle, space, time, position, mass,
force), Newton's second law, and the constraints for mass and force,
standard expositions of classical particle mechanics contain something
else - some further conditions which cannot be understood as inter-
theoretical links either. When considering our reconstruction of CPM,
the reader might already have asked himself where we have left such
important laws of classical particle mechanics as Newton's third law
(the actio-reactio principle), the law of gravitation, or Hooke's law. Our
answer is: They all constitute different but interrelated theory-elements
of classical particle mechanics. The whole array, in turn, constitutes
what we might call "the theory-net of classical particle mechanics". The
same holds for other advanced theories of empirical science. In the case
of simple equilibrium thermodynamics, besides the fundamental equa-
tion and the constraints and links (which, admittedly, provide much of
the content of this theory), one would like to see Nernst's "Third
Principle of Thermodynamics", Gay-Lussac's law, and other more
special laws. Many of these more special laws of the theory are,
moreover, associated with particular constraints and, possibly, partic-
ular links, besides those already explicated when dealing with the
"basic" theory-elements. In other words, the consideration of all these
further requirements will end up in the reconstruction of a whole series
of different theory-elements, which, however, have the same basic
structure. Because of this similarity of structure, we can speak of a
theory-net and not just an amorphous set of single, isolated theory-
elements.
    One could very well wonder why we need all these different but
related theory-elements: Why not simply lump together all those further
laws and constraints in just one big theory-element, containing all laws
                             THEORY-NETS                               169

(as fundamental laws defining the set-theoretic predicate), all con-
straints, all links?
    We could do this (even at the price of tremendous clumsiness) if all
laws, constraints, and links really stood on the same footing and if they
were applied to the same range of intended applications. But this is not
the case. We have to take into account the fact that our theory-concept
includes not only the formal structure known as the "core" but also the
range of applications I. Once we remind ourselves of this, we under-
stand immediately that the different laws cannot be on the same footing.
It is clearly not the same to try to apply, say, Newton's second law and
Hooke's law. The latter has a much more restricted scope of empirical
application and is in a sense subordinate to the acceptance of Newton's
second law. We do not try to apply a very special law of a theory when
we know that the fundamental law and constraints do not apply to this
case; but the converse, of course, is not true.
    From a model-theoretic point of view the addition of more special
laws to the already existing fundamental laws can be regarded as
"carving" out of the set of actual models M(T) a subset M' (T) deter-
mined by a set-theoretic predicate satisfying more restrictive conditions
and intended to apply to a more limited empirical range, i.e. to a subset
of I(T). For example, by adding Hooke's law to basic classical particle
mechanics we define a set-theoretic predicate the models of which must
satisfy Newton's second law together with Hooke's law, thereby forming
a subset of M(CPM). These models are supposed to apply to cases of
elastic forces as exemplified by the so-called free harmonic oscillators.
This range of application clearly is much more limited th~m the whole
range of intended applications of CPM. In the process, we might also
(though this is not necessarily always the case) add some more special
constraints and links. The result of this construction will be a theory-
element that will have a more restricted scope than the original one, but
the same conceptual structure, i.e. the same primitive concepts and the
same distinction between the theoretical and the non-theoretical level.
In other words, though the classes of actual models, constraints, links,
and intended applications of the new theory-element will be subsets of
the original ones, the classes of potential and of partial potential models
will be the same sets. The relationship between the two theory-elements
considered can be called a relation of specialization. The new theory-
element is "more specialized" than the original one (though belonging
to the same "conceptual structure"). Other equivalent expressions for
170                         CHAPTER FOUR

this situation would be: That the new theory-element "presupposes" the
original one, that it "gives a more detailed picture", that it is "less
fundamental" or "less basic", etc. Foqnally, we define the relation as
follows. As in Ch. II, we shall define the concepts of idealized speciali-
zation, idealized specialization nets, etc., but informally omit the label
"idealized" until we come to Ch. VII.
DIV-I:       If T = (Mp, M, M pp ' GC, GL, I) and T' = (M~, M', M~p,
             GC', GL', 1') are idealized theory-elements, then T' is an
             idealized specialization of T (abbreviated as T' a T) iff:
         (1) M~ = Mp and M~p = Mpp
         (2) M' ~ M, GC' ~ GC, GL' ~ GL, and I' ~ I
By DIV-I we formally have defined a binary relation a on the class of
all possible theory-elements. This relation a, restricted to any given set
of pairs of theory-elements will be called a specialization relation.
    We note in the following theorem that the specialization relation on
theory-elements has some intuitively desired properties. Specializations
apply to "special cases" of the initial range of intended applications I
(TIV-Ja below). Specializations narrow down the empirical content of
the initial theory-element-core (TIV-I-b). When constraints are transi-
tive the applications for the specialization are always in the empirical
content of the initial theory-element-core, provided its own applications
are (i.e. provided its claim is true) (TIV-J-c).
TIV-J:       If T and T' are theory-elements, if T has transitive con-
             straints and T' a T then:
         (a) I' ~ I
         (b) Cn(K') ~ Cn(K)
         (c) ifl E CoCK) then I' E Cn(K)
   Proof: TIV-J-a is just a direct consequence of DIV-I-2. As for
TIV-I-b and c they can very easily be derived from DIV-J-2 by
assuming that constraints are transitive. #

Let us explicitly illustrate this general notion of a specialization by
means of a rather simple but important example taken from physics.
The fundamental law of classical collision mechanics, as we have seen,
is the law of conservation of momentum, which is supposed to apply to
all kinds of collisions (at not too high velocities). However, we can add
more content to the theory by' specializing the basic set-theoretic
                              THEORY-NETS                                171

predicate, CCM into structures which are applicable to more special
kinds of collisions and which add more quantitative information about
them. Two such specializations are the cases of elastic collisions and of
perfectly inelastic collisions. Historically, they already played an im-
portant role in the development of collision mechanics in the 17th
century, and today they still are of didactical and practical significance.
In order to deal with the first kind of collisions most adequately, we
add the law of conservation of (kinetic) energy to the law of conserva-
tion of momentum. For the second case, we require that the velocities
of all particles after collision be the same. The corresponding set-
theoretic predicates determined by this additional requirements are,
respectively, as follows.

172                         CHAPTER FOUR

                          IV.2 THEORY-NETS

Any given theory-element may be connected by the specialization
relation with quite a number of other theory-elements, either by being a
specialization of them or by having them as specializations. In other
words, the specialization relation can impose a structure on some given
set of theory-elements by telling which theory-elements are speciali-
zations of which others in that set. The resulting structure can be
graphically depicted as a net the knots of which are theory-elements
and the cords of which represent the specialization relation. Such a
structure we call a theory-net. We are going to consider some examples
of theory-nets below. For the time being let us define the general
concept.

It is easy to see that any theory-net N is a poset (a partially ordered
set). That is, the specialization relation defined on a set of theory-

ordering the set of theory-elements.

    Proof: According to DIV-J, the specialization relation between

identity and inclusion are both reflexive, transitive, and antisymmetric it
follows immediately that the specialization relation also is reflexive,
transitive and antisymmetric. #

  Therefore, the notion formalized in DIV-2 is still too general for our

  is violated if the net consists of subnets which are not really con-

  rule out such cases of "anarchical" theory-nets in principle and this is
  why we have held DIV-2 very general. These abnormal nets might be
  applicable in some cases. However, they do not seem to correspond to
  the real cases of theories we have in mind. Normal theory construction
  does not seem to be prone to such forms of "anarchism" but rather
  (pace Feyerabend) to a highly hierarchized ordering of theory-elements.
  Therefore, it seems convenient to introduce a more stringent notion of
  a theory-net, which excludes the former abnormality and which seems
  to be applicable to all relevant cases. This notion is that of a connected
  theory-net. We obtain this concept by requiring of a theory-net N that
  any two different theory-elements of N must be either specializations of
  some other common "superior" theory-element, or else must have a
  common specialization themselves. The example of Figure IV-1 b is
  thereby excluded.

                              THEORY-NETS                              175

which are singletons, that is, those N for which there is a unique
To E t with B(N) = {Tal. It is an interesting fact about science that all
scientific theories we have reconstructed so far have this property. They
appear to have a single basic or "fundamental" theory-element (of a
quite general conceptual nature) such that all other theory-elements in
that theory are its specializations. This roughly means that there is one
single fundamental law which is intended to apply to the whole range of
intended applications, whereas all other laws are applied only to partial
domains of this range. (Of course, besides the fundamental law of this
basic theory-element, there will also be its basic constraints and links
playing an analogous role with respect to more special constraints and
links.)
   The graphs representing connected theory-nets with a single basic
element might be called trees. This denomination is, intuitively speak-
ing, not very appropriate for a natural tree does not only have a trunk
and branches but also roots ramified in the opposite direction. How-
ever, since that term is used for similar graphs in logic and mathematics
we will adopt it here and call theory-nets of this type tree-like theory-
nets, or for short, theory-trees.

DIV-5:     N is an idealized theory-tree iff:
       (1) N is a connected theory-net.
       (2) B(N) is a singleton.

It seems that most entities that we call "scientific theories", at least in
the relatively advanced branches of science, have the structure of a
theory-tree. All theories dealt with in this book certainly have this
structure. The tree of classical collision mechanics as reconstructed
before is a very simple one:

176                          CHAPTER FOUR

We conjecture that all theories of mathematized science, in particular
those of physics, are tree-like. This, in turn, would lend some plausi-
bility to the structures of scientific theories intuitively propounded by
the metatheories of Kuhn and Lakatos, respectively. This issue will be
discussed with some more detail in the next chapter. Of course, there is
also a possibility that in other branches, or in a less developed stage of
science the implicit structure of theories will not appear to be tree-like.
It could be the case, for example, that at the beginnings of a new
discipline, theories are constructed by starting from different, though
compatible, bases which then "converge" into a common specialization,
which is, so to speak, their intersection. In these cases, connected
theory-nets, but not tree-like ones would be adequate in order to depict
the situation. However, since we have not explored this possibility in
concrete cases, we shall say nothing more about it here.
   The ordering of the theory-elements of a theory given by the speciali-
zation relation into a theory-net gives rise to corresponding orderings
of their respective component parts, i.e. their cores and ranges of
applications. In other words, the construction of a theory-net induces
the construction of a corresponding net of cores and of a corresponding
net of ranges of applications. Of course, this is valid not only for nets in
general but also for connected and tree-like theory-nets. Thus, once we
have any of these kinds of theory-nets we can define the corresponding
core-nets and application-nets.

      IV.3 THEORY-NET CONTENT AND EMPIRICAL CLAIM

In Chapter II the empirical claim of any theory-element T = (K, I) was
construed as a propostion of the form I E CoCK). Now, in the case of a
theory-net we have as many particular empirical claims as there are
theory-elements in the net. The global claim of the theory-net will be
just the conjunction of all these particular claims.
DIV-8:       If N = (t, a) is an idealized theory-net, then we define as
             its empirical claim the proposition:
             For all (K, I) E t: I E CoCK).
In the case of a non-connected theory-net with possibly unrelated
subnets, its global claim will consist of just a more or less amorphous
conjunction of particular empirical claims. In the case of a connected
theory-net the global claim will be a bit more substantial, since all its
particular claims will refer to the same "empirical ground" Mpp (accord-
ing to TIV-3). But the really interesting case is the global claim for a
178                         CHAPTER FOUR

theory-tree. Here, all particular ranges of intended applications I; of the
theory-elements in the net are subsets of the basic range 10 of the basic
element (K o, 10). In this case, the global claim is that the basic range 10
can be subsumed under the basic core Ko and that the particular
subsets I; of 10 can be dealt with by adding some more restrictive
conditions to those of K o, namely the conditions defining the different
K;. Note that the claim for the basic element (Ko, 10 ) (the "basic
claim"), i.e. that 10 E Cn(Ko) may be vacuous, because of Cn(Ko) =
Po(Mpp), and yet the global claim of the net may be non-vacuous
because Cn(K;) ;;: Po(Mpp) for at least some specializations K; of Ko.
Even if the basic claim is not vacuous, it can be "very weak" (as appears
to be the case in CPM); however, the theory as a whole may produce
an empirical claim that is not at all weak, because very strong speciali-
zations are added (again, this appears to be so for CPM).
   The form of the claim treated in DIV-8 appears particularly simple
but it may be doubted whether this is the only form of empirical claims
to be encountered in science. As soon as there is more than one theory-
element at hand, other forms of empirical claims are possible. We can
imagine two types of claims different from that of DIV-8. In one type
the assignment of cores to sets of intended applications might be
weakened, and might become part· of the claim itself. In DIV-8 this
assignment is taken as given: sets of intended applications and cores are
assigned to each other in the same way as they are in the theory-net.
But we can imagine realistic situations in which just this assignment is
doubted. The claim then will not be that each set of intended applica-
tions is in the content of "its corresponding" core. The claim will be that
there is an assignment of sets of intended applications to cores (pos-
sibly different from the one given by the theory-net) such that each set
of intended applications is in the content of the core so assigned to it.
One possible way of formalizing this is the following.
DIV-9:     If N is an idealized theory-net and if N* = (I, a*) and
          *N = (K, *a) are the corresponding application~net and
          core-net associated with N then the generalized empirical
          claim of N is that there is some c ~ 1 X K such that
      (1) for all K, K' E K and alII, I' E I:
          if (I, K) E c and (I', K') E c then: K a* K' iff I ~ I'
      (2) for all K E K: U {I/(I, K) E c} E Cn(K)
The claim formulated in DIV-9 intuitively may be rendered as follows:
                            THEORY-NETS                               179

there is an assignment c of sets of intended applications to cores such
that: (1) under this assignment the specialization relation *a among
cores corresponds to set-inclusion (~) among the assigned sets of
intended applications, and (2) for each core K, the union of all sets of
intended applications assigned to K is in the content of K. Requirement
(1) guarantees that the core-net together with an arbitrary choice of an
assigned set of intended applications for each core will be a theory-net.
Condition (2) represents the generalization of DIV-8. It is interesting to
compare the empirical claim of a theory-net N with its generalized
empirical claim, and especially to state conditions under which the
latter implies the former. Such investigations, however, involve com-
plicated theorems which we do not want to present here.
   A second type of claim can be obtained by strengthening the claim
of the form as given in DIV-8. In order to see how this might be done
let us go back to DIV-8. The empirical claim formulated there says that
the intended applications of each theory-element T can be augmented
to a set X of potential models such that X is a set of models of T and
satisfies T's constraints and links. From this it does not follow that
among the different sets J( of augmentations thus obtained we have the
same kind of inclusions that obtain among the corresponding cores K j
by means of the *a-relation. It might happen that Kl *a K2 but not
Xl ~ X 2 , where Xi is the theoretical augmentation of set I j (for i = 1,
2), and in some realistic situations this leads to the empirical claim of
the net being inadequate. The simplest way of excluding this possibility
is the following. We just add a further claim to that of DIV-8, namely
the claim that the respective theoretical augmentations are ordered
by set-inclusion in the same way the corresponding cores or theory-
elements are ordered by the *a or a-relation.
DIV-lO:   If N = (t, a) is an idealized theory-net then the restricted
          empirical claim of N is that
          for all T, T' E t there are X, X' such that
      (1) X E Cnth(T) and X' E Cnth(T')
      (2) TaT' iff X ~ X'
      (3) I ~ r(T)(X)
The requirement is that to each theory-element T of the net (at least)
one theoretical array X is assigned such that the arrays are ordered by
set-inclusion in the same way the theory-elements are ordered by a.
   It should be emphasized that there are various other possibilities for
180                         CHAPTER FOUR

formulating empirical claims for a given theory-net. It will be a difficult
task for future research to obtain some survey of all the possibilities, to
filter out the "reasonable" ones, and especially to find examples from
the history of science exhibiting such forms of claims.
    In the second part of this chapter we reconstruct two examples of
theory-nets in some detail: the net for classical particle mechanics
(abbreviated as N CPM ) and the net for simple equilibrium thermo-
dynamics (abbreviated as N SETH ). Neither of these reconstructions will
be totally complete, since specializations other than the ones considered
here could certainly be found in the literature, especially in literature of
the engineering sciences. However, we do believe that the nets con-
sidered here actually contain the most important and frequently used
specializations appearing in standard expositions of both theories. We
also believe that the structure of the nets offered here quite fairly
represents the present-day structure of both theories, even if some
specializations have been left out. In other words, we think the net-form
offered in both cases is essentially adequate for representing the
present-day state of the theory; the reader familiar with more "remote"
specializations of CPM or SETH could complete the net by following
the main lines of the form given here.
    The nets to be reconstructed here will be incomplete in still another
sense. In all the specializations considered we shall explicitly formulate
the special laws and special constraints that are added to the basic core.
We shall also indicate informally the restricted range of intended
applications in each case. But we will not formulate the (possible)
intertheoretical links that might playa role in different specializations.
The main reason for this omission is that the formal reconstruction of
links would involve us in the reconstruction of other theories, which we
still do not have at our disposal. On the other hand, the consideration
of this further complication would not essentially alter the picture of the
nets offered here.
    The main task is finding the most adequate set-theoretic axiomatiza-
tion of the special laws of each specialization. As for the special
constraints, for the most part they will be equality constraints, and
therefore their explicit formulation a quite straightforward matter. In
some cases, we shall leave it to the reader.

IV.4 THE THEORY-NET OF CLASSICAL PARTICLE MECHANICS

All specializations of CPM come from restrictive conditions put on the
                             THEORY-NETS                               181

force functions. Forces are thereby put in relation not only to the
product of mass times acceleration but also to some combinations of
other parameters suited for specific kinds of applications. Many of
these specializations are, at the first move, still of a rather general and
"abstract" character. They can subsequently become more concrete by
adding further conditions successively. We have detected four main
"lines of specialization" of CPM's basic core. They are independent in
principle, though not incompatible, and can therefore be combined with
each other and yield "mixed" kinds of specializations. Each "specializa-
tion line" can have, of course, its "sublines". The four main lines can be
characterized as follows: (1) symmetry forces; (2) position-dependent
forces; (3) velocity-dependent forces; (4) time-dependent forces. They
represent the most used "pure" kinds of forces appearing in standard
expositions of mechanics. We have concentrated on line (2) especially,
since it contains some of the most important specializations of CPM.
   In a number of important applications of mechanics we can postulate
that any force acting on a given particle is counterbalanced by another
force of the same magnitude and opposite direction. This is the content
of Newton's third law or "actio-reactio" principle ("the action equals the
reaction"). It expresses a sort of dynamical symmetry within a physical
system. Since Newton was the first to postulate this principle and he
apparently thought that it should be applied to all mechanical systems,
it might be appropriate to call such symmetry forces also "Newtonian
forces" and the systems where they appear, "Newtonian systems". The
CPM-models satisfying this principle are determined by the following
set-theoretic predicate.
M(NCPM): x is a Newtonian classical particle mechanics (x E
          M(NCPM)) iff there exist P, T, S, c 1, c2 , s, m, f, cp, P*
          and N* such that
      (1) x=(P,T,S,N,fR,c],c2 ,s,m,j)
      (2) x E M(CPM)
      (3) 0 'i- P* ~ P and 0 'i- N* ~ N
      (4) cp: p* X N* .... P* X N* is bijective
      (5) for all p, q E P* and i,} E N*: if cp(p, i) = (q, j) then:
             (5.1) p 'i- qandforallt E T:f(p, t, i)=-f(q, t,})
             (5.2) r(p, c](t)) (8) f(p, t, i)=-r(q, c](t)) (8) f(q, t,})
cp is the relation expressing that forces are counterbalanced. Force
number i applied to particle p is cp-counterbalanced by force number
} applied to particle q. Though the two corresponding forces should
182                         CHAPTER FOUR

 be intuitively "of the same kind" the indices i and j need not be the
 same, for the enumeration of forces for p might be different from the
 enumeration of forces for q. cp is defined on a subset of all particles and
 of all indices for forces (N*). These subsets can be (but need not be)
 proper subsets. That is, contrary to some expositions of CPM we do
 not require for a mechanical system to be Newtonian that all forces
 applied to all particles are counterbalanced. In other words, in order
 to consider a system Newtonian we do not require that it be dynami-
 cally isolated. It is fruitful to consider systems as models of NCPM
 which have dynamically isolated subsystems while not being themselves
 dynamically isolated. Whether to call such systems still "Newtonian" or
 not is a purely terminological question. We have opted for calling them
 so because they contain "Newtonian forces".
    Requirements (5.1) and (5.2) say that forces acting on two "cp-
balanced" particles are inverse to each other (5.1) and act along the
straight line which connects both particles (5.2).
    Some readers may wonder why we take the famous principle of
action and reaction as a specialization and not as a fundamental law on
the same footing as Newton's second law. There is certainly a long
tradition in mechanics, starting with Newton himself, which regards
Newton's second and third laws as the "basic axioms" of mechanics.
Still, we do not think that this tradition in the interpretation of me-
chanics should be taken too literally. The actio-reactio principle cannot
be considered as fundamental as the "Second Law" for the very reason
that it is not universally valid, i.e. it is not presupposed in all CPM-
applications - whereas the second law is always presupposed in CPM.
There are two sources of restriction in the applicability of NCPM.
First, it is simply not the case that all applications of CPM are treated
as dynamically isolated systems or as systems containing isolated sub-
systems. For example, when we study the motion of a projectile near
the earth's surface, we always consider the force of attraction exerted
by the earth on the projectile, but nobody cares about the supposed
"reaction" due to the "attraction" exerted by the projectile on the earth.
Of course, the orthodox Newtonian tradition tells us that, "in principle",
the latter force should also be considered but is so small as to be
"negligible". This means nothing but the recognition of the fact that the
talk about the counterbalancing force is a piece of metaphysical orna-
ment with no bearance whatsoever upon the real-life applications and
calculations of the theory. That "the Universe" as a whole is a dynami-
                               THEORY-NETS                                      183

cally isolated system, is an interesting ontological commitment of some
Newtonians, but we do not see how it can have any relevance for the
reconstruction of the actual functioning of the theory.
   The second source of limitation of NCPM is of a more theoretical
nature: In some applications of CPM, there are forces that cannot even
"in principle" be considered to be counterbalanced by another equal
and opposite force. This is the case when we apply CPM to the
description of moving charges in an electromagnetic field, where we
apply the notion of a Lorentz-force (see below).
   Since dynamically isolated systems play an important role among
Newtonian systems, we define them separately.
   To facilitate this definition and other similar ones it is convenient to
introduce a "meta-definition" which from certain given set-theoretic
predicates produces new, "relativized" set-theoretic predicates in which
just some of the components which originally were bound by existential
quantifiers are taken out of the scope of quantifiers and treated as
constants. This is necessary because in the following definitions of
specializations we shall refer not only to the original components P, T,
S, el , e2 , s, m, f of CPM but to additional components which, however,
do not explicitly occur in the structures.

is constituted by the so-called "conservative forces". There is some
terminological confusion over conservative forces in the literature.
Sometimes, forces are called "conservative" only in the case they are
solely dependent on position. In other expositions other parameters are
admitted as well, as long as they are not velocity or time. For simplicity
we adopt the former alternative.

respectively.

We have constructed the set-theoretic predicates for position-depen-

they are not mutually incompatible. Further specializations could be
built by combining them and, perhaps, adding some new requirements.
An important example of this are Lorentz-forces, which are position-,
velocity-, and time-dependent forces altogether (but not symmetry
forces). They are introduced when we apply classical particle mechanics
to a charged particle moving through an electromagnetic field.

   It would be natural to introduce equality constraints for Q, E, B, and
C for a complete reconstruction.
   At this point, some might question whether it is proper to regard the
Lorentz force law as a proper part of classical particle mechanics
190                         CHAPTER FOUR

 (CPM). Is it not, more plausibly, to be taken as a part of a distinct
 physical theory "classical electrodynamics"? This view could be sup-
 ported by noting that all "proper" laws of CPM are invariant under
 Galilean transformations while the Lorentz force law is not. Implicit in
 this view is that "invariance" principles constitute a part of the identity
 criteria for, at least some, empirical theories. We are sympathetic to
 this view. However, we have avoided including invariance principles
 explicitly and formally in our account of empirical theories for two
 reasons. First, the technical apparatus required to do this in a sys-
 tematic and elegant way is formidable and not easily accessible. Second,
 it is far from clear that invariance principles are, in fact, a part of the
 identity criteria for all empirical theories. This claim is most plausible
 for mechanical theories. But even here, it could be challenged. For
 example, few would deny that frictional forces are a proper part of
 CPM. Yet, in its usual formulation, the laws for different kinds of
frictions are not Galileo invariant. To this, one might reply that an
 "equivalent", Galileo invariant formulation of the frictional force laws
 "could be found". This is so. But, the only equivalent formulation we
know, which involves describing the "form" of a force function and then
existentially quantifying over forces, requires that some force function
of the specific form exists in all coordinate systems related by Galilean
transformations, provided it exists in one. In fact, this same "trick"
works for Lorentz forces - provided we let the "velocity of light"
parameter take different values in different coordinate systems. Of
course, this is widely believed, with good reason, to be incompatible
with empirical evidence. Those interested in exploring these issues may
consult Sneed [16]. A more adequate treatment of invariance principles
can be provided within the framework of category theory. Carrying out
the details of such a treatment is simply beyond the scope of the
present work.
    By taking the abbreviations CPM, NCPM, PCPM, etc. we have just
used names for the corresponding specializations (special constraints
and links included); we are able now to depict the graph corresponding
to the theory-net of classical particle mechanics as reconstructed so far.
As we see, this is the graph of a theory-tree having CPM as its only
basic element. The lines indicate the relation of specialization: The
lower labels are to be understood as specializations of the upper labels
with which they are linked by one or more lines.
