                   IV.S THE THEORY-NET OF SIMPLE
                   EQUILIBRIUM THERMODYNAMICS

  As to be expected, most specializations of the basic core of SETH are
  specifications of the "abstract" entropy-determination t S (or, alterna-
                                           t
  tively: of the energy-determination U ) appearing in the fundamental
  equation of SETH. By successively specifying the form of p (or U )  t
  one gets different lines of specialization for applying SETH to partic-
  ular cases. However, the first specialization we consider is not of this
  form: Nernst's law, also called the "third law of thermodynamics" in the
  literature, does not come from any specification of p, but from a
  condition relating the states with minimal energy to those with minimal
  entropy.
      As in the case of "Newton's third law" in mechanics, some readers
  familiar with the thermodynamic tradition might wonder why "Nernst's
  third law" is not considered here as a fundamental law belonging to the
192                         CHAPTER FOUR

basic core of thermodynamics. Leaving aside traditional evaluations of
this law, the fact is that the scope of application of Nernst's law (which
was originally only intended for explaining the behavior of systems at
very low temperatures) is much more restricted than that of the axioms
stated in the core of SETH. For one thing, one can do a lot of work
within equilibrium thermodynamics without worrying about Nernst's
law at all. Historically, it is also a fact that thermodynamics developed
rather well for several decades while this law was not known. There are
many applications of thermodynamics which do not presuppose
Nernst's law. Still worse, there are special laws of thermodynamics, like
Gay-Lussac's, which are incompatible with Nernst's law - which does
not prevent thermodynamicists from applying Gay-Lussac's law when-
ever they find it convenient. Finally, recent literature points to the result
that there are some intended applications for which the validity of
Nernst's law even at low temperatures appears to be very doubtful (for
all this see e.g. Buchdahl, [5], pp. 110-112, Landsberg [10], pp. 112-
114 and 196, and Callen [6], p. 27).
    Consequently, it seems more plausible to take Nernst's law as a
specialization, and not as a fundamental law of SETH - though, if we
wish, we can label it a "very general specialization", as in the case of
Newton's actio-reactio principle.
   To formalize Nernst's law within the present framework we first
need two auxiliary definitions.
AUX 3 (SETH): For any x = (Z, N, IR, I, ze, V, N, U, S) E Mp(SETH)
              we define:
              Zmin(S) = {zlz E Z and for all z' E Z, S(z) ~ S(z')}
              Zmin( U) = {zlz E Z and for all z' E Z, U(z) ~ U(z')}
That is, the states in Zmin( S), respectively in Zmin( U), are those of
minimum entropy, respectively minimum energy.
M(NSETH):      x is a Nernst simple equilibrium thermodynamics (x E
               M(NSETH)) iff there exist Z, I, ze, V, N, U, S, P such
               that:
           (1) x = (Z, N, IR, I, ze, V, N, U, S) and x E M(SETH)

stated in the literature: All "minimum" states have the same energy- and
entropy-values in all systems.

We obtain very different specializations of SETH by specifying the
entropy or the energy determinations in a number of different ways. An
important group of specializations obtained in this way are all the laws
of gases, especially the laws for one-component gases. This charac-
terization means that the system is regarded as consisting of just one
chemical substance (though not necessarily a chemical element) - call
it i; that is, the potential models x for one-component gases are such
that Ix = \ ij. Moreover, by the usual understanding of these laws it is
implicitly assumed that the system is neither loosing nor gaining matter,
i.e. the quantity of the gas is kept constant: DN(i, z) = O. Among the
laws of gases, the most famous one, both for historical reasons and for
its simplicity, is the law of ideal gases, also known as Gay-Lussac's law.
It was noted already that this special law, though widely used in
equilibrium thermodynamics, actually is incompatible with Nernst's law.
Its intended applications also are quite different from those of Nernst's
law: They are homogeneous gases at high to room temperatures. For
gases whose behaviour substantially departs from the law of Gay-
Lussac, laws of more complicated forms have been devised, like the
laws of Van der Waals and Berthelot. These two laws, the latter of
which usually gives somewhat more accurate results than the former,
not only fit the behaviour of so-called "almost ideal gases" but of gases
near the condensation point and some liquids as well. For higher
pressures or densities (i.e. higher values of N(i, z)/V(z», none of the
laws above-mentioned is applicable, and more complicated specializa-
tions· are needed. Actually, the laws of Gay-Lussac, Van der Waals,
Berthelot, and some others we could add as well, may all be recon-
structed as specifications of one "big" specialization of SETH, the
so-called ''vi rial expansion". This comes from a rather schematic speci-
fication of p, out of which the more special laws of gases may in turn
be obtained by successive specifications. In the following pages we
reconstruct this process in detail.

Another specialization which is worth introducing formally at this point
is the so-called "phase rule". This specialization is important from a
historical and systematic point of view, since from the very beginning of
SETH's evolution it was a driving force helping to spread this theory
and to find for it a wide range of successful applications. It is also quite
interesting from our metatheoretical perspective, since it is the only
example we have found so far of a specialization which solely consists
of a constraint - not adding any special law to the basic core. That is,
here we have a case of a special constraint not essentially connected to
any special law, thereby contradicting the view sometimes advanced in
previous discussions that all special constraints must appear in connec-
tion with some law.
    Of course, usual textbooks of thermodynamics label the phase rule
a "law", but this is only because of the fact that scientists normally don't
use different terms for what we call "laws" and "constraints". In order to
make clear that the phase rule actually is a special constraint, we need
some terminological clarifications.
    The usual wording of the phase rule is this: If a system containing r
different chemical substances consists of p different coexisting phases
(i.e. phases in mutual equilibrium), then the number n of free intensive
parameters (i.e. intensive functions of state that may vary independently
of the rest) is given by the equation:

           n = r - p + 2.

For example, if we have a system containing only water (r = 1) in its
three different phases (solid, liquid, gaseous) coexisting in equilibrium
(p = 3), no intensive function of state can be varied (n = 0) in any of
the phases without thereby modifying the values of all other functions
in all phases. This also fits the experimental findings.
   The problem here is to find out what the notion of a "phase" in
                                 THEORY-NETS                                     201

general means and how a "system consisting of several phases" has to
be conceived within our metatheoretical framework. Now, standard
textbooks of thermodynamics usually don't provide any general defini-
tion of the notion of a phase but restrict themselves to pointing at
intuitive examples, like the coexistence of two different phases of water
- e.g. ice and liquid water - in one and the same system, or the
coexistence in a saturated solution of dissolved salt and solid salt.
However, this intuitive understanding certainly is insufficient. A more
advanced textbook gives the following characterization, which also
agrees with the original intention of SETH's founder (see Gibbs [8],
p.96):

"A phase is a closed or open thermodynamically homogeneous region of space, whose
thermodynamic functions may be uniquely specified by its internal energy U, volume v,
and the number of molecules nb ... , nx of the various chemical species contained in
it." (see Landsberg [10], p. 153).


This characterization of a phase is actually equivalent to our notion
of a simple system, i.e. a model of SETH. This, in turn, naturally leads
to the idea that the "system consisting of different phases", which is
needed in order to formulate the phase rule, is nothing but our com-
pound system, i.e. it is a system Z resulting from the concatenation of
a number of previously identified systems: Z = ZI 0 . . . 0 Zp. The
concatenation should be realized in such a way that each Zj is in a total
thermodynamic equilibrium with the rest of the Zj. Then, each Zj is
"a phase" of Z. More exactly, the "system" to which the traditional
wording of the phase rule refers to is a potential model of SETH
coming out of a particular sort of concatenation of a number of actual
models of SETH. It then is quite straightfoward to interpret an asser-
tion constraining the possible values of the intensive functions of the
different Zj composing a Z - which is what the phase rule amounts to
- as nothing but a constraint in our sense.
   The phase rule may only be applied to those cases where a con-
catenation of the kind wanted is empirically obtainable - which not
always is the case. Or, to say it more accurately, we may always
concatenate a collection of systems ZI' ... , Zp but it is not always
guaranteed that among the concatenated states of the collection there
will be at least one which is a state of generalized equilibrium. Also, the
202                         CHAPTER FOUR

phase rule presupposes that the particular form the fundamental law
of SETH(M(SETH)-a-S» taken in each one of the models involved
does not depend on the form it takes in some other model; this
condition is usually, though not always, satisfied, as Tisza has noticed
(see Tisza [18], p. 141). These restricting conditions on the applicability
of the phase rule make it clear that, though it is a constraint widely
applicable in a variety of cases, it should not be viewed as a general
constraint of SETH, i.e. it is not on the same footing as the equality and
additivity constraints, or Gibbs' Maximin Principle, which all belong to
SETH's basic core. Therefore, we conclude that we have to reconstruct
the phase rule as a special constraint applicable to its own range of
intended applications, which does not cover all collections of intended
applications in SETH. In order to formulate this constraint adequately
we need an auxiliary definition.

     THE DIACHRONIC STRUCTURE OF THEORIES



                         V.O INTRODUCTION


In the preceding chapters we presented a detailed synchronic account
of empirical theories. The most complex entity detected in our analysis
so far is what we have called "a theory-net". It is the formal counterpart
of the intuitive idea of "an empirical theory" many people appear to
have in mind. However, this correspondence between the intuitive and
the formal notions only holds when a purely synchronic point of view is
adopted. When empirical theories are viewed as a part of the history of
human culture, as cultural items in process, the concept of a theory-net
is clearly insufficient to represent them. The reason simply is that the
concept of a theory-net does not contain any provision for representing
changes of conceptual structures within historical time. On the other
hand, most people would like to have a clear concept of an empirical
theory as a kind of entity that has "a history" like any other cultural
product - an entity that emerges, develops, and ultimately dies. There-
fore, we need a still more complex notion of a theory including those
diachronic aspects that some people feel are essential to a complete
notion of an empirical theory. In this chapter, we shall introduce a
notion of this kind under the label of "theory-evolution". The concept
of a theory-evolution rests on the synchronic concept of a theory-net,
but it is not just the latter's "diachronic translation" - it substantially
goes beyond the scope of the notion of a theory-net. A theory-evolution
is a sequence of theory-nets in historical time subject to some constric-
tions. Intuitively, a theory-evolution is a changing theory-net. More
intuitively still, a theory-evolution may be visualized as a "living" net
growing and/or shrinking in different directions over historical time.
   Our concept of a theory-evolution and related notions associated
with it are not intended to cover all diachronic aspects of empirical
theories. Their target is almost exclusively what may be called "the
normal kinematics of a theory". This means that two essential limita-
tions are self-imposed on the applicability of the notion of a theory-
evolution. First, the more "dynamical" aspects of science diachronics,
                                   205
206                          CHAPTER FIVE

 i.e. the historical "causes" or "forces" that produce changes in a theory-
 net are, on the whole, left out of the scope of the notion of a theory-
 evolution. Nevertheless, we believe that the apparatus here introduced
 may serve for a future precise account of the dynamics of theories.
 After all, in a diachronic study of culture (as in a 'mechanical study of
 nature), a precise dynamical analysis must be preceded by a precise
 kinematical description. To provide this starting point is our aim here.
 Moreover, some hints on how to make a dynamical use of the notions
 here introduced will appear along with the discussion.
     Second, the present chapter concentrates on the "normal" evolution
 of science. This consists of comparatively long and frequent periods in
the history of science when the most fundamental parts of a theory-
net are not questioned. The scientific activities characteristic of such
periods have been subsumed under the label "normal science" by Kuhn
 [25], "scientific research programmes" by Lakatos [27] and "[research]
 relying on an ideal of natural order" by Toulmin [54]. According to
 these authors, such periods in the history of science are characterized
by the existence of a particular conceptual structure - called "para-
digm" by Kuhn and Toulmin, "ideal of natural order" by Toulmin,
"disciplinary matrix" by Kuhn, and "hard core" by Lakatos - which is
very general in scope and nature, and which guides the more specific
research work that is being done during those periods. Now, we claim
that the basic features of these rather vague notions like "normal
science", "paradigm", "core of a research programme", and so on, can
be rendered precise and also subject to historical check by means of the
concept of a theory-evolution and its associates. On the other hand,
there are other sorts of phenomena in the history of science outside
"normal science" which we do not claim to fall under our notion of
theory-evolution. We mention four types of these together with specific
examples of each. There may well be others.
    First, the initial emergence of a "paradigm" or "hard core" or "ideal"
in a field or discipline where there was no previous well-established,
generally accepted paradigm, after a long period of discussions, special
assumptions, and results of a narrow scope. Kuhn has called these situa-
tions "initial revolutions". Possible instances could be: the emergence of
Aristotelian dynamics and of Ptolemaic astronomy. No coherent and
generally agreed upon theoretical picture of the motions of physical
bodies in general seems to have been available before Aristotle's
Physics. Note that no empirical research was done on the basis of
             DIACHRONIC STRUCTURE OF THEORIES                        207

 atomism and that this view was never accepted by the bulk of people
interested in explaining physical nature in antiquity - whereas Aristo-
telian dynamics was the paradigm for doing specific physical research
during the Hellenistic and medieval periods. Also, no coherent and
generally agreed upon description of planetary motions seems to have
been available before Ptolemy's Almagest. The work of the Babilonians
and of older Greek astronomers like Eudoxus was significant but never
achieved the status of a general system. Possibly, what we now call the
Ptolemaic system could already be considered as a well-established
paradigm in Hipparchus' times, but historical data are insufficient to
decide upon this question. In any case, whoever the founder may have
been, the important thing to notice is that the so-called "Ptolemaic
system" seems to have been the first widely accepted theory of plane-
tary motions.
    Second, the gradual emergence of a paradigm in a field where there
 had been another paradigm, which already "died" some time ago and
was followed by a considerably long period of "disorganized" research
and trials in different directions. These periods may be called "periods
of crystallization". During such fluctuational periods the new ideas that
will eventually crystallize in a clearly conceived paradigm are formed
gradually, and usually not in a coherent and systematic way. A case in
point here is probably the establishment of Gibbsian thermodynamics
as a research paradigm for all thermodynamicists. This conceptual
structure crystallized in the 1870s and became widely known and used
as a base for doing further research before the end of the 19th century,
whereas the previous well-established paradigm in the same field, the
caloric theory, had already been abandoned in the 1830s. In the mean-
time, a rather appalling and confused conglomerate consisting of
Carnot's "cycles", Joule's and Helmholtz' "mechanical equivalent of
heat", Helmholtz' hybrid construct of "force" and "energy", Clausius'
"disgregation", and "entropy", and more generally a mixture of kinetical
and phenomenological considerations, painfully prepared the terrain
for Gibbs' "classical" formulation. A similar process might be detected
in the history of dynamics during the first half of the 17th century:
From Stevin through Galilei and his disciples to Descartes we are
confronted with a very convoluted development of dynamical concepts
that had already left the ground of Aristotelian dynamics but still had'
not coalesced into a coherent system of general scope.
   Third, the quite sudden appearance of a new paradigm replacing and
208                         CHAPTER FIVE

totally rejecting the previous one. Here we have a deep cut in the
conceptual development of the discipline, which is usually accompanied
by ideological clashes of a very general kind. The appearance of
Lavoisier's chemical theory and its uncompromising rejection of the
phlogiston theory is probably a clear case of this kind. Perhaps the
transition from Ptolemaic to Copernican astronomy and from Cartesian
to Newtonian dynamics are two further examples, though their struc-
ture is less clear. Kuhn's genuine concept of a "scientific revolution" is
applicable to this sort of historical phenomenon - and only to it.
   Finally, the shift from an older to a newer paradigm which has better
prospects of success, but nevertheless does not completely reject the
older paradigm and tries to "save" as much as possible of it, to view it
as a "good approximation", "a partial truth", etc. Many historical
instances are of this sort: the passage from Kepler's planetary theory to
Newton's theory of gravitation, from Newtonian mechanics to relativity,
from both these to quantum electrodynamics, from geometrical optics
to undulatory theory to Maxwell's electrodynamics, from phenomeno-
logical thermodynamics to statistical mechanics, from Mendelian to
molecular genetics, etc. Kuhn apparently thought also of these cases
when he introduced the term "scientific revolution", but it seems quite
clear that the logical and methodological features of this kind of
changes are remarkably different from those of the previous kind.
Instead of "revolution", the classical terms "reduction" or "approxima-
tion" would seem to be more appropriate here.
   Presumably, the foregoing list could be enlarged by intermediate
forms or even by very different sorts of diachronic phenomena. How-
ever, it is not our purpose to engage in speculations about a "typology"
of scientific change. Rather, the purpose of these remarks is only to
make clear that the notion of a theory-evolution as we shall introduce it
in this chapter is not intended to apply to the four types listed above -
nor to other possible ones. It is only intended for historical processes of
a quite well-determined kind - the ones known as "normal science" or
"research program". We shall show in detail how our formal notion
applies to two specific historical examples: the evolution of Newtonian
mechanics during one century and the evolution of Gibbsian phe-
nomenological thermodynamics during half a century. Other plausible
candidates for a reconstruction in these terms might be: Ptolemaic
astronomy (for more than a millenium), Cartesian collision mechanics
(for more than half a century), classical hydrodynamics (since more
             DIACHRONIC STRUCTURE OF THEORIES                         209

than two hundred years ago), Daltonian atomic theory (for almost a
century), and most "post-classical" physical theories of the present
century. Presumably, the development of biological theories shows the
same pattern. Whether or not the same is true of theories outside the
natural sciences we would like to leave as a completely open question.
Perhaps they are "too young" to allow for a genuine application of this
kind of diachronic analysis.
   Two different sorts of reactions are possible against the idea of
neatly separating what we call the "normal evolution of a theory" from
other, more complicated, and deeper, changes in the history of science.
Both reactions can be found in the literature on philosophy of science.
Some authors, like Shapere [44] and Toulmin [55], dismiss the distinc-
tions made here by maintaining that there is no "essential" difference
between a period of normal science and other, more "fluid", periods -
the difference being only a matter of degree. Our answer to this sort of
objection is that it might well be that the difference between "normal"
and "non-normal" changes in science is only a matter of degree, but we
should not forget that differences in degree can nevertheless become
very strong and significant enough as to warrant a difference in philo-
sophical treatment. Moreover, in Ch. VI we shall show in what exact
sense something more than a "mere difference in degree" may be
involved in many cases. On the other hand, Popper [39], Feyerabend
[12], and other enemies of "normal science" would like to find that
normal science really does not exist and that science is (or should be) in
a state of "permanent revolution". It is not always clear whether their
claim is to be understood in a descriptive or in a normative sense. With
respect to this Trotzkyan view of science, we contend that, whatever the
moral evaluation of "normal science" may be, as a matter of fact
scientists do not change their most fundamental concepts every couple
of days, and that they normally stick to previously attained basic ideas,
abandoning them only under very strong pressure. We think that the
standard and comparatively "peaceful" development of science we shall
formalize as a theory-evolution is both historically real and worth
considering.
   As for the other cases typified in the list above, it should be clear
that a different sort of conceptual apparatus is needed - an apparatus
that is presumably much more sophisticated than what we have con-
sidered thus far. For the last type of change above-mentioned - what
we have called "reduction" or "approximation" of theories -, we shall
210                         CHAPTER FIVE

introduce the appropriate formal notions in Chs. VI and VII and show
how they work in some examples. With respect to the first three cases
of the list we have nothing to say. However, whatever is ultimately
proposed to explicate the "deep changes" in the history of science, we
believe that an accurate explication of the "smaller changes" is a pre-
requisite. Speaking in very broad terms, it should be clear that the
structure of such things as "scientific revolutions" cannot be well-
understood unless the structure of "normal evolutions" has previously
been well-understood. The latter is the task we set ourselves now.

              V.I PRAGMATIC PRIMITIVE CONCEPTS

In the synchronic analysis of theories offered in the previous chapters
we already encountered some features that could not be treated in a
purely syntactic-semantical manner. We had to introduce some notions
that essentially referred to the relationships between the scientists and
the theory they use. That is, we had to consider pragmatic aspects in a
narrow sense - in the sense of the relationship 'conceptual structure -
user of the conceptual structure'. This was particularly apparent when
we treated the theoretical vs. non-theoretical distinction as well as the
notion of range of intended applications. Therefore, the synchronic
study of science is dependent on some irreducibly pragmatic notions,
though their role is rather narrowly confined. A great deal of the
synchronics of science can be reconstructed from a purely syntactic-
semantical point of view.
   On the other hand, pragmatics pervades the diachronic study of
science in a much more essential way. In this case, "pragmatics" not
only includes "pragmatics-in-the-narrow-sense" as explained above, but
also sociological and historical notions at large. This does not mean that
the diachronic study of science reduces to a sociological history of
science. All it means is that, in this domain, the philosopher of science
has to rely on socio-historical notions and results more heavily than in
other cases.
   Generally speaking, pragmatic aspects of science are more difficult
to treat formally than the syntactic and semantical ones. This has led
some philosophers to the assertion that pragmatic, and especially
diachronic, aspects of science cannot be dealt with in any reasonably
precise way - they have to be left forever to the "feelings", "intuitions",
and vague metaphors of the analyst. We see no warrant for this
              DIACHRONIC STRUCTURE OF THEORIES                           211

romantic view of diachronics. Admittedly, only a small portion of
pragmatic concepts may be formalized in a completely satisfactory way.
But, some can actually be treated in this way through our set-theoretic
tools. And, what is more important, a great deal of the rest can be
reconstructed with a high degree of precision and systematicity, though
not formally. And this is all we need to escape the swamp of vague
rhetoric. We can make those concepts precise enough to be amenable
to intersubjective check and controlled emendation.
   In order to build up the general apparatus fo dealing with the
"normal" evolution of theories, we shall need five basic pragmatic and
socio-historical concepts that will appear as primitive notions in the
present context. These are
            historical periods
            historical precedence
            scientists
            scientific communities
            scientific generations
Clearly, these concepts are common intellectual currency. They have
been used by many authors in a more or less implicit way. We shall
consider each of them successively and try to make it as clear and
explicit as we can.

V.1.1 Historical Periods
It is assumed that the evolution of a theory can be divided in rather
well-defined periods, each one with its specific features. The historical
periods hi are supposed to constitute a finite sequence, i.e. an ordered
tuple - the first period of the sequence marking the theory's "birth"
and the last one its "death" (or at least the last period considered in our
reconstruction of the theory). Let us call such a sequence of hi'S a
theory'S "history", H. Each theory-evolution has its own H and it is a
contingent matter whether or not the same H can be used to represent
the evolution of a different theory. The set of all historical periods in all
histories we shall symbolize by "HIST".
   It is possible that the historical periods hi could be determined as
intervals of real numbers - numbers standing for years or other dates.
However, this determination is not necessary, and presumably not even
convenient. In fact, in many cases the most convenient strategy appears
212                          CHAPTER FIVE

to be to take the historical periods as objects of a ''fuzzy'' qualitative
kind rather than as numerical intervals. We may use numbers repre-
senting years for marking the periods in an "appropriate" manner, but
this is for grounds of mnemotechnics and of cross-reference, rather
than for systematic reasons. For example, in the cases treated in this
chapter we may say that the "founding period" of Newtonian mechanics
goes from "the 1680s to the 1720s", and that of Gibbsian thermo-
dynamics takes place in the 1870s. But these dates should not be taken
too seriously; more important is to see that this period was followed by
another one of rather different characteristics. Numerically, historical
periods might even overlap (actually, this will be the usual case); but
this does not impinge on their ordering.
   Of course, all these remarks on historical periods should in no way
be taken as true only of the history of science. Any periodization in any
branch of the history of culture reveals the same patterns. This is
obvious; however, it had to be said explicitly since some systematic
treatments of history tend to convey the impression that dates are very
significant. Certainly, chronology is quite important for history, but not
so chronometry. In short, the concept of a history is a comparative,
rather than a metrical concept.


Y.1.2 Historical Precedence

In the following, we assume the concept of a historical period as well
understood; at any rate, we introduce it as a primitive (non-definable)
notion within our meta theoretical framework. A further primitive
notion we assume in this context is the dyadic relation of historical
precedence between historical periods. We shall use the symbol" <." to
denote the relation "historically precedes or is the same as" between
historical periods. It is intuitively clear that <. should be taken to be an
antisymmetric, transitive relation. A history will then be a structure
consisting of a set of historical periods together with <. defined on it,
such that <- is not only antisymmetric and transitive but also connected
in that set. That is, a given history will be a totally ordered structure of
historical periods. We don't assume that <. is connected in general; we
have no use for the notion of a universal history. We shall use capital
"H" with indices for histories and small "b" with indices for historical
periods.
              DIACHRONIC STRUCTURE OF THEORIES                          213

V.l.3 Scientists
Another obvious primitive concept we need here is the notion of a
scientist, i.e. the (potential) user of theory-elements and theory-nets.
Usually, one tends to take for granted that scientists should always be
human; that is, one tends to assume that the class of scientists is a
special subclass of the class of human beings. But, in our era of artificial
intelligence, some might feel this explication of the notion of a scientist
is an old-fashioned one and would like to include special sorts of
computers among the class of scientists. Whether or not this proposal
makes sense, we shall just assume in the following that some more or
less operational identity criteria for scientists are available. We shall
denote the class of scientists by "SOPH".

V.l.4 Scientific Communities and Scientific Generations
Scientific communities are special subsets of SOPH. They, in turn, may
be divided in more particular subsets we call 'scientific generations'.
Though we take these two notions as primitives as well - and in need
of further sociohistorical clarification - we shall try to narrow down
their meaning as much as we think it possible. Some of the features that
may be said to belong essentially to both concepts are the following:
(A) A scientific community (SC, for short) normally lasts more than
    the active life-span of any of its individual members. In other
    words, a SC should be viewed as a genidentical entity.
(B) The boundaries of a SC are usually fuzzy. For some particular
    scientist it may be a matter of historical debate whether he/she/it
    belongs to a given SC or not. Usually, SCs are not highly institu-
    tionalized groups of people.
(C) Any given SC consists of (usually several) subsets of SOPH called
    "scientific generations" (Gs, for short). Each G within a SC is
    uniquely associated to a historical period, viz. the period during
    which a group of people belonging to a SC is scientifically active.
    Formally, this means that a function g may be constructed such
    that, if COMM is the class of all scientific communities, then:

           g: HIST X COMM --+ Po(SOPH)

     such that g is bijective within Rge(g). Each value g(hi' SCj) of g is
214                         CHAPTER FIVE

      a scientific generation. We write: g(hj, SCi) = G k . We call g a
      "generation function".
This notion is another primitive here. We shall not further explicate it,
but it is plausible to assume that different generation functions may be
used on different levels of historical analysis. In the following, we
assume that a chosen g is fixed throughout the whole analysis, that is we
introduce our notions with respect to a fixed g. Since g is bijective, g-l
is also a function. Instead of "(g-l(G))t we write "h G " and instead of
"(g-\G))2" we write SC G • The means used to construct g for a given SC
should be the ones admissible for the study of the history of ideas:
direct or indirect quotation analysis, influence analysis, etc. What kinds
of methods are really effective in this context is not a matter we feel
able to discuss here; we just assume some such methods are available.
For a fixed SC we denote g(hb SC) by "Gt. That is, g(hj, SC) =
G j ~ SOPH. As scientific communities and historical intervals are
"fuzzy" objects, it is only natural to suppose that scientific generations
are fuzzy as well - presumably "doubly" fuzzy. Note, finally, that our
notions of a scientific community and generation don't preclude the
possibility of the same individual person p belonging to two different
generations and also to two different communities. He/she will belong
to two different generations within the same SC whenever his/her
active scientific life within SC lasts for more than one period. He/she
will belong to two different scientific communities whenever he/she is
simultaneously or successively engaged in the use of different (evolving)
theory-nets.
(D) The members of a G communicate with each other in a specific
    "scientific language" which only they master as a group and which
    differs from ordinary natural languages more or less sharply. This
    scientific language has a vocabulary of its own and frequently also
    special rules of formation and transformation.
(E) The members of a G share particular techniques for observing,
    classifying, and systematizing their objects of study; in quantitative
    sciences they also have specific measurement techniques and
    devices, and calculation procedures for testing hypotheses.
Characteristics (A) to (E) can be said to be analytically implied by the
notion of a Sc. They are necessary conditions for belonging to a given
SC or G. It may be discovered that SCs and therefore Gs are also
             DIACHRONIC STRUCTURE OF THEORIES                        215

intimately connected with other kinds of entities such as "fundamental
laws" or "paradigmatic examples". However, this connection should be
considered as an empirical fact, not as a merely conceptual question.

V.l.S Scientific Propositional Attitudes
SCs and Gs may have some propositional attitudes towards the con-
ceptual items they use. The following are essential to our purposes. For
the sake of simplicity, we shall restrict ourselves to generations in the
following, but many of our remarks may be applied a fortiori to whole
scientific communities.

(A) Given a theory-element core K = (M pp ' M p' M, GC, GL), a G
    may want to use K to explain, make predictions on, or otherwise
    systematize a given y E Mpp. We shall say that "G intends to
    apply K to y". The set of y's satisfying this condition at a given
    time is a subset of Mpp and, of course, it is nothing but our well-
    known "range of intended applications" I. But now the qualifica-
    tion "intended" has a very definite meaning: These applications
    are intended by someone, viz. by a particular SC, at a particular
    historical time. (Alternatively, we may say they are intended by a
    particular G j within a SC.)

(B) If a G uses a theory-element T = (K, I), where I is an intended
    application structure with 10 as the corresponding subset of para-
    digmatic examples (see e.g. [46] and [49]), then we shall say that G
    acknowledges the elements of 10 as being paradigmatic for other
    elements of I. In other words, a necessary condition for an
    element of I to become also a member of 10 is that it be acknowl-
    edged as paradigmatic by the SC at a given time. Again, we take
    the relation "x is acknowledged as paradigmatic for y by z" as a
    primitive epistemic notion within our reconstruction.

(C) "G admits proposition p" means: "most members of G consider p
    as a proposition well-confirmed or corroborated by testing proce-
    dures typically used by SC". On the other hand, notice that, in the
    present context, "Person X assumes that p" will just mean what it
    means in ordinary language; there is no reference either to a
    particular G or to specific testing procedures.

Diachronic specialization is not just a "diachronic translation" of (syn-
chronic) specialization within a net. The underlying idea is somehow
intermediate between core-specialization and (theory-)specialization,
when they are conceived diachronically. It implies core-specialization,
but it is not purely formal since it also contains a condition on the
relation between the two respective domains of intended applications:
                 DIACHRONIC STRUCTURE OF THEORIES                       217

They must have some intended applications in common. This condi-
tion, however, is clearly weaker than the inclusion requirement in
(theory-)specialization. Two theory-elements that are diachronically
related by a specialization relation must contain some common cases of
applications but it is not necessarily the case that either I' ~ I or I ~ I'
(though neither one of these cases is excluded by principle). In the
historical passage from T to T', some intended applications of T may
be "forgotten" by T' while T' considers some new ones. This implies
that, contrary to the case of (synchronic) specialization, 0d is not
transitive. In principle (though this will not be the usual case in the
actual history of science), the following situation could arise: T" is a
diachronic specialization of T', T' is in tum a diachronic specialization
of T but T" is not a diachronic specialization of T because I" n 1= O.
This would mean that, in the course of the theoretical evolution, the
theory-elements have gone so far apart that they have no application in
common anymore. It is important to keep this (conceptual) possibility
in mind for the discussion to follow.
   Note that DV-2 allows for saying that one theory-element at a given
period is a specialization of another theory-element at a different,
previous period, but of course, it can also be a specialization of a
theory-element of the same period. In this case, our definitions guar-
antee that the generation involved in both theory-elements will be the
same.

to a given theory-evolution E. We denote it by "SC(E)". Condition (B)
             DIACHRONIC STRUCTURE OF THEORIES                         219

 of the last definition is crucial for the genidentity of "a theory" in a
 theory-evolution: In order to have a theory-evolution that can properly
be regarded as the evolution of "one and the same theory", every
theory-element in a newly constructed theory-net must be connected by
the specialization relation to a theory-element (which can be the same
up to historical period) appearing in the previous theory-net of the
 sequence. The core-specialization implicit in the specialization relation
 ad is the "identity thread" that runs through the whole evolution, but
this identity thread is not purely formal since there is partial pairwise
coincidence between successive domains of intended applications (as is
implicit in ad as well). The history H consisting of the corresponding
sequence of historical periods hi can be said to represent the history of
the theory in question.
    Notice that for the genidentity of a theory-evolution in general it is
not necessary that all domains of intended applications which may
appear in the course of the evolution have some intended applications
in common; it is only required that, at each step of the evolution, there
be some common applications that make recognizable the fact that two
nets, one of them immediately following the other, are not related only
from the purely formal point of view but really come out from quite
similar purposes of explaining a certain domain of phenomena -
though the purposes may not be exactly identical: some new applica-
tions may be added, some old ones may be disregarded as "uninterest-
ing". In the long run, however, the intentions of application may
become ever more different from the original ones. In an extreme case,
they would become completely different in spite of the fact that the
cores would still formally be related. There is presumably no historical
example for this extreme possibility, but we think it conceivable. And
we think that, even in such an extreme case, we would be entitled, in
historical perspective, to say that we are dealing with one and the same
theory-evolution as a coherent unity of scientific development. Con-
sider the following, admittedly fictitious, but nevertheless conceivable
example. Suppose that, in his younger years, Newton would have
devised the first theory-net of CPM (say, the "Second" and "Third
Laws" and the law of gravitation) with the sole purpose of explaining
tidal phenomena - not caring about planetary motions, comets, free
fall, etc. Later on, he and his disciples might have seen that their
theory, conveniently specialized, also applied to these other "interest-
ing" cases and much more - the tides becoming less and less interest-
ing. Eventually, in view of the troubles that tides caused to the precise
220                          CHAPTER FIVE

application of CPM they were removed from the domain of intended
applications of CPM and assigned to another theory (as Laplace really
did a century after Newton). We think that, in such a case, it would still
be natural to say that the whole historical process corresponded to one
theory-evolution, namely the evolution of CPM.
   Two further peculiarities of this concept of a theory-evolution should
be noted. First, a history H is uniquely associated to a given theory-
evolution, but the converse is not necessarily true; therefore, in the
present scheme, it is possible to have two different theory-evolutions,
e.g. different SC's postulating different K's but intending to apply them
to the same (or "corresponding") I's coexisting or competing during the
same history H or at least during some .h; occurring in H. Whether or
not such cases may be found in the actual history of a discipline, we
would like to leave as an open question. But, if they could be found,
they would be clear instances of Lakatos' intuitive idea of "competing
research programmes". On the other hand, it seems that an important
part of Kuhn's account of the history of science consists in the more or
less implicit assertion that such cases do not occur in mature science.
At any rate, we have now a precise way of stating and checking these
two rival hypotheses.
   Another peculiarity of our concept of a theory-evolution is that it
does not preclude the possibility that a new theory-net in the evolution
contains fewer theory-elements than the preceding theory-net - instead
of more, as we would presume in the normal case. There is nothing in
history of science which would seem to preclude a priori such cases of
"theory-regression". Moreover, they could represent the kind of situa-
tion that Kuhn has called "a crisis" or, still better, what Lakatos calls "a
degenerating research programme".
   We may analyze the concrete features of a theory-evolution by intro-
ducing finer distinctions. In particular, we may consider the epistemic
relationship of SC towards the intended applications of its theory-nets.
Some applications in I will be admitted by SC during h as well-
confirmed applications of K. Let us call this secured subset of I "the
confirmed or firm domain of applications", F(I). There may be other
members of I which are not well-confirmed during h but are only
assumed by some subgroup of SC, say SC Q (possibly consisting of just
one person), to be real applications of K. Let us call this complemen-
tary subset of I "the assumed domain of applications", A(I). By the very
concept of I we take as an analytical truth that: F(I) U A(I) = I. Ideally,
             DIACHRONIC STRUCTURE OF THEORIES                        221

it should also be the case that F(I) n A(I) = 0, i.e. F and A should
provide a partition of I. The exact boundary between F(I) and A(I)
could be taken as determining a particular historical interval h: a shift
of some elements from A(I) to F(I) would mean a change in historical
period.
   Of course, the notion of a confirmed domain of applications F(I) is
not to be taken in an absolute sense. It is relative to a given theory-
evolution and even to a particular period within a theory-evolution.
Certain applications which are viewed as firm in one period can be
questioned or even removed from the domain of applications later on.
We shall meet at least two examples of this situation in one of the
particular theory-evolutions reconstructed in this Chapter, viz. the
evolution of CPM. First, tides were regarded by Newton and his
collaborators as firm applications of particle mechanics; the theory-
element they developed in order to account for tides was the so-called
"equilibrium theory of tides". But less than a century afterwards,
Laplace dismissed tides from the domain of particle mechanics and
treated them rather as an application of hydrodynamics by means of his
"theory of waves". This development took place because only a portion
of tidal phenomena could be considered as firm applications of particle
equilibrium theory; the rest proved to be recalcitrant to this theory-
element of CPM. Another example is moon theory. Although the
earth-moon-sun system was considered to be a firm application of
CPM in the first period of the theory-evolution, much later Euler came
to the point of questioning this. Our remarks on the relativity of the
notion of a firm application are intended only as a reminder that this is
a pragmatic notion depending on the attitudes of the Sc. The aim
of the present conceptual framework is not to attack the unsolved
problems of confirmation theory.
   Let us then use the notions of firm and assumed intended applica-
tions to define the particular cases of a progressive and a perfect
theory-evolution.

In DV-7(A), the intuitive idea is captured that a theory-evolution is

 or at least not diminishing, with every shift to a new theory-net. This
 concept reminds of Lakatos' "progressive research program".
    In D V-7( B), a kind of "utopian" theory-evolution is formalized: a
theory-evolution that is not only progressive, but proceeds in such a
way that any presently assumed intended application will prove to be a
 confirmed application some time in the future. Probably, there is no
historical example of a perfect theory-evolution, and probably there will
never be such a thing. However, some theory-evolutions may come
closer to this ideal than others, and, in this sense, the concept may be
historically significant. For all we know, the evolution of SETH since
 Gibbs' times seems to approach this ideal (see Sec. VA).
    Kuhn's diachronic theory of science has played a central role in the
philosophical discussion of the last decades. It may prove to be fruitful
to try to give it a more precise form within our scheme so that it may be
checked against historical examples. The crucial notion for doing this is
that of a paradigm-guided evolution, and for this we need, in turn, a
clear notion of a paradigm in Kuhn's sense.
    As Stegmiiller has shown in detail in his [47], at least two different
components have to be distinguished in Kuhn's paradigm concept: a
formal-theoretical component (corresponding to our notion of a theory-
element-core) and a pragmatic-empirical component (corresponding to
our subset 10 of an intended application structure). Of course, 10 has to
be acknowledged as paradigmatic for other applications by the scien-
tific community. A Kuhnian paradigm, according to this interpretation,
will be a pair (Ko, 1o) consisting of a theory-element-core and a set of
intended applications.
    Now, we can try to make precise the idea that the whole evolution is
guided (or "dominated") by a paradigm by saying that all cores that
might appear in any net of the theory-evolution will be core specializa-
tions of the paradigmatic core K o and further that the elements of any
intended application in any net will stand in the appropriate similarity
relationships of an intended application structure with the elements

some of the paradigmatic intended applications) to appear after the
theory-evolution was initiated. That is, some intended applications may
be acknowledged as paradigmatic only "after a while".
   A special case of a Kuhnian theory-evolution that might come even
closer to Kuhn's own intuitive ideas is the case where all nets in the
theory-evolution are tree-like. Let us call such cases "Kuhnian theory-

It is plausible to assume that in Kuhnian theory-evolutions in the strong
sense, the paradigm will coincide in part or in toto with the basic
element of each net of the evolution. But we would like to leave this as
a hypothesis. It is not conceptually necessary. In an obvious way, we
could add the concepts of being progressive and perfect to Kuhnian
theory-evolutions, but we spare ourselves the formal definitions.
   Now, the time has come to apply the formal apparatus introduced so
far. Let us try to depict the evolution of classical particle mechanics and
of simple equilibrium thermodynamics in the way described above.


                    V.3 THE EVOLUTION OF CPM

We reconstruct the evolution of classical particle mechanics during its
first hundred years, i.e. from Newton's founding work by the end of the
17th century to Laplace's first culmination of the program at the turn of
the 18th to the 19th century. Given the historical and conceptual
224                          CHAPTER FIVE

 complexity of the process, our picture will necessarily be a sketch only;
 many details will be left out of the present reconstruction; we claim,
 however, that the essential content of this theory-evolution will be
 reproduced in the scheme to follow.
   Though strictly speaking unnecessary, we wish to make the following
remark in order to avoid possible misunderstandings about the scope of
the present reconstruction. The concept of classical particle mechanics
is not identical to the concept of classical mechanics, much less to the
concept of mechanics. (Whether or not the latter concepts may be
defined in a sufficiently precise way, we want to leave as an open
question here.) Accordingly, we shall focus our reconstruction on the
evolution of the very particular theory-net known as "CPM" we have
synchronically defined in previous chapters. The evolution of CPM was
undoubtedly connected to the evolution of other mechanical theories
(hydrodynamics, acustics, rigid body mechanics); especially when we
examine the evolution of the domain of applications we notice several
gradual shifts from CPM to other theories; for example, motions in
resisting media and tides gradually shifted from particle mechanics to
hydrodynamics. Therefore, to get a complete picture of the process, we
should consider the evolution of other theory-nets, say hydrodynamics,
and their connection to CPM. However, as not all can be done at once,
we shall not consider these possible relationships between different
theory-evolutions. Consequently, here the evolution of CPM is recon-
structed as a single evolving structure. This is, of course, an idealization;
but we claim that the idealization is not too unrealistic and that it
furthermore is suitable to prepare the ground for future research on
interconnected theory-evolutions.
   The evolution of CPM until the beginning of the 19th century is
attached to the original work of Isaac Newton in a quite precise way. It
may be viewed as a development of Newton's own program - much
more so than subsequent developments in the 19th century. There-
fore, it seems appropriate to characterize this theory-evolution as
"Newtonian" and name it "N". That is N:= E(CPM) roughly from
1680 to 1800. We shall use this abbreviation in the following.
   Before the formal representation of N is offered, let us give an
informal account of its content. This account heavily relies on historio-
graphical sources - though the original writings, especially Newton's,
have been used in a few dubious cases. Therefore, concrete historical
statements made in the present reconstruction are mainly based on the
              DIACHRONIC STRUCTURE OF THEORIES                          225

methodological assumption that the descriptions and interpretations
contained in the relevant historical studies are, on the whole, accurate.
Diachronic philosophy of science starts where the historiography of
science ends.
   N's theory-evolution from the 1680s to the end of the 18th century
has been divided into four main periods (= historical intervals); this
division has, of course, a schematic character, but it appears to have
some factual historical support. The first period is the founding one.
It was restricted to Newton and his close collaborators (Halley, Flam-
steed, Clarke, Taylor) in England. During the second period, Newton's
formalism was adopted, developed, and further applied mainly by the
Basel group (Herman, Euler, the Bernoullis). The third period is the era
of the French 'geometres' (Clairaut, D'Alembert, Lagrange, and also
Euler); they made great efforts to solve difficult many-body problems in
celestial mechanics - not always with success. The fourth and last
period is mainly typified by two quite different aspects: young Laplace's
impressive solutions of some very difficult problems in celestial me-
chanics, and Coulomb's success in treating electrostatic and magneto-
static forces in analogy to gravitational force. The different groups of
people just mentioned for each historical period represent what we
think are the "hard cores" of successive scientific generations into which
the scientific community of the "Newtonians" may be divided during
the history considered.
   Let us describe the basic features of each period with some more
detail by using the conceptual framework introduced before. First,
notice that from a purely chronological point of view, the different
periods distinguished partially overlap. This gives support to the gen-
eral statement that the purely topological ordering relation <. is to be
preferred to the numerical :::; for the representation of historical issues.
   In the first phase of the first period (the early 1680s), CPM's basic
theory-core, K(CPM), including the fundamental concepts, Newton's
Second Law, the principles of inertia and of the parallelogram (which in
our reconstruction may be obtained as theorems) together with certain
other less important theorems are constructed by Newton in a series of
manuscripts with the generic title De motu (cf. Newton [32]). In the
First Book of the Principia (1687) they all reappear with slight changes
and the actio-reactio principle, i.e. K(NCPM) is added. The basic'
core is immediately specialized to a theory-element consid.ering solely
distance-depending forces, which is, in turn, specialized to gravitational
226                         CHAPTER FIVE

forces in the Principia's Third Book. In the Second Book, among some
complex and rather dubious hydrodynamic considerations, he proposes
a velocity-dependent force-law which. actually is applicable to simple
cases of friction. Therefore, by using our symbolic notation, we may
say that, by 1687, Newton essentially had constructed the following
theory-cores: K(CPM), K(NCPM), K(PCPM), K(CCPM), K(ISCPM),
K(GCPM), K(VCPM), K(SFCPM). The main task during subsequent
years of this first period was to provide as much evidence as possible
for the empirical applicability of these specialized cores, i.e. to deter-
mine and extend as much as possible the corresponding domains Ii.
    The construction and successful application of the gravitational
theory-element was the main result of this revolutionary period. Almost
all firm applications of the period are applications of this theory-
element. This is why Newtonian theory was almost identified with the
theory of gravitation which, from our present point of view, was only
one theory-element among many others of the theory-net. Certainly,
Newton thought that his original theory-net could be expanded by way
of inserting non-gravitational theory-elements in order to account for
hydrodynamical, elastical, optical, chemical, electrical, and magnetical
phenomena; but, with the possible exception of some rather simple
cases of frictional motion, all these further projects remained, for the
time being, only a vague promise without secured ground.
    The strikingly confirmed applications obtained in the first period
belong to celestial mechanics: all known planets; some comets; the
earth-moon system; Jupiter with its satellites; Saturn with its satellites.
But we should not forget the terrestrial applications of gravitation
theory which also gave it splendid confirmation; mainly, free fall near
the earth's surface, simple pendula, and some tidal phenomena but not
all of them (cf. Defant [8]).
    Besides these firm applications of the gravitational theory-element,
two interesting cases should be noted which were direct empirical
applications of the basic core (the fundamental laws): first, the para-
digmatic application of Newton's rival theory - Cartesian mechanics -
namely, particle collision, was derived quite directly and naturally from
the Newtonian core without further specializations (cf. Newton [331,
Corollaries III, IV, VI; cf. further Home [21]), secondly, the problem of
the vibrating string was attacked by Taylor with partial success by using
only Newton's basic core. 'Partial success' means here that only simple
cases of the vibrating string couid be explained by Taylor (cf. Szabo
[531; Truesdell [56]).
              DIACHRONIC STRUCTURE OF THEORIES                          227

    As for the assumed applications of the theory at this stage, Newton
and his collaborators explicitly thought that, through future research, all
celestial phenomena, including many-body systems and all examples
of comets, would fit the gravitational theory-element (ct. Truesdell
[56)). Further, Newton believed that new theory-specializations could
be developed in the future that would explain a great diversity of
phenomena: the behaviour of light rays, chemical cohesion, electricity,
and magnetism. He himself made serious attempts for the first class of
applications (ct. Truesdell [56]); the last ones he just posited as 'queries'
to Nature in his Opticks.
    The second period is essentially characterized by the detailed elabo-
ration of the Newtonian theory-net by the Basel school. A new line of
research is developed with much success: non-gravitational distance
forces for oscillating systems. From our formal point of view, this
means the successful addition of new theory-specializations to the
former net, among them our T(HCPM) of Ch. 4. Euler's elaborate
theory of different kinds of harmonic oscillators can be viewed as the
culmination of this theoretical work (cf. Truesdell [56]).
    A different trend is represented by the successive efforts made by
D'Alembert, Euler, and Daniel Bernoulli to get a completely satisfac-
tory treatment of the (discrete) vibrating string. Lagrange also assumed
in this period that the more general case of the continuous string could
be fitted into the framework of particle mechanics; but, afterwards, the
criticisms of D'Alembert persuaded Newtonians that the continuous
string does not properly belong to the domain of applications of
particle mechanics. So, this particular application was taken away from
this theory-net (ct. Truesdell [56]).
    During the third period, Clairaut, Euler, D'Alembert, and Lagrange
devoted their greatest efforts to get rid of all inaccuracies in celestial
mechanics. But they did not always succeed, since the problems con-
fronted were mathematically very difficult. Certainly, a splendid con-
firmation of the gravitational theory-element as applied to celestial
phenomena was Clairaut's treatment of the complicated system com-
posed of Halley's comet, Jupiter, Saturn, and the sun - which allowed
him to make a very accurate prediction of the orbit of Halley's comet
(ct. Pannekoek [36]). However, other problems in celestial mechanics
proved to be more recalcitrant. Especially, the earth-moon-sun system
almost led some researchers to reject the gravitational theory-element
and look for something new: Clairaut assumed for a while that a factor
1/ r 4 should be added to the accepted law of gravitation in order to
228                         CHAPTER FIVE

account for the recalcitrant data in measuring the orbits; and Euler
came to the point of doubting altogether that the earth-moon-sun
system could be fitted into anything like the law of gravitation (cf.
Pannekoek [36]). In order to simplify the formal representation of
the theory-evolution, we are not going to take these two interesting
developments into account. However, they could be formalized within
the present framework without difficulty. Clairaut's proposal can be
interpreted as a substantial change in the existing theory-net, which
consisted in replacing the accepted gravitational theory-element by
another one; it is interesting to note that Clairaut's proposal was not
considered by the Newtonian community as a revolutionary departure
from Newtonian mechanics - which incidentally indicates that the law
of gravitation does not belong to the basic core of the theory. As for
Euler, his negative attitude towards the earth-moon-sun system means
that he took this system away from the domain of applications of the
gravitational theory-element; again, this was not felt as a revolutionary
proposal against Newtonian particle mechanics, but rather as the hope
that a different, still to be invented, theory-element would cope with the
problem. A quite different result belonging to the "other line" of the
theory-evolution was Euler's successful addition of certain kinds of
many-body systems to the domain of applications of distance forces for
oscillating systems (d. Truesdell [56]).
   The fourth period is the culminating phase of this theory-evolution
- mainly due to the work of Laplace, but also, to a lesser extent and in
a different sense, to the findings of Coulomb. Laplace's great mathe-
matical skill allowed him to surmount practically all the difficulties in
celestial mechanics that had plagued the previous generation. A partic-
ularly impressive aspect of Laplace's results was his confirmation that
the Jupiter-Saturn-sun system and the moon-earth-sun system really fit
into the gravitational theory-element with the required accuracy (d.
Shapley and Howarth [45]). A negative aspect to Laplace's work was
his dismissal of the tides from the domain of applications of particle
mechanics (d. Defant [8]).
   Other examples of successful additions to the domain of the gravita-
tional theory-element were Olbers' calculations of the orbits of all
comets (cf. Pannekoek [36]), and Herschel's discovery of Uranus in the
same period. Coulomb's work on electrostatic and magnetostatic phe-
nomena has the following meaning within our conceptual framework.
He introduced two new theory-specializations into the basic theory-net:
               DIACHRONIC STRUCTURE OF THEORIES                      229

he specialized the distance-forces theory-element to electrostatic and
magnetostatic so-called Coulomb forces, and furthermore confirmed
the application of these new theory-elements to the case of two-particle
systems; that is, he got a quite successful pair T(ECPM) and T(MCPM)
(cf. Hund [23]).
   After this brief informal summary of the theory-evolution, its formal
reconstruction will appear clearer. Unless otherwise indicated, the
labels for the different theory-elements have the same meaning as in the
synchronic reconstruction of CPM in Ch. IV.
