The suppression of tidal phenomena from the domain of applications
of particle mechanics was undertaken by Laplace, who propounded a
hydrodynamical theory instead; but it should be noticed that not all
members of the Newtonian community accepted this revision, and for
many years some Newtonians still tried to handle all tidal phenomena
within particle mechanics (ct. Defant [8]). So, the treatment of tides
remained a disputable issue.
   It is easy to check that the sequence of the four nets considered
is a theory-evolution in the sense of DV-6; moreover, if we leave aside
the disputable issue of tides and Laplace's decision, then we can
consider the theory-evolution as (roughly) progressive in the sense of
DV-7(A). However, it is certainly not a perfect theory-evolution, since
many intended applications assumed by Newton did not prove to be
firm applications in the long run (especially optical and chemical
phenomena).
   If we now look for a paradigm guiding this theory-evolution, an
unquestionable choice is more difficult to take, since this question
depends on a non-trivial interpretation of the historical data. It appears
rather unquestionable that the theoretical part of the evolution-guiding
paradigm was constituted by Newton's fundamental concepts, axioms,
and theorems, i.e. K(NCPM). The question is more difficult to decide
for the paradigmatic applications. There are certain applications which
undoubtedly were paradigmatic for the subsequent developments: the
planetary cases successfully explained by Newton. Also, collisions and
free fall could be added. However, a more interesting point is that, if we
are not misinterpreting the data, it seems that not only those applica-
tions explicitly and successfully dealt with by Newton had a para-
digmatic role for subsequent work: paradigmatic examples were prob-
ably also some applications that Newton intended but did not solve
successfully (like three-body systems in the planetary system) and even
applications that do not appear to have been of particular interest to
              DIACHRONIC STRUCTURE OF THEORIES                        233

Newton (freely oscillating particles). On the other hand, more com-
plicated applications which appeared in the theory-evolution should
certainly not be taken as paradigmatic examples (for this theory-
evolution) - for example: tides, complicated many-body systems,
forced oscillations, electric and magnetic phenomena. These assertions
are, of course, substantial historical claims; they could be refuted by
future investigation. The issue is difficult to settle beyond doubt,
because it not only depends on detailed historical research but also on
the clarification of the criteria for something being a paradigmatic
example - which we still badly need. In any case, and assuming that
the present interpretation is not inaccurate the important point for the
philosophy of science that arises from this discussion is the hypothesis
that some intended applications played the role of paradigmatic exam-
ples for the evolution of CPM without having been dealt with (or even
propounded) by Newton himself. If this interpretation were accurate,
then we should adopt a more flexible and "liberal" concept of para-
digmatic application than the one offered by Kuhn and refined by
Stegmiiller in their well-known works on the subject. Paradigmatic
applications are not necessarily only the first ones successfully ex-
plained by the founder of the theory. This possibility is contemplated
by our precise notion of a Kuhnian paradigm introduced by DV-8. In
the same vein, we should notice that the first element of all theory-nets
in the theory-evolution does not fully coincide with the paradigm of the
theory-evolution.
   In the present case, the paradigm of the theory-evolution of Newton-
ian particle mechanics seems to be formally this:
P = (K(NCPM); F*(IJ(NGCPM)) U A*(IJ(NGCPM)) U
     U F(Iz(HCPM))) where F*(IJ(NGCPM)) C F(IJ(NGCPM)) and
    A*(IJ(NGCPM)) = {certain many-body planetary systems}
We see that this paradigm does not coincide with the basic theory-
element of the successive theory-nets. The task of determining the
paradigm should be viewed as conceptually independent of the task of
determining the basic theory-element.
   It seems plausible to admit that P actually satisfies the conditions of
D V-8 of being a paradigm for the evolution of classical particle
mechanics. The only problematic point is condition D V-Be b); it seems
that for any application found in this theory-evolution, a certain subset
of the paradigmatic domain in P actually had the role of a paradigm.
234                          CHAPTER FIVE

But this is a factual historical issue for which we can only offer intuitive
criteria at the time. Let us only conclude that it appears very plausible
to describe the evolution of CPM during the four periods considered as
a Kuhnian theory-evolution in the sense of DV-9.


                   V.4 THE EVOLUTION OF SETH

The second example of a theory-evolution we reconstruct here is the
evolution of simple equilibrium thermodynamics from the time of its
beginnings with the work of J. Willard Gibbs until the first post-war
period, i.e. roughly from the 1870s up to the 1930s. This history we
shall divide in three main periods, corresponding to three "generations"
in our technical sense: the "initial" or ''founding'' period of Gibbs him-
self; the generation of the Dutch school of physical chemists together
with some German and French thermodynamicists around the tum of
the century, and finally the epoch of the Nemst school. Most of the
methodological remarks and caveat with which we introduced our
reconstruction of CPM are applicable as well to the present case, even
to a higher degree. The sketchy and hypothetical character of the
picture provided will become even more apparent than in the case of
CPM's evolution. On the other hand, we think that we have been able
to collect enough historical evidence for the claim that the essential
features of the history considered fit well into the general framework
provided at the beginning of this chapter.
   The development of equilibrium thermodynamics since Gibbs is a
much less well-known story than the emergence of Newtonian mechan-
ics. Systematic historical studies are much rarer and the existing ones
tend to get involved into the more dramatic issues of "energetics" and
the would-be reduction of thermodynamics to statistical mechanics.
Both topics completely fall outside our aim. Due to this lack of a well-
established historiographical corpus on the history of thermodynamics
proper after 1870, we have felt obliged to venture into a certain
amount of direct hermeneutical examination of the primary sources
involved. To give some support to our (admittedly non-standard)
interpretation of the historical data, more biographical, chronological,
and bibliographical details than in the CPM case will be given in the
informal account to follow.
   As in the reconstruction of CPM's evolution, we have tried to isolate
as much as possible the evolution of one single theory, viz. simple
             DIACHRONIC STRUCTURE OF THEORIES                       235

equilibrium thermodynamics. But more so than in the CPM case, much
of what will be said about the evolution of this theory could be
extended without problem to the whole of equilibrium thermodynamics.
However, since in this book the only thermodynamic theory recon-
structed has been SETH, we shall focus on the evolution of SETH as a
"paradigm case" for phenomenological thermodynamics. This also
means that the intriguing connections of this theory-evolution to the
emergence of physical chemistry, the kinetic theory of gases, electro-
dynamics, quantum mechanics, etc. will be ignored - to say nothing of
the quite problematic issue of the alleged reduction of SETH to
statistical mechanics.
   If it can be said that the "founding act" of the CPM research
program was the work of one single man, viz. Newton, then, in a
strikingly similar sense, it can also be said that SETH was initiated by
just one person, viz. Gibbs. And in the same way we nowadays speak
of "Newtonian mechanics" as a "scientific style", we could speak of
"Gibbsian thermodynamics" as another fundamental style of science.
The parallelism Newton-Gibbs was already noticed by a scientist who
mastered both "styles" as no-one else did in his time: Ludwig Boltz-
mann. Indeed, he characterized Gibbs as "the greatest synthetic philos-
opher since Newton" (quoted in Arveson [lD. This evaluation might
seem to run counter the widespread idea that thermodynamics was
founded some twenty to thirty years before Gibbs started his own
work. The names of Sadi Carnot, R. J. Mayer, Joule, Helmholtz, and
Clausius - not Gibbs - are usually associated with the beginnings of
thermodynamics. This is, however, no real contradiction to our (and
Boltzmann's) historical interpretation. We are not saying that thermo-
dynamics as such was invented by Gibbs alone; what we do claim is
that the first encompassing theory or "paradigm", synthetizing all pre-
vious results into one conceptual mould and giving rise to a quite
definite tradition and "way of looking" at thermodynamic systems was
Gibbs' feat. Modern mechanics was not invented by Newton either.
Newton's synthesis presupposed the scattered discoveries, concepts,
and laws of almost a century of previous mechanical investigation,
starting with Stevin and Kepler, and going through Galileo and his
disciples, Descartes and his school, Huygens, and many others up to the
Royal Society in Hooke's times. In the same way, Gibbs' work must be
seen as the "classical synthesis" after a complicated crystallization
process which had started with Carnot half a century before. (In further
support of this view see also Duhem [11 D.
236                         CHAPTER FIVE

   The only other possible candidate as a founder of a thermodynamic
theory-evolution in our sense would be Clausius. Some historians seem
to evaluate him in this sense. Ironically enough, Gibbs himself, with his
characteristic modesty, essentially contributed to this evaluation (ct. his
quite remarkable review of Clausius' work in [17], p. 262). Of course,
there is no question about Clausius' great merits in providing the first
complete analysis of the Carnot cycle, both for reversible and irrever-
sible processes, and in introducing the entropy concept; nor is it our
intention to play Clausius down to favour Gibbs and get thereby
involved into a sort of "personalities struggle". The interesting issue for
us is to find out whether a theory-evolution in our sense may be
detected within thermodynamics and when its origins are to be located.
We claim that these origins are quite definitely identifiable with Gibbs'
monograph On the Equilibrium of Heterogeneous Substances of 1876
(in the following abbreviated as Equilibrium) in quite the same way as
CPM as such started with Newton's Principia, and not before. Actually,
to give a more flexible picture of the emergence of SETH's theory-
evolution we could include in this phase Gibbs' two initial articles of
1873 (cf. [14] and [15]), which in a significant way prepared the ground
for the "great synthesis" of 1876. They could be compared to the role
Newton's manuscript series De motu played in preparing the ground
for the Principia. Neither the historical process leading from Galileo to
Newton's De motu nor the one leading from Carnot to Gibbs' papers of
1873 seem to be definite theory-evolutions; they rather belong to the
category of "crystallization'1 processes for which a different kind of
formal scheme still has to be devised.
   The main reasons we have for identifying SETH's birth with Gibbs'
writings published between 1873 and 1876 and not with, say, Clausius'
monograph "Mechanische Wiirmetheorie" of 1865 are the following.
Gibbs' work for the first time introduced or explicitly constructed.:

   the idea of a conceptually independent phenomenological theory of
   thermodynamics, completely freed of the conceptual remnants of
   the caloric theory and also of any molecular notions. Clausius and
   others made thier conceptual frame dependent on the molecular
   hypothesis. Gibbs' approach was "pure thermodynamics" for the
   first time, though he by no means was opposed to the me>lecular
   hypothesis, as his later work demonstrated; he just neatly differen-
   tiated both approaches;
             DIACHRONIC STRUCTURE OF THEORIES                       237

   the notion of a thermodynamic system in its most general sense, not
   restricted to cyclic processes and the like;
   the concept of entropy in a clear and distinct way as a function of
   state on a par with inner energy, and independent of the concepts of
   heat, cyclic process, etc. and also independent of any molecular
   hypothesis - contrary to Clausius (see Clausius [6] and [7]; for
   Clausius' inability to introduce entropy as a fully independent
   concept, not to be "defined" in terms of a body's "disgregation" plus
   the transformational content of its heat, see further Garber [13] and
   Klein [24]);
   the fundamental law of SETH as a functional relationship between
   entropy and the rest of extensive parameters, or equivalently be-
   tween energy and the rest. In his papers of 1873 Gibbs for the first
   time expressed his ''fundamental equation" by putting energy as a
   function of entropy and volume solely, whereas in Equilibrium he
   generalized the idea to cover systems with material exchange (see
   Hornix [22]); there, the fundamental law already appears in the
   same form as in present-day textbooks, which is also the form we
   have reconstructed in this book in Ch. III as M(SETH)-a-5;
   the notion of a chemical potential as a brand-new SETH-theoretical
   concept (d. Bmnsted [5]);
   the additivity constraints for entropy and energy (see Gibbs [14], p.
   36);
   the Maximin Constraint for entropy and energy in equilibrium states
   (see Gibbs [16], p. 56; and Duhem [11]);
   most important theorems directly derived from the basic core, like
   the so-called "Gibbs-Duhem" and "Gibbs-Helmholtz" equations (cf.
   Duhem [11], Hiebert [20]);
   the phase rule (d. Duhem [11], Partington [37]).

In sum, there is to our mind little reason to doubt that the SETH
paradigm emerged within a quite definite lapse of time between 1873
and 1876 and that it was the work of Gibbs alone. Moreover, this
paradigm, though almost completely ignored in the country of its birth,
soon gave rise to a "normal science" tradition abroad, especially in
Continental Europe. Physicists like Maxwell, Boltzmann, Duhem, and
Nernst, and physical chemists like Pirie, the Dutch school (Van der
Waals, Van't Hoff, Rozeboom, etc.), Berthelot, Le Chatelier, Ostwald,
and many others, soon grasped the paradigm's basic core and made
238                               CHAPTER FIVE

important contributions to it. By the end of the history of this theory-
evolution, one of its most conspicuous protagonists, Le Chatelier,
writing about Gibbs, felt compelled to say in a characteristic "normal-
scientist" mood:

"This creation of his [= Equilibrium] was so complete and perfect as it came from his
hands that the fifty years that have passed have been able to add little or nothing to it.
The numerous scientists who have in the meantime concerned themselves with like
questions have accomplished little more than a paraphrase of his work. They have
perhaps completed some points in more detail; but more often they have only applied
to particular cases laws formulated by Gibbs" (quoted in Stevens [52], pp. 161-162).

Though Le Chatelier is obviously making the typical understatement of
a "normal scientist" involved in a fruitful research tradition, the expres-
sion of his feeling about the state of equilibrium thermodynamics in the
 1920s gives further support to our hypothesis that here we are con-
fronted with a clear case of a theory-evolution in our sense.
   Before we represent SETH's evolution within our formal scheme, let
us informally summarize the content of each period of this history. We
shall denote the whole theory-evolution by "G" for "Gibbsian thermo-
dynamics". The first period starts with Gibbs' preparatory papers:
'Graphical Methods in the Thermodynamics of Fluids' and 'A Method
of Geometrical Representation of the Thermodynamic Properties of
Substances by Means of Surfaces'. Both were published in 1873. Their
modest titles do not reflect the "revolutionary" significance of their
content. They already introduced energy and entropy as "parallel"
functions of state in the present-day sense and SETH's fundamental law
for the simple case where there is no change in the mole numbers of the
substance(s) in the system. The additivity constraints explicitly appear
in the second paper. In 1876, Gibbs publishes the first part of his
epoch-making monograph On the Equilibrium of Heterogeneous Sub-
stances. The second part had to be published in 1878. Only the part of
1876 will concern us here, since it is the one devoted to simple
equilibrium thermodynamics. The 1878 extension falls outside the
scope of SETH: It introduces further basic concepts in order to deal
mainly with strained solids, capillarity, and electrochemistry. The last
part of the 1876 paper also falls outside SETH since it briefly con-
siders gravitational systems.
   In Equilibrium (1876), Gibbs introduces the fundamental law in its
complete form (which includes consideration of changes of masses of
              DIACHRONIC STRUCTURE OF THEORIES                        239

the different substances involved and the novel notion of a chemical
potential), the "Maximin" Constraint for entropy and energy, and the
constraints for the intensive parameters (i.e. our C3 (SETH) of Ch. III).
In sum, the essential elements of K(SETH) are fully and explicitly
constructed.
   Furthermore, Equilibrium contains a detailed exposition of the
formalism's application to ideal gases and the novel statement of
the phase rule. Therefore, of the core specializations of SETH
we reconstructed in Ch. N, Equilibrium contains K(ISETH) and
K(PRSETH).
   Gibbs was not very explicit about concrete applications of his
formalism, but from the context it becomes clear that he thOUght it was
obviously applicable to all usual kinds of thermodynamic processes
known before him, especially gases at high to room temperatures. His
new applications were composite systems of the same substance in
different phases (like water in the gaseous, liquid, and solid phase),
equilibrium between saturated solutions and the corresponding crystals,
and some cases of chemical equilibrium sensu stricto, which belonged
also to the field of interest of the chemist G. Pirie, one of Gibbs' first
followers.
   The first well-known scientist to react very positively to Gibbs' work
(even before the publication of Equilibrium) was Maxwell. He immedi-
ately saw that Equilibrium offered a new and most fruitful approach to
thermodynamics (cf. Maxwell [29]), and avowed that he had been
confused about the basic notions of thermodynamics before (see
Garber [13]). Subsequently, he started promoting Gibbs' ideas as
energetically as he could. He was quite successful in that some physical
chemists, especially Pirie, studied Equilibrium and applied it to prob-
lems of chemical equilibrium already during this first period (see Pirie
[38]; further Seeger [43]).
   The main advances in SETH during the second period, theoretically
and also (even more) on the level of the intended applications, were
made by the Dutch group of physical chemists. Early in the 1880s, Van
der Waals became acquainted with Gibbs' work and made Rozeboom
aware of it. Rozeboom, Van't Hoff, and other Dutch scientists sub-
sequently applied SETH's formalism, especially the Maximin Principle
and the phase rule to many problems of chemical equilibrium, e.g. the
behaviour of hydrates of sulphur dioxide, much dilluted solutions,
mixtures, and alloys. Rozeboom popularized Gibbs' paradigm in his
240                         CHAPTER FIVE

 treatise, Die heterogenen Gleichgewichte vom Standpunkt der Phasen-
 lehre (1901-1904), which may be seen as a sort of culmination of
 SETH for this period (cf. Partington, [37]). Also, the behaviour of gases
 was studied more systematically and new laws were devised. Van der
 Waals had stated his law already in his Dutch dissertation indepen-
 dently of Gibbs' formalism, but after its translation into German in
 the 1880s it became integrated into the new theoretical framework by
 Van der Waals' own collaborators (cf. Partington [37]). The intended
 applications of the law of Van der Waals were mainly liquid-gas
equilibria at the crucial point, though other systems were subsumed
 under this law as well (cf. Rowlinson [41]). A very important specializa-
 tion of SETH obtained in this period by the Dutch group was the virial
expansion: Kamerlingh Onnes formulated this law in a version slightly
different from the present one in 1901; in 1912 he and Kesson brought
it into the present form (cf. Partington [37], Rowlinson [41]).
    In the 1880s and 1890s several French scientists, especially the
group around Berthelot, incorporated SETH's ideas into their own
 researches. Within this context, Berthelot formulated his law for real
gases in 1899. German scientists also began to know and use Gibbsian
thermodynamics in the early 1880s. Stefan had found his law of black-
body radiation in 1879 quite independently of any thermodynamic
ideas; but Boltzmann grounded it on thermodynamics in 1884 (cf.
Boltzmann's [2] and [3]; also Landsberg [28]). Though Gibbs is not
explicitly mentioned in Boltzmann's short papers on black-body radia-
tion, he himself documented that he had grasped the full significance of
the Gibbsian approach in 1883, just before he derived Stefan's law
from thermodynamics (see Boltzmann, [4]). A great German follower of
Gibbs was Ostwald. He translated Equilibrium into German (1892),
thereby making it available to a wider public, since the American
original paper was very difficult to obtain; but more importantly he
used SETH's formalism for a great variety of concrete applications in
physical chemistry (cf. Hiebert [20]). He also speculated about using
SETH as the conceptual grounding stone for his "energetics" program.
    We may summarize the content of the second period by saying
that it was characterized on the theoretical level by the addition
of some important laws for real gases and solutions (M(WSETH),
M(BSETH), M(VSETH)), and the incorporation of black-body radia-
tion (M(BBSETH)); on the level of applications, besides those directly
implied by the addition of the new laws, a very wide range of direct
              DIACHRONIC STRUCTURE OF THEORIES                         241

applications of K(SETH) itself and of K(PRSETH), notably in the field
of non-gaseous systems, was added to the ones considered by Gibbs
himself.
    The most characteristic feature of the third period is the introduc-
tion, modification, discussion, and ever-growing application of Nernst's
so-called "Third Law" (K(NSETH». This is not to say that the other
specialization lines of SETH lapsed into oblivion. Much work on and
with M(VSETH) was done before and after the First World War. Quite
useful new laws for real gases, like the law of Beattie-Bridgman, were
developed in the 1920's, and surprising applications of the phase rule
continued to be found (see e.g. Partington [37], Rowlinson [41 D. We
have omitted detailed consideration of these developments because
they would add nothing to the essential argument. On the other hand,
Nernst's law really meant a striking new development for equilibrium
thermodynamics in general, both theoretically and on the I-domain.
    Strictly speaking, we should have divided the third period into two
sub-periods: the first from around 1906 to the end of First World War,
the second comprising the period between the wars. During the first
one, Nernst himself was very much involved in "his" law. He (and
Planck) reformulated it several times and he started a huge experi-
mental program on processes at very low temperatures to confirm its
validity. Afterwards, he became disinterested in active research on it,
while some of his followers pursued research in this empirically elusive
field with much ingenuity. The most remarkable among them was Franz
Simon, who confirmed the applicability of K(NSETH) beyond doubt in
the late thirties, after strong criticisms had been raised against Nernst's
claims (for all this, see Hiebert [18] and [19D. It is to be remarked that,
from the very beginning Nernst used Gibbs' basic core quite explicitly.
To arrive at his "Third Law" he essentially made use of the Gibbs-
Helmholtz equation, which is a central theorem of K(SETH). He even
preferred Gibbs' own original formulation and notation for this the-
orem (ct. Hiebert [19D.
   With all this in mind we may go on to G's formal representation.

The structure of G during the history (hI, hz, h3) here considered is
clearly that of a theory-evolution in the precise sense of D V-6. If we
take the structure (K(SETH); F(II(SETH») as a "paradigm", then it
seems also plausible to consider G as a Kuhnian or paradigm-guided
theory-evolution in the sense of DV-8. However, a detailed examination
of the historical construction of the specializations BBSETH and
WSETH, as specializations of SETH, might make this claim, especially
for BBSETH, more problematic than in the case of N and its succes-
sive nets, since it is not clear to what extent the inclusion by Boltzmann
of Stefan's law into the conceptual framework of equilibrium thermo-
dynamics was really guided by Gibbs' original formalism and applica-
tion cases. A similar case might be made for the incorporation of the
law of Van der Waals. We don't want to decide upon this question here;
we just lack enough historical evidence to take a decision in one or the
other sense. What we feel entitled to say is that, at least approximately,
244                                CHAPTER FIVE

G was a paradigm-guided theory-evolution. For all we know, there is no
question about considering G a progressive theory-evolution in the
sense of DV-7(A). It might even be contended that it very nearly
approaches the ideal of a perfect theory-evolution (DV-7(B)).

             INTER THEORETICAL RELATIONS



                         VI.O INTRODUCTION

Up to now our approach to the concept of an empirical theory has
been "from the inside": We have developed ever more adequate (and
more complex) pictures of the way theories look like by concentrating
on the theoretical apparatus and on the intended applications of one
particular, isolated theory. We thus got a succession of ever more
complex notions: theory-element, specialization-net, theory-evolution;
but all these notions were "closed" in the sense that they dealt with only
one theory in isolation, as if there were no other theories around. In
reality, of course, science does not consist of isolated "theories" but of a
complex web of theoretical structures and different applications. It is
this real complexity that causes the difficulties in explicating the
(seemingly) simple notion of an empirical theory. Should we take an
empirical theory to be just a theory-element? Or do specialization nets
grasp their structure more adequately; or theory-evolutions? Or should
we go even further, and take into account all the "relevant" relations
which such a "theory" has with others and which would be essential to
its own identity?
    We do not pretend to provide a quick and straight answer to these
questions. Before taking a decision it is better to study how things
appear, and to look at examples. We propose to do so now, and to turn
to the investigation of the relations which a "theory" may entertain with
other "theories". However, at this point the question arises: If we want
to talk about such relations, do we not have to presuppose some
definite concept of a theory, and do we not therefore have to make a
decision with respect to its identity criteria? There are three aspects
relevant to this question here. First, as we saw in Chapters IV and V,
the more complex structures of specialization-nets and of theory-
evolutions essentially are built up from theory-elements as "units". It
seems plausible therefore to expect that this feature will extend to
relations among theory-nets and theory-evolutions as well. We expect
that a relation between two theory-nets will somehow be built up from
                                   247
248                          CHAPTER SIX

 relations among the respective theory-elements that constitute those
 nets, and similarly for theory-evolutions. It seems reasonable to start
 the investigation by considering relations among theory-elements, and
 eventually to extend these relations to more complex structures in a
 second step.
    Secondly, even if the procedure indicated above were confronted
with serious difficulties (which we do not now see), there is some
strategical point to it. Up to now we applied the strategy of first
studying simple, "local" phenomena ("theories") and only then passing
to more complex ones. Even if the "local" results first obtained were
not fully adequate, still the strategy remains sound as long as at some
later stage the results become incorporated into a more adequate
overall picture. For it is very unlikely (as confirmed by a great amount
of philosophical literature) that by immediately jumping into the most
encompassing context one gets precise ideas. Also, we believe that our
"local results" as summarized in the notion of a theory-element are not
essentially inadequate, and just have to be adjusted "approximately" in
the course of further developments. These are our strategic grounds for
starting with a study of the relationships among theory-elements.
    Thirdly, it may be argued (as already suggested) that the relations we
are going to consider are - at least in part - essential to the "theories"
so related. Therefore the concept of a theory employed in the study of
intertheory relations cannot be the ultimately adequate one. It will be
affected by the very results of these studies. In such a situation one
would like to be a bit vague about the concept of a theory. But this on
the other hand seems to lead into a vicious circle because if we start too
vaguely we shall not arrive at interesting intertheoretical relations.
    For all these reasons in most of this chapter we shall use "theory" in
the sense of "theory-element", and extend our considerations to the
more complex variants only occasionally, whenever it appears possible
and fruitful to do so. We shall start from a "given" theory(-element) T*
and look at the context, i.e. the "surroundings" into which T* is
embedded. We shall see that other theories, different from T* are
"relevant" for the proper understanding or application of T*, and that
there are many different ways in which other theories may be "relevant"
toT*.

         VI.1 GLOBAL INTERTHEORETICAL RELATIONS

In Ch. II we introduced the notion of an (intertheoretical) link as
                  INTERTHEORETICAL RELATIONS                           249

an essential part of the identity of a theory-element: one of the
components of a theory's core consists in a set of links tying the
models of this theory to other, structurally different theories. In Ch. II
we introduced links within the context of the discussion of theoreticity:
An important class of links for a theory-element T* are those that
provide the "data" for T*, i.e. those that determine the T*-non-
theoretical functions by identifying them (or somehow connecting them
uniquely) to some functions appearing in an underlying (presupposed)
theory-element T. Because of the role they play in tying up a theory
to its presupposed theories, we shall call them "presupposition links".
We then indicated that such presupposition links do not constitute
the only kind of essential links to consider when examining a theory,
so that the general idea of a link refers to a much wider context than
the issue of providing T*'s non-theoretical base. In Ch. III, when
reconstructing the core of SETH, we already met an example of a link
that had nothing to do with the unique determinations of T*-non-
theoretical functions: the equation relating hydrodynamic pressure to
the partial derivative of energy with respect to volume in thermo-
dynamic equilibrium states. This link is not a presupposition link. We
immediately see this because of the fact that it does not determine
thermodynamic energy uniquely. But this is not the really essential
reason why it is not a presupposition link for SETH; the fact
mentioned is only a "symptom". The true reason is that this link is not
considered to be valid unless the values of energy it links to pressure-
values have been obtained by presupposing SETH's fundamental
equation and usually some other special laws as well. That is, internal
energy is a SETH-theoretical concept at any rate - whatever links it
may have to functions of other theories. This shows that the presence of
a link for a given concept in a theory T* does not on its own imply that
the concept in question is T*-non-theoretical. T*-theoretical concepts
may be tied to concepts of theories T', T·, ... , in a variety of ways
without loosing their theoretical character because these ties may only
be accepted when we deal with (actual) models of T*. Links of a
T*-theoretical concept f to other theories may help to determine f in a
more accurate or expedient way, but if we always thereby presuppose
T*'s fundamental and some special laws, then f will continue to be
T*-theoretical. The situation is somewhat similar to the presence of
constraints. Requiring that a certain theoretical function fulfills a given
constraint helps in determining its value, but it does not· eliminate its
theoretical character.
250                           CHAPTER SIX

   It is very likely that if we examined fully developed examples of
empirical theories more closely, we would find numerous instances of
links of the sort just discussed; that is, links that somehow tie the values
of (a) given function(s) in one theory with values of some other
function(s) in another theory without thereby "subordinating" or
"making dependent" one theory with respect to the other. These are,
one could say, isolated links that do not belong to a "general strategy"
of tying a whole T* to a whole T. These links are useful for the modest
purpose of determining some values of some function(s) by means of
some values of some other function(s). However, they will not be the
main subject of our concerns in this chapter. What we are mainly
interested in now is in links that are part of an overall strategy of
relating a whole theory to another whole theory (and not justa function
to another function). Usually, these links appear in "bunches" and,
taken together, provide what we may call a "global intertheoretical
relation" ("g.i.r."). These global relations may belong to different
categories or types. Each type may be defined through certain general
conditions that should be precisely specifiable without resorting to
particular links. The question whether a set of links established between
two theories T* and T "adds up" to a g.i.r. of the kind envisaged will
normally be a non-trivial issue. Some times we may even feel entitled to
change some of the proposed links in order to get the g.i.r. we want.
Speaking more precisely, the situation in general will be this. We define
a g.i.r. R of kind K by stating some general model-theoretic conditions
C" ... , Cn ; then, for each pair of theories (T*, T) which we expect to
be in the relationship R we carefully reconstruct the assumed links A"
... Am between T* and T and then investigate whether they all taken
together satisfy Cr, ... , Cn .

                     VI.3 TYPES OF REDUCTION

 Specialization and theoretization are only two kinds of g.i.r.'s. Other
important kinds which have been discussed in the literature and which
 are particularly significant for the diachronics of science at large are:
 reduction, equivalence, and intertheoretical approximation. Especially
 reduction has been the object of much controversy among philosophers
of science, because this relationship has been connected, rightly or
wrongly, to far-reaching epistemological issues, like "scientific prog-
 ress", "realism", etc. It seems to us that in real-life science reduction
plays a much more modest role than general discussions tend to
assume. Many would-be cases of reductions on a closer scrutiny reveal
themselves as cases of approximations - which is a rather different
form of g.i.r. Some of these intertheoretical approximations (though not
necessarily all of them) show formal analogies with reduction that are
strong enough to warrant the label "approximative reductions", as a
subcase of intertheoretical approximation. At any rate, we do not want
to deny that the analysis of (exact) reduction has a genuine interest for
the philosophy of science; it is only that its role seems to have been
over-estimated. In the following, we intend exactly to depict the
structure and role of reduction in science. Afterwards, we shall examine
equivalence as a kind of "two-way" reduction. In the next chapter, we
investigate approximation in general and approximative reduction in
particular.
    Historically, it sometimes (though not very often) appears that a
theory T is replaced by a "new" and conceptually distinct theory T*
with related or somehow "similar" intended applications. In these cases
the question arises of how to compare and how to assess the achieve-
ments of T and T* in relation to each other so that the transition from
T to T* may be justified. Usually it appears that in such a process the
preceding theory T will turn out to be "contained" in some way or other
in the succeeding theory so that T's achievements are preserved in the
transition. However, the argument leading to such a result is not
straightforward, and often has been the subject of much controversy. It
is sometimes contended that proposed ways of comparison miss an
essential point in not achieving the incorporation into T* of all of T in
its original meaning. It is argued that because T and T* are semantically
incommensurable no such incorporation is possible in principle. This
sort of argument suggests that a conceptual clarification of reduction
may prove to be quite a difficult task.
                   INTERTHEORETlCAL RELA TlONS                            253

    This task is further aggravated by the fact that there is not one
 unique intuition about reduction in general but several, at least two of
 which can be clearly distinguished. The first intuition is inspired by
 consideration of some "dramatical" epoch-making transitions, like those
from Aristotelian to Galilean concepts of motion, from Ptolemy's to
 Copernicus' to Kepler's and finally to Newton's theory of planetary
 motion, from Cartesian to Newtonian mechanics, from phlogiston
 theory to Daltonian chemistry, from caloric theory to phenomeno-
logical thermodynamics to statistical mechanics, and from classical to
 special relativistic to general relativistic theories of space-time. In these
 cases the intuition about reduction is that the preceding theory T
"reduces to" the succeeding theory T* in a way that transmits the main
achievements of the preceding theory so that they can also be regarded
as achievements of T*. Let us call such kinds of reduction historical
ones because they are induced or necessitated by the historical
occurrence of new theories. Another, different intuition arises from
problem-solving situations in which theories and their theoretical
equations are applied. It often happens that solving some theoretical
problem or equation is difficult; it may presuppose deep mathematical
results or require complex calculations which are very difficult to obtain
or very costly. In such situations, the following procedure may be
applied. One tries to simplify ("to reduce") the theory used by
consciously omitting some "parts" of it which for the problem at hand
do not distort the "correct" solution too much so that the simpler
theory will produce a solution approximately equal to the "correct" one.
By using the simpler theory one then solves the problem in a "coarse"
version and thus obtains an approximate solution of the original
problem. In some cases, the solution thus obtained may even be equally
satisfactory from the empirical point of view. In these cases we shall
speak of practical reduction because it is mainly performed for the
practical reason of solving some given problem. Typical examples of
this kind of reduction are the use of the theory of rigid body instead of
particle mechanics, or of an electrostatic instead of an electrodynamic
theory. Such reductions appear to be the basis of much engineering
practice.
   Besides these two kinds - historical and practical reduction - there
is also talk in the literature about whole disciplines reducing to other
disciplines, like biology to chemistry, chemistry to physics, or psychol-
ogy to physiology, and there also is talk about laws reducing to other
laws. The "reduction" of disciplines is a rather speculative topic, and
254                           CHAPTER SIX

 of no concern to us here. On the other hand, talk about reduction of
 laws will be included in our treatment implicitly because laws may be
 represented through corresponding classes of models and these by
 theory-elements. As for the distinction between historical and prac-
 tical reduction it seems that though both concepts may be clearly
 distinguished from an intensional point of view, their formal explica-
 tions tum out to be similar, if not identical. More precisely, it appears
 that "practical" reduction of a theory T* to a theory T formally is just
 the converse relation of the general scheme for a "historical" reduction
 of T to T*. For example, we may say that, when we nowadays "reduce"
 electrodynamics to electrostatics in order to simplify some calculations
 in a given practical problem, what we are doing is to "deconstruct" the
 historical process which led in the 19th century from pure electrostatics
 to its reduction to electrodynamics. From this standpoint, the term
 "reduction" simply has two usages, one of which is the exact opposite of
 the other - at least with respect to their formal structure. We know of
 no counterexample to this general hypothesis, so that in the following
 we shall assume that we only need one formal scheme - both for
 historical and practical reduction. To fix terminology, in the following
 we shall use the manner of speaking of historical reduction; that is,
 when we say that T reduces to T* it will be assumed that T* is the more
 complex or "better" theory.
    There is another distinction cross-cutting the one between historical
and practical reduction, namely that between "exact" and "approxima-
tive" reduction. To our view, this is a more important distinction than
the previous one, since it gives rise to formally different schemes of
explication of the corresponding concepts. We shall deal in this chapter
with exact reduction and, omitting the adjective, simply speak of
reduction. In the next chapter we shall treat approximative reduction.
The difference between both kinds intuitively becomes manifest
through the logical relation between the two theories involved. If, after
some "straightforward translation", the axioms of T* imply those of T
we speak of exact reduction; if some approximations have to be taken
during this process we speak of approximative reduction. Of course,
these remarks need further clarification.
    So far, we have set the stage as follows. We shall study reduction as a
relation between theories (or between theory-elements as their. consti-
tuting building blocks) in the context of achieving a more detailed
picture of theories including their relations to other theories in their
                  INTERTHEORETICAL RELATIONS                         255

surroundings. We distinguish from the outset between exact reduction
(or simply: reduction) and approximative reduction. The task then in
this chapter is to obtain some explication of a general concept of
reduction and to exhibit its merits. A brief review of the literature on
reduction shows that even for this restricted task there are quite a
number of different approaches. We therefore shall be cautious in
claiming that the concepts presented here are "the" adequate ones.
Rather we offer our explications as candidates to be evaluated against
other candidates. We shall not, however, engage in such an evaluation
because this would necessitate a treatise on its own.

    Let us now see whether CCM, in fact, can be "incorporated" into
 CPM. A first observation is that most of CCM's concepts are identical
with the corresponding ones in CPM. This is certainly true for
"particle", "instant" and, we claim, also for "mass". The concepts of
particle and time are non-theoretical in both theories, and therefore
obtain their meaning independently of both. So, their· meaning is the
same in CCM and in CPM. With respect to mass one might hold the
view that, because "mass" is theoretical in both theories, the meaning of
this term is determined in each theory, respectively, by means of the
axioms in which it occurs, i.e. by means of the law of momentum
conservation in CCM, and by means of Newton's second law in CPM.
And because these laws are different, so one might conclude, the
meaning of "mass" is different in CCM and in CPM. This view is an
instance of a radical view about meaning held, for instance, by
Feyerabend [10] which implies that most historically related theories
are "incommensurable" in the sense that not all of their terms can have
identical meaning in both theories. Although we believe that there is an
interesting concept of incommensurability which can be exemplified by
real cases, we do not think that the present example exhibits features of
incommensurability. We shall devote a section to this topic below,
where an explication of incommensurability will be proposed. At
the moment we only remark that for incommensurable theories the
meaning of some "common" term must be different in the sense that its
denotation in any two appropriately related models of both theories is
drastically different. This condition is not satisfied for CCM and CPM
for there are "appropriately related" models in which the m-functions
are the same - namely pairs of models such that the CPM-model also
satisfies momentum conservation. With respect to "absolute space" S
the situation seems to be such that, historically as well as conceptually,
this notion is not really needed as a fundamental concept for CCM. So,
though it occurs in CPM, it has no counterpart in CCM.
   The question whether the T -non-theoretical functions of CCM and
CPM are the same or not, especially as far as the velocity and the
position functions are concerned, is somewhat more involved. Of
course, in present-day standard expositions of mechanics the usual way
to deal with this issue is to say that the velocity of colliding particles is
nothing but the derivative of position with respect to time: v = Drx '
Thus, we would say that v is just a definable magnitude in CPM so that
CCM and CPM should be viewed as having the same T -non-theoretical
258                           CHAPTER SIX

 structures. However, if we take CCM as an autonomous unit, this does
not appear to be the most natural way to look at the matter. Actually,
for CCM we don't need any differentiable function; all we need is mean
velocity and, also from the historical point of view, it is not plausible to
 require that such a velocity function should be defined in terms of a
 differentiable position function. More on this point will be said below.
At any rate, this simple example already shows that we should not
presuppose that, for historical reduction to obtain, the reducing and the
reduecd theory must have the same non-theoretical structures. Some-
times these structures will coincide but there is no reason to suppose
that this will generally be the case in reduction. On the contrary, a
certain amount of "conceptual disparity" between the. reducing and the
reduced theories, both at the theoretical and the non-theoretical level,
should be expected to be the rule.
    The possibility of conceptual disparity in reduction has, in tum,
some implications for a central tenet of "traditional" concepts of
reduction, namely that the laws of the reduced theory (in this case:
CCM) should formally be derivable from those of the reducing theory
(here:CPM). If the structures of one and the other theory are
conceptually disparate to a certain degree, then it is clear that no
derivation in a straightforward sense is possible. In the present case, if
we take CCM's velocity function as conceptually independent of CPM's
position function, as we think it should be done in a neat treatment of
both theories, then logically we may not derive CCM's fundamental
law (1) (momentum conservation) from CPM's fundamental law (4)
(Newton's second law). In order to allow for a derivation we have to
add some statement connecting v and s, a particular link between both
theories; in the present case, this "bridge principle" intuitively will be
that v is required to have the same vector values as the first derivative
of s. However, because of our particular treatment of space and time
we cannot formulate this in a straightforward way. Rather, we have to
use the mathematized function rx • The "bridge principle" may then be
expressed by the statement that for any two potential models x of CCM
and x* of CPM for which Px = Px* and Tx ~ Tx':
           for all p E Px and t E Tx: v(p, t) = DrAp, c,(t))
(where c, is the "time-coordinate-mapping" in x*). Note that this
statement does not only involve the two terms we want to relate but
other terms as well: the P's, T's and the coordinate-mappings cl , c2 of
                  INTERTHEORETICAL RELATIONS                           259

 x*. Even if we adopt this bridge principle, (1) still does not follow from
 (4). If (1) followed from (4) then in each model of (4), that is, in
 each model of CPM, the law of momentum conservation would hold.
 But there are many models of CPM in which this law does not hold.
 This exemplifies another general feature of historical reduction. Usually
 the reducing theory T* on its own does not allow for a derivation: It is
 rather some specialization of T* that does the job. In the example
before us the actio-reactio principle (Newton's third law characterizing
Newtonian classical particle mechanics NCPM as defined in Chapter
IV) is such a specialization. From the axioms of NCPM plus the bridge
principle just discussed (1) can be derived logically. These considera-
tions about derivability reveal that in the present example - and in
general as well - two additional items have to be present before a
genuine derivation can be achieved. First, there has to be some
appropriate specialization of T* serving as the premise in the deriva-
tion, because the basic laws of T* alone will not suffice. In the general
case, this specialization must not be invented just for the purpose of
reduction; it rather has to be acceptable on independent grounds.
Second, there has to be some link establishing a connection between
those terms which do not identically occur in both theories (because of
conceptual disparity). Instead of links we might also speak of a
"translation" of the languages of the two theories. In the present
example one would say that the language of CCM has to be translated
into the language of CPM, where by "language" here we mean a
formalized language consisting of the primitives of the respective theory
(providing non-logical symbols) plus some suitable logical apparatus of
variables, connectives, quantifiers and formation rules. It is clear how to
proceed in the present example. The terms "particle" and "mass" are
translated identically, the terms "before" and "after" are translated into
two "instants" in CPM, and the term "velocity" is translated into
"derivative of position with respect to time". On the basis of this
procedure we obtain a mapping <I> assigning to each sentence A (in the
language) of CCM its translation <I> (A) which is a sentence of CPM.
    However, there are two difficulties associated with this sort of
translation. First, it seems that assigning arbitrary instants to the terms
"before" and "after" will lead to inadequate results. Of course, one
would like to have that the instants so assigned have the right order (as
real numbers) so as to indicate the ordering of "before" and "after", and
that they have the same "distance in time" as have the two instants in
260                           CHAPTER SIX

 CCM. But these requirements clearly involve further concepts which
 are not available in our reconstructions. One might conclude from this
that our reconstructions are not adequate because they do not contain
 enough concepts to state the relation under discussion. But it is very
likely that any other formal reconstruction of the two theories will
be confronted with similar objections. Formal reconstruction always
involves some cutting down of the richness of informally stated
theories. We therefore rather tend to conclude that the concept of
a translation as given by a mapping of terms and sentences is an
inadequate reproduction of what we have in mind when speaking of
translation.
    A second difficulty with the translation at hand is that the translation
of "velocity" by "derivative of position" leaves much room for the
choice of a corresponding position function in CPM. Since v in CCM is
defined only for two arguments, we may choose any corresponding s in
CPM - the derivation of which at two points has the same values as v.
By this requirement s is not determined in any interesting way, and
again it seems that in many situations the proposed translation will yield
inadequate results in that the position function employed in CPM will
not be the one correctly describing the system under consideration.
Again one could use this as an argument showing that our reconstruc-
tion of CCM is inadequate. But if we would replace the simple "before-
after" picture by a continuous velocity function defined on some real
interval the situation would not improve. For then a translation will not
be possible in all cases. There will be models of CCM in which v may
not be integrable, and therefore will have no counterpart, no translation
in CPM. Still, one might defend translatability by proposing to include
the requirement of integrability of v among the axioms of CCM. One
might say that physicists always are sloppy in formulating the mathe-
matical properties of the functions they are dealing with, and that in the
present case "of course" it is always understood that v is well-behaved.
This amounts to saying that, even in historical perspective, CCM
cannot be understood and applied at all unless from the very beginning
v were taken to be a differentiable function, which in turn means that,
appearances to the contrary, when such people as Descartes and
Huygens developed and applied CCM they were already (unknow-
ingly?) using the whole battery of kinematical notions of Newtonian
mechanics. This further move in the argument does not at all seem to
be plausible to us. However, we do not want to pursue this- kind of
                  INTERTHEORETICAL RELATIONS                          261

"dialogue" with potential defenders of "translatability". We wanted to
show that talk about translatability of historically reduced theories is
confronted with difficulties even in the most simple cases of "commen-
surable" theories. This is why we will avoid this way of talking. Instead,
we shall remain on the model-theoretic level, and just talk about
relations among the potential models of both theories. By dropping the
requirement of translatability we gain a lot of freedom which in the
present situation is needed in order to be able to deal with concrete
examples.
   The price to be paid for this is that we cannot talk about the
"derivability of translated axioms" in a direct way. It is possible,
however, to find a model-theoretic analogue to this expression so that
actually not too much is lost. We postpone a detailed discussion of the
questions around the concept of a translation until our abstract concept
of reduction is at hand. Let us now use the results of these informal
considerations in order to introduce a "reduction relation" p among the
potential models of both theories.

So far we have dealt with purely formal requirements but mere formal
comparison cannot determine any kind of reduction. If formal require-
ments similar to those considered above were sufficient to establish
reduction then many theories would reduce to other theories in quite
unexpected ways. Exchange economics, for instance, could then be
reduced to thermodynamics which is an obviously unintended result. It
will always be necessary to refer to additional pragmatic features which
in our conceptual frame are covered by reference to intended applica-
tions. In the case of historical reduction, an important additional
pragmatic requirement is that the "new" theory T* should be able to
deal successfully with all successful applications of the "old" theory T.
The problem here is to say what "a successful application" of a theory
is. To say simply that it is a system that can be extended to a model
would be too hasty because this would ignore the constraints which
usually play an important role in "applying" a theory. What, then, about
a system x for which there is some X E Cn(T) such that x E X?
Though here constraints are taken into account there still is a problem,
namely that X may consist - besides of x - of abstract unintended
systems only. In this case one would not say that x is a successful
application of T because such a "success" would appear as fictitious.
We thus are led to the formulation that x E I E Cn(T), that is, x is an
intended application which, together with the other intended applica-
tions, satisfies the empirical claim of T. Under this interpretation
the above requirement may be expressed by saying simply that the
empirical claim of T is entailed by the empirical claim of T*.
    It turns out that this condition is satisfied as soon as each intended
application of T has some intended application of T* p-related with it
- provided p is such that parts (b), (d) and (e) of TVI-J are satisfied. It
                 INTERTHEORETICAL RELATIONS                          265

is not quite correct to talk about p-related non-theoretical structures,
because p formally is defined on the "theoretical" level of both theories
including theoretical as well as non-theoretical concepts. We therefore
have to introduce the restriction of p to the non-theoretical levels,
which is defined just by omitting the functions m and fin DV/-2 and
denoted by "p".

Parts (b) and (c) of the theorem state that the reduction relation p
"transports" the whole theoretical and non-theoretical content of
NCPM into CCM. By TV/-2-d the question of whether the success of
266                         CHAPTER SIX

T also is a success for T* - because it is entailed by T* being
successful- is reduced to the assumption of the conditional in (d).
    Whether this assumption is satisfied in the present example can only
be decided on pragmatic grounds. Typical applications of CCM involve
particles moving on straight lines in situations where frictional forces
may be ignored. Paradigm applications of CCM are so-called "billiard
ball collisions" and collisions of pendulae whose amplitudes are small
relative to their length. Note however that treating billiard ball colli-
sions as intended applications of CCM ;md CPM as well is a matter of
some delicacy. It requires that we ignore the frictional forces respon-
sible for their rotation as well as other aspects of the situation that
make it - strictly speaking - a model for rigid body mechanics.
Without fully discussing the various ways of treating these situations in
mechanical theories, it appears relatively clear that every intended
application of CCM is an intended application of CPM. But according
to the assumption in (d) we must also assume that each intended
application of CCM corresponds to some intended application of
Newtonian CPM, i.e. of NCPM which is not obvious. It is easy to state
this proposition but not so easy to establish it beyond reasonable doubt.
What do members of I(NCPM) look like? Intuitively, in order to
describe members of I(NCPM) we apply CPM's theoretical apparatus
and we try to find out whether the forces acting on each particle may be
balanced out by forces acting on other particles. It is not clear how to
describe this procedure in a purely non-theoretical way. Typical
applications of NCPM are systems in which all particles exert relevant
- i.e. non-negligible - forces on each other, in which moreover there
are no external forces acting on the system "from outside", and in which
it is clear which pairs of forces between different particles "match up".
Paradigm intended applications are the harmonic oscillator and sub-
systems of the solar system.
    Now, what about the crucial assumption in TVI-2-d,. that is,
the condition I(CCM) ~ p(I(NCPM))? Corresponding to our rough
description of both sets of intended applications we have the puzzling
situation that the relevant factors for determining members of
I(NCPM), namely forces, loose their relevance with respect to CCM
because in CCM they are zero. Of course, zero-forces balance out
trivially. But this does not contain any idea of "actio equals re,actio".
How else can. we imagine the actio-reactio principle in CCM? Intui-
tively, we can think of the total momentum of all particles before the
                  INTERTHEORETICAL RELATIONS                          267

collision as representing the "actio" and of the total momentum after
the collision as representing the "reactio". Stated in this way the models
of CCM clearly satisfy the actio-reactio principle. Although this
description does not fit the general requirement for the determina-
tion of I(NCPM), namely that it should be clear which forces "match
up", it is by no means excluded by the latter requirement, for the
description in terms of momentum covers cases in which a description
in terms of balanced forces does not work - when forces are zero. It
seems possible to accept the description of actio-reactio in terms of
momentum as an extension of the "balanced forces" description for
some special cases. On these general intuitive reflections we may
therefore conclude that I(CCM) ~ p(I(NCPM)). If this is so then by
TVI-2-c, in fact, CCM's empirical claim can be deduced via p from that
of NCPM.

VI.3.2 The Reduction of Rigid Body Mechanics to Classical Particle
       Mechanics
As a second example let us consider the reduction of rigid body
mechanics (RBM) to CPM. According to the distinction between
historical and practical reduction this is an example of a practical
reduction. The reduced theory RBM historically was introduced after
the reducing theory CPM. Essentially, RBM provides some mathe-
matical apparatus for dealing with rotating rigid bodies by referring to
their centre of mass which is much simpler than the application of
CPM's "pure" apparatus. This indicates that the reduction is practical.
It will turn out that this case formally does not differ from the previous
one which could be viewed as a historical reduction. So the two
examples also provide at least some evidence for our working
hypothesis of the structural identity of both types of reduction. In order
to state the reduction relation in detail we have to introduce the models
and potential models of RBM. We restrict ourselves to systems
consisting of exactly one rigid body. Systems with more than one body
can be treated similarly but the intertheoretical relation becomes
somewhat more complicated.
   Consider a rigid body b (see Figure VI-1) from the point of view of
a frame of reference K. A marker is fixed on b and its path in time
relative to K is given by a position function u. Thus u(t) yields the
marker's position relative to K at time t. We imagine a second frame of
268                             CHAPTER SIX



                                    F(i,t)

 reference K' being rigidly fixed on b so that the axes of K' are rigidly
tied to b. K' moves and rotates the way b does, K' is needed in order
to describe b's rotation relative to K. Formally, this can be achieved by
means of a function cp assigning to each instant t a matrix cp(t) such
that cp(t) describes angles of rotation of K' relative to K (at time t). It
is well known that such angles of rotation are given exactly by
orthogonal matrices with determinant + l. In Figure VI -1 one of the
angles, CPl(t), the angle between the I-axis of K' and the I-axis of K at
time t, is depicted. It is easy to see that - as far as rotation is
concerned - it is irrelevant at which point of b we imagine K' to be
fixed. The angles will remain the same if K' is fixed at any other place
of b.
    The data given by the two functions u and cp are sufficient for a
complete description of b's motion relative to K. The aim of RBM is to
treat (or to "explain") such motions as being "caused" by suitable forces
and masses which obey laws similar to those of CPM, The idea is that
several forces Fi may act on b causing, first, a movement of b's centre
of mass R, and second, a rotation of b around R. The centre of mass R
again is a function of time which for any instant t gives the position of
b's centre of mass relative to K. The motion of R is treated as the
motion of a particle in CPM: it satisfies Newton's second law, where
the relevant mass is the total mass of b and the component forces are
just the different forces acting on b. b's rotation around R is covered
by a law stating that b's angular acceleration - multiplied by a "mass"-
factor, namely the moment of inertia - equals an expression containing
the forces and information about where the forces are impinging on b,
                    INTERTHEORETICAL RELATIONS                        269

The latter information is given by a function p which assigns to each
"component force index" i and each instant t a vector P(i, t) which has
to be imagined as being fixed at R(t). The tip of P(i, t) indicates
the point at which we have to imagine Fi'S action. These intuitive
considerations are made explicit through the following definitions.

especially M(RBM)-2, and by supporting b only at its geometrical

these considerations we shall treat R as RBM-theoretical.

The reason for the failure of compatibility of p with the distinction
between theoretical and non-theoretical terms is that in D VI-4 the

   As in the previous example, formal properties like those proved
above do not on their own establish reduction. Further pragmatic
requirements have to be satisfied. Again, the most important such
requirement is that each successful application of RBM also is a
successful application of RCPM. Again, however, the term "successful
application" is not entirely clear, and reflection about it leads us to
rephrase the requirement as stating that the empirical claim of RBM is
entailed by the empirical claim of RCPM.
   Because of TVI-3-e, this inlplication cannot be "reduced" to a simple
connection between intended applications such as the one expressed in
 TVI-2-d. On the other hand, intuitively all intended applications of
RBM also are intended applications of RCPM because each applica-
tion of RBM arises from the consideration of some CPM-system which
in terms of RBM is easier to calculate. So if we start with the set of
intended applications of RCPM, and trace its transformations through
our formalism, it is clear that the resulting subset of Mpp(RBM) will
contain all intended applications of RBM. We first have to 'adduce
theoretical terms to the terms occurring in the structures of I(RCPM)
thus obtaining a set X E Cnth(RCPM). Next, X via p is mapped onto a
                 INTERTHEORETICAL RELATIONS                          275

subset p(X) of Mp(RBM) which by virtue of TVI-4-c and d is an
element of Cn1h(RBM). Finally, p(X) is projected on the non-theoretical
level in RBM and we obtain r(RBM) (p(X)). Since in each step of this
chain the structures involved are directly linked with the original
intended applications of RCPM and since among these there are all
intended applications of RBM, we may conclude that
I(RBM) ~ r(RBM) (p(X)), and thus that I(RBM) E Cn(RBM). This
informal argument seems to us to be sufficient in order to state that, in
fact, RBM is reduced to RCPM by means of p.

           VI.4 A GENERAL CONCEPT OF REDUCTION

In order to obtain a general concept of reduction, let us summarize the
essential aspects which were revealed in the course of the investigation
of the examples above. Again, let us denote the reduced theory by T,
and the reducing one by T*. First, we saw that we cannot in general
assume that the respective concepts of T and T* will be the same and
therefore it is necessary to employ a kind of "translation" in order to
derive T from T*. Within our model-theoretic frame we simply use a
relation p, the reduction relation, relating potential models of both
theories. Because of the difficulties with the concept of translation we
have pointed out before, we do not assume that the reduction relation
amounts to, or even yields, a mutual translation of the languages of
both theories.
   Second, and most important, there is the requirement that the laws of
T should be derived from those of T* through the mediation of p. We
rephrase this by the general condition of "derivability":
  (D)      for all x*, x: if (x*, x) E p and x* E M* then x EM
In order to include the higher order laws expressed by constraints we
require that p be compatible with the constraints of both theories:
  (C)      for all X* ~ Dom(p):ifX* E GC*thenp(X*) E GC.
Similarly, we may consider a condition for the links which eventually
occur in T and T*.
  (L)     for all x*, x: if x* E CL* and (x*, x) E p then x E GL
One also might consider a condition of uniqueness as being contained
in the idea of constructing T out of T*. The condition is that each
276                          CHAPTER SIX

reducing x* E M: has precisely one x E Mp p-related with it, i.e.
   (0)     for all x*, x, y: if (x*, x) E p and (x*, y) E P then x = y.
Though this further requirement would simplify the treatment of
reduction a great deal, we do however have some reservations about
imposing this condition in general. Usually, the concept of a construc-
tion does not imply uniqueness. We may construct according to given
different rules several new objects out of a given object, and we may
obtain various different objects in this way. More important, the study
of examples shows that this condition often is not satisfied. The case of
RBM and CPM above is only one case among others. We therefore
will treat this condition as a "specialization" of the general concept of
reduction.
   Fourth, we may consider the requirement that
  (T)      Rge(p) = Mp.
That is, each potential model of T is p-related to some structure of T*.
Intuitively, (T) might be rephrased by saying that all concepts of T
(making up all of Mp) can be translated into T*.
   Fifth, there is a requirement stating that p should not by itself yield
(D); this might be called a requirement of "independence" of the
derivation expressed by (D) from the definition of p. Without such a
requirement we simply could define a p-relation for two given theories
by (x*, x) E P iff (x* E M: and x EM), and obtain (D) in a trivial
way. This is excluded if we impose on p the condition that
  (I)      not: Rge(p) ~ M
A sixth condition to be thought of is one expressing the compatibility of
p with the distinction between theoretical and non-theoretical terms in
both theories. This condition formally says that

where r* and r denote the respective functions cutting off theoretical

below. However, it also is a rather strong condition, and actual
reduction relations do not always seem to satisfy it (see the example
RBM-CPM). We therefore will treat (CT) as a "special case" of
reduction, just like (U).
                  INTERTHEORETICAL RELATIONS                         277

conceivable examples.

The conditions we have stipulated for reduction and the theorems that
follow from them quite clearly show that reduction, even in its weakest
version, is a rather complex g.i.r., much more complex, at any rate, than
the two previous g.i.r.'s we had considered so far: specialization and
theoretization. Since the question of the relationship between these
three g.i.r.'s has been discussed in the literature (see e.g. [6]), it may be
convenient to examine it at this point. First, it is quite clear that
specialization and theoretization are mutually independent, since
specialization requires that the potential and the partial potential
models be kept the same, whereas theoretization violates precisely this
condition (unless M; = M;p = Mp = Mpp which would be a completely
uninteresting case both for specialization and theoretization). As for
theoretization and reduction, since reduction involves more substantial
requirements than theoretization, it is clear that the last may not imply
the former; on the other hand, reduction does not imply theoretization
either since we do not require for reduction that T and T* have any
concept in common. By applying this same argument, it becomes also
clear that reduction does not imply specialization. Finally, let us
consider whether specialization may imply reduction in one direction or
the other. Suppose we have T* a T. Does this imply T p T* of'T* P T?
By DVI-5-3 (the implication-of-Iaws condition) the only possibility
would be to have T p T*. But then, by DVI-5-5, to every intended
                  INTERTHEORETICAL RELATIONS                             281

 application of T there should be a p-corresponding intended applica-
 tion in T*, which, in the present case, means that I ~ 1*. Since by
T* a T we have at any rate that 1* ~ I, we would obtain I = 1*. That is,
 specialization may imply reduction only in the rather uninteresting case
where there is no change at all in the intended applications.
    In general, therefore, the three g.i.r.'s considered so far are logically
independent. This does not mean, of course, that they should be viewed
as mutually incompatible. We just have seen a possible case of
specialization which, ceteris paribus, may result in a reduction. A more
interesting case of coincidence is the following one. We could have a
case of reduction where the potential models of the reduced theory just
happen to be (part of) the partial potential models of the reducing
theory. We might even conceive of real-life examples of this kind.
Though this does not seem very likely to happen, we do not see any a
priori grounds for considering such a case as counter-intuitive. In some
cases, we might really want to reduce a theory to its theoretization.
There are some historical data which seem to point to real-life cases of
such attempts. For example, by the end of the 19th century, when
Gibbsian thermodynamics already was well-established, Ostwald tried
to derive all basic concepts and laws of stoichiometry from Gibbsian
thermodynamics (which we have reconstructed as SETH in this book),
being at the same time well-aware that Gibbsian thermodynamics had
been built on the previously existing stoichiometric theory (see Hiebert
[16], p. 463). Though nobody formally showed the untenability of
Ostwald's endeavour, his motivation for undertaking it, viz. to prove
that stoichiometry makes sense even if we don't assume the atomic
hypothesis, was only shared by a small group of anti-atomistic
energeticists and his attempt soon became obsolete and forgotten as
everybody became convinced of atomism on independent grounds at
the beginning of the 20th century. Within our own conceptual frame-
work, it is quite straightforward to interpret Ostwald's aim as showing
that, while stoichiometry constitutes part of the non-theoretical struc-
ture of Gibbsian thermodynamics (the latter clearly being a theoretiza-
tion of the former in the weak sense), it may be reduced to full-grown
thermodynamics. Our point here is not to argue in favour of the
feasibility of Ostwald's endeavour, but just to indicate that its very
conceivability shows that there is no formal contradiction in assuming
that a theory may be reducible to one of its theoretizations. Other
examples of this sort, perhaps issuing from the relationship assumed
282                           CHAPTER SIX

between kinematics and general relativity theory, could probably be
found in the literature. However, since we have not reconstructed any
of these further potential examples, we shall leave the discussion of the
relation between theoreticity and reduction at this point.
   Let us now briefly speculate abut how to extend the reduction
relation to the more complex notions of theory-nets and theory-
evolutions. We say "speculate" because no concrete examples of such
"global" reductions have been studied, and even it is not entirely clear
whether examples of this sort exist at all. Formally, at any rate, the
extension seems to involve no great difficulties. Consider first the
extension to theory-nets. The main interest here belongs to historical
reduction. Some well-established theory, described by a theory-net N, is
replaced by a better theory. Of course, we cannot expect that, typically,
a whole theory-net N* built at once will replace N in one single step.
The typical picture we expect from the discussions about research
programs and theory-dynamics is rather this. N will be a tree-like net
with a unique basic element T. The replacement of N begins with the
"revolutionary" introduction of a new "basic" element T* such that T
reducesto T*, i.e. T* is better than T. But T* provides only a frame in
which all the specializations of T which already exist in N have to be
"repeated" as specializations of T*: This is part of the "promising"
research program associated with T*. In this situation, the "promise" is
warranted formally, for, in fact, "plausible" specializations of T in N can
be replicated by a specialization of T* such that the original p-relation
reducing T to T* also will reduce the original specialization to the new
one. This follows from our definitions of "theory-net" and "reduction".
We state this result as a theorem.

   By means of TV/-6 the existence of a theory-net N* over T* is
guaranteed such that N* replicates the "successful" specializations of T

a natural way extends to theory-nets.

we actually want to find an axiomatic description of Ti. TV/-6 is a

theorem cannot be applied if on the side of T* we already have some

constructed in the proof will be among those actually appearing in N*.
