   The situation appears to be analogous if we go one step further and
284                           CHAPTER SIX

consider theory-evolutions. TVI-6 may be applied to any theory-net of
a given theory-evolution, provided the net is based uniquely on some
theory-element T and T reduces to some other theory-element T*. In
this way we might "replicate" the theory-evolution by replacing all of its
formal parts by corresponding reducing ones. However, this idea is still
more fictitious than that of the automatic reduction of theory-nets
because, on the basis of a given theory-evolution one hardly would
repeat the historical development as described by nets in order to get
some specialization net on the basis of a new, reducing basic theory-
element. One rather would cancel all specializations in the original
evolution which did not survive until the appearance of the historically
"last" theory-net in the evolution, and simply "project" the ones
remaining from all historical intervals onto one single theory-net over
T*. So it seems unlikely that we shall ever find two theory-evolutions
such that one reduces to the other in a piecemeal fashion retaining the
historical and systematical structure of the "earlier" evolution. At most
one would expect a kind of reduction in which theory-evolution E
reduces to E* in a way that does not respect the historical order.
Specializations from different historical periods in E may be reduced to
specializations of one theory-net in E*, or even to specializations
occurring in E* in reversed order of time (as compared with their
occurrence in E). We shall not engage in proposing definitions to cover
this situation, since there are no concrete examples at hand that might
control their historical adequacy.

                  VI.5 EMPIRICAL EQUIVALENCE

The theme of equivalence is closely related to that of reduction. Two
approaches to equivalence can be clearly distinguished. First, there is
the approach concentrating on empirical equivalence. This approach
focusses on the non-theoretical level of real systems, that is, on the level
of intended applications. From this point of view, theories are regarded
- roughly - as instruments used to explain the phenomena "captured
by" the intended applications and to solve problems occurring in this
domain. In order to assess empirical equivalence, the particular struc-
ture of the theory, i.e. the structure of their full theoretical apparatus,
can be neglected as long as both theories yield the "same" explanations
and solve the "same" problems for the "same" systems, i.e. if they have
the "same" empirical content. A second approach also takes into
                  INTERTHEORETICAL RELATIONS                         285

 account the theoretical terms of both theories. Two theories are
 equivalent if their full theoretical structures are in some sense
"isomorphic", and if both theories are about the "same" phenomena.
Intuitively, the second approach is stronger than the first one, and we
expect empirical equivalence to be just a special case of equivalence.
However, few examples have been studied, and our preconceptions
might easily be in need of adjustment. We therefore do not start with
the more general concept in connection with which it is tempting just to
apply formal ideas from logic and mathematics. In fact, standard cases
of "equivalence" (like that between CPM and LAG) seem to exemplify
only the weaker notion of empirical equivalence.
   One basic feature common to both approaches is that some identity
or "sameness" is involved: both theories have to be about "the same
things". Without this feature we would be left with purely formal
equivalence which, as in the case of reduction, cannot separate the
"intended" cases of equivalent empirical theories from those in which
just the same formalism is applied in two theories dealing with quite
different phenomena. A naive account of two theories T and T* being
about the same things would consist of taking their classes of partial
potential models and of intended applications as identical:
           Mpp = M:p and 1* = I.
Reference to examples shows that this is too restrictive. CPM and LAG
are usually claimed to be "equivalent" but their non-theoretical struc-
tures are not identical.
   A less naive picture of "identical" phenomena is this. We start with a
given set of real, yet "conceptually unstructured" systems. We may then
look at each system from the perspective of either T or T*. Depending
on which perspective we choose the system will be conceptualized
differently: in one case we obtain (we "see") an intended application of
T, in the other case an intended application of T*. This picture has
some heuristic value, at best. We have no more access to a set of
conceptually unstructured systems than we have to Kant's Ding an sich.
And the notion of seeing the "same system" in two different concep-
tualizations (i.e. as two systems) is poorly understood.
   Basing considerations of equivalence on this picture would mean to
"define" equivalence in terms of a mysterious, or at least badly
understood relation of "sameness". We believe this to be a bad strategy.
We suggest a re-orientation. Instead of defining or characterizing
286                           CHAPTER SIX

equivalence by means of an identity of "unstructured systems" or
"phenomena" we propose to go the opposite way: to define or charac-
terize this kind of identity by means of equivalence. The concept of
equivalence of theory-elements can be defined rather precisely, and
with only a small residuum of pragmatic requirements. If theories are
about the "same things", and if they yield the "same" results and
solutions or ''isomorphic'' pictures then they are equivalent. So equiva-
lence is a necessary condition for two theories being about the "same
things".
   With this in mind let us now tum to empirical equivalence. Consider
two theories (theory-elements) T and T* which are claimed to be
empirically equivalent. As already said it would be too restrictive to
insist that M,p =  M:  p' Both theories' non-theoretical concepts may be
different. Now what kind of requirements could we employ in order to
"zero in" identity of the underlying phenomena T and T* are dealing
with? A first idea is to require that there be some bijection ~ between
both sets of intended applications:
           ~:I*'" I

by means of which the applications on both sides are "identified".
 ~(x*) = x then intuitively would mean that x* and x both "capture" the
same "real system", but in different terms. A moment's reflection will
show that such a requirement still may be too strong. There is a long
way to go from "real systems" to partial potential models. There may be
various different partial potential models "coming out" of one "real
system" even in terms of one single theory. Think of our solar system as
"real" and of partial potential models of CPM which "describe" this
system. There are infinitely many different such partial potential models
according to the different possibilities of choosing a frame of reference
in which the position function s is posited. Of course, among these
"descriptions" there are equivalent ones: those in which the frames of
reference chosen are not accelerated relatively to each other, and there
even may be one "preferred" class of such descriptions, namely those
whose frame is not accelerated relatively to the sun or the fixed stars. In
the long run we may be able to close this gap between real systems and
partial potential models by means of a series, of intermediate steps
involving appropriate relations of equivalence. But before this'is done,
some weakening of the requirement under discussion appears to be a
more adequate procedure. If we have two theories, and one common
                  INTERTHEORETICAL RELATIONS                            287

real system can be captured and described in both theories in various
different ways then it may be formally difficult to map those descrip-
tions one-one onto each other. In fact, this suspicion is not purely a
priori; it is confirmed by the study of examples (like that of CPM and
LAG below). We therefore shall require only some relation between the
intended applications of the theories (which need not be a function):
            <I> ~ 1* X I.
Intuitively, "( x*, x) E <I>" still means that x* and x capture and
describe the same underlying real system. A natural requirement for <I>
would be that each intended application on each side has some <I>-
image on the other side, i.e. all intended applications on each side are at
least related with some on the other side. Formally this means: for all
x* E 1* there is some x E 1 such that (x*, x) E <I> and for all x E 1
there is some x* E 1* such that (x*, x) E <I>.
   A second point to be noted in this connection is that, in concrete
cases, it will be difficult, if not impossible, to describe a relation
between intended applications because the sets of intended applications
cannot formally be characterized. In order to give some (formal)
characterization of a relation like <I> we have to move to the formal
level of partial potential models. We may therefore require that there
be some relation v by means of which partial potential models are
"identified":
            v ~ M;pX Mpp.
   Such a v has to fulfill at least one further global condition: In some
sense it has to "respect" intended applications. Intuitively, the <I>
introduced above will have to be a subrelation of v: <I> ~ v. That is,
whenever two intended applications are "identified" by means of <I>
they will also have to be formally related by v. We then may omit
reference to <P altogether, and simply define <I> as the restriction of v to
1* X I: <I> =: v n (1* X I). The above requirement for <I> then would
become a requirement for v: for all x* E 1* there is x E 1 such that
(x*, x) E v and for all x E 1 there is x* E 1* such that (x*, x) E v.
This constitutes a first step towards expressing "sameness" (as repre-
sented by <I» in terms of formal relations between the structures of the
theories involved.
   Given such a very weak "identification" we may ask how to use it in
order to express empirical equivalence. The most natural move is to say
288                          CHAPTER SIX

that T and T* are empirically equivalent if they have the same empirical
content. On our account of a theory's content (compare Ch. II) this
would mean that Cn(T) = Cn(T*) which implies that the partial
potential models of T and T* are of the same type, that is, T and T*
employ the same vocabulary. In the light of what has been said before,
this seems too strong a requirement. But our discussion of how to
present the identity of phenomena on the level of non-theoretical
structures hints at some kind of generalization. We may express that T
and T* have the "same" content by saying that there is some relation v+
"identifying" the elements of Cn(T) and Cn(T*):
           v+ ~ Cn(T*) X Cn(T).
If we think about how such a v+ may be defined we are led back to v.
v+ has to relate sets of partial potential models of T* with sets of partial
potential models of T, and the most natural way to define such a
mapping is to start with some mapping v on the level of single partial
potential models and then to "lift" v to the level of sets of partial
potential models. More formally, the procedure is this. We start with
           v ~ M:pXMpp
and we define a relation v+ between the respective power sets
           v+ ~ Po(M:p) X Po(Mpp) by
           v+ = {( U, V)/Vu E U3v E V«u, v) E v) /\ Vv E V3u
           E   U«u, v) E v)l
The identification v+ of the contents of T* and T then may be taken to
be just v+, restricted to Cn(T*) X Cn(T).
   Finally, it seems reasonable to require that v be defined for all
partial potential models on each side. That is, all partial potential
models of M:p are v-related to members of M pp , and vice versa.
Without such a requirement, some "parts" of one of the theories might
not enter into the relation, and one would say that only a "part" of this
theory is equivalent with the other theory. By summarizing these ideas
we obtain the following definition of empirical equivalence.

It should be clear by now that, generally speaking, the relation V of
sameness we are looking for to state empirical equivalence is nothing
but an intertheoretical link. To describe it more precisely, V should be
conceived of as the non-theoretical portion of a g.i.r. - call it 11- -
constituted by at least one (usually several) links imposing restrictions
on (some of) the non-theoretical concepts of T* and T, respectively.
This means that, in order to obtain empirical equivalence between T*
and T, a relation 11- ~ M: X Mp is needed such that 11- is constituted by
a series of links AI, ... , An with the following property:
           For any i(l ~ i ~ n) and for all x* EM:, x E M p ,
           ii, . .. , it, i l ,· .. , im E N:

           j* E {ii, ... , it}, j E {iI' ... , in}: (x*)j* is a component of
           r*(x*) and (x)j is a component ofr(x).
Then, v may be defined as the projection of 11- to the non-theoretical
levels - just the way p was defined in terms of p. In other words, the
links we need to determine an empirical equivalence as a g.i.r. only
affect non-theoretical terms of each theory. The rest of 11- we may forget
about. It has no relevance at all for the question of empirical equiva-
lence and may be constructed in any way we like. Therefore, we may
restrict our attention to v.
   Whether or not the links constituting v belong to the "essence" of
the theories involved, i.e. whether or not they are part of GL*(T*)
and/or GL(T) cannot be decided upon in general terms. Sometimes
they will, sometimes they won't. This question can be decided only
through partly formal, partly pragmatic examination of each particular
example~ In the following general discussion we need not take any
                  INTERTHEORETICAL RELATIONS                             291

 stance on this issue and we shall not explicitly mention or use the links
that belong to any couple of theories involved in a relation of empirical
equivalence. In the following, we consider v as a g.i.r. without further
 analysis into its components.
    There are other formulations of empirical equivalence in terms of
"solved problems", "observation sentences" or of "observational predic-
tions". We do not attempt to fully incorporate these formulations into
our frame because it seems difficult to make them precise. We restrict
ourselves to a few remarks. First, it is clear that sets of observation
sentences can be represented by substructures or sets of substructures
of partial potential models. If x = (DI' ... , D k ; AI, ... , AI; R I , ... ,
 Rm) is a partial potential model, Ri ~ Ti(DI' ... , AI) and a E Ti(DI'
... , AI) then "a E R/' is an atomic proposition representing an
observation sentence, namely that object a "has the property" R i •
Conversely, if we start with a collection of observation sentences all
stated about the same system we can take together the corresponding
atomic propositions and thereby obtain some "fragment" of a partial
potential model. In this way a formulation. of equivalence in terms of
observation sentences might be incorporated into our conceptual
framework, at least if we generalize our notion of non-theoretical
structures to include "fragments" or substructures of the kind just
mentioned. In a similar way it should be possible to deal with observa-
tional predictions which just are a subclass of observation sentences.
    Concerning the approach to equivalence by means of "problems"
there is the task of saying precisely what a problem is, and what a
solution of a problem is. Here we do not expect a simple and complete
answer. It seems that in many cases, problem-solving can be repre-
sented as calculation of unknown data by means of known data with the
help of the theory. Consider the problem of generating a certain
collision of billiard balls in the frame of CCM. The "known" data are
those about velocities after the collision: these are to be generated and
therefore are to be treated as given. Also, the masses of the billiard
balls may be assumed to be known. The solution consists in assuming
that CCM applies to the situation, and in calculating velocities "before"
the collision which by means of CCM would lead to those required
"after" the collision. In this example the "problem" might be repre-
sented by the "given data", i.e. by some partial structure, and the
"solution" is represented by filling out this partial structure in order to
obtain a full model (eventually with further, special properties) of the
292                           CHAPTER SIX

theory. It seems possible to represent such situations in our present
frame if we use a concept of substructure more general than that given
by partial potential models. The question here is of course whether all
kinds of "problems" can be treated in this way. Since a notion of
problem general enough to be used in our context has not been made
very precise in the literature on "problem-solving", it is idle to deal with
this question with more detail here.


VI.S.1 The Empirical Equivalence of Lagrangian and Classical
       Mechanics

As an example of equivalence let us consider the pair consisting of
LAG and CPM. Both theories have been described in Ch. III. Let us
recall some features of LAG. The partial potential models of LAG are
of the form x = (h, T, ~, c, ii) where h is the number of degrees of
freedom of the system described by x, T is the time interval, and ii is a
function comprising the generalized coordinates iii of the system.
Moreover, we employ a coordinatization function c: T ..... ~ by which
the structure required is imposed on T. The partial potential models of
CPM have the form x* = (P, T, S, N, ~, cl , c2 , s) where P is the set of
particles, T the time interval, S "space", s: P X T ..... S is the position
function, and coordinatizations cl : T ..... ~ and c2 : S ..... ~3 are used.
    We want to "identify" the partial potential models of one and the
other theory by means of a relation v ~ Mpp(CPM) X Mpp(LAG). The
problem here is to relate degrees of freedom and particles in an
appropriate way or - which amounts to the same - to relate the
generalized coordinates iii and the components of the position function
Sj: P X T ..... ~ (j = 1, 2, 3). If we start from the side of CPM we may
easily associate some Lagrangian system with any x* E Mpp(CPM): just
take iiI' •.. , iih to be, respectively, Sl (PI' .), S2(PI, .), slpI' .),
Sl(P2' .), ... , s3(Pn' .) (if P = {PI' ... , Pn} and the dots indicate the
places for the arguments), and if needed, shift and rotate the whole
system. Though this procedure does not yield a unique result it seems
that intended applications are preserved: if x* is an intended applica-
tion of CPM then each of the systems x E Mpp(LAG) obtained in the
way indicated will also be an intended application of LAG. On the
other hand, it is clear that in this way we do not obtain all the
interesting cases. For instance, we do not get systems which are
obtained from CPM-systems by rewriting them in polar coordinates.
                  INTERTHEORETICAL RELATIONS                            293

   The situation becomes more difficult if we start from the side of
LAG. If we have just h abstract degrees of freedom and h generalized
coordinates qi: T .... IR, how should we group them together in order to
obtain position functions sp = (sp,t, Sp,2' Sp,3)? This seems to be
possible only if we got the generalized coordinates from the position
functions of some real system by means of previous transformations.
Only in this situation we may go back to the original CPM-description,
and "globally" relate the LAG-system to the CPM-system by means of
the latter transformations. This process also preserves intended applica-
tions. If x E I(LAG) and if x is related to some x* E Mpp(CPM) in the
way just described then x* is a CPM-description of the same real
system, and the interest in this system from the side of LAG may
be assumed to go over to the side of CPM. But couldn't there be
intended applications of LAG which are not obtained from previous
CPM-descriptions? The answer seems to be: no. If x is an intended
application of LAG then x has to describe some real system of moving
particles. But if there is some theoretical interest in this real system then
it will also be an intended application of CPM. Even if the generalized
coordinates may have been read off from the system without detour via
CPM we always can make such a detour, and thereby obtain some idea
about how the two descriptions are related.
   This discussion may be summarized in two points. First, the relation
we want to establish seems to be far from being unique - at least if we
take intended applications and their preservation into account. Second,
preservation of the intended applications in the sense of DVI-9-2 seems
to hold - at least if the relation is defined along the lines discussed.
Such a very general relation has been proposed in Jamison [18] which
we take up with slight modifications. In fact, this relation we used
already in defining the link for LAG in Ch. III.

                   INTERTHEORETICAL RELATIONS                        295

notion of empirical equivalence should be extended to whole theory-
nets. This might be done by requiring that there be some bijective
mapping of the theory-elements of the two nets such that any two
related theory-elements under this mapping become empirically equiva-

respect to new specializations as well as lack of fully worked out
examples prevent us from looking deeper into this possibility.


                         VI.6 EQUIVALENCE

In comparison with empirical equivalence (full) equivalence puts more
weight on the relationship between the full conceptual structures of the
theories involved, i.e. between the potential models. In addition to this
we also have the requirement that both theories be about "the same
things" and that the relation among potential models yield some
satisfactory comparison between intended applications. In the preced-
ing section we saw that the latter requirement in isolation does not
presuppose the formal relation employed to be bijective. "Being about
the same things" may be captured by a many-many relation. This
suggests that there also is some indeterminacy in choosing "the"
adequate requirements for the relation between potential models. Let T
and T* be two theory-elements, and
           p <;;   M: Mp
                     X

be the candidate by means of which "equivalent" potential models
should be related. An account of equivalence similar to that of
empirical equivalence just would require p to yield a reasonable
relation between intended applications (along the lines discussed in the
preceding section), and to "preserve" models and constraints in a way
whiCh implies "equivalence" of the theoretical contents, the contents,
and the empirical claims of both theories.
    A first requirement on p is that all potential models on each side be
p-related to some structure on the other side. Without this condition,
some potential models would have no p-counterparts at all which
means that not "aU of" the respective theory is related to the other
theory. Intuitively, in this case one would say that only "part of" the
first theory is equivalent to the second. We therefore require that
  (1)      Dom(p) = M: and Rge(p) = Mp
296                           CHAPTER SIX

Very often, p also will be a function but for reasons already mentioned
in connection with reduction we hesitate to regard this as a general
requirement for equivalence.
   Next let us consider the requirements of p's preserving models and
constraints. As far as models are concerned there is a straightforward
formulation:
   (2)     for all x*, x: if (x*, x) E p then (x* E M* iff x E M)
As in the case of reduction, for the sake of simplicity we may assume
that it is not necessary to modify this condition with an explicit
reference to linked models. Taken together with (1), (2) implies that
every model of M* is p-related to a model of M, and vice versa. In
addition, (2) implies that the models in M* are not p-related to any
non-models in M p ' and vice versa. A similar requirement has to be
formulated for the constraints. We have to use an appropriate relation
p+ induced by p on the level of power sets, and to require that
   (3)     for all X*, X: if (X*, X) E p+ then (X* E C* iff X E C)

           (X*, X) E p+ iff (for all x* E X* there is x E X such that
           (x*, x) E p) and (for all x E X there is x* E X* such that
           (x*, x) E p)

  (4)      for all y*, y: if (y*, y) E P then (y* E 1* iff Y E I)

           (r*(x*) = r*(xi) iff rex) = r(xl))

Again, our choice is motivated by some difference concerning the
formal implications (especially TVI-JO below).

As mentioned earlier one would expect that equivalence implies
empirical equivalence. Unfortunately, the relation between the two
notions is rather complicated, and we are not able to prove such a
theorem without further assumptions. Intuitively, the difficulties arise
from the fact that we allow for "proper" relations which may be
many-many. There were general reasons as well as examples which led
us to these weaker formulations, so we do not want to adjust one of the
two notions of equivalence or of empirical equivalence just in order to
prove the theorem. We rather want to stick to the concepts as defined
above, and leave it to formal investigations whether one implies the
other or not. Without proof we state:
TVI-ll :   If p is a relation of equivalence between T and T* and (a) p
           is bijective or (b) the constraints of T and T* are transitive
           then p is a relation of empirical equivalence between T and
           T*.

our general definition of reduction in DVI-5, and DVI-1l-6 is slightly
stronger than the double-sided version of DV/-5-5. We also note that
DVI-1l-6 is not just a double-sided version of DVI-8-a.

We admit that this example, too, does not look very interesting. The
physicist will say that the example is trivial and the philosopher of
science will say that the two "theories" are really only two versions of
"the same" theory. (We shall come back to this below). We agree. In
fact, it seems difficult to find simple examples of equivalent empirical
theories which are so different in their formulation that one would not
just call them two versions of the same theory. If this is so, then one
might conclude that the concept of equivalence in reality does not have
the weight philosophers and philosophers of science sometimes attach
to it.
   In physics, the standard examples of equivalence are LAG-CPM,
CPM-Hamiltonian mechanics, and the matrix and wave formulations of
quantum mechanics. We can only consider the first example, because
we do not have reconstructions of the other theories at hand. So, what
about CPM and LAG? Are they equivalent? This question turns out to
be highly non-trivial. The first move in answering it is to consider the
relation defined by Jamison [18] between potential models of LAG and
CPM, which is slightly stronger than the link L(LAG) which links LAG
to CPM (see Sec. 111.6.3). If this relation is denoted by p ~ MP{CPM)
X Mp(LAG) then Jamison [18] has shown that if (x*, x)Ep and
x* E M(CPM) then x E M(LAG). But the converse of this fails. If
x E M(LAG) then, in general the conditions of L(LAG) will not imply
that the x* to which x is linked is a model of CPM. This may be shown
by constructing counterexamples. That is, p is not a relation of
equivalence between LAG and CPM.
   Next, let us try the relation already considered in Sec. VI-5-1. To
each CPM-system we assign a corresponding LAG-system by letting ij
be just the tuple of the component position functions, after suitable
transformations if needed, and by defining K and Q along the lines of
Jamison [18]. Again, this will yield a derivation of "x E M(LAG)" from
"x* E M(CPM) /\ (x*, x) E p", but not of the opposite implication.
304                           CHAPTER SIX

Intuitively, lamison's conditions as well as the weaker conditions of
L(LAG)-(4) and (5) defining K and Q are not suited to come to grips
with m and f, if we start from K and Q.
    SO what about trying to start from LAG? We might contemplate a
p-relation which to each LAG-system x assigns some CPM-system x*
as follows. Divide the number h of degrees of freedom by 3 with result
 k + i (i E {O, 1,2)). Take x* to consist of k + 1 particles PI' ... ,
PHI with component position functions Si(Pj' t) = qU-I)+i(t) plus
constant functions to "fill up" if needed. But again, how may we come
from K and Q to m and f, at least in a way so that Newton's second
law will follow from that of LAG? We have no solution.
   From three unsuccessful attempts we cannot, however, infer that
there is no relation of equivalence between LAG and CPM. Reflection
on the purely formal possibilities indicates that the mere existence of
such a relation may come out to be a rather trivial fact for logical
reasons, provided both theories are "rich enough" (compare Haring
[17]) - which is the case of CPM and LAG. If there is some such
relation for purely formal reasons then the question centers on whether
it yields a "reasonable" relation among the intended applications. This
is difficult to decide without having any concrete p-relation at hand.
We would not expect that formal results assuring double-sided inter-
pretability will yield sensible relations between the intended applica-
tions. Without definite arguments we thus should not expect LAG and
CPM to be equivalent.
   A final point we want to discuss in connection with equivalence is
that of "equivalent descriptions". Intuitively, the idea is the same as
with equivalence: there are two different but "equivalent" descriptions
of the "same" phenomena. If we replace "description" by "theory" and
remember how "sameness" was treated earlier then we just have the
situation of two equivalent theories. Thus, to say that we have two
equivalent descriptions of something just means that we have two
equivalent theories ("about that something"). This does not sound very
new and fascinating. But it provides a way of stating within our frame-
work what it is for some metatheoretical statement to be invariant
under equivalent descriptions. Consider some metatheoretical sentence
B(Tl' ... , Tn) where T I , . . . , Tn are variables for empirical theories.
Then
                  INTERTHEORETICAL RELATIONS                             305

            B may be said to be invariant under equivalent descriptions
            iff, for all T I, ... , Tn' TT, ... , T~ (ranging over empirical
            theories): if for all i ~ n, T j and Tt are equivalent then:
            (B(T I' ... , Tn) iff B(TT, ... , T~))
This kind of invariance becomes important in connection with inter-
theoretical relations. If, for instance, B(TI' ... , Tn) states that a certain
intertheoretical relation obtains among T I, ... , Tn then it is desirable
that B be invariant under equivalent descriptions. That is, B should not
depend on the particular way the theories in question are formulated,
or on the particular language or vocabulary used. In general, the
requirement of invariance under equivalent descriptions may be
regarded as a necessary condition on g.i.r.'s and on metatheoretical
statements about empirical theories.
   Let us apply this idea to some examples of g.i.r.'s we have introduced
up to now.

This failure suggests considering "invariant" definitions of specialization
and theoretization of the following form. If T, T* are theory-elements
then T is an invariant specialization of T* iff there exist T I, Tf such that
T, T 1 and T*, Tf are equivalent, respectively, and T I is a specialization
of Tf in the sense of Ch. N. Analogously, we may say that T* is an
invariant theoretization of T iff there exist T I, Tf such that T, TI and
T*, Ti are equivalent, respectively, and Tf is a theoretization of Tl in
the sense of DVI-J. It is clear from TVI-JO that the relations so defined
are invariant under equivalent descriptions. These invariant versions are
the adequate concepts to be used in general metatheoretical contexts. In
connection with concrete examples, one will of course refer to
particular formulations.


 VI.7 REDUCTION, LANGUAGE, AND INCOMMENSURABILITY

In this last section we want to discuss three topics in the context of
reduction involving explicit reference to language - which we tried to
avoid up to now. We do not have deep reasons for avoiding explicit
                  INTERTHEORETICAL RELATIONS                             307

reference to language in our general concepts of theories, theory-nets
etc. Our reasons are rather of a practical kind. Reference to language
creates certain problems which we do not find uninteresting in them-
selves but which tend to distract us from the issues we believe belong to
philosophy of science proper. Reference to language requires further,
complicated definitions concerning formal syntax which are not really
used in our metatheoretical studies. Also, it appears to us that the use
of formal languages in reconstructions of empirical theories has had on
the whole a more negative than positive effect in making things look
more complicated than necessary and obscuring those features of
theories which are really interesting to philosophy of science. This said,
we readily admit that there are topics which are most natural and
profitable to discuss by reference to language; some aspects of reduc-
tion may belong to them. This does not create any problems within our
concept of an empirical theory. It is straightforward to consider the
class Str( r) of all structures of a given type r = (k, m, aI' ... , an)
(compare Ch. I) to be just the class of structures for some "underlying"
language L in the sense of mathematical logic (compare, e.g. Shoenfield
[331 for a definition of this notion in the case of first-order logic). (Note
that the term "underlying" is intuitively misleading from our perspec-
tive.) We shall introduce such an "underlying" language in the way that
is common in formal logic, and we shall assume that the reader is able
to fill in the technical details. Though this procedure is of little help to
the logically unsophisticated reader we believe that he, too, will be able
to grasp the essentials of what will be said even without precise
knowledge of all details.
DVI-13:    Let r = (k, m, OJ, ..• , an) be a type.
           L is a language of type r iff L is a (k + m )-sorted language
           such that Str( r) is the class of all interpretations for L (or
           structures for L) in the sense of model theory. L is a
           language for structure species ~ (or for theory-element T) iff
           ~ is of type r (or the potential models of T are of type r)
           and L is a language of type r.
Intuitively, L consists of a set of non-logical symbols corresponding to
the terms RI , ••• , Rm of Str( r) plus suitable variables of different sorts
and types plus logical symbols and some formation rules telling how to
construct the formulae of L. We do not specify the formation rules so
that the language is not uniquely determined. Most naturally, one would
308                          CHAPTER SIX

admit quantification of variables ranging over individuals, and also of
variables of the types used in the inductive construction of aI' ... , an'
So if some of the 0i contains two or more occurrences of "Po" the
corresponding language most naturally would be of higher order.
However, we do not want to require this explicitly, leaving room for the
"quantificational apparatus" being stronger than necessary. It should be
noted that languages of type T are not precisely the languages in which
the axioms a i for some structure species of type T could be formulated
(see DI-4). For these axioms may contain non-logical symbols different
from those denoting the relations R I , ••• , Rm. Since the following
considerations are of more general nature, and will not really be
applied to concrete examples, we leave it with the present definition
which saves us much complication.
    Let us now turn to three special problems about reduction whose
discussion has been stimulated by the work of D. Pearce [29, 30]. The
first problem is whether we are justified in talking about "derivation" in
connection with condition DVI-5-3 of the definition of reduction.
Recall that we were considering theory T (directly) reducing to T* and
that DVI-5-3 says
   (A)     for all x*, x, ifx* E M* and (x*, x) E p then x EM.
In the discussion of the concept of reduction we used to paraphrase this
(not without qualification) as stating that
   (B)     The laws of T can be derived (under translation) from those
           ofT*.
It is entirely clear that the proposition 'x* E M*' does not express the
same as that T* is true or that the laws of T* are true, and similarly with
x E M. So it is not clear whether (B) may be used for paraphrasing
(A).
   Nevertheless, we want to show now that, under certain restrictions
and plausible interpretations, (A) and (B) are equivalent. Even if the
additional assumptions to be used may not be realistic as far as they do
not provide a frame in which empirical theories could easily be
formalized, their existence to a large extent justifies our using (B) to
translate (A).
   Let T and T* be theory-elements and L, L * be languages for T and

consist of a mapping of the sentences of the respective languages into
each other. A translation of L into L * then is at least a mapping
           trans: Sent(L) --> Sent(L *).

A second question about reduction and language we want to consider is
whether reduction implies translation, that is, whether the existence of
some relation p of direct reduction implies the existence of a transla-
tion of the corresponding languages of the theories in question (if we
assume that the latter are given in a unique way). Let us begin by stating
the relevant result from logical theory which is just a generalized
application of the well-known interpolation theorem (compare
Feferman [9]).
   If the following conditions are satisfied:
  (1)        T and T* are (idealized) theory-elements having no auxiliary
             base sets and p directly reduces T to T*
  (2)        Land L * are languages for T and T* with disjoint sets of
             sorts and non-logical symbols, but identical otherwise
  (3)        p respects isomorphy and can be defined by a compact set
             of axioms
  (4)        The logic employed in T (given by logical axioms and rules
             of derivation) is the same as in T* and is such that the
             interpolation theorem holds
  (5)        p is unique (compare DVI-8-h)
then we may conclude that there exists a function trans: Sent (L) -+
Sent (L *) such that for all x* E Dom(p) and all a E Sent (L): x* 1=
trans ( a) iff p(x*) 1= a
By premiss (5) p is a partial function so that we can write p(x*) in
order to denote the function-value of x*, provided x* is in the domain
of p: x* E Dom(p). The first part of premiss (3) then caQ be stated as
312                          CHAPTER SIX

follows: if xj and x~ are isomorphic then so are p(xi) and p(xn,
provided that xj, x~ E Dom(p). And isomorphy can be defined in
terms of canonical transformations. The second half of (3) usually will
be satisfied in applications, and therefore may be regarded as a mere
technical assumption. The theorem then essentially says that if the logic
common to both theories has the interpolation property then there
exists a mapping trans of the sentences of L into those of L * which
"corresponds" to p, where "correspondence" is expressed by the
following diagram, which in a certain sense "commutes". Still more
briefly: reduction implies a mapping of the languages.
                                           p
                             M*::3 x*-x=p*(x*) E M
                               p    lr            lr            P
           Sent(L*) ::3 trans(a) = a * - a E Sent(L)
                                          trans


It is tempting to call trans a "translation". Certainly, any translation
from L to L * has at least to be a mapping by which sentences of L are
mapped ("translated") into sentences of L *. The existence of such a
mapping is a necessary condition for L to be translatable into L *. But
this condition is only necessary, and by no means sufficient. A further
common requirement for translation is that it preserve meaning. The
above diagram may be regarded as going in that direction. We may call
the "upper" level the level of semantics and of meaning so that p
represents a relation at least between possible referents of the terms of
Land L *. If meaning were reference we could say that p somehow
relates the meanings attached to the terms of Land L *. The diagram
then might be paraphrased as expressing that if a * is the "translation"
of a then the "meaning" of a * as given by all possible x* E M; for
which x* 1= a*, is p-related to the "meaning" of a, as given by all
x E Mp for which x 1= a. And conversely, if the "meanings" of a* and
a and p-related then a* is a "translation" of a.
   Tempting though it may be, we cannot infer from this diagram that
trans is a proper translation. Certainly the requirements expressed in
the diagram go into the direction of "preservation of meaning" but they
do not go all the way: they still are too weak. This is obvious in the case
of translations of natural languages where model-theoretic semantics
does not lead very far. Even if we manage to introduce semantical
structures for some fragments of two natural languages being translated
into each other we tend to have strong reservations about these
                  INTERTHEORETICAL RELATIONS                            313

 structures capturing the "full" meaning, and even more about their
 being related by some p which "preserves" meaning. But also in
 contexts of axiomatized scientific theories we find examples showing
 that the above diagram is too weak to guarantee preservation of
 meaning and thus real translation. Think of SETH and statistical
 mechanics. It is believed that there is some p which (perhaps approxi-
 matively) reduces the former to the latter. Also, there is a mapping
 trans of the sentences of the former into sentences of the latter, and it
 seems plausible that p and trans satisfy the above diagram. But there
 are strong reservations (at least among philosophers of science) about
 saying that trans is a proper translation, preserving, e.g., the meaning of
 the term "state". Such cases of "incommensurable" theories - which
 will be considered in more detail below - provide evidence for the
 claim that the conditions on p and trans stated above are not sufficient
for calling trans a translation proper.
    If they were sufficient then the theorem roughly would say that
reduction implies translation, provided the logic used has the inter-
polation property. That is, at least for some restricted domain of
application - given by theories which can be axiomatized in systems of
logic with the interpolation property - reduction would imply transla-
tion. Counterexamples show that this is not so, the reason being that the
mapping guaranteed by the theorem in general need not preserve
meaning and thus need not be a proper translation. In other words: our
concept of reduction is weak enough not to imply preservation of
meaning.
    The third problem with reduction and language which we touched
upon already is that of incommensurability. The problem may simply
be formulated by means of this question: Are there incommensurable
theories? Of course, the answer will depend on what we mean by
"incommensurable", and the pre-systematic notion here seems to be
rather vague and controversial - in spite of much discussion in the
literature. We intend to advance a precise concept of incommensu-
rability for theory-elements. Unfortunately, we do not have at our
disposal examples which are worked out in full detail. Thus we will, as
is common in most discussions of this issue, confine the discussion of
our proposal to brief, informal and admittedly somewhat speculative
remarks.
    Advocates of the so-called "incommensurability thesis" have pointed
out the fact that theories that are supposed to be closely related to each
314                            CHAPTER SIX

other, both historically and systematically, show, on closer analysis, the
phenomenon of conceptual disparity between their most basic notions.
Favorite examples of pairs of theories appearing in this situation
are supposed to be the following: Aristotelian and post-Aristotelian
theories of motion, Ptolemaic and Copernican astronomy, impetus
theory and Newtonian mechanics, equilibrium thermodynamics and
statistical mechanics, classical and special relativistic kinematics, classical
and special relativistic mechanics, classical mechanics and general
relativity. In all these cases, and others one could add from non-
physical disciplines as well, it is claimed that, though both theories in
each pair seem at first to be conceptually linked, they really are not.
Their concepts are only lexicographically the same. Their meanings are
essentially different and therefore may not be put in any logical
relationship (like identity, inclusion, partial overlapping, etc.). The
respective conceptual frameworks are as different as those of two
unrelated cultures, i.e. they are "incommensurable".
    In order to discuss the incommensurability thesis in a fruitful way, it
is important not to trivialize the concept of incommensurability
involved - as some defenders as well as opponents of this thesis
sometimes tend to do. We should distinguish "trivially incommensu-
rable" from "non-trivially incommensurable" theories. Examples, rather
than general descriptions, will help in clarifying the distinction we
intend to make. All cases listed above are to some extent plausible
candidates for pairs of theories which are non-trivially incommensu-
rable. On the other hand, the relation between Marxian theory of value
and classical particle mechanics, or that between simple equilibrium
thermodynamics and a psychoanalytic theory of the unconscious are
instances of trivial incommensurability. A philosophically interesting
explication of incommensurability has to apply to the first kind of
examples - not to the second. It may be that some radical "meaning-
variance theorist" would like to claim that our distinction between
trivial and non-trivial incommensurability is unwarranted and that
his/her claim is precisely that all cases of theories with a conceptually
different framework - as slight as the difference might appear
superficially - are trivially incommensurable in our sense. They
absolutely have nothing to do with each other. He/she would claim that
the connection between e.g. classical and relativistic mechanics is
exactly the same as the one between classical mechanics and Marxian
value theory - namely none. We shall not indulge in a detailed
                  INTERTHEORETICAL RELATIONS                            315

 argument against this claim. We just assume that there are amply
justified reasons, coming from a combination of historical case studies,
 formal reconstructions and plain common sense, for considering the
 claim of the radical meaning-variance theorist to be manifestly wrong.
    On the other hand, the possibility of non-trivial incommensurability
is worthwhile considering. Of course, it could be the case that the
intuitive notion of non-trivial incommensurability proves to be, after
 some analysis, a vacuous notion: Though logically conceivable, there
would be no real cases where the notion of non-trivial incommensura-
bility is applicable. That is, all pairs of theories found in scientific
literature would be either cases of trivial incommensurability or else
their concepts would be "mutually translatable". The latter alternative
would apply to the list of examples given above, among many other
cases. Though we have no formal proof of the falsity of this claim since
the relationships between the theories in question have not yet been
reconstructed in full detail and in a generally convincing manner, we
think that the intuitive arguments advanced by the "meaning-variance
theorists" with respect to a number of historical examples cast serious
doubts on the alternative just mentioned. For example, it has been
argued that one cannot "translate" the term 'natural motion' as it
appears in impetus theory into the same term as it appears in
Newtonian mechanics without loss of meaning; or that the meaning of
'mass' in Newtonian mechanics cannot be embedded into the meaning
of 'mass' or 'rest mass' in special relativity by any ascertainable "rule of
translation"; it could probably be argued in a similar (though perhaps
less evident) way that the meaning of 'state' in thermodynamics cannot
be equated with a collection of certain 'coordinates' in statistical
mechanics. In all these cases, it is argued that even if we might
encounter lexicographically the same term or expression or symbol in
both theories of the pair considered, the meaning changes so drastically
that not only must we say that we are confronted with two different
concepts expressed by the same word (which in itself would not be a
serious problem), but also that there is no way to construct the meaning
of one of the concepts out of the meaning of the other one. Though we
have no definite proof for this claim, we may envisage the possibility
that at least some of the cases above-mentioned correspond to the
situation just depicted. Therefore, it does not seem to be an idle task to
try to explicate within our meta theoretical framework the following
"(non-trivial) thesis of incommensurability":
316                          CHAPTER SIX

   (TI)   There are pairs of theory-nets N 1, N z succeeding in histori-
          cal time such that:
      (A) Nl and N z are not trivially incommensurable.
      (B) (Some of) the basic concepts of Nl and N z are not mutually
          translatable (in a meaning-preserving sense).

 Clearly, this formulation of the thesis of incommensurability still is
 rather vague. In order to discuss its likelihood it is convenient to make
 it more precise. Condition (A) of (TI) may be rendered as the claim
 that there is some kind of formally ascertainable connection between
NI and N z. Typically, this connection would be a p-relation or some
sort of approximative p-relation. (In view of the examples listed above,
the second possibility appears to be more likely to be applicable.
However, since a precise notion of approximative reduction will be
introduced only in the next chapter here we shall concentrate our
discussion on reduction tout court.) Other kinds of intertheoretical
relations may come into scene as well. The only important point on this
level of generality is that some plausible g.i.r. between two non-trivially
incommensurable nets N 1, N z be found such that it may be constructed
out of some identifiable links Ai ~ Mp(N 1) X MP(Nz). Nothing in the
way of the examples listed nor of the general epistemological arguments
brought forward by the meaning-variance theorists gives any reason to
preclude the existence of such g.i.r.'s in the case of incommensurable
theories.
    Condition (B) of (TI) is more difficult to formulate precisely. Just
difference of meaning will certainly not do. Even if a term tl in theory
NI has a meaning different from a term tz in N z, it could be translated
into some logical transformation of tz (presumably in combination with
other terms of N z). If NI contains, say, the concept of a bachelor and
N z the concepts of male and of being married, then we could translate
any sentence of the form 'x is a bachelor' appearing in NI into a N z-
sentence of the form 'x is a male and x is not married' in spite of the
fact that the word 'bachelor' doesn't have the same meaning as either
'male' or 'married' - whatever 'meaning' may mean. What we need in
order to be confronted with the phenomenon of incommensurability is
the impossibility of equating the meaning of the terms of NI with any
logically describable transformations and combinations of terms of N z.
(These transformations and combinations may include all kinds of
mathematical operations as well.)
                 INTERTHEORETICAL RELATIONS                          317

    A fortiori, mere change of reference in the terms of one and the
 other theory will be no guarantee at all for the presence of an
 incommensurability relationship. Whether or not the meaning of a term
 is exhausted by its reference - a question which we would like to leave
 open now -, a generally accepted idea is that, at least in scientific
 contexts, reference is a (proper or improper) part of meaning. There-
fore, the general argument according to which mere change of meaning
 does not imply incommensurability also applies to reference. Neverthe-
less, we think that a particular sort of change of reference does playa
 role in incommensurability. Since it is convenient to examine this
question with more detail, let us first see why mere change of reference
does not give any reason for concluding that we face two incommensu-
 rable theories.
    In the case of theories using metrical concepts (which encompasses
all the examples analyzed in this book) some of their basic concepts are
functional terms whose reference is constituted by sets of tuples of
empirical individuals together with real numbers. Each real number
expresses the value of some magnitude for each empirical object. A
change in the real number assigned to one and the same empirical
object would clearly be a change in the reference of the functional term
in question, since we would immediately get a different set of tuples.
However, even if the change of value takes place within the same
metrical scale, the same frame of reference and the same class of
admissible approximations, unless some further aspects are involved
nobody would consider such a minor modification as a symptom of a
"dramatic" change implying conceptual disparity or incommensu-
rability. It would rather be considered as a typical instance of the
everyday business of science, presumably due to some "accidental"
misfit between our theoretical calculations and the non-theoretical data,
or at inost to a small change in the set of special laws used or the
intended applications considered. All such a change of reference
amounts to is a change of the potential model used or considered with
respect to a given intended application. Even if this kind of change
would occur with all intended applications, this would not be dramatic
enough to conclude incommensurability. For example, by adding a new
fundamental law or a new general constraint we might systematically
change the values of some magnitude assigned to all empirical objects
constituting the theory's intended applications. This more drastic
modification might possibly be regarded as a change of theory, but still
318                          CHAPTER SIX

 the old and the new theories would not be considered as "incommensu-
 rable" in any intuitive sense, nor would the change be a conceptual
 "revolution". We need much more to be justified in speaking of
 incommensurability.
    What we think one needs for (non-trivial) incommensurability is an
"ontological" change in the reference of the basic terms of all p-
 corresponding potential models of both theories. What is an "onto-
logical" change? We think that a substantial change in the extension of
the principal base sets and/or in the typifications of the relations
constructed upon them will be felt as a sufficiently drastic change in our
"worldview" (= in the "furniture of the world") to warrant speaking of
incommensurability. Of course, put in this way we immediately see that
incommensurability is a matter of degree - as it should be. The more
base sets change their extensions and the more substantial this change
is, the "more incommensurable" the theories are; the same goes mutatis
mutandis for changes in the typifications of corresponding relations.
Such a gradual concept of incommensurability is more likely to be
applicable to historical examples than an "all-or-nothing" concept. It is
plausible to say that in the passage from Kepler's to Newton's theory of
planetary motion there is "less incommensurability" involved than in
the passage from Newtonian to special relativistic mechanics, and this
pair of theories is, in turn, less incommensurable than CPM and
general relativity. Incommensurability should be used as a comparative
rather than dichotomic concept. To see this, we define a "minimal" and
a "maximal" concept of incommensurability. To simplify the exposition,
we shall refer incommensurability to a g.i.r. of the p-type only; we
could, of course, extend our definitions to other g.i.r.'s which might be
felt as worth considering in this context. For more perspicuity we shall
also restrict our considerations to basic theory-elements instead of
whole theory-nets.

DVI-14:   Let T, T' be basic theory-elements and p a reduction
          relation such that p directly reduces T to a specialization of
          T'. Then:
      (A) T and T' are (non-trivially) incommensurable in the weakest

             (1) (X)i is a principal base set of x' and, for all j E N, if

Incommensurability in the weakest sense is not very interesting (as
incommensurability) since, especially in the case where only condition
(A)-(l) is fulfilled and the intersection (x'); n (x)j is always much
bigger than the difference (x');\(x)j it is not really plausible to talk of
any conceptual disparity at all. On the other hand, incommensurability
in the strongest sense, though theoretically interesting, is not very likely
to occur when there is (approximative or exact) reducibility between
theories. Our hypothesis is that real cases of incommensurability will lie
somewhere between the two extremes just defined. Our final version of
the incommensurability thesis runs, consequently, as follows:
   (TI*)   There are pairs of theory-nets N 1 , N2 succeeding in histori-
           cal time such that their respective basic theory-elements T 1
           and T 2 are in a g.i.r. of the p-type and they are incom-
           mensurable in a sense which lies between DV/-14-A and
           DVI-14-B.
A completely formal explication of the thesis of incommensurability, as
we understand it here, should make precise in what particular sense the
incommensurability assumed between two basic theory-elements "lies
between" the conditions stated in DVI-14-A and those stated in
DVI-14-B. It is very likely that there is no general criterion to specify
what this "lying between" here means. Very likely, the precise sense in
which the incommensurability conditions "lie between" those two sets
of conditions will depend on each particular pair of theories con-
sidered. Our general hypothesis, however, is that "interesting" cases of
320                                CHAPTER SIX

incommensurability will be those in which conditions DV/-14-B-I and
-2 taken together will be weakened, but not "too much". For example,
we may envisage as an interesting case of incommensurability one in
which, for each principal base set, the "size" of (X)i n (x')} is "com-
parable" to the "size" of (x)Nx')}, and in which some of the most
important functions - though not all of them - fulfill DV/-14-B-2.


                                  BIBLIOGRAPHY

Work on global intertheoretical relations anteceding the approach
presented in this chapter is contained in [3, 6, 7, 26], and [35] below.
