                             CHAPTER VII




                         APPROXIMATION



                        VII.O INTRODUCTION

Any empirical theory can be effectively applied to its domain of
intended applications only under the assumption of allowing for some
degree of inaccuracy or approximation in the use of the theory and in
the theoretical reconstruction of the data. As a matter of fact (and
perhaps also as a matter of principle), no known empirical theory of
any complexity works exactly. The degree of inaccuracy with which the
theory works may be expressed numerically or qualitatively, according
to the type of theory and application. In "mathematized" empirical
theories, that is, in those theories that use metrical concepts, there will
be a tendency to express their degree of inaccuracy (partly) in
numerical terms, whereas in "qualitative" theories, that is, in those
theories that only use classificatory or comparative concepts, the degree
of inaccuracy implicitly or explicitly assumed will be given by non-
quantitative comparisons. Only in qualitative theories of a very simple
kind is it possible to avoid the (implicit or explicit) use of approxima-
tions, but only at the expense of producing quite trivial claims - claims
that have almost no empirical content and lack technological applica-
bility. In qualitative theories with a minimal amount of sophistication as
well as in the more fully mathematized theories of the natural and
social sciences, the use of approximations will be absolutely essential
(though frequently implicit). For example, when we apply some intelli-
gence test to two different persons and assign them the same I.Q.,
thereby concluding that both "have the same intellectual ability", we
know that, if the test is reasonably sensitive, the responses of those two
persons to the test will not be, in general, exactly the same. Neverthe-
less, this does not hinder us in assigning them the same intellectual
level, if we consider that the differences in response are below the test's
discrimination threshold. Thus, any theory of personality using (com-
parative) concepts like intelligence, neuroticity, introversion, etc. and
reasonably sophisticated detection devices (tests), will necessarily apply
those concepts in an approximative way. Obviously, these considera-
                                   323
324                        CHAPTER SEVEN

tions could be generalized to any theory, either "mathematized" or
"qualitative", either from the natural or from the social sciences.
    The importance of approximation for empirical science is obvious to
experimental scientists and technologists, but it has been neglected by
most theoretical scientists, and only recently it has attracted the
attention of some philosophers of science. Usually, when two different
theories "should" be related in some simple and direct way, but are
obviously not so, some rather unclear words are said about "limiting
cases", "constants tending to 0 or infinity", etc. There is not much
philosophical insight to be gained from such phrases. In any case, laws,
theories, and empirical results are very often presented without saying a
word about their approximative character and the problems involved in
it. A similar picture is offered by many historians of science, who write
much about, say, Newton's discovery in the seventeenth century that
the planetary system "obeys" the law of gravitation, but usually forget to
tell us about the painstaking efforts made during the 18th century and
afterwards to make sure that Newton's law actually fits the astronomical
observations "with quite good an approximation".
    Of course, everybody knows - or should know - that scientific laws
and theories can be applied to reality only up to a certain degree of
approximation, and that competition between different laws, theories,
and "research programs" is, in many cases, nothing but competition to
attain a better degree of approximation. Systematic accounts in the
philosophy of science seem to have regarded this as an uninteresting
accidental feature of the scientific enterprise - something not really
belonging to the "essence" of science and not worth deserving a
detailed analysis. We believe this attitude to be fundamentally mis-
leading. It is misleading to take for granted that the canonical situation
the philosopher should account for, is the situation in which a theory
with perfectly exact concepts perfectly fits the facts it is supposed to
systematize. There is at present no significant empirical theory in which
this really happens, and we see no reason to suppose it will ever
happen. An adequate logical reconstruction of empirical science must
take approximation as one of its essential features.
    The program is, then, to define appropriate approximation concepts
and structures to be included in adequately extended metatheoretical
structures.
                           APPROXIMATION                               325

                 VII.1 TYPES OF APPROXIMATION

Let us try to become a bit more systematic as to what counts as an
approximation in empirical science. First of all, the logical category of
the approximation concept in general seems to be that of a dyadic
relation: Something is an approximation of some other thing. It also
seems that scientific research uses many different kinds of approxima-
tion in many different contexts. But perhaps they are not so many. Let
us try to get at a crude typological classification of different approxima-
tion cases. There appear to be four main types:
   (1)     model construction approximation
   (2)     application approximation
   (3)     law approximation
   (4)     intertheoretical approximation.
We shall briefly and intuitively discuss each, in turn, before moving on
to a more technical discussion.
   First, there is the case where we try to systematize some empirical
data within a given conceptual framework, and in the process we have
to make some "idealizations" and "simplifications" (read: approxima-
tions) in order to obtain a manageable model. In our terms, this is the
case when we start constructing a potential model or a partial potential
model out of some given empirical data. For example, we approximate
the motion of a macroscopic body by considering it as a particle on a
continuous path; or from a finite number of geodetical measurements
we conclude that the earth is an ellipsoid - thereby forgetting all its
mountains and valleys; or we consider a visible light ray in our room as
representing a geometrical straight line. This level of approximation (or
"idealization") may be called the level of model construction. A first
step towards a logical reconstruction of this level has been made by
Suppes [23].
   Second, at the next level we approximately apply some law or theory
to a "constructed model", that is, we try to subsume a conceptually
systematized collection of data under a propounded law. In our terms,
we try to make a potential or a partial potential model into an actual
model, perhaps also taking account of the constraints and links to other
theories. For example, we try to make plausible that the body falling in,
front of us is a case of Galilei's law of free fall, or that the earth's
motion around the sun obeys the law of gravitation, or that we can
326                           CHAPTER SEVEN

apply the law of reflection to a(n) (idealized) ray of sun light. This we
shall call 'application approximation'.
    Third, when we consider a law as an approximation of another, more
complicated law of the same theory - both laws therefore belonging to
the same conceptual framework - we have an approximate relationship
on a purely theoretical level which we call 'law approximation'. In such
cases, we do not worry about the empirical facts "outside" the theory -
we are only doing mathematics within the theory. This comparison of
laws is very common in physics. For example, Galilei's law is taken as
an approximation of the law of gravitation; or the ideal gas law is taken
as "approximately true" with respect to the law of van der Waals, and
this is itself an approximation of a still more complicated expression -
the virial equation of state; or the law for the simple pendulum (relating
its period r to gravitational force g):

                        1 ) 112
           r= 2:n ( -
                     g

is an approximation of a more realistic expression when the amplitude
a is not "small enough",




which is in turn an approximation to a power series. Many examples of
this sort can be found in any physics textbook. It is common in such
cases that the simpler or "less exact" law derives from the more
complicated one by substituting a fixed numerical value (usually 0 or 1)
for a parameter (a constant or a real function) which appears in the
approximated law. For example, van der Waal's equation (with "p" for
"pressure", "V" for "volume", "T" for "temperature" and constants
a, b, R)




"reduces" to the law of ideal gases (compare Ch. III) by taking a = b =
O. Not all cases are that simple, of course. But commonly the "approxi-
mation trick" consists in changing (and fixing) the value of some
magnitude appearing in the law.
                           APPROXIMA TION                             327

    We are speaking here of a given law approximating another given
 law. But in many cases the expressions approximating or being approxi-
 mated do not really deserve the label of "laws" in the usual sense. They
 do not appear in the systematic exposition of the theory. That is, they
 don't determine the actual models of a "serious" theory-element of the
 theory-net; they are just devices for calculation introduced for some
 rather special purpose - usually approximation needs in technological
 applications. Formally, there is no clear-cut distinction between genuine
 laws and those more special devices calculation; but most scientists
 would feel that those "engineers' equations" do not really deserve the
 label of a "law". Take the case of the systematization of the motion of a
motor vehicle when we take its mass as time-dependent (fuel mass
 being lost): Should we call the resulting dynamical equation a physical
law? Nevertheless, in spite of the misgivings about this strained usage of
the term, for brevity'S sake we shall continue to use the general term
"law" in the following - keeping in mind that this label is intended to
 cover both "serious laws" and "mere devices for calculation" introduced
 ad hoc for dealing with particular applications, especially in approxima-
tion contexts.
    As already noted, approximation between laws is, in a certain sense,
a purely theoretical endeavour, a paper-and-pencil operation. Never-
theless, this fact does not preclude us from admitting an intimate
relation between this kind of approximation and the approximation of
the second kind mentioned, that is, the approximative application of a
law to an empirical constructed model. Suppose we have applied some
law L1 to an empirical domain D with some success, but we are still not
very satisfied with the degree of approximation thus obtained; we may
try to construct a second law Lz such that L1 is taken as an approxima-
tion of L z and L z applied to D gives a better degree of approximation.
Or, conversely, L1 applies "quite well" to D, but the calculations made
with the help of L1 are very tedious: We would like to have a simpler,
even if cruder, way of systematizing D. So, we look for a Lo which,
while being a simpler approximation of L 1, may be applied to D with a
degree of approximation that is sufficient for our purposes. A more
formal account of this relationship between both levels of approxima-
tion will be given below.
    Finally, there is a kind of approximative relation at the most theo~
retical level, which does not seem to be reducible to the approximative
relationship between laws: approximation between two general theories,
i.e. between whole structures with different conceptual framework and
328                        CHAPTER SEVEN

different fundamental laws. Let us call it "intertheoretical approxima-
tion". Kinds (2) and (3) in contrast may be termed 'intratheoretical
approximation', whereas (1) would be termed 'pretheoretical approxi-
mation'. Intertheoretical approximation seems to hold between classical
and special relativistic mechanics, between phenomenological thermo-
dynamics and statistical mechanics, between geometrical optics and
electrodynamics. It is fairly obvious that these cases cannot be
subsumed under exact reduction as treated in the previous chapter.
Often, the label "approximative reduction" is used. In fact, some
authors take approximative reduction to be just a generalization of
strict reduction, obtained by "adding" features of approximation to
strict reduction. Some examples have already been worked out along
these lines (cf. Mayr [8]; Moulines [10] and [11]). However, in our
opinion such a notion of approximative reduction may turn out to be
too narrow in order to cover all cases of intertheoretical approxima-
tions that might be expected to occur. We therefore prefer to keep the
more general label, but occasionally we also will speak of approxima-
tive reduction. In this book we are not going to discuss in detail
problem context (1) since we do not have anything new to say about it.
We shall concentrate on clarifying the approximation issues subsumed
under (2), (3), and (4).

           VII.2 INTRA THEORETICAL APPROXIMATION

We have got now to be more precise about the kind of entities to be
compared with each other in an approximative relationship of types (2)
or (3). A first thought could be to take statements as the entities to be
compared. Most philosophers of science that have taken approximation
into consideration have assumed the "statement view" more or less
explicitly, that is, they have taken empirical statements (either laws or
their instantiations) as basic units of analysis and have considered
approximation as a relation between some statement and "the truth" -
i.e. as a relation between some (false) empirical statements that we
know and true empirical statements that we do not know. Along these
lines the concept of verisimilitude was introduced as a property of
those statements that appear in real science. Such statements would be,
strictly speaking, false but more or less verisimilar or likely. (A ,survey
of work done within this approach is contained in Niiniluoto [13];
see, further, his more recent [14].) This account faces difficulties of
                            APPROXIMA TION                               329

epistemological nature as well as of applicability to real-life examples.
We can avoid these difficulties by shifting the level of comparison from
sentences to models.
   The basic idea is to take set-theoretic structures rather than state-
ments as the entities to be compared in an approximative relationship.
This approach to the particular case of approximation is in accord with
the general metatheoretical methodology propounded in this book. To
see how this idea might work, just remember that when we use a theory
to describe some empirical state of affairs, the first thing we do is
describe this state of affairs by means of some potential model of the
theory. And also remember that, given a state of affairs, there will
normally be a large number of potential models that fit it. Among the
host of potential models that formally correspond to it, some pairs will
be considered more similar to each other than other pairs; and the
"degree of similarity" between possible mathematical descriptions of
some facts may be an important question to consider when we try to
apply the theory to those facts.
   For example, if we try to apply a dynamic theory to the motion of
some physical system S consisting of a set of particles P during some
time interval T in a spatial region S by means of a position function s, a
significant question to ask is what degree of similarity beween two
possible descriptions of this system may be required. A possible answer
may be given in the following terms. If x and yare possible descriptions
of S (i.e. two potential models of the dynamical theory that are
conceptual reconstructions of the same physical system), we shall be
satisfied with their similarity if they fulfill the following condition for
some previously agreed upon real numbers e and 0:
  IS]      Px = Py, Sx = Sr' Tx = Ty, and, for all p E Px, t E Tx:
           Irx(p,t)-rip,t)1 < eandID2rxCp,t)-D2rip,t)1 < O.
If this condition is fulfilled, we shall say that x is an approximation of y,
and conversely. Note that, in order to state this approximation condi-
tion, no proper axiom (empirical law) of the theory is needed. This
means in our terminology that we are working on the level of potential
models.
    The present approach towards a general explication of approxima-
tive notions mainly rests on the proposal of taking approximation as a
relation between two potential models of a theory-element, i.e. as
dyadic relation on a given class Mp. The concrete features of the theory
330                         CHAPTER SEVEN

are totally irrelevant for the realization of this program. We do not
need to suppose that we are dealing with a "quantitative" theory (i.e. a
theory with metric functions) nor that approximation rests upon some
special measurement methods. The level of generality of the present
explication is such as to be applied to very crude and qualitative
theories as well. The only assumption needed is that we can axiomatize
the theory and distinguish the structural from the proper axioms, i.e. Mp
from M. Now we are in a position clearly to state the explicandum we
are after. It is a metatheoretical statement of the sort: "potential model
x is an approximation of potential model y in theory-element T". What
is the way to its explicans?
    Potential models of a theory element T are all elements of the same
class Mp of T. As said above, the particular form the elements of this
class may take does not matter on the general level. We· therefore may
just ask how to define an approximation relation between any two
elements (or "points") of a given class or set. There is a well-known
method for defining such a relation in topology, namely to introduce
the concept of a uniform structure (see e.g. Bourbaki [2]). Therefore, we
reconstruct model-theoretic approximation by defining a uniform
structure on the class of potential models. In the following, we shall
abbreviate "uniform structure" to "uniformity".
    Before going on to the formal definition of a model-theoretic
uniformity let us offer an intuitive picture of it. For a given class (in the
present case Mp), a uniformity determines a whole array of subclasses
of it, each of them representing a "degree of approximation", "degree of
similarity", or "measure of inaccuracy". Let us introduce a neologism to
denote such subclasses. Let us call them "blurs". They are instruments
to transform sharp claims into blurred ones. Entities playing a similar
role in other metatheoretical studies of empirical approximation have
been given different names: Ludwig [5] called them "Unschiirfemengen";
Moulines [10] "fuzzy-sets", D. Mayr [7] "inaccuracy-sets", and Hart-
kamper and Schmidt [3] "imprecision-sets". The idea behind all these
labels is pretty much the same. However, there are some non-trivial
differences, either of a formal or of an intuitive kind. Therefore, even at
the cost of terminological inflation, we choose still another name for
our formally defined degrees of approximation.
    A blur consists of pairs of elements of the original class (Mp in this
case). If a pair (x, y) is in a blur u, this means that x and y approximate
                           APPROXIMA TION                             331

each other in at least the degree given by u. We could alternatively say:
x and y coincide at least up to u. Or still: x and yare u-nearly equal. In
the case of a set of real numbers, where we have a standard metric (the
absolute value of the difference) we can define the standard uniformity
where each blur is determined by a particular e:



But this is a special case only. The concept of a uniformity does not
depend on the concept of a metric; it is more general. The determina-
tion of empirically relevant blurs can be much more complicated than
the previous example, or even not expressible in metrical terms.
   Such a general concept is precisely what we need for explicating the
comparison of potential models. For the general treatment of approxi-
mation we need not bother about the specific terms of the models
(mainly functions) involved in the approximation. Besides brevity, this
abstract treatment has two other advantages. First, we are completely
flexible in defining a particular blur by reference to whatever com-
ponents of the potential models we please. In a concrete case, a given
blur could be defined by referring, say, to the function Rl occurring in
the potential models, but we might as well define blurs with respect to
R z, or also with respect to Rl and R 2 • For example, in a gravitational
study of the earth-sun system we may state the approximation condition
by considering lIm(sun) to be "almost" zero, or alternatively by
considering the force which the earth exerts on the sun to be "very
small"; the same degree of approximation is obtained by considering
masses and by considering forces. Second, and still more important, in
a general treatment we need not assume that the blurs used in some of
the theory's applications are determined by any completely specifiable
conditions: It may be the case that a specific inaccuracy degree depends
on the "personal knowledge" of the scientists, on their "intuitions",
changing pragmatic needs, and so on. All we need to know is that the
blurs used are elements of a uniformity associated with the theory'S Mp.
   For the formal definition of a uniformity, we need the following
special notation: If M is a class, then ~(M) is the "diagonal" of M, i.e.
the class of all pairs of identical elements of M. If u is a set of pairs
then u- 1 denotes the set of ordered pairs of u in which the order of the
components is reversed, u- 1 = {(y, x)/(x, y) E u}. Finally, if U J and Uz

We call the elements of U "blurs". Note that, formally, a blur is a dyadic

small variation in the first axiom). The following axioms (4)-(6) are
specific of the uniformity concept.
   Let us try to interpret this formal structure in terms of model-
theoretic approximation to see whether it appears intuitively adequate.
First note that the pragmatic ground for associating a uniformity U with
the class Mp of a theory-element T is to allow for a liberalization in the
application or manipUlation of T. Should we assume that T applies
exactly to its domain, or that the relations between its special laws are
always of an exact kind, we would bump into falsification quite soon.
Formally, this would mean that we only allow for the use of the
diagonal - as a "degenerated" blur - in the manipulations of T. The
use of the diagonal represents absolute exactness. But real scientists are
more liberal than that. They use "proper" blurs in their manipulations
of a theory. The size of the specific blur used depends on the different
kinds of applications and manipulations of T. The bigger the blur, the
easier to stay out of trouble. Of course, if a certain limit is exceeded,
the theory becomes completely useless. But this is a point we neglect
for the moment; we shall consider it in the next section.
   As a kind of slogan for an intuitive understanding of the conditions
in DVII-J let us say that: To associate a uniformity with a theory is a
way to immunize it against troubles in its applications. (The limits to
                            APPROXIMA TION                               333

 this kind of immunization will be discussed later.) Suppose we have
 constructed a uniformity U for theory-element T, and we are using
 some special U E U for a given application of T. This means that we
 have "immunized" this application up to degree u. For example, the
 application may consist in the following. (This is only one possible
 case.) Given a system S, we make some theoretical calculations using T
 and predict that S will have the mathematical form described by
 potential model x. But then, after some "empirical observations", we
 come to the conclusion that S should better be described by potential
 model y, with x ¥- y. If (x, y) E u, then we are satisfied, at least for the
 time being. If (x, y) $. u, there are two possible reactions: Either to be
 still more liberal and admit that, after all, we would also be satisfied
with a u' E U such that u C u' and (x, y) E u'; or to reconsider T
and/or the mathematical description of S. Both kinds of reactions are
copiously exemplified in everyday science. The more pairs (x, y) you
let in u, the safer you are; and, of course, the less you can really do with
the theory.
     Leaving aside the purely structural axiom DVII-J-J, let us translate
the rest of them into the "immunization language". DVII-J-2 states that
if the theory is immunized by a blur u!, it will also be immunized bya
bigger ~ including u!. DVII-J-3 says that if we immunize T by using u!
and by using ~, we may put both of them together and immunize T by
using their intersection. This axiom is, perhaps, less obvious than
DVII-J-2, but it seems quite plausible - at least as an idealization.
(Note that the intersection cannot be vacuous, by DVII-J-4: It always
contains at least the diagonal.) If we are satisfied with approximation
degree u in some application, whatever this degree may be, we will also
be satisfied with exact application, if this fortuitously happens; that is,
exactness is included in every blur. This is the content of DVII-J-4.
However, it is not assumed that the diagonal is itself a blur. This cannot
be derived from the axioms. And we think this is all right. It is science
fiction to assume that a theory will ever be supposed to apply with
absolute exactness. Condition DVII-J-5 is obvious under the present
interpretation: The order of the models of a pair in a blur has no
significance at all for the "immunization degree" of the theory-element.
D VII-J-6 is a critical axiom. It roughly states that for any given blur u!
immunizing T, a sharper ~ may be found such that ~ still immunizes
T; ~ is at least twice as sharp as u!. For an easy appraisal of this last
axiom, consider a very simple example. Suppose the model-theoretical
334                        CHAPTER SEVEN

blurs of a geodesical description are determined by an approximation
condition on the position function of "particles" or "points":

Such an axiom certainly represents an idealization of actual scientific

ever attain ~, i.e. exactness.)

VIT.2.1 Blurs on Two Levels

When the distinction between T -theoretical and T -non-theoretical
                           APPROXIMA TION                              335

 concepts for a given theory-element T is introduced, i.e. the distinction
 between Mp and M pp ' a natural question to ask is whether the "global"
 approximations undertaken on the level of Mp (which involve all of T's
 concepts) could be "confined" to the non-theoretical level of Mpp- This
 question gets its significance from the fact that all one needs for having
 an approximate version of the empirical claim of a theory-element T is
 to apply the blurs to the T-non-theoretical concepts. On the other hand,
 since we also make theoretical calculations using the T -theoretical
 concepts which have some bearance on the T -non-theoretical concepts,
it is clear that we cannot just consider uniformities on M pp ' but rather
 must retain the uniformities on Mp. A first question then is how the
 "global" approximation undertaken on Mp is related to or reflected in
 the "empirical" approximation on Mpp. The second question we have to
deal with in this context is how all these approximation structures are
 reflected in the formulation of the empirical claim. The first problem is
attacked in this section, and the second problem in the two following
sections.
    The first move is formally to express non-theoretical approximation
by using a uniformity defined on Mpp in quite the same way we did it
for Mp. We introduce a class of relations V ~ Po(Mpp X Mpp) satisfying
the axioms of DVIJ-l. Its elements may be called "non-theoretical
blurs". This means that, in principle, we may associate two kinds of
uniformities with a theory-element T: a U for Mp and a V for Mpp- Our
intuitive understanding of the situation leads us to expect some
relationship between a uniformity on Mp and a "corresponding"
uniformity on Mpp; or still more intuitively: Approximation on the
Mp -level is performed for the sake of approximation on the Mpp -level.
    To make these intuitions somewhat clearer, let us consider the
example of Newtonian gravitation theory GCPM and its applications
once again- (see Ch. IV). Recall that the potential models for GCPM are
structures of the form (P, S, T, N, ~, cI , c2 , s, m, f) with the standard
interpretation of the components: P is a set of particles, S is a spatial

F acting on a particle at a given time may be constructed out of f:
F(p, t) = LEN f(p, t, i). It is the resulting force that interests us now.

(within one theory).

    However, from a completely general standpoint there is no guarantee
that this mechanism will always work. There is, in principle, no
guarantee that a uniformity on Mp will induce a "corresponding"
uniformity on Mpp - notwithstanding the intuitive plausibility of the
idea. In fact, there is no general proof to the effect that this induction is
always possible. The critical axiom DVl/-J-6 is the trouble-maker here:
Assuming the present concept of uniformity, it cannot generally be
proved that ever increasing sharpness of the theoretical blurs induces
an ever increasing sharpness of their corresponding non-theoretical
restrictions. The basic reason for this impossibility lies in the fact that
many theoretical models correspond to only one non-theoretical
model. It is easy, though somewhat lengthy, to see that this fact has the
effect mentioned above.
   In spite of the difficulty just mentioned, we should not give up our
hopes too hastily. It can be shown that by restricting the original
concept of a uniformity with a further plausible requirement one gets
the desired theorem. The uniformity thus modified we shall call an
"empirical uniformity" - "empirical" in the sense that it is significant
for empirical theories only (i.e. for theories with the distinction between
theoretical and non-theoretical concepts). It can be proved, then, that
an empirical uniformity on Mp always induces in a natural way a
corresponding empirical uniformity on Mpp. Our aim may be roughly
stated as the proof that the non-theoretical restriction of any blur is
itself a blur. To prove this formally we need some further auxiliary

level always induces a corresponding uniformity on the non-theoretical
level in a natural way. This means, intuitively, that the distinction
between Mp and Mpp does not enforce the separate introduction of two
uniformities - one for Mp and one for Mpp. It is sufficient to introduce
just one empirical uniformity on the Mp-Ievel, which then becomes
automatically translated into the Mpp-Ievel.

the notion of an empirical theory, it would seem natural to introduce
the empirical uniformity on Mp that we need for expressing all kinds of
approximations within a theory formally as a component of our notion
of a theory-element. If U is the empirical uniformity needed for
"matching" K with I in a given synchronic theory-element, then we

of the ideal (K, I). The diachronic version of the theory-element would
become similarly expanded into (K, U, I, G). However, in spite of the
apparent plausibility of this move, our final version of a theory-element
will not include the whole of the uniformity needed, but only a part of
it. The reasons for this restriction will become understandable after the
discussion of admissible approximations in the next section. The part of
the uniformity associated with a theory-element that we shall introduce
formally as a component of the final version of a theory-element will be
the class of so-called "admissible blurs".

VI1.2.2 Admissible Approximations

The content of the axioms of a uniformity was explained above by
 interpreting the use of blurs as a way to immunize a theory up to a
 certain degree. We already mentioned in passing that the "bigger" the
blur we use, the "safer" the theory becomes but the weaker the content
 of its claims. It is clear that if no restriction is placed upon the elements
of U that we are allowed to choose for using the theory, then we can
match everything with anything, but of course the price is that we shall
not be saying much of interest. The theory becomes useless. Therefore,
when we consider questions of empirical applicability of a theory, it is
clear that not every blur will do. Blurs that are "too big" in an intuitive
sense should be ruled out. Size is the most significant, but not the only
relevant consideration for selecting admissible blurs; there are other,
more subtle factors to take account of. In this section we are going to
consider the question of the admissibility of those blurs that we need to
state the empirical claim of a theory.
    The question of what still is a good approximation and what already
is a bad one when applying a theory is a much involved issue and we do
not claim to provide a final answer to it here. We only aim at depicting
the main lines of the problem and describing it as precisely as we can.
From the very beginning, it should be clear that the degree of
inaccuracy that will still be considered admissible in a theory, is an
issue that heavily depends on the particular intended application we are
dealing with. When applying, say, the law of gravitation to planetary
motion, we do not expect the same degree of approximation as in the
case we apply it to the attraction between two large lead spheres on the
earth's surface, making measurements by means of a delicate torsion
balance. However, the admissible degree of inaccuracy not only
depends on the particular application at stake. It also depends on the
stage of scientific evolution. The expectations of the scientific com-
munity with respect to approximation change in time, according to
varied and informal factors, like technological progress in detection and
measurement, mathematical progress in the theoretical calculations,
previous success attained by rival theories, etc. These are strongly
pragmatic factors. It is unlikely that they will ever become completely
and formally explicable. On the other hand, they are very important for
the admission of a given blur for a particular application. In the
                           APPROXIMA TION                              343

 reconstruction of the empirical claim of the theory-element, we should
 take them somehow into account.
    Here, we are facing a problem similar to that of formally determining
 the concept of an intended application, which is also strongly prag-
 matic. All the philosopher may be asked to do in such cases, is to find
 some (weak) necessary conditions for the determination of the concept
in question. This is what we shall try to do here for the notion: "class of
 admissible blurs" (for the application of a theory-element at a given
 time). Let us denote this class by A.
    What can we say in general about A? One thing for sure is that it
 must be a proper subclass of U. But there are other requirements that
we can see it must always satisfy. To see the kinds of factors that are
involved here, let us consider again the example of a kinematical
description of a system of celestial mechanics. Suppose we are com-
paring two kinematical descriptions of the "same system" - i.e. we
are comparing two partial potential models of Newtonian particle
mechanics. One typical situation in which we may say that there is a
good approximation between both descriptions (and that therefore we
are using an admissible blur) is the situation expressed in formula [S]
previously in this chapter. That is, we have the same base sets P, S, and
 T for describing, say, the planetary system, while the position and
acceleration of each celestial body in the two descriptions may differ by
an amount of f and 0, respectively, whereby f and 0 are "small enough".
    We may envisage some further complications of this standard
picture. For example, we may not only approximate the position and
acceleration functions, but also allow for some non-metric approxima-
tions with respect to the set P of bodies considered. These may refer to
just the number of particles considered. It is likely that if one of the
kinematical descriptions of the planetary system coincides with the
other one in everything but the fact that one of them forgets about one
of Saturn's minor satellites, then we shall probably regard both partial
potential models as "almost equivalent" and we may say that the model
in which that satellite is missing is a good approximation of the model
in which all satellites are present. On the other hand, no serious
astronomer will say that a description of the planetary system in which
Jupiter is missing is a good approximation of a description that includes
this planet. Note that, in approximative considerations of this kind
about the set that constitutes the domain of each model (a set of
344                        CHAPTER SEVEN

 particles in the present example), both the differences in number of
 the elements considered and the differences in theoretical significance
 attributed to each one of the elements play an important role. That
 some minor satellites or asteroids of the planetary system are dis-
 regarded, may appear to be relatively unimportant in order to calculate
the orbits of the rest; but to take Jupiter away is absolutely unaccept-
 able. These approximative comparisons about the number and signifi-
cance of the elements contained in P are "qualitative" in the sense that
they are not expressible in "epsilontic" terms, i.e. through the standard
metric on the real numbers.
    Another sort of qualitative approximative considerations are those
referred to in the description of the nature of each one of the elements
of P. For example, for a given planetary theory (let us say, in some
historical period of the development of celestial mechanics), a descrip-
tion of the planets as spheres may have been regarded as a good
approximation of their description as ellipsoids of small excentricity
("slightly flattened spheres"). But in some other theory-element (in a
later historical period, say), the same approximation may not be
regarded as satisfactory: At most, the relation between an ellipsoid and
a geoid would be considered as a good approximation. Such differences
usually are not of the kind to be expressed in "epsilontic" terms.
    According to what has been said thus far, in the global approxima-
tive comparison between two planetary kinematics a number of
different factors have to be accounted for: metrical differences between

differences between the descriptions of each element's geometrical
form, and perhaps some other factors as well.

Not every blur which is admissible with respect to given -, E, 0 will be
really admissible in an absolute sense. It is clear that the bijection
implicit in - must be properly chosen, and that E and 0 must be small
enough. The choice of the particular -, E, 0 will certainly depend on
the particular application we have in mind and on some changing
pragmatic factors. However, there are some general conditions of
admissibility that can be stated in a quite precise and systematic way.
Let us discuss this question in more detail.
    The most essential condition for admissibility in general is the
existence of what may be called an "upper bound". Intuitively, it means
that, beyond a certain degree of inaccuracy, the disparity apparent in
the comparison between two models will be considered unbearable.
Thus, there will be an upper bound for the portion of the uniformity
which is effectively used in the theory. Otherwise, empirical theories
would cease to do empirical work.
    In the following we shall always assume the existence of boundaries
of approximation, and we shall say that any blur which is "smaller" (that
is, stricter) than a given boundary will be admissible for stating the
empirical claims of the theory-elements. In general, we shall define the
set of such boundaries of all admissible blurs of a given uniformity U as
follows:
DVII-5:    If U is a uniformity (either on Mp or on Mpp) and A ~ U,
           then:
           Bound(A) =: {ulu E U, and for all u' E U: if u ~ u', then
                       u' $. A, and if u' C u, then u' E A}.
The intuitive requirement of the existence of upper boundaries
in approximation will then become formally the requirement that:
Bound(A) ¥- 0.
   A straightforward corollary of the definition is this.
TVII-6:    If U is a uniformity and A ~ U, then:
           if u E U and u E Bound(A), then u $. A.
A sensible question to ask about Bound(A) is this: How many elements
does Bound(A) contain? A simple answer could be: Just one. In this
case, we would be claiming that, when we want to subsume a given
domain of applications I under a given core K, there will be exactly one
boundary for the degree of inaccuracy we still want to admit for the
"match" between I and K. This boundary would be the same for all
 348                         CHAPTER SEVEN

  applications. However, this simple answer is not plausible in general.
  With regard to different applications of the same theory-element
  usually different degrees of inaccuracy will be accepted. This is true
  even in a synchronic cut in the theory's development. Clearly, when
  making measurements of kinematical magnitudes, we shall not require
  the same accuracy on the astronomical and on the laboratory scale.
, Applications that allow for measurements with very sensitive instru-
  ments will not use the same blurs as those that are treated with less
  developed technology. Therefore, the boundaries of admissibility will
  somehow depend on the particular features of the application we have
  in mind. Whether or not some non-trivial and precise conditions of a
  generalizable kind can be stated about this dependence, we do not
  know. We want to leave it as an open question. In general, Bound(A)
  will have more than one element, it may have infinitely many.
      Up to this point we have discussed the requirements for admissibility
  of blurs taking only Mp into account, that is, without the distinction
  between theoretical and non-theoretical terms. Once this distinction is
  made, a further requirement seems natural to be imposed on admissi-
  bility: The admissibility of a given blur should be invariant with respect
  to purely theoretical changes in the models it contains; that is, if u fully
  coincides with u' with respect to its non-theoretical components, and u
  is admissible, then u' should also be admissible.
      Finally, an obvious additional requirement to impose on admissi-
  bility is that this notion be invariant with respect to mere change of
  order in the consideration of the potential models; that is, if u is
  admissible, then also u- 1 should be so.
      With all these requirements in mind, let us introduce the notion of
  admissile blurs formally. Since we do not want to preclude the possi-
  bility that some further general conditions of admissibility be found in
  future research, we shall state the set of present requirements as a
  necessary but non-sufficient set of conditions. That is, the next "defini-
  tion" is not a genuine definition in a formal sense, but rather a list of
  up-to-date identified necessary conditions.

admissibility of the blurs will not be independent from the particular

is expressible in general terms we do not know.

VII.2.3 The Approximative Version of an Empirical Claim

Consider a synchronic idealized theory-element T = (K, I), that is, an
element without "diachronic" components like G. The idealized empiri-
cal claim of T is the global statement that 1 can completely be
subsumed under K. In Ch. II this was defined formally as the set-
theoretic statement: 1 E Cn(K). At the beginning of this chapter, it has
already been pointed out that, if we want to be realistic about the way
minimally developed empirical theories function, then we have to take
account of the fact that the "match" between 1 and K will never be
exact, i.e. the empirical claim will express a blurred relationship
between 1 and K. How much blurring is allowed for will depend on the
particular class of admissible blurs we happen to use for the particular
idealized theory-element T. This means that the idealized empirical
claim "I E Cn(K)" has to be transformed into a more realistic blurred
claim of the same sort which makes use of admissible blurs.
   Since the match between K and I, which is expressed by the
empirical claim of T, normally will not obtain unless we use a class A of
admissible blurs, it is plausible to conclude that A essentially belongs to
the "constitution" of a theory-element. Therefore, we have to add A to
K and 1 in order to constitute a synchronic theory-element. Let us
define this formally. Recall that in Ch. II we only introduced the notion
of an idealized theory-element, and that we omitted the adjective
"idealized" thereafter only for reasons of brevity. We are now at a point
where we have to use the full label in order to keep clear about the
distinction between idealized and "realistic", i.e. approximative theory-
elements.
DVII-8:   T is a theory-element iff there exist M p' M, M pp ' GC, GL, I,
          U, A, such that
      (1) T = (Mp, M, M pp , GC, GL, A, I)
      (2) (Mp, M, M pp, GC, GL, I) is an idealized theory-element
      (3) U is an empirical uniformity on Mp
      (4) A is a class of admissible blurs in U for (Mp, M, M pp , GC,
          GL,I)

idealized empirical claim of the form 1 E Cn(K), a(n) (approximative)
theory-element (K, A, I) will be used to make a(n) (approximative)
claim. The question now is how to make this notion precise.

VIL2A Approximations in Theory-Nets and Theory-Evolutions
So far, we have dealt with approximation within a single theory-
element. This is the most typical case of intratheoretical approximation
and intuitively corresponds to what we have characterized as approxi-
mate application of a law to a constructed model at the beginning of
358                       CHAPTER SEVEN

 this chapter. There we also noted that there is another case of
 intratheoretical approximation, intimately related to the previous one,
 which may intuitively be characterized as approximation between laws
 of the same theory. In our terms, what we have here is an approxima-
 tive relationship between different theory-elements of the same theory-
 net. This situation may be analyzed synchronically, in which case we
 have to take account of just one theory-net, or else diachronically, in
 which case we have to make approximative comparisons of theory-
 elements across a theory-evolution. Both cases still belong to the
 context of intratheoretical approximation, since not only the general
 conceptual structures, but also the approximative structures "hang
 together" in a quite straightforward sense. This will become clear along
 the discussion in the present section.
    The first basic idea is that the elements of a theory-net should
become "approximatively connected" in the sense that they make use of
commensurable "approximation devices" - the approximation relations
they use are "of the same kind". Ultimately, this means that they all use
blurs of the same uniformity. The question could be raised whether we
may not go a step further and claim that all theory-elements of a net
use the same class of admissible blurs, and consequently, that they all
share the same bounds of inaccuracy. However, a little reflection shows
that this would be too strong a claim. Normally, depending on the
particular law we happen to apply to a particular domain of intended
applications, the degree of admitted inaccuracy will vary. The blurs we
are ready to admit for applying Hooke's law in mechanics are not
necessarily the same we are ready to admit for the application of the
law of gravitation. They will be of the same kind, that is, they will
belong to the same empirical uniformity, but they will not have the
same boundaries of inaccuracy - not even for intended applications
that happen to be common applications of both laws.
    Nevertheless, we should not too hastily give up the idea that there
must be some connection between different degrees of admissible
inaccuracy and different theory-elements of the same net. Consider two
idealized theory-elements T and T' such that T' is an idealized
specialization of T. Roughly speaking, this means that T' is obtained
from T by adding more laws to the ones already postulated in T. This
implies, in tum, that a priori the possibilities of application, of T'
decrease as compared to the possibilities of application of T. It seems
quite obvious that, in such a case, we are not going to be more srict as
                           APPROXIMA TION                             359

to the degree of admissible inaccuracy with respect to T' than with
respect to T; that is, the boundaries of admissible inaccuracy for T' will
be at least as big as those for T. Or, to see it from the opposite
perspective, the fewer the laws we want to apply to a given class of
intended applications, the more accurate the results we expect from the
application. When many laws are simultaneously at stake, we are more
tolerant with respect to inaccuracy than when only one or two laws are
being applied. Therefore, when an idealized theory-element is a
specialization of another, its boundaries of admissibility will be bigger
or equal to the boundaries corresponding to the other one. This seems
to be an analytic implication of the notions of admissible inaccuracy
and specialization.
    In addition to this effect that specialization has on admissibility,
we have to take into account the consequences for the construction
of a theory-net which arise from considering approximative theory-
elements, and not just idealized theory-elements. Since the elements of
the theory-net represent "blurred" ties between a core and a domain of
applications, which only match by means of some blurs, it is natural to
conceive the relationships the elements might have among them as
"blurred" relations as well. In particular, this means that the idealized
specialization relation will also become an approximative relation. That
is, if we want T' to be a specialization of T, we shall only require that
the class of models of T' approximately be a subclass of the class of
models of T, and analogously for the constraints and the corresponding
domains of intended applications.
    Before we define this relationship systematically, it is convenient to
introduce the notion of two theory-elements being connected with
respect to approximation.

The inclusion of approximation structures into an idealized theory-
evolution is a rather straightforward matter. We shall have a sequence
of theory-nets (with approximation) connected by an idealized speciali-
zation relation throughout historical time as in Ch. V. The idealized
specialization relation is now "blurred", but besides this, nothing
362                       CHAPTER SEVEN

changes in the explication. The question may be raised whether changes
of period in a theory-evolution will not also be accompanied by
some systematic changes in the approximation structures, i.e. in the
whole class of admissible blurs or in the boundaries. They would be
systematic insofar as we could characterize them by some law-like
proposition. A little reflection shows that it is not safe in general to
assume that there will be any systematic changes of accuracy in the
application of laws: Some theory-elements might increase their accuracy
in the match of K with I, while at the same time others might
experience a (still admissible) decrease of accuracy, and still others
might altogether be abandoned because new observations and/or
calculations show the gap between K and I to be too big. Also, changes
in the admissibility of inaccuracy might be prompted by factors that
have nothing to do with changes in K and I, but rather with changes of
experimental technology or of the "external" influence of other theories
that tell us what degree of inaccuracy is still admissible in the theory
presently considered. All these changes could lead to changes of the
boundaries of admissibility in any direction.
    On the other hand, it is true that we would positively assess any
theory-evolution that experiences an overall increase of accuracy; that
is, we expect a tendency towards smaller boundaries from a "good"
theory-evolution. In other words, a progressive theory-evolution should
be conceived not only as one with increasing successful specializations
(D V- 7), but, moreover, as one with increasing accuracy. Though we
cannot state any general conditions on approximation for a theory-
evolution of any sort, we shall require of a progressive theory-evolution
that it tend towards an increase of accuracy. We make these ideas
explicit in the following definitions. Analogous to the notion of an
idealized diachronic specialization (remind DV-2) we first need the
notion of a(n) (approximative) diachronic specialization relation. (The
concept of a diachronic theory-element would be introduced in the
obvious way - which we spare ourselves here - as a structure {T, A, I,
G) by just adding an admissible set A to the structure as defined in
DV-l.)

           VII.3 INTERTHEORETICAL APPROXIMATION

For the rest of this chapter we shall deal with intertheoretical approxi-
mation. In the present section we introduce a general scheme for
constructing approximative relationships between conceptually different
theories, or to be more precise, between theory-elements that differ not
only with respect to their laws and applications (as in the case dealt
with in the previous section) but also with respect to Mpp and/or Mp.
   The explication of a general concept of intertheoretical approxima-
tion has not only an interest in itself, but is of relevance to a more
general issue within recent discussion in the philosophy of science: the
question of incommensurability of theories separated by a deep
conceptual change we touched already in the previous chapter. Here,
we shall not expand on this issue. Let us only remark the following. We
are not claiming that all cases of radical theory change that have been
identified as cases of incommensurability by some historians and
                            APPROXIMA TION                               365

 philosophers of science can be reconstructed simply as instances of
 intertheoretical approximation in our sense. What we do claim is that
 some important examples of pairs of allegedly incommensurable
 theories that have been mentioned in the literature could be subsumed
 under our general scheme of intertheoretical approximation. These
 examples are the following: Kepler's planetary theory vs. Newton's
 theory of gravitation; Newtonian particle mechanics vs. special rela-
 tivistic particle mechanics, Newtonian particle mechanics vs. quantum
mechanics; (a part of) equilibrium thermodynamics vs. statistical
mechanics; geometrical optics vs. undulatory theory. Possibly, some
other historically relevant examples could be added. We are not going
to attempt a proof of the truth of this claim for all the examples
mentioned. In this chapter, we shall prove the claim only for the first
example of the list. The second example has been treated in Pearce and
Rantala [17] in a different setting but it could easily be treated in our
frame, too. For the remaining examples we can only hope that future
research shows our claim to be on the whole acceptable. We think that
both the general treatment of intertheoretical approximation and the
particular instantiation of it offered in this chapter make the general
claim plausible to some degree. To avoid misunderstandings, let us
emphasize at this point that we are not claiming that all aspects of
alleged incommensurability which have been noticed by historians and
philosophers may completely be covered by structuralist analysis. In
particular, we do not have anything to say about the change in
metaphysical worldview and in microsociological structure that are
supposed to accompany radical theory changes. But we do claim that
important issues of a semantical and methodological kind usually
associated with scientific revolutions may be rendered precise and fully
understandable by using the notion of intertheoretical approximation.
In fact, if theories that are separated by a replacement process and
apparently have different conceptual structures can nevertheless be said
to approximate each other in a well explicated sense of "approxima-
tion" then this sheds new light also on incommensurability.
    When we speak of a general notion of intertheoretical approximation
we mean a concept that could be applicable to different sorts of
"blurred" intertheoretical relations. The general notion should have a
sufficient degree of flexibility in order· to cover different specific kinds,
of approximation between theories. Accordingly, in this section we first
introduce a general scheme for the relation of intertheoretical approxi-
366                         CHAPTER SEVEN

mation. Then, we modify it to the more special case of what we call
"approximative reduction".
   "Intertheoretical approximation" is a generic name for any kind of
blurred intertheoretical relation between two theory-elements T, T'
such that MpP(T) "# Mpp(T ') or MP(T) "# Mp(T'). In other words, the
theory-elements being compared by means of intertheoretical approxi-
mation belong to different (synchronic) theory-nets. It should be clear
that in the present context we have to work with the approximative
version of the notion of a theory-element, as introduced earlier in this
chapter. Consequently, intertheoretical approximation will be a rela-
tionship between theory-elements of the form (K, A, I) and (K', A', I')
where not only K and K' are conceptually different but also A and A'
playa role in the establishment of the relationship.
   By definition, if Mp and M~ are different then A and A' also will be
different. Therefore we shall not have "common" blurs to express the
model-to-model relationship between T and T', as we had in the case
of intra theoretical approximation. It makes no sense to use an u E A
(or an u' E A') to formulate a statement of the sort "(x, x') E u".
Therefore, we have to introduce some special device in order to
express intertheoretical approximation. The basic idea is to work with
neighborhoods derived from blurs instead of using the corresponding
blurs directly.

VI!'3.1 Approximative Reduction
Approximative reduction certainly may be construed as a biro In
372                        CHAPTER SEVEN

addition, we expect that approximative reduction should be obtained
simply by blurring strict reduction, as indicated by the very label.
Indeed, we will take this route and introduce the concept of approxima-
tive reduction as "blurred exact reduction". In doing so there is some
danger of being misled, by taking exact ,reduction to be the more
important or more fundamental concept because approximative reduc-
tion is "derived" from it "just by blurring". In view of real examples
from the sciences quite the contrary is true. There are several clear-cut,
interesting instances of approximative reduction which we mentioned
above, whereas we have no interesting example of exact historical
reduction (at least if we take the case of CCM and CPM treated in Ch.
VI as "not interesting"). Intuitively, strict reduction derives its interest
from being closely connected with logical derivation (remember the last
section of Ch. VI). In fact, then, we seem to be confronted with two
concepts each of which has some interest on its own: strict reduction
with its logical interest, and approximative reduction with its applica-
tions to interesting cases of progressive shifts in the history of science.
In the light of these considerations the fact that approximative reduc-
tion comes out "just" by blurring strict reduction no longer can be
regarded as obvious and expected, rather it has to be viewed as an
interesting fact about the development of empirical science, namely that
all those transitions which are subsumed under "approximative reduc-
tion" contain features of very strong connections as expressed by logical
derivations.
   In view of the previous section there are still several ways of
obtaining the concept of approximative reduction by blurring exact
reduction. Let us recall the definition of direct reduction in slightly
different terms.
           If T and T* are theory-elements then p directly reduces T to

VII.3.1.1 The case of the Kepler-Newton relationship. We want to show
now that the relationship between Kepler's planetary theory and the
gravitational theory-element of Newtonian particle mechanics is an
instance of almost exact approximative reduction of type wi.
   In this endeavour, we shall rely on the previous analysis of this
example as expounded in Scheibe [20]. In this essay, Scheibe gave
the particular conditions determining the relationship between both
theories without deriving them from a general intertheoretical scheme.
In the last part of the present section we shall come back to those
conditions which follow from our general concept of approximative
reduction.
   To begin with, it is necessary to define the theory-element that has to
be reduced, namely Kepler's theory, in a modern formulation. We
restrict considerations to two-particle systems which constitute the
essential aspect of Kepler's theory. Also, we assume that there are no
constraints and no links involved in the reductive relation so that these
components of the theory-element are trivial.

Third Law. Thus, the historically purist reader may interpret our
endeavor as reconstructing the relationship of Kepler's first successful
planetary theory to Newton's law of gravitation.

    Let us close this chapter by comparing our account with Scheibe's.
His study of the present example may be summarized by means of
three conditions which are relevant for the relation between KEP and
GCPM.
    (a) Each Kepler-system can be approximated by gravitational
        systems (op. cit., p. 114, (20»
   (b) Each gravitational system satisfying further appropriate condi-

omitted so that (b) and (c) are compatible.
   These conditions have some general plaUSibility, and one might
382                         CHAPTER SEVEN

 expect that similar conditions be satisfied in other cases of approxima-

priate versions of these - in general.
    Let us reformulate (a)-(c) in precise terms. The terms "Kepler-
system" and "gravitational system" refer to partial potential models
which can be extended to models, respectively. So r(M(KEP)) and
r*(M(GCPM)) are the classes of Kepler-systems and of gravitational
systems, respectively. As already noted: Mpp(KEP) ~ Mpp(GCPM), so
r(M(KEP)) ~ Mpp(GCPM). "Approximation of a Kepler-system by
gravitational systems" therefore can be understood in terms of the
uniformity introduced on Mp(GCPM), or simply, its projection on the
level of Mpp(GCPM). Let us denote the corresponding blurs by DE
(compare U(KEP)-a-l and 2). Then, that "Kepler-system x is approxi-
mated by gravitational systems" means that, for each c > 0, there is
some gravitational system y such that (x, y) E DE' Especially, this
implies that y also is a two-particle system. "Approximation of a
gravitational system by Kepler-systems" can be understood analogously.
With this in mind conditions (a)-(c) can be restated as follows.
    (a)' for all x E r(M(KEP)) and all c > 0 there is some x E
          r*(M(GCPM)) such that (x, y) E DE
    (b)' for all y E r*(M(GCPM*)) and all c > 0 there is some x E
         r(M(KEP)) such that (x, y) E DE
    (c)' there is some y E r*(M(GCPM)) and some c > 0 suth that for
          some x E r(M(KEP)):not(x,y) E DE
    In this formulation all three conditions are satisfied. (a)' is proved in
Scheibe's paper (p. 114); (b)' follows from the proof of TV11-13. (c)' is
trivial because of our restriction to two-particle systems on the side of
KEP. If we take y to be, say, a suitable three-particle system then, with
the uniformities used, y cannot be approached by two-particle systems.
    Scheibe's conditions are satisfied in the present example. But does
this indicate that they are "in general" contained in the concept of
approximative reduction? Closer inspection reveals that (a)' -(c)'
follow from the definitions of the models and uniformities in the case at
hand. The assumption that KEP is approximatively reduceable to
GCPM does not add anything to the proofs. Of course, conditions
(a)' -(c)' then also follow from the fact that KEP is approximatively
reduceable to GCPM - but in a trivial way. So in order to lend
plausibility to the concept of approximative reduction and to its com-
prising the three above conditions further consideration is necessary.

this condition which really creates some asymmetry. If (c)* could be

open question.
