         THE GLOBAL STRUCTURE OF SCIENCE



                        VIII.O INTRODUCTION

In this final chapter we continue our strategy of extending the
"surrounding" of an "isolated" theory. The ultimate object of study we
thereby approach is something like the structure of "all of science". Of
course, the concrete investigations - "concrete" in the sense of being
accompanied and "tested" by concrete examples - of the preceding
chapters did not lead us very far on the way towards this globl;ll object.
The structures we investigated, like specialization nets, theory-evolu-
tions, and global intertheoretical relations, still are rather "local" in
comparison to "all of science". But before we venture to make any
claims about the structure of the whole of science, some further
intermediate levels must be distinguished and reconstructed, levels
which still are relatively local but more comprehensive than theory-nets
or theory-evolutions. If we shift to ever larger complexes the role of one
single theory-element in such a complex will become less and less
important. There will be some maximal size of such complexes which
still may be reasonably regarded as depicting the surrounding of some
particular, "basic" theory-element. More comprehensive complexes will
have to be regarded as qualitatively different from mere "surroundings".
The question of how to characterize this distinction in an intrinsic way
- though being of great metascientific relevance - seems to have
received little attention, perhaps because of the lack of precise concep-
tual tools. We don't intend to offer a criterion for this distinction here,
we just want to pose the problem. Anyway, the main subject of this
chapter are theory-complexes large. enough not to count as just the
auxiliary apparatus of one particular theory-element.
    At the moment what we can offer in order to study such complexes
is some general conceptual apparatus. We are not in a position to
present concrete examples in order to show that our concepts capture
some real scientific phenomena - we hope to work out such examples
in the future. This does not mean, however, that the concepts to be
introduced are completely arbitrary or a priori, and are not to be
                                   386
                 GLOBAL STRUCTURE OF SCIENCE                          387

preferred to other approaches toward more global structures in science.
We shall try to demonstrate their value by applying them to the analysis
of some problems of a more philosophical nature. These analyses do
not aim directly at solutions of those problems. Rather they aim at a
clarification of the issues at stake and at making them more precise in a
way that may eventually lead to some solutions - if there are any at all.
We believe that the gain of clarity and precision achieved by our
conceptual apparatus - as measured against the standards of the
philosophical literature dealing with these same problems - is sizeable
enough to indicate that our apparatus is useful as a basis for further
investigation of phenomena lying in between theory-evolutions and "all
of science".
   What we are looking for are concepts that may plausibly capture
chunks of empirical science larger than theory-evolutions such as the
ones exemplified by labels like 'mechanics', 'classical physics', 'natural
science', and 'science'. We expect that our strategy of describing more
comprehensive parts of science in terms of "atomic" building blocks
(theory-elements) and relations between these (intertheoretical rela-
tions) per sued in the preceding chapters will also be successful in the
area we now approach.

                       VIII.l THEORY-HOLONS

To start with the discussion from a synchronic point of view, imagine a
piece of science bigger than a theory-net which we want to analyze in
terms of theory-elements and their relations. The concept of a theory-
element has been clarified to a great extent and not much further
adjustment or modification of it is to be expected in the present
context. The question therefore is what kind of intertheoretical relations
are met "in reality" and have to be employed in order to obtain an
adequate metascientific picture, and what kind of further structure such
a complex of interrelated theory-elements may have.
   As concerns the kinds of intertheoretical relations to be met, a
survey of the relations introduced earlier shows that there is a plausible
candidate depicting intertheoretical relations in general, namely the
concept of an intertheoretical link. We indicated on several occasions
- though not heavily stressed - that intertheoretical relations: special-
ization, theoretization, reduction, equivalence, may be regarded as
particular kinds of combinations of intertheoretical links. Furthermore,
388                        CHAPTER EIGHT

the concept of a link is a very general one on purely formal grounds. In
fact, if we drop the requirement put forward in Ch. II, namely that a
link should not properly be composed of relations among all of the
terms of both theories involved, it is hard to imagine a binary relation
between theory-elements which does not have the form of, or at least
induces, some link. It has to be noted here that in actual science there
may occur links relating more than two theory-elements at the same
time. Such links formally would have to be treated as "n-ary links"
where 11 is greater than two. A treatment of such links by extending the
present approach does not create essentially new problems. On the
contrary, it yields the possibility of investigating structural features
of "theory-complexes" beyond those treated below. Our reasons for
sticking to the case of binary links are that - up to now - we have not
met real examples of ternary or n-ary links (with n > 3), and that
things become much simpler if we consider binary links only.
    Let us introduce the term 'theory-holon' for sets of theory-elements
which are related by arbitrary intertheoretical links. We choose not to
use the label "theory-net" because this has been used earlier for
specialization nets which essentially grasp a specific surrounding of
some basic theory-element, and because we want to stress the shift
away from "surroundings" to "global structures", or wholes. Besides
taking only binary relations into consideration, a second special feature
of our notion will be that we assume at most one link to exist from a
given theory-element T to another given theory-element T'. This
assumption certainly is quite strong if we think of the matter in realistic
terms. We may well imagine two "different" links, that is, two links we
can easily separate conceptually, to lead from T to T'. On the other
hand, it seems to hold in general that the "conjunction" of two links -
set-theoretically given by their intersection - will be a link, too. We
therefore may consider just one link between any two theory-elements
which eventually "really" is a conjunction of several different links. As
long as there is no gain in keeping these separated our assumption of
only one link between T and T' does not represent any serious
restriction. Of course, we might come to a stage where it is necessary to
differentiate between different kinds of links leading from T to T'. The
following account then would have to be generalized in an obvious way.
We also note that the present account concentrates on the formal,
theoretical level. Relations among the intended applications are treated
as being induced by the links between full theoretical structures. Since
                  GLOBAL STRUCTURE OF SCIENCE                           389

in the following general discussion we do not need to refer to the
special terms which are properly involved in the links considered we
may here profitably use the notion of an abstract link introduced in
DII-4-a. Recall that an abstract link from Mp to M~ was just a binary
relation L ~ Mp X M~. We write A(f, T') instead of L in the following
in order to make explicit that the link is from T (i.e. from Mp(T)) to T'
(i.e. Mp(T')). Also we will not always use the proper label "abstract
link" in the following. "Link" will always mean "abstract link". If A is
such a link between T and T', then for given x E M p' x' E M~, we
shall sometimes write, for abbreviation's sake, "A(X, x')" instead of "(x,
x') E A". Note that this notion of a link involves a specific direction in
which the link operates. The temptation of formally identifying a link
from T to T' with its reverse from T' to T leads astray as will become
clear below. It is just this directedness that gives rise to some non-trivial
global features of theory-holons. The general notion of a theory-holon
now may be introduced as a set of linked theory-elements satisfying
some further minimal requirements concerning the global structure of
the complex.
D VIII-J : H is a theory-halon iff there exist N and A such that H =
           (N, A) and
       (1) N is a non-empty set of theory-elements
       (2) A.: N X N -> U {Po(MP(T) X Mp(T'))/T, T' E N} is a
           partial function
       (3) for all T, T': if (T, T') E Dom(A) then A(T, T') ~ Mp(T) X
           MP(T')
       (4) if N contains more than one element then, for all TEN,
           there exists T' EN such that (T, T') E Dom(A) or (T',
           T) E Dom(A)
       (5) for all T, T', TN: if (T, T') E Dom(A) and (T', TN) E
           Dom(A) then (T, TN) E Dom(A)
We do not require N to be finite. This is useful for the discussion of
some philosophical issues below. Formally, we represent the link from
theory-element T to theory-element T' as the function value A(T, T') of
a partial function A mapping pairs of theory-elements in a set of entities
which have the correct form to be links. A being a function expresses
the assumption discussed above, namely that there is at most one link
from T to T' for given T, T' E N. A being partial leaves room for pairs
of theory-elements in N which are not linked together at all. DVIII-J-3
390                         CHAPTER EIGHT

 says that the function value of A for a given pair (T, T') actually is a
link from T to T'. This is not yet implied by part (2) of the definition,
by which A(T, T') might be a subset of some MP(Tl) X Mp(T2) with T 1,
T2 different from T and T'. DVIII-J-4 is a condition of connectedness:
all theory-elements of N should be linked at least to one other theory-
element of N. Theory-elements which would fail to satisfy this condi-
tion might be called "isolated": they have no connection at all to the
other parts of the holon, and thus may be excluded. Requirement (5),
finally, says that the notion of being a link from ... to --- is transitive.
This is a kind of "synthetic" requirement as opposed to the others
which are of a more analytic nature. This kind of transitivity is actually
present in concrete cases, and no counterexamples are known to us.
Note that transitivity and connectedness together do not imply that
each theory-element in N is linked to each other. This is due essentially
to links being directed.
    Let us consider the new possibilities opened by this definition by
way of comparison with our earlier concepts. As already mentioned,
the definition of a link is general enough to comprise all other inter-
theoretical relations studied so far. Specialization gives rise to two links.
If T is a specialization of T' then, first, the potential models of both
theories may be linked by means of mere identity: (x, y) E Al iff x = y.
That is, Al = Mp(T) X Mp(T '). But the inclusion of models, M ~ M',
also yields a link which may be defined by (x, y) E A2 iff x = y and
x EM. If T is a theoretization of T', there is a link A3 from T' to T,
defined by (x, y) E A3 iff r(y) = x, where r is the function cutting off
the terms of T which are "new" wrt T ' (compare Ch. II). Reduction and
equivalence, finally, are directly defined with reference to some relation
between the potential models of both theories, that is, with reference to
a link. As far as sets of interrelated theory-elements are concerned, on
the synchronic level we considered only specialization nets. It is
straightforward to show that any connected theory-net is a theory-
holon. If Al above is used the result is trivial. If A2 is used, DVIII-J-4
and 5 have to be proved as consequences of DIV-2 and the definition
of A2 , respectively. Now what is new in D VIII-J? First, of course,
D VIII- I admits for "proper" links which involve only very few concepts
of both theories, like the link considered in Chap. III between HD and
SETH linking pressure with energy and volume. Second, we might
consider theory-holons in which all links are part of theoretization
relations. Or we might consider "reduction-nets" in which all links
                  GLOBAL STRUCTURE OF SCIENCE                          391

constitute reduction relations. We do not expect to find "interesting"
theory-holons of these "pure" types in reality, "interesting" in the sense
that the structure of how the theory-elements are linked is not com-
pletely trivial. The real advantage, however, of theory-holons is given by
the possibility of "mixing" proper links with global intertheoretical
relations (like p, a, r) and eventually with further relations to be
revealed by future studies. This yields the possibility of analyzing
portions of science which are more than mere surroundings of one
theory-element, and eventually may contain several "self-dependent"
basic elements plus their respective surroundings, or even bigger
portions.

              VIII.2 THEORETICITY RECONSIDERED

As already indicated in Ch. II our informal criterion of theoreticity may
be sharpened by reference to other theory-elements which, together
with the theory-element T under consideration, form a bigger con-
nected entity. Our concept of a theory-holon seems to be adequate to
represent the latter entity. So let us present here the sharper form of the
criterion which - besides T - takes into account a given theory-holon
H to which T belongs.
   Recall the paradigm of mass in CCM. As stated in Ch. II mass is
CCM-theoretical only if we restrict quantification over "all possible"
mass measurements in the criterion of theoreticity to those measure-
ments which can be described by potential models of CCM, that is, if
we exclude measurements via force laws which do not imply conserva-
tion of momentum. There, we saw that mass turns into a CCM-non-
theoretical function if we - realistically - also quantify over measure-
ments which are not potential models of CCM but are potential models
of some other well specified theory-elements like CPM. This example
shows general features which may be expected to occur in other cases
as well.
   The idea of how to extend our criterion to a given theory-holon H =
(N, A) is clear: just quantify over all measuring models which are
potential models of some theory-element in the holon. That is, term Ri
of T is T-theoretical wrt H iff: for all x': if x' is a measuring model for
Ri and a potential model of some T' E N then it follows that there is
some x which is a model of T and also an intended application of T. In
other words: measurement of Ri - possibly by means of some other
392                          CHAPTER EIGHT

theory-element T' of N - presupposes T, or implies that T has some
real model. The relation of entailment referred to may be explained by
means of the links in H. Let us introduce the concept of an entailment
link as a link A from T' to T which carries models into models, and
intended applications - via theoretical emendations - into intended
applications.

DVIII-2: If H = (N, A) is a theory-holon and T, T' E N then
          A(T " T) is an entailment link iff
      (1) for all x, x': if x' E M(T') and (x', x) E A(T', T) then
           xEM
       (2) for all y', y: if y' E I(T') and there are x', x such that
           r'(x') = y', rex) = y and (x', x) E A(T', T) then y E I(T)

By restricting considerations to those theory-elements T' which are
connected with T by an entailment link we obtain the following
sharpened form of the criterion.

D VIII- 3:   (Criterion of Theoreticity for Theory-Holons)
             Let H = (N, A) be a theory-holon, TEN and R be a term
             ofT. R is T-theoretical wrt H iff:
             for all x', if (a) x' is a measuring model for R and (b) there
             is T' E N such that x' EMiT')
             then (c) x' E M(T') and (d) (T', T) E Dom(A) and A(T', T)
             is an entailment link

According to this criterion, if R is T-theoretical wrt H then, if there is a
measuring model x' for R at all, there also is some real model of T,
i.e. some x E M(T) such that rex) E I(T). For, by the definition of
measuring models, x' will have as a reduct an intended application of
T', and so by the definition of entailment links the image of x' under
A(T', T) will be a real model ofT.
    Note that this version indeed is a sharpening of the original version
described in Ch. II, because now, for term R to be T-theoretical, more
measuring models have to be considered than in the original version,
and so the chance that all those will yield models of T becomes
smaller. Note also that the example of CCM fits into this definition.
Mass as a primitive concept of CCM would be CCM-theoretical only in
case all measuring methods for mass appearing in the holon to which
CCM belongs were to imply CCM's fundamental law. In particular,
mass as measured in CPM should always imply not only Newton's
                   GLOBAL STRUCTURE OF SCIENCE                             393

Second Law but conservation of momentum too. This, however, is
certainly not the case. The link from CPM to CCM is not an entailment
link, so there are measuring models x' E MP(CCM) which, though
being actual models of CPM (since they make use of certain force laws)
do not presuppose momentum conservation and therefore are not
necessarily models of CCM. Therefore, mass is CCM-non-theoretical
with respect to a holon H containing at least CCM and CPM. This is
also the result we informally obtained in the discussion of Ch. II.


                        VIII.3 GRAPHS AND PATHS

The "net structure" of theory-holons may be more complex and
interesting than the structure of specialization nets - not only from the
formal point of view but also from that of philosophy of science. The
"net structure" of a theory-holon roughly consists of the global way in
which the various theory-elements are linked with each other. In
DVIII-J above, this structure is implicitly captured by function A. In
order to facilitate the succeeding discussions it seems helpful to make
this net structure more explicit. There are two ways to proceed. We
may consider the net induced by a given theory-holon. This is a kind of
"theory-net" (N, ::;;;) in which the binary relation among theory-
elements obtains whenever there is a link from one theory-element to
the other:
           T ::;;; T'   iff   (T, T') E Dom(A).
In order to avoid terminological confusion we will speak here of the
graph of a given theory-holon. Another way to proceed is to introduce
the notion of a path leading from one theory-element to another one.
This notion can be taken over from graph theory if we consider the
graph of the theory-holon. For each such graph just is a connected
directed graph in the sense of graph theory (see TVIII-J below). But
also we can directly introduce the notion of a path in a given theory-
holon thus avoiding the detour via the graph. This definition will be
most easily used in the following.

   In the same way as theory-evolutions were constructed out of
specialization nets in Ch. V we may "dynamize" theory-holons by
means of considering sequences of these, ordered by historical time
intervals - and eventually enriched by further pragmatic concepts as in
Ch. V. We shall not expound the definitions here, the reader will have
no difficulty in providing them. With these conceptual tools. at hand
we now tum to some philosophical problems which may be profitably
analyzed in our terms.


      VIII.4 LOCAL EMPIRICAL CLAIMS IN GLOBAL THEORY-
                           HOLONS

In the previous discussion we have said nothing about the content or
                 GLOBAL STRUCTURE OF SCIENCE                         395

 empirical claim of theory-holons. One might suppose that this could
 easily be done. Intuitively, the content of a theory-holon is simply the
 collection of partial potential model classes that satisfy both the laws
 and the links of the holon. More precisely, the content would be a
 graph whose objects were these 'partial potential model classes. It is
 natural to think that there is something - some graph I on some
 specific set of partial potential models - that is the intended applica-
 tion of a theory-holon. This I is just the information or data we have
 that we claim has the properties of the structures in the content of the
 holon. But this idea becomes somewhat less plausible when we think of
 our holon H as representing the whole of empirical science at a given
 time. How do we describe I? What is outside H that can be used to tell
how we obtain the values of the components that appear in members of
 I?
    Our intuitions are much firmer in the case of single theory-elements.
Here it seems clear that we should be able to say something clear about
what they claim about the world - albeit this claim may be relative to
the net in which the theory-element appears. It seems intuitively evident
that single theory-elements do have relatively clear ranges of intended
applications associated with them that are to some degree specified by
the theory-element's links with other theory-elements. What can we say
 about how this works? It might be possible to give a coherent picture of
the whole of empirical science in which the concept of an intended
application appeared only in connection with local pieces of the picture,
but not in connection with the global picture. Roughly, there need not
be anything that we claim to be the intended application of all of
empirical science. But for each sufficiently small piece of empirical
science, it is possible to identify, or at least characterize rather
precisely, what its intended applications are. For reasons of simplicity
our treatment here will ignore the role of constraints and, together with
this, the possibility that some theory-elements may have more than one
range of intended applications.
    Let us then consider how we are to regard the empirical claim of a
single theory-element in a theory-holon. In Ch. II we suggested that the
theory-element T = (K(T), I(T») claims that I(T) E Cn(K(T». We have
been somewhat vague about what I(T) is and how it is specified -
suggesting that there were irreducibly pragmatic elements involved in
its determination that eluded precise formulation (Secs. II.6, V.l). I(T)
just was conceived as some sub-class of the non-theoretical structures
396                        CHAPTER EIGHT

of T - Mpp(T). Roughly, the claim of T was that all members of I(T)
can be filled out in some way with theoretical components of members
of Mp(T) to yield a model of T - a member of M(T). This seems
intuitively plausible just in that it renders the empirical claim of T as a
claim about its data and nothing else.
   To say more about I(T), let us think about what a single theory-
element contributes to the "content" of a theory-holon. In this context,
we may restrict considerations to interpreting links - links that
intuitively provide interpretations for the non-theoretical terms of a
theory-element. We say that theory-element T' interprets T (in H), and
also that T' is an interpretor of T (in H) iff (T', T) E Dom(A) and
A(T', T) is an interpreting link. A single theory-element T in holon H
has effects on the content of H that go in both "directions" from it.
Among other possibilities, it may narrow down the content of all the
theory-elements that interpret it and it may contribute to the interpreta-
tion of other theory-elements. Very roughly, T is used to make a claim
about models of the theory-elements that interpret it and, in turn,
theory-elements that it interprets make claims about its models. In the
absence of constraints we may think of the local theoretical content of
T in the hoi on - Cnth(TIH) - as the class of models of T that are
consistent with the links in the holon - ':consistent" in the sense that, if
they are linked at all to other theory-elements they are linked to models
of these theory-elements that are, in turn linked to other models of still
other theory-elements, if they are linked at all, and so on. Furthermore,
we require that members of Cnth(T IH) should be interpreted by all of
T's interpreting links. That is, members of the theoretical content
should be fully interpreted in the sense that all the interpretative
apparatus pertaining to T can be brought to bear on them. For
example, we would not consider a model for SETH to be in the
theoretical content of SETH unless the values for the mole-number
function were actually obtained from a link to a stoichiometric theory.
Unless this were the case, we would simply regard them as "meaning-
less numbers". The local content - Cn(T/H) - is just the non-
theoretical parts of the members of Cnth(T/H) - the r*-image of
Cnth(T IH) (compare D VIII-8 below).
   As a first cut, it seems natural to think of the intended applications
of T as being provided by models of the theory-elements that are linked
to T by interpreting links. But not all of these models will provide
acceptable data for T. Some may be ruled out because they themselves
                 GLOBAL STRUCTURE OF SCIENCE                          397

are not "interpreted" by theory-elements that are still "further back" in
the holon. Others may be ruled out by restrictions imposed by other
theory-elements, besides T, that they interpret. Clearly, we do not want
to include the restriction imposed by T itself. Doing this would make
T's claim trivially true. Further, it appears that we would not want to
include restrictions imposed by theory-elements that T interprets. The
reason is that the laws of T have an "indirect" effect on what these
theory-elements rule out in the other theory-elements that are "behind"
them. This suggests that we should think of the intended applications
for T as being provided by the "global content" of interpreting theory-
elements immediately "behind" T in the holon H. But, the "holon"
whose content is relevant here is not H. Rather, it is H, less everything
in H that is "before" T that T interprets. Roughly, we should think of
the intended applications for T as being provided by the content of a
net in which T and all other theory-elements whose interpretation
"presupposes" T have been removed.
    We may make these ideas more precise in the following way. The
first thing to note is that we have no formal criterion for distinguishing
between interpreting and non-interpreting links. Some cases may be
easily decided in this respect but the decision seems to involve features
of the particular case. We therefore have to treat this distinction as
basic. To the theory-holon H = (N, A) under consideration we add a
function E assigning to TEN the set E(T) of T -interpreting links
occurring in the hoi on. Formally, E(T) is a subset of the range of A:
           E(T) ~ Rge( A)
(recall that A maps pairs of theory-elements on links) satisfying the
additional requirement that for all 1 E E(T) there is some T' E N such
that 1-= A(T', T). This requirement is no more than an indication of the
direction in which 1 works.

        VIII.S INTENDED APPLICA nONS RECONSIDERED

The question emerging from the above definition of the intended
applications of T induced by H is of course whether the requirements
specified are, in fact, necessary and sufficient for some x E M:P(T) to
count as an intended application of T. If we go back to the pragmatic
concept of I(T) introduced in Ch. II we may say that in the previous
section we have, in effect, specified necessary conditions for the
intended applications in I(T). That is, we require at least that
           I(T) ~ I(T IH).
It may even be tempting to regard these conditions as sufficient as well.
If we regard H as including all of empirical science, we might hope that
it included enough to rule out all "empirically meaningless" structures.
Were this so, we could replace "~" above by "=". Note that even if
I(T) c I(T/H) it is still quite plausible to render the local claim of Tin
                 GLOBAL STRUCTURE OF SCIENCE                        405

Has I(TfH) ~ Cn(TfH). For, clearly, this entails that I(T) ~ Cn(TfH).
Further, there are strong pragmatic reasons to think that whenever
I(T) ~ Cn(TfH) is true, I(TfH) ~ Cn(TfH) will, as a matter of fact, be
true as well. Thus we seem to be on reasonably solid ground when we
represent the empirical claim of T in the holon H by I(TfH) ~
Cn(TfH).
    It should be emphasized that our discussion of intended applications
and non-theoretical structures in this and the preceeding section
depends essentially on the concept of an interpreting link. We have
already noted that this concept is a pragmatic one. Though we can
provide some formal necessary conditions on interpreting links, we can
not completely characterize them by purely formal conditions. From
this it follows that the concepts of intended application and non-
theoretical structure are as well features of the practice of empirical
science that elude completely formal characterization. This should not
be too surprising. We should not expect the use we make of our con-
ceptual tools to be completely determined by their formal properties.
The major virtue of the present treatment of these matters is that it
localizes the pragmatic aspets of non-theoretical structures and
intended interpretations in the concept of an interpreting link. Earlier
formulations of the distinction between theoretical and non-theoretical
components in potential models depended on the clearly pragmatic
idea of "methods of determination in existing expositions of the theory"
(cf. Sec. II.3.3). We have simply replaced this somewhat vague prag-
matic idea with the more precise, but still irreducibly pragmatic,
concept of interpreting link. By doing this we have, not only provided
an improved version of the informal criterion for "theoreticity relative
to a given theory", but also brought the concept of intended application
somewhat further into the realm of formal characterization. We have
sketched, at least, how the concept of intended application can be
captured by formal methods on the assumption that the whole of
empirical science has been formalized in a theory-holon and inter-
preting links in this net have been identified.
   However, this first account of intended applications of T induced by
H, and of the corresponding local empirical claim of T in H still
contains two restrictions which may be questioned from a still more
global perspective. First, in the definition of I(TfH) we restricted
ourselves to the use of purely conceptual means that are in principle
formalizable. Other means sometimes discussed in the philosophical
406                         CHAPTER EIGHT

 literature, like ostensive definitions or pure intuition were excluded. In
 the case of pure intuition we do not think that much is lost in the
 present context since this is, by its very nature, an irremediably obscure
 notion. But with respect to ostensive means the situation is more
 delicate. In logical empiricism the role of "observation" as an ingredient
 of knowledge which cannot be reduced to formal "theoretical" descrip-
 tion has been stressed over and again, and more recently, causal
 theories of reference have been propounded to "anchor" theoretical
 knowledge in "real events". Moreover, it may be pointed out that any
 formal characterization is subject to indeterminacy "up to isomor-
 phisms": if some structure - like our I(T/H) - is formally charac-
 terized in some intrinsically clean way then every structure isomorphic
 to it also will fall under the given characterization. But certainly part of
 the idea of intended applications is to refer to those real systems we
 actually find around us, as opposed to merely possible ones which are
isomorphic to the former. If we do not want to exclude the possibility
 of such non-conceptual means to contribute to a determination of the
intended applications we have to admit for the possibility of I(T), the
"real" intended applications, being a proper subset of I(T/H). By
 extending these considerations to arbitrary theory-elements of H we
will have to admit for the possibility of some genuine set I(T ') of
intended applications for each T' in H.
    A second restriction in the above definition of I(T/H) is that we
precluded the possibility of circularities from the outset, by the very
construction of I(T/H). Recall that in the definition of I(T/H) only
those interpretors of T were considered which were not already
themselves interpreted by T. If, for instance, the situation is like in the
graph below with arrows indicating interpreting links then N\ (N:f) is
{T6 }, Cnth(T'/H\(HT')) = M(r), and so I(T/H) = App(T', T)(M(r)) n
App(T6' T). One might ask why e.g. T4 should not be used for the
determination of I(T/H) as well, and the same goes for T3 and T 2 • Of
course, then, we arrive at a similar question with respect to T \. What
can be seen from this example is that in the presence of "interpretation
loops", that is, loops of interpreting links in H, the definition of I(T, H)
contains some conventional element, namely in cutting off such loops in
between theory-elements one and two steps "before" T (like T' and T 4
in Figure VIII-I) in the interpretation relation.
    In a second move we will now present an approach not subjected to
the two kinds of restrictions discussed. To do so we concentrate on the

   In order to clarify the meaning of I*(T) as defined above (and
analogously for the next definition) it is convenient to discuss some
possible objections that may be raised against this way of conceiving the
determination of the intended applications. A first, rather harmless
objection, could be the following. It may be said that the present
definition of I*(T) provides at most a partial determination of the
intended applications of T, for the base sets D j , • • • , Dk of each
application are not determined at all by this procedure. This is true, but
the strength of this objection may be weakened by two remarks. First,
we don't pretend hereby to be able to define the intended applications
of T in the strict sense of "defining". (This is why we previously,put this
term in quotation marks.) It would perhaps be more accurate to speak
just of a "determination". We don't even claim that the procedures
                  GLOBAL STRUCTURE OF SCIENCE                            409

 determining the relations R 1 , ••• , Rm of the intended applications via
 links constitute real definitions. In general, the links employed may not
 be functions, and so the procedure may yield non-unique results.
 Second, it is plausible to assume that similar determinations of the base
 sets as well could be found by analyzing concrete cases. Though we
 have no real-life example at hand, there is some reason to think
 (especially in the case of reductive relationships) that different base sets
 may be linked through interpretation links. Formally, it would be easy
 to include the base sets into the determination via links, if needed. In
 the following, when discussing the question of determining applications
 via links we shall just assume that inclusion of the base sets into the
links would not change the essentials of the discussion.
    Another technical objection that may be put forward is that we have
not included the operation of constraints or other kinds of links which
may be relevant in the determination of the intended applications. As
shown by the examples of CPM and SETH, constraints may play quite
an important role for determinations. To be quite complete, therefore,
the present account should be emended so as to include constraints at
least. We have not undertaken this emendation because this would
require additional technical apparatus of a complicated kind. On the
other hand, it would not drastically change the picture we are offering
now of the way intended applications are determined.
    A more fundamental objection against DVIII-J1 is that it seems to
involve an infinite regress or a vicious circle. In order to "define" I*(T)
we need to know already all sets I*(Tj) for all Tj from which there is an
interpreting link to T. In order to know every such I*(Tj) we have again
to apply DVIII-J1 and to look at all those theory-elements T j in N from
which there are interpreting links to Tj and we have to know the
respective sets I*(Tj) of their intended applications. And so on. To see
whether or not this situation leads to some basic difficulties, it is
convenient to make use of the idea of paths and loops introduced
earlier. It should be noted at this point that the usage of these notions in
the following should be understood in a purely synchronic manner;
whether or not the introduction of a diachronic perspective in these
issues may change some of the conclusions reached, will be discussed
afterwards briefly.
    Consider some path P = (Tl' T 2 , T 3 , ••• ) in N such that Tl = T and
for each i E I\J there is an interpreting link from Tj to Tj_ 1. In the
determination of I*(T) we have to run along all such paths and for each

interpreting sort are meant.)
   (a)     P is not circular and is finite.
   (b)     P is circular, i.e. T 1 is among T 2, T 3' •.•
   (c)     P is not circular but infinite.

   (a)     The determination of I*(T) involves only finite and loop-free
           paths
   (f3)    Some circular path is involved

       VII1.6 FOUNDATIONALISM VERSUS COHERENTISM

The previous discussion leads us back to the consideration of the three
fundamental cases we might encounter when analyzing the overall
structure of interpreting links in a given theory-holon. This issue has
some relevance for general epistemology. Let us start with the last
alternative, (r), where at least some of the paths are infinite. It seems to
be quite clear that such a possibility should be ruled out for repre-
senting actual science. The presence of an infinite path would imply, by
412                        CHAPTER EIGHT

DVIII-5, the existence of an infinite number of theory-elements. Now, it
should never be forgotten that our theory-elements are intended
formally to reproduce really existing pieces of science as cultural
products, and these will always be finite in number (both synchronically
and diachronically). The collective human mind which produces science
will never have an infinite number of theory-elements at hand. This
is an empirical matter of fact and a quite obvious one. Against this way
of viewing scientific products, the objection could be raised that they
may be infinite in number in the same way mathematical entities like
numbers are, i.e. as potential outcomes of rule-determined operations
or constructions. This certainly is a logical possibility. But there is no
ground to believe that it may ever actually be realized. The idea of
an algorithm producing different scientific theories ad infinitum is
not plausible at all. At any rate, nothing like this is envisageable in
the present state of science. The fact that the formal characterization of
theory-elements may include mathematical entities such as sets of real
numbers and numerical functions (which constitute infinities in the
peculiar sense of mathematics) should not be confused with the idea
that they themselves coincide with those mathematical universes.
Ontologically speaking, theory-elements are more like symphonies or
political ideologies than like numbers. That they apparently are more
amenable to formal representation than other cultural products is a
purely contingent fact that has nothing to do with the possibility of an
infinite construction.
   Let us now consider the two other alternatives for representing the
global structure of science and see whether they look more plausible.
Case (a) with all paths loop-free and finite presumably reflects the
explicit or implicit understanding of science characteristic of philoso-
phers of a so-called ''foundationalist'' bent. For all the intricacies and
length that interpreting links departing from a given theory-element
may show, they eventually reach a solid end, a bed-rock that grounds
the empirical content, however indirectly, of the given theory-element.
Note that, to become compatible with the finitude of real-life science, a
further condition has to be imposed on alternative (a). For, in the way
( a) has just been stated formally, there need not be a boundary
common to all the lengths of all paths occurring in the definition of
I*(T) since (a) as such does not rule out that there may be· infinitely
many different paths of increasing length. That is, without further
assumptions we cannot represent the "determining ground" for a given
T by a "last" In(T) for a fixed n. On the other hand, the additional
                 GLOBAL STRUCTURE OF SCIENCE                          413

 assumption necessary for such a representation is rather natural: that,
for each TEN, E(T) be finite. Let us call "(F)" the conjunction of (a)
and this further assumption. It can then be said that (F) reproduces in
our formal terms the essential tenets of a foundationalist epistemology.
If (F) holds, then, in fact, we may represent I*(T) by some In(T) for a
fixed n. Each path necessary for the determination of I*(T) will also be
present in In(T), and by means of the inductive procedure we can trace
back each path up to its end. There we arrive at a ''final'' theory-
element P' which still has its original intended applications I(TtlJ)
associated with it (because there are no interpreting links to some
previous T'). Note that, for a given T, if (F) holds, there will normally
be several such TjtlJ, since many determining paths will come out of T
and of its underlying, intermediate theory-elements. Let us call these
(possible) final theory-elements relative to a given T 'bed-rock theory-
elements (for the interpretation of T in H)'. Clearly, the determination
of In(T) then is given by those bed-rock theory-elements and the links
which, via various paths, "import" empirical data from the bed-rock
theory-elements into T. If (F) holds, the global structure of science is
that of a building, or a hierarchy: Theory-elements appear at different
levels or ''floors'' of determination, the whole structure resting on
a ground of (perhaps very many) bed-rock theory-elements. If the
arrows indicate that a theory-element is determined by another one,
the graph of this view of science (or at least of a "closed" theory-holon)
may appear something like this:




                  T21




                  T31                                 P3



                 TW1          Tw2      TW3

                                Fig. VUH.
414                        CHAPTER EIGHT

 A possible concrete realization of (a part of) this picture would be
 the following. Take SETH as a specific example of a level-O theory-
 element, i.e. the level where we start our investigation. On inferior
 levels (for example, levels 1 and 2 in our picture) these theory-elements
 may appear: Euclidean physical geometry (say, level 2), classical hydro-
 dynamics of compressible fluids (level 1), and Daltonian stoichiometry
 (level 1 as well); their links to SETH determine (at least some of)
 the SETH-non-theoretical concepts, viz. volume, pressure (as the
negative of the partial derivative of energy determination with respect
to volume) and the mole numbers, and a fortiori SETH's domain of
intended applications. The intended applications of each one of these
three theories are, in turn, determined by other theory-elements of
inferior levels. For example, we may say that at least part of each
intended application of physical geometry is determined by a realiza-
tion of an extensive measurement theory of length, which in turn rests·
on a purely qualitative topology of the "longer-than" relationship.
Perhaps this last would be one of the T {" we were looking for -
say, Tf. A similar path could be traced for hydrodynamics and
stoichiometry until we reach, say, Tf and Tf. In this way it should
become possible, at least in principle, exactly to point out the bed-rock
theories a given theory rests upon and, consequently, to identify the
"real content" of its empirical base.
    In order to avoid possible misunderstandings or objections that
would be besides the point, it should be noted that this picture of
science does not imply either an empiricist epistemology of any sort nor
a reductionistic methodology. Though, historically speaking, founda-
tionalism has often been associated with empiricism and/or reduc-
tionism, there is no reason why this must be so. In our understanding of
foundationalism, this view of science would involve an empiricist tenet
only if some further claim is made about the content of the bed-rock
theory-elements. For example, if one would say either that the empirical
content of the T {" is "pure observation" or that, immediately ''under-
neath" the T{" we find non-conceptualized "pure experience", then, of
course, we would have an empiricist foundationalism. However, such
interpretations of the T {" are by no means a natural outcome of the
present explication of foundationalism and a foundationalist reconstruc-
tion strategy for science is in no way committed to them.
    Secondly, foundationalism does not imply reductionism. The appear-
ance of non-definable or, more generally speaking, non-eliminable Ti-
                  GLOBAL STRUCTURE OF SCIENCE                          415

 theoretical terms on any "floor" i each path comes through, suffices to
 dismiss the idea that the content of the theories on the upper levels is
 nothing but a "summary" of the bed-rock theories. Even if the "build-
ing" picture of science foundationalism offers would be the right
 metaphor, this would not make reductionism more plausible. "To
ground" is not the same as "to reduce". Therefore, arguments that have
been set forth against empiricism (e.g. the "theory-Iadenness of all
observation") or against reductionism (e.g. the non-eliminability of
theoretical terms) in no way affect the tenability of a foundationalist
view of science.
    At this point, we may ask whether changing from a synchronic to a
diachronic perspective somehow modifies our interpretation of founda-
tionalism. The answer is that nothing is essentially changed but that,
diachronically, two different versions of foundationalism may thereby
be distinguished, one of which is "less pure" (and more plausible, for all
we know). than the other. Synchronically, however, they are equivalent.
One diachronic version of foundationalism would claim that, once you
reach a bed-rock theory-element, you can rest on it forever. Bed-rock
theory-elements, once obtained, would be permanent. In other words,
the property of being bed-rock for a theory-element would be trans-
historical. Let us call this view 'absolute foundationalism'. Its rival
would be a 'relative foundationalism': What scientists construct as bed-
rock theory-elements depends on the contemporary state of science;
what is regarded as bed-rock at one period may become not so at the
next one. Bed-rock theory-elements would always be provisional. In
the present age of historical relativism, it is understandable that relative
foundationalism is more likely to become popular than its static
absolute counterpart - even for those people who claim not to be
historicists. On the other hand, through relativizing the notion of a bed-
rock theory-element, foundationalism looses much of its conceptual
strength. However, we shall not engage in a discussion of the relative
merits and demerits of both foundationalistic views. We think it is more
profitable to detect the intrinsic difficulties any version of founda-
tionalism reveals on closer scrutiny. As far as we can see, these
difficulties are quite independent of the issue whether bed-rock theory-
elements are transhistorical or historically changing. They rather come
from the very idea of a bed-rock theory-element, be it permanent
or provisional. To see this, it does not matter whether we take a
synchronic or a diachronic point of view.
416                          CHAPTER EIGHT

    By definition, if po is bed-rock (for the interpretation of T in H)
 then there is no interpreting link from any other theory-element of N to
 po, for if there were, TW could not be the final element of some path.
 But, if there is no interpreting link to TW then, under the assumption
 that the concept of a term determined by an interpreting link and the
 concept of a non-theoretical term are co-extensive, it follows that TW
cannot have any TW-non-theoretical terms. Thus, if we take seriously
the idea that (non-) theoreticity may be expressed in terms of the net
 structure of interpreting links, then a bed-rock theory-element TW (so
long as it is acceptable as bed-rock) will contain only T-theoretical
terms. Is this plausible?
    In order to decide upon this question it is first necessary to be quite
clear about what it means for a theory TW that all its terms are TW-
theoretical. In our formalism, this means first of all that Mpp(TW) = 0,
since now there are no terms of TW that may be singled out as TW-non-
theoretical. Further, since we have always characterized the domain of
intended applications as a subset of M pp , we have in this case I(TW) =
o and, therefore, the theory's empirical claim becomes trivially true. It
just states that you may always add to the empty set whatever TW_
theoretical terms you like, which is certainly true but not very informa-
tive. Of course, it could be replied that all this situation shows is that, in
the case of bed-rock theory-elements, it is not adequate to characterize
the domain of intended applications as a subset of Mpp; in the case of
TW we should take I(TW) ~ Mp(TW). It is not at all clear what the
procedure to pick out the intended applications would then look like.
But even if this move were made, a more serious counterintuitive
consequence would still be left.
    The most significant consequence of the fact that all terms of TW are
Tw-theoretical is that all methods of determination for all terms of TW
presuppose the validity of the laws of TW; that is, if we denote by
"Mm(Tw)" the class of all methods of determination for all terms of TW,
it has to be the case that Mm(TW) ~ M(TW). Intuitively speaking, no
"correct" determination of any parameter of TW, and consequently no
determination of any term appearing in the elements of I(TW) -
whatever they may be - may ever cast any doubt on the validity of the
laws of TW. These laws thereby become unfalsifiable. The only kind of
trouble a bed-rock theory-element might get involved into would then
be a sort of "internal conflict": Either because the laws of TW are
                 GLOBAL STRUCTURE OF SCIENCE                          417

inconsistent - in which case M(T aI ) = 0 - or because they are
incompatible with the constraints - in which case Cnth(TaI) = 0. In
both cases we could find out the inadequacy of Tal by just looking at
Tal itself and forgetting about the rest of our knowledge, that is, on
purely a priori grounds. The base of empirical science becomes then a
system of a priori theories. If their claims are false, it is only because
they are inconsistent; if they are true, they are a priori true. Bed-rock
theory-elements of empirical science would have exactly the same
epistemological status as formal systems of logic.
   By pointing at this conclusion, we don't want to imply that founda-
tionalism is necessarily a false view of science. But, curiously enough,
this analysis shows that, if pushed far enough, foundationalism turns out
to be quite similar to its opponent, viz. coherentism, for the foundations
of science have to be conceived as self-sustaining conceptual entities
whose only validation criterion is internal consistency. Bed-rock theory-
elements are a sort of epistemological monads. If formally consistent,
they last forever, according to the absolute foundationalist, or else they
come and go, according to the relative foundationalist, but they come
and go on grounds that may be sociological, psychological or whatever,
in any case not epistemic. They are not dependent on the rest of our
knowledge. Whether a convinced foundationalist would like to espouse
this conclusion, we do not know. It seems to us, however, that it does
not accord very well with the original "spirit" of foundationalism.
   The issue of foundationalism would become very much clarified, of
course, if at least one path could be traced within a given portion of
science that would lead to a corresponding bed-rock theory-element
whose identity as such would be quite clear to everybody. In such a
case, perhaps the nature of such entities would reveal itself as less
strange than it seems in an abstract discussion. Unfortunately, to our
knowledge no attempt made which could be interpreted in that sense
has come out with satisfactory results; and unless such an example be
produced in all detail, foundationalism will remain a speculative
possibility with not much prima facie plausibility.
   Are there better prospects for case ({3)? First, notice that in order
for ({3) to become a real alternative to (a) it should be reworded in
stronger terms. It should not only assert the existence of loops but also
deny the existence of any loop-free paths. Otherwise, we would agam
get involved in the difficulties of foundationalism just mentioned in
418                         CHAPTER EIGHT

addition to the ones characteristic of loops. Thus, if we want to get
rid of the problems of foundationalism, we have to assume that all
paths in science are either loops or contain loops in an essential way.
("Essential" means here that there is no ''way out" of the loops towards
some bed-rock theory-elements.) Let us call this stronger claim against
( a) the "thesis of coherentism" (C). Besides "pure" loops like this,

                                           TO




                                 Fig. VIII-5.

(C) could admit loop-like structures of a more complicated form like



              (.
      p6
                            or




                       T,


                                 Fig. VllI-6.

and so on. A radical coherentist view of the global structure of science
might even contend that the latter consists of one single "big" loop
made up of a great number of "smaller" loops inside. But, for our
modest interpretation (C), it is not necessary to accept such a global
coherentism. (C) just asserts coherentism for theory-holons, not for the
whole of science.
   Let us envisage a possible example of a loop in a complex of empiri-
cal science. It 'is very plausible to think of the intended applications of
                  GLOBAL STRUCTURE OF SCIENCE                           419

rigid body mechanics as being determined by classical kinematics; the
latter's intended applications are in part described by means of physical
geometry; this, in tum, is only applicable to systems that may be
conceived as rigid rods and the like, i.e. to systems that are to satisfy the
laws of rigid body mechanics. Summarizing, in order to determine the
intended applications of RBM we have to assume that RBM's laws are
applicable to them. Generally speaking, a loop indicates that we may
not take something as an intended application of a theory unless we
don't assume that it can be subsumed under the models of that same
theory. In more formal terms, a loop from T back to T itself, means
that, for any system y E Mpp(T), "y E I(T)" implies "there is an x such
that x E M(T)". In other words, T may have intended applications only
if its class of actual models is not vacuous. The intended applications
cannot be incompatible with the actual models. This situation is
nothing but a radical form of auto determination: The theory itself
determines in all cases which systems are to be regarded as its intended
applications - namely only those structures which may be augmented
to actual models.
    At first sight, the autodetermination effect of loops in coherentism
looks very much like the a priori character of bed-rock theory-element
in foundationalism. The unfalsifiability effect would now become even
more exaggerated, since not only a very particular class of theory-
elements (the bed-rock ones) but every possible theory-element would
become unfalsifiable. However, this would be too hasty a conclusion.
Theory-elements belonging to loops are less immune to conflicting
knowledge from outside than bed-rock theory-elements. Even if all
theory-elements constituting a loop were internally consistent, there
would still be room for trouble. In a sense, and even at the cost of
paradox, coherentism is less coherentistic than foundationalism. The
reason is that the self-consistent units of coherentism will normally be
much bigger than the corresponding units of foundationalism, so that
there will be much more chance for a misfit. To clarify this point let us
take a very simple-minded example.
   Suppose we have the most simple case of a loop we may think of (a
very unlikely one, anyway): a loop only between two theory-elements, T
and T', that are supposed to be each one internally consistent, i.e.
Cnth(T) i' 0 and Coth(T') i' 0. Being a loop between T and T'
means, according to the explication above, that, in order to know
whether any given y E Mpp(T) also is an element of I(T), we have to
420                        CHAPTER EIGHT

look for an x' E M(T ') and an interpreting link A such that A(y, x')
 determines y, i.e. determines the values of all terms appearing in y.
 Now, by definition, r'(x') E Mpp(T'). In order to know whether x' is a
"reasonable" model we have to see whether r'(x') is an element of
I(T '). But on the assumption of a loop between T and T', this question
 may only be answered in the affirmative if there is an x E M(T) and an
interpreting link A' such that A'(r'(x'), x) determines r'(x'). This is
precisely the loop. Notice, however, that there is no warrant at all for
concluding from the previous description of the situation that r(x) = y.
(Interpreting links are generally not model-theoretic identities; only in
this latter case should we assume r(x) = y; but then it should also be
the case that x = x', i.e. T = T' - so we can altogether dismiss this
possibility.) Now, if y = r(z) for a z =f x with z E M, it could well be
the case that x and z are incompatible because of the constraints; it
could be the case that {x, z} $ GC(T). In this case, T would run into
trouble. In a sense, we could interpret this situation as a kind of
"falsification", or at least of "anomaly" in the sense of Kuhn. In spite of
the internal consistency of each theory-element taken on its own and in
spite of the loop, or rather just because of the loop, we could tell that
something is wrong with T (or with T', or with both). It is easy to
understand that, if not only constraints, but also other links to theories
different from T' (even if they too make up loops) are part of T
and also if the loops are much bigger than the "degenerate" case just
depicted, the probability for a situation like the one just discussed will
rapidly increase. The more the loops, the more likely that they collide
with each other. As the number of theory-elements and of their mutual
links increases with the development of science, ever more incom-
patibilities and collisions will arise in the whole of a theory-holon. This
is just what one would expect from a coherentist point of view.
    Of course, if coherentism is the right perspective for viewing science
as a whole - and we are by no means claiming that it is - a number of
cherished ideas should be abandoned. Among them is the idea of a
hierarchical structure of scientific knowledge built upon "solid" founda-
tions. There would still be differences in the "caliber" of theories, which
could be detected especially by considering the number and signifi-
cance of links that "depart from" or "arrive at" each single theory; but
the image of a building with a succession of floors resting on a
basement would be a totally misleading metaphor for grasping the
global structure of science. In this way, it appears that claim (C) comes
out in a more favourable light than claim (F).
                 GLOBAL STRUCTURE OF SCIENCE                          421

    Against the way of comparing the relative merits and demerits of
 tenets (F) and (C) we have offered here it could be argued that it rests
 on a purely synchronic perspective, and that our understanding of the
 situation would change significantly if we were to consider it diachroni-
 cally. In this case, it may be contended, (C) becomes completely
 implausible and only (F), or something similar to it, has any prospect of
 representing the actual structure of science. After all, when you intend
 to build something, you start from some solid basement and then go on
 step by step. This is the plausible diachronic claim implicit in (F),
whereas the diachronic view of science implicit in (C) would rather
 seem to be that of a "bootstrap" strategy not better, only more com-
plicated, than the strategy of the Baron of Miinchhausen. According to
 (C) there would not be any starting point in science, therefore science
could never have been developed, which would be, of course, an absurd
consequence.
    The obvious reply to this kind of argument is that the results of a
diachronic analysis in no way necessarily reflect the synchronic struc-
ture of global science. Even if we have some reason to think that there
were some first theory-elements built up in ancient time, they were
 historically, not methodologically or epistemologically the first. Only in
the case of theory-evolutions in our precise sense, some degree of
parallelism between the synchronic and the diachronic reconstruction
can be detected. However, notice that, first, specialization nets are a
quite different thing from theory-holons (specialization links normally
not being interpreting links) and, secondly, theory-evolutions cover
only a particular sort of diachronic phenomena. In general, therefore,
there is no reason to assume that the first theory-elements constructed
in the -historical beginnings of a discipline were bed-rock theory-
elements with their a priori flavour. On the contrary, if there actually
are bed-rock theory-elements of the kind foundationalism envisages, it
is very likely that they will come out as the result of rather recent
investigations. For example, if (F) is right, then theories of fundamental
measurement will presumably be theory-elements that are quite near to
the bed-rock (F) assumes; but such theories appeared only in the last
hundred years. It is more likely that the historical starting point in a
discipline is not bed-rock in any sense. Why should the historically first
theory-elements of a discipline not be mutually linked by loops from
the very beginning? Actually, some historical material seems to point
in that direction. For· example, classical kinematics and classical
mechanics, which are very likely linked by interpreting links, seem to
422                        CHAPTER EIGHT

 have emerged and evolved together in a complicated interaction
 process. Be that as it may, it does not appear that diachronic analysis
 has any bearing upon the alternative (F) vs. (C).
    A more fundamental objection against the whole way we have
 formulated the issue between foundationalism and coherentism, and
 therefore, the question of the global structure of science could be that
 our explications all rest on a misleading assumption - that the domain
 of applications of a theory is "defined" or determined by interpreting
 links to other theories. It could be argued that this hypothesis is wrong
 from the very beginning. Whatever the roles links may play in the
 functioning of a theory, they are not there in order to define the
intended applications. We immediately acknowledge that this may be
true. As a matter of fact, at the beginning of this section we suggested
the hypothetical character of our claim that intended applications are
determined by a special sort of links to other theories. However, two
things may be said in favor of this hypothesis - an inductive and a
deductive argument. The inductive one is that, in all examples recon-
structed so far, this seems to be actually the more natural way to
understand how intended applications are determined. The other
argument is that it is hard to see how else they could be determined.
    The only rival hypothesis that comes to our mind is the claim that
the intended applications of a theory are "directly given" without the
need for any previous theoretical concepts and laws. To be a bit more
precise, the intended applications of a theory T would be determined
by a verbalization (partially) in terms of T of a "direct encounter with
reality". This encounter would proceed presumably by means of "pure
observation", "direct intuition" or something similar. For example, when
describing the intended applications of CPM as "paths of particles",
everybody would immediately know what we mean by that: No
kinematical, geometrical, chronometrical, mereological notions and
regularities should be known in order to assess whether something is
the path of a particle. Needless to say, this view seems to us to be
extremely naive. The idea that the ordinary English words "path" and
"particle" are simple verbalizations of some "direct experiences with
reality" is a hazardous hypothesis about natural language only few
semanticists would be ready to defend nowadays. But even if this
hypothesis were true, we should take into account that the ordinary
English usage of "path" and "particle" is only remotely associated with
the use of these same words in a physical theory. If we try to unearth
                    GLOBAL STRUCTURE OF SCIENCE                                   423

what is concealed behind those words in physics, we immediately find a
highly sophisticated theoretical apparatus that only makes sense if one
knows a good deal of kinematics, geometry, etc. As far as we can see,
the determination of the intended applications of a theory is a highly
theoretically-dependent business - it essentially depends on the funda-
mental concepts and laws of other theories. All we claim, then, is that
this dependence may be reconstructed formally as the presence of some
interpreting links. If this is accepted, we are led back to the starting
point of our discussion and the issue between foundationalism and
coherentism or, more precisely, between theses (F) and (C) is not a
pseudo-issue at all but a crucial matter for a correct appraisal of the
global structure of science.
   Let us conclude this discussion by noting that, so far we can tell,
coherentism shows some a priori advantages of a conceptual kind over
foundationalism. Its essential disadvantage with respect to the latter is
only the fact that, psychologically, it appears more difficult to assimi-
late; but it seems to be better defendible from a methodological point of
view. Nevertheless, let us stress that this last remark by no means
purports to decide the issue. After all, the question whether founda-
tionalism or coherentism is right cannot be answered on purely a priori
grounds but depends on the careful analysis of much more material
than we have been able to reconstruct so far.
